Is China behind a wave of AI fake videos targeting Taiwan?
- Published
Taiwan's ruling party is being repeatedly targeted with AI videos spreading false claims about its leader and other key members ahead of crucial local elections, BBC Verify has found.
A China-linked network has pumped out more than 500 fake videos about the Democratic Progressive Party (DPP) in the past year, which experts suggest is part of a long-running campaign to influence the outcome of the elections.
The videos appear to try to smear President Lai Ching-te by claiming he holds a US green card - and would abandon Taiwan if war broke out with China - which Taiwan's presidential office says is completely false. Deepfakes also appear to show Puma Shen, who is running to be the mayor of capital Taipei, using drugs, which he denies. Others seek to undermine or ridicule the politicians by showing them in children's clothing or as popular film characters.
The Taipei mayoralty has traditionally served as a springboard to the presidency. Experts say this has made Shen, who has been openly critical of Beijing, an obvious target for disinformation campaigns. The current mayor, Chiang Wan-an, is part of Taiwan's Kuomintang (KMT) party, which favours closer ties with China.
Taiwan is a self-governing island that China claims as part of its territory. Beijing and Taipei have long observed an uneasy status quo under which Taiwan, backed by the US, neither formally declares independence nor unites with China.
But tensions have risen since the DPP came to power in 2016. Beijing has repeatedly accused the party of pursuing independence while China's leader Xi Jinping, who has said "reunification" with Taiwan is a key goal, has stepped up pressure against the party with increased military activity around the island.
Experts believe the current disinformation activity is part of a broader campaign against Taiwan designed to undermine trust in its democratic process.
"The account operators are trying to make people distrust the DPP politicians so that they will not believe whatever they say," Austin Horng-En Wang, an expert in cognitive warfare at the University of Nevada, Las Vegas, told BBC Verify. "If you don't trust that candidate then you will not listen to what they say," he added.
The videos, many of which were shared from an account called "noxparable" or carried a watermark with the same name, have been viewed tens of millions of times across several social media platforms since May 2025.
More than half of those views were tracked in the past four months as the activity has ramped up ahead of the elections. Many of the accounts involved in spreading disinformation listed their locations on social media as mainland China and Hong Kong, while a number of the clips carried labels showing they were generated with AI. Many people who engaged with the videos were often seen repeating the false claims or attacking DPP figures in the comments, while others appeared to treat the clips as entertainment.
One of the most widely shared videos targeted Shen by superimposing his face onto a man who is seen holding a lighter and exhaling smoke alongside claims he is smoking drugs. The video appears to build on accusations from Taiwan's opposition party that he supports drugs decriminalisation, which Shen denies, and was debunked by a local news network.
Shen has taken legal action against people sharing deepfakes, local media reported, while his campaign office said AI videos showing the candidate appeared to be part of a "classic tactic China uses to smear specific targets". BBC Verify contacted the Chinese embassy in London for comment.
Other debunked claims include allegations that Lai's predecessor Tsai Ing-wen had fraudulently obtained her PhD from the London School of Economics. The university pushed back on identical allegations in 2019 and confirmed it had awarded her the doctorate.
A number of the social media accounts BBC Verify identified as sharing the disinformation videos appeared to be linked to Chinese firm Borderless, which produces websites that blend apolitical content with pro-China messaging. The network has also been investigated by journalists at the Taiwanese independent media outlet The Reporter, who shared their findings with BBC Verify. Borderless has previously been accused of carrying out "cognitive warfare" against Taiwan by Taipei's National Security Bureau and the firm has been contacted for comment.
Analysts confirmed to BBC Verify there were also linguistic clues that the accounts, which presented themselves as based in Taiwan, were actually posting from China. The posts occasionally used a simplified Chinese script introduced by the Communist government which was never adopted in Taiwan.
The posts mostly appeared during regular office hours, which Wang suggested showed a "professional" operation, while the accounts originating outside Taiwan showed evidence of election interfering. "When they pretended to be citizens in another country and used these accounts to manipulate the public opinion of the other country during the campaign, it is definitely election interference," Wang added.
Earlier this month, Taiwan's central election commission aired an advert warning voters to "beware of AI-generated deepfake videos" circulating online that could seek to influence the upcoming election. It comes as government officials flagged nearly 2,700 social media accounts to Meta that it claimed were part of a Chinese information warfare campaign, Reuters reported. Meta said it had removed the accounts.
Andrew Yeh of the China Strategic Risk Institute said the ultimate goal is not to favour any party. "China's information operations succeed not just by backing one candidate or opposing another, but by diluting Taiwan's policy debates, driving polarisation and degrading Taiwanese citizens' trust in their democratic processes," he said.
"Regardless of whether the KMT or DPP comes out on top, a more fractured and more divided Taiwan is in Beijing's interests."

John Travolta rarely connects with all his characters. Sometimes, he even loves to hate them.
“They say you have to find something you like,” the actor explains. “But I’ve never felt that. I think you have to like the result, pulling it off. That’s where the joy comes from. To become these people, you don’t have to identify with them or enjoy being them. You just have to be excellent at executing them.”
Even so, Travolta faced one of the biggest challenges of his career playing a rather literal executioner in Roland Joffé’s “November 1963,” which opened the Torino Film Festival with its international premiere.
On paper, Johnny Roselli seems right in Travolta’s wheelhouse: a real-life wiseguy turned showbiz fixer, an Al Capone protégé whose career took him from Hollywood to Las Vegas to the Bay of Pigs, leaving a trail of bodies along the way.
“He was an odd mix,” says Travolta. “He was the guy who asked Sinatra to connect Kennedy with the mob. He hooked Kennedy up with Marilyn Monroe. He was a Hollywood icon of sorts, and had this other, darker side as a hitman. That’s complex. I’ve done dark subject matter before, but this was real. It actually happened, and that’s the difference.”
Roselli was purportedly a CIA go-between and sharpshooter. “November 1963” takes that history a step further, imagining him as a key triggerman on the Grassy Knoll, directly responsible for the killing that shook a nine-year-old boy in Englewood, New Jersey, and still haunts the actor to this day.
“It was the biggest crime of the century,” says Travolta, instantly transported back to second grade. “The announcement came at 11 a.m. Eastern Standard Time that the President had been shot, and then three hours later, at 2 p.m., they confirmed that he had passed. We all went to our homes, and all I can remember is being home with my father, glued to the television, sitting on his lap and trying to make sense of it all.”
Travolta carried that weight onto the set, where, he says, he was asked “to play a very evil man with moments of humanity.”
“The actors were all suffering because everybody who was hired was a very decent person, and we all had to play, to some degree, people who were not,” he continues. “So it was harder to go home every night. It took a glass of wine and a nice dinner to snap out of the zone.”
That feeling returned in full force when Travolta finally watched his finished performance at Torino’s opening night, prompting a kind of out-of-body experience.
“I thought, ‘Wow, I can’t believe that’s me,’” he says. “I’ve never seen myself lose my soul in a film, and [here] I was soulless. I was very proud that I could portray that, because it’s against my very essence. When I looked at it on screen, I went, ‘Oh my god, he’s the devil.’”
Written and produced by family members of Windy City crime boss Sam Giancana, “November 1963” foregrounds the Chicago Outfit’s role in the assassination plot, leaving CIA and government involvement for a possible follow-up.
“This is not history; it’s about human beings,” Travolta says. “There will be lots more to tell, but you can’t do it all at the same time.”
That deliberately incomplete picture appealed to Joffé, who translates the murky history into a mise-en-scène of skewed angles and funhouse reflections.
“That’s how history comes to us,” he says. “I’d say this story is probably 90% true, insofar as no one will ever know what really happened. What’s most important to me is whether it’s credible. And has that mindset changed? The transactional mindset, the mafia mindset, the idea that power is all that counts and loyalty has to be bought at the point of a gun. My feeling is that it doesn’t disappear. It transmutes. It may become a political party. It may become the way business acts.”
In one telling revision, the film casts slain Dallas policeman J.D. Tippit, whose murder was attributed to Lee Harvey Oswald, as a key conspirator. Joffé uses the twist to further muddy the waters while dismissing the notion of a neatly orchestrated plot.
“I reject the conspiracy theory,” he says. “If it were a conspiracy, we would have known by now, and we absolutely do not. What it was is collusion, and collusion is very different. Collusion is subtle. It happens in the shadows. It’s a nod, a wink, a knowing glance. It’s putting a gun in the right place.”
The distinction, he argues, is that no grand design is required. The CIA and organized crime had already worked together on plots to kill Fidel Castro, but that didn’t mean anyone had to convene a committee to plan Kennedy’s assassination.
“It’s not about control,” Joffé says. “It’s about the fact that life is chaotic, and the killing of the President comes out of that. We made a film about chaos.”

ASI hands over 12th-century bronze idol, 2 other repatriated antiquities to Tamil Nadu Police
ASI DG Yadubir Singh Rawat handed Somaskanda, Saint Sundarar with Paravai Nachiyar and Saint Kannappa Nayanar to the Idol Wing CID at Dharohar Bhawan
Three repatriated antiquities, including a 12th-century Chola-period bronze idol, were on Thursday handed over by the Archaeological Survey of India (ASI) to the Tamil Nadu Police at a function held at the ASI headquarters here, marking a "significant step" towards the recovery and restitution of India's cultural heritage, officials said.
The antiquities comprise two bronze idols repatriated from the Smithsonian Museum in the US and one from The Hague in the Netherlands. They were formally handed over to the respective police officers, the ASI said.
Also read: BJP office-bearer chants ‘kamal khila de’ at Taj Mahal, Archaeological Survey of India files plaint
The antiquities include Somaskanda (Lord Shiva and Uma), a 12th-century Chola-period bronze idol photographed in 1959 at the Siva Temple, Sri Visvanatha in Alattur, Mannargudi Taluk, Thanjavur district of Tamil Nadu. It was repatriated from the Smithsonian Museum, the ministry said.
Another antiquity, Saint Sundarar with Paravai Nachiyar, is a 16th-century bronze idol belonging to the Vijayanagara period. It was photographed in 1956 at the Shiva Temple, Sri Narisvara in Viracholapuram, Kallakurichi Taluk, Tamil Nadu, and was also repatriated from the Smithsonian Museum, it said in a statement.
The third antiquity, Saint Kannappa Nayanar, is a Chola-period bronze idol from Arulmigu Agneeswarasamy Temple in Thirupugalur, Nagapattinam district in Tamil Nadu.
It depicts the Shaivite saint in a 'tribhanga' standing posture, with his right hand raised towards his eye. The idol was repatriated from The Hague, the ASI said.
"In a significant step towards the recovery and restitution of India's cultural heritage, the Archaeological Survey of India today handed over the three repatriated antiquities to the Idol Wing CID, Tamil Nadu Police, at Dharohar Bhawan, New Delhi," it said.
Also read: ‘Total callousness’: SC slams Delhi civic body, ASI over neglected heritage sites
The formal handover was undertaken by ASI Director General Yadubir Singh Rawat, along with other representatives of the organisation.
The restitution of the antiquities marks an important milestone in India's ongoing efforts to bring its cultural treasures back to their rightful home, officials said.
The ASI continues to work towards identifying, recovering and repatriating India's lost heritage in coordination with national and international agencies, they added.

Nothing’s Ear (note) is a pair of earbuds with built-in AI notetaking
I was more excited for Nothing’s latest device when I thought it was an AI vape pen.
Ahead of December 8 and too many coordinated leaks to count, Nothing has officially announced its first "AI-native" device. Somewhat anticlimactically, the Ear (note) is a pair of earbuds with built-in AI notetaking. As the company told Bloomberg, the earbuds can transcribe and summarize in-person conversations, calls, online meetings and voice memos, in addition to offering traditional audio playback with Hi-Res audio support.
"Ear (note) is part of Nothing's vision to build the hardware context layer of AI, bringing intelligence closer to the moments, conversations and experiences that shape our everyday lives," the company wrote in a press release it shared with Engadget.
No information on pricing or specs just yet, but Nothing promised to share more details soon. The company describes the Ear (note) as a "new approach to personal productivity," but Nothing is not the first to announce earbuds with built-in AI transcription. This past August, Plaud debuted its own pair of AI-forward earbuds in the form of the Plaud One. That said, if you're a fan of Nothing's design, you'll be sure to appreciate the Sony Walkman-like design the company has gone for, especially when it comes to the new Record and Talk buttons along the bottom of the aluminum case.
The Ear (note) will launch on December 8.

For more than a decade, my colleagues and I at the Center for Research Innovation in Biotechnology have tracked every experimental medicine that enters human testing anywhere in the world. Last December, I wrote in STAT that China had reached parity with the United States in terms of the absolute number of new drugs introduced into clinical trials each year. Starting in 2018, the rate of U.S. contributions began to stagnate. Meanwhile, in 2013, Chinese organizations had introduced about 30 new experimental drugs. A decade later, the number topped 400. And there is no reason to expect the momentum in either country is changing.
Over the past month, both governments have seemingly been moving to wall themselves off. On Oct. 16, Beijing proposed barring foreign acquisition of its companies’ proprietary cell and gene platforms. Within a week, the U.S. Department of the Treasury proposed restrictions that would bar Americans from taking equity stakes, forming joint ventures, or making limited-partner investments in Chinese biotech companies and their equipment suppliers.
The proposals from Beijing and Washington do not impact licensing. American drugmakers can keep licensing Chinese molecules, and Chinese companies may develop new medicines to sell to the U.S. and European companies.
That open door matters more than either wall. Data show that the U.S.-China contest in biotechnology is not one race but several. Restricting investment will not help America win the races it is already losing. The bigger threat to U.S. leadership is not Chinese capital. It is the erosion, at home, of the research enterprise that built America’s lead.
The Center for Research Innovation in Biotechnology’s newest analysis, published in September in Drug Discovery Today, emphasizes the importance of these continued engagements. My colleagues and I evaluated the 17,000 new drugs that first entered human trials between 2000 and 2024, separating them into eight different modalities. These ranged from conventional pills to gene therapies. The convergence in the numbers of overall active ingredients that we reported last year turned out to be anything but uniform when looking at the details.
The growth by China was concentrated in a key subset of biologics. By the late 2010s, Chinese sponsors often had introduced more, and more novel, cell therapies annually than American sponsors. By the early 2020s, China had matched or exceeded the U.S. in the introduction of new monoclonal antibodies, a commercially important class of biologic drugs. China took a commanding lead in certain categories of monoclonals, such as multispecific antibodies and drug conjugates.
The U.S. still holds a larger share in two categories: nucleic acid drugs and gene therapy. Dominance in both technologies reflects tools built over decades of Western public and private investment. Examples include lipid nanoparticles that conveyed SARS-CoV2 vaccines, viral vectors, and CRISPR gene editing.
Those differences help explain why the two governments are building different walls. Beijing’s proposal shields cell and gene therapy from outside entities, areas where they have a demonstrated or aspirational determination to lead the world. Platforms must remain domiciled in China while individual products can be marketed abroad. That is a coherent industrial strategy, and it is paying off well. Chinese financial regulators report that foreign deals for Chinese biotech assets reached $120 billion through August 2026, up more than a third from the year before.
Washington’s proposal works differently. The Treasury Department proposal prevents American investors from punting on a piece of Chinese biotech and yet still allows American companies to pay for Chinese molecules. In areas where China now leads, the combined effect would seem at best to be a division of labor. As my co-author and I pointed out in our earlier STAT article, China increasingly invents and owns while American firms are more prone to take licenses, complete late stage development, and pay royalties.
To be fair, biotechnology raises real national security questions, from genomic privacy to research that could be misused for nefarious purposes. Imposed limits on capital flows are a legitimate tool. I am certainly not arguing that U.S. investors should fund Chinese state-linked companies without scrutiny. Nor do our data indicate that all Chinese products are comparable in terms of quality or originality. Higher counts may overstate the number of genuine breakthroughs.
Nonetheless, a decision to cut off scientific and/or economic engagement would seem detrimental to both nations.
Restriction is a defensive move. It does not put a single new medicine into the clinic. It treats “biotech” — which comprises drugs, devices, diagnostics, ag-tech, and many other areas — as one thing. Each of these competitive races is being run at different speeds and with entirely different players, outcomes, and pole positions.
The fundamental problem is the one described in our December 2025 article. American output of new experimental drugs has been flat since 2018. In our earlier study, China’s public sector, including universities and state-linked enterprises, contributed more than twice as many new drugs in 2024 as their American counterparts. All the while, the U.S. universities that built our lead in nucleic acids and gene therapy face shrinking federal research support as has been highlighted by STAT.
A competitor lacking fuel will lose the race even if regulators try to slow the opposition.
Three steps would accomplish more than walls ever can.
First, subject matter experts should take advantage of the public comment period the Treasury Department has opened through Dec. 7.
Those comments should press Treasury on several points. If it does impose restrictions, and it is not obvious that it should, they should be aimed narrowly at transfers of platforms and capabilities rather than at all investment. More clarity is also needed to address “NewCo” deals, in which a Chinese licensor takes a stake in a new U.S. company. Importantly, the regulator should set a date and objective criteria to review whether any new rules are working as intended.
Second, policymakers should prioritize and incentivize investment in areas where America leads or could lead. Nucleic acid and gene therapies depend on academic discovery and specialized manufacturing. Stable funding for proven models such as translational research by the National Institutes of Health, ARPA-H, and domestic manufacturing is the most obvious and reliable way to protect a declining margin. In cell therapy, policymakers should ask candidly why so many early trials now start in China (regulation, investment, technology, or combinations thereof), and how we might alleviate domestic hurdles.
Third, Washington should measure the race in a more nuanced way, such as by drug or disease type. The totals of new experimental drugs, such as those we have previously emphasized, can hide more meaningful long-term outcomes, such as FDA approvals as well as market and public health improvements. Federal agencies could start by tracking first-in-human trials by drug type and sponsor country. As this will take time, it should become a long-term indicator, ignoring annual variations. Policy aimed at the aggregate and/or based solely on short term measures will miss key details.
Walls are what you construct when you think you are under attack or are losing. In the technologies that will define the next generation of medicines, from RNA drugs to gene editing, American institutions still lead. The biggest threat does not come from abroad but from changes in domestic policy, such as cutting biomedical research. Our current lead in these fields was built with reliable investments by the public and private sectors, not barriers.
Michael S. Kinch is a professor of pharmacology at Stony Brook University and the author of six books on pharmaceutical innovation.

UN peacekeepers are preparing to leave southern Lebanon. There’s no plan for what comes next
The U.N. peacekeeping force in southern Lebanon is preparing to end a 50-year mission as tensions between Israel and Hezbollah remain high
NAQOURA, Lebanon -- Among the few buildings still standing in the Lebanese border town of Naqoura are an abandoned hotel occupied by Israeli soldiers, its walls draped with anti-drone netting, and the compound housing the headquarters of the U.N. peacekeeping force.
The roads passing through the once-idyllic seaside town, now largely reduced to rubble, are empty except for the occasional military patrol or convoy of peacekeepers escorting civilians or supplies.
The end of the nearly 50-year mandate of the UNIFIL peacekeeping force is looming in just over a month, and still there is no plan for what comes after it.
The peacekeepers' impending exit, in parallel with an ongoing occupation by Israeli forces and a debate over the disarmament of the Hezbollah militant group, leaves the future of southern Lebanon in limbo.
Lebanon wants the U.N. force to stay. But the U.N. Security Council voted last year to terminate UNIFIL’s mandate at the end of 2026, bowing to demands from the United States and its close ally Israel.
Israel says the mission was a failure, citing Hezbollah’s military buildup over the years. The peacekeepers say they helped preserve calm for 17 years before Hamas’ 2023 attack on southern Israel ignited a regional conflict.
“My mandate is not to disarm Hezbollah,” UNIFIL’s commander, Maj. Gen. Diodato Abagnara, told The Associated Press in an interview. “My mandate is to support the Lebanese Armed Forces, to create the best conditions for the Lebanese Armed Forces to take full control here in the south. It’s not to fight against Hezbollah.”
UNIFIL is set to begin a gradual drawdown of its 7,500 peacekeepers on Jan. 1. Whatever comes after that, he said, “It’s very important to avoid a security vacuum in the south.”
UNIFIL wasn’t able to stop Hezbollah from launching missiles or Israel from carrying out airstrikes in two recent wars. But many residents of southern Lebanon say they still feel safer with its presence.
Mohammed Aoun was late to start harvesting his olive groves this year in the village of Halta, just outside of the Israeli-occupied area. On the first day of harvest earlier this month, as a UNIFIL patrol stopped at the orchard, an Israeli drone was buzzing overhead. The thud of a distant airstrike echoed through the valley.
Aoun said he was hesitant to start picking, but he had already lost out on the previous two years’ harvests. He is apprehensive about the impending departure of UNIFIL forces.
“Of course we feel more secure when we see patrols coming and going; it’s a sort of protection,” he said. “Their presence is important with regards to the security situation. We don’t know what will happen after they leave.”
The U.N. Interim Force in Lebanon was created in 1978 after Israel invaded southern Lebanon to fight Palestinian militants. Israel invaded again in 1982 and didn't withdraw until 2000. During that period, Hezbollah, backed by Iran, emerged as a guerrilla force.
After a monthlong war between Israel and Hezbollah in 2006, UNIFIL was tasked with monitoring violations of U.N. Security Council Resolution 1701, which ended the fighting. When a ceasefire ended another Israel-Hezbollah war in 2024, UNIFIL was part of the mechanism overseeing its implementation.
The Lebanese army was to take over security in southern Lebanon after the U.N. force's exit.
But then another war broke out between Israel and Hezbollah in March, linked to the wider Iran war. Israel now occupies large swaths of southern Lebanon, where its soldiers have emptied and demolished dozens of villages.
About 11,000 people remain in a handful of mostly Christian villages in the occupied area, Abagnara said. They depend on UNIFIL to escort the convoys that keep them connected with the rest of the country.
An agreement between Lebanon and Israel for Israeli forces to withdraw in exchange for the disarmament of Hezbollah has floundered, and negotiations between the two countries have stalled.
Lebanese President Joseph Aoun said in a statement Wednesday that “Israel continues to engage in hostile acts in the south” and his government and France — a Security Council member with close ties to Lebanon — both want an extension of UNIFIL's mandate. Any alternative force should continue to operate under the 1701 framework, with some possible amendments, he said.
U.S. officials have expressed willingness for some sort of international force to remain, but not in its current form. They have suggested that it could be a civilian force or private defense contractor.
Israel wants its military to coordinate directly with the Lebanese army to remove what remains of Hezbollah’s weapons.
Israel’s ambassador to the U.N., Danny Danon, said earlier this month that Hezbollah had "exploited UNIFIL’s presence."
“We do not rely on any international force," he said. "We trust only our own soldiers.”
Lebanon opposes the idea of a civilian contractor and has rejected direct military coordination with Israel.
France is working on a Security Council resolution that would authorize a new international force, a U.N. diplomat said. A Western diplomat said there are also discussions of slowing down UNIFIL's withdrawal and maintaining certain missions to avoid a “power vacuum.”
They spoke on condition of anonymity because they were not authorized to comment publicly.
In January, the Lebanese army announced that it had finished removing Hezbollah weapons caches from the border area south of the Litani River.
Hezbollah did not actively oppose the effort but has refused to give up its weapons elsewhere in the country and threatened to fight any attempt to forcibly disarm it.
The Lebanese army has been cautious about any move that might provoke a civil conflict. A Lebanese security official, who spoke on condition of anonymity to discuss sensitive matters, said the army’s current policy is to stop weapons shipments from moving around the country — a change from the past, when Hezbollah freely transported arms — but not to raid the militant group’s storage sites.
Hezbollah supporters in the past accused UNIFIL of spying for Israel and sometimes attacked peacekeepers. Now the group says it would accept UNIFIL or another U.N.-mandated force, but not a private security contractor or a force seen as supporting Israel's occupation.
———
AP staff writer Edith Lederer in New York contributed to this report.

We weren't able to confirm, as of this writing, precisely how many barrels of lead azide would be exploded.
In mid-November, a rumor spread online that the U.S. Army had plans to set off two detonations to destroy an old cache of lead azide — a highly explosive compound — in Middletown, Iowa, on Nov. 20.
"The Army found 68 barrels of the explosive that had been stored at the plant for more than 20 years," one Facebook post read (archived). "Lead azide becomes more unstable as it ages and can detonate with slight movement or friction, making it unsafe to move off site."
The claim spread across other platforms, with several Snopes readers also contacting us for answers.
In short, the claim is true. Here's what we know:
Army confirms explosions will take place
The Iowa Army Ammunition Plant launched a campaign to inform the public about the upcoming explosions, including an open house on Oct. 15 and a notice (archived) on Nov. 15 warning people in the affected area to evacuate and inviting residents to shelter at the Armed Forces Reserve Center during the explosions if needed.
In a document titled "Keeping Our Community Safe," the Army described how plans to reduce harm from the explosion by using specialized water misters and cleaning and removing affected soil and debris once the operation ceases.
(U.S. Army)
The public warnings issued by the Army to residents in the area were as follows:
- Consider avoiding the affected area.
- If you are inside of the affected areas, avoid outdoor air by staying indoors.
- Keep windows and doors closed.
- If it is safe to do so, set heating and cooling systems to "recirculate" to minimize outdoor air exposure and maximize indoor air filtration until the plume passes by your community.
- Avoid unnecessary travel through impacted areas.
- After the US Army determines the air exposure period has ended, consider cleaning indoor and outdoor surfaces such as play surfaces for children and windowsills.
- If your car was parked outside, consider washing your car at a car wash to minimize your contact with potentially exposed surfaces.
Is the circulated 'blast zone' map accurate?
In the circulated map shown in the Facebook post above, the blast zone appears to stretch approximately 100 miles northeast from the blast site. We compared this map to maps the Army released ahead of the planned detonations and found they aligned.
(Facebook user Live Storm Chasers and U.S. Army)
As Nov. 20 draws closer, the Army's maps will be updated. Residents in the area were encouraged to regularly check for updates.
What is lead azide and how did it get there?
According to the Environmental Protection Agency, lead azide is a "hazardous waste that exhibits the characteristic of reactivity (energetic) and exhibits the characteristic of toxicity for lead." In a public notice (archived) Nov. 16, the EPA wrote:
The recrystallization of the stored lead azide has increased the material's sensitivity to friction and shock, and disturbing the containers of lead azide could create an unacceptable risk of unintentional detonation. The Army's evaluation of a range of potential alternatives for the treatment of lead azide culminated in the secretary of the Army selecting in-place, controlled, intentional detonation for the treatment of lead azide.
The material is used to initiate munitions, according to a Q&A document the Army published.
It's unclear precisely how the lead azide stores came to be stored at that underground location. While a number of media outlets reported that 68 barrels would be detonated, we were unable to confirm that amount. We contacted the Army seeking more context and information about the history of the lead azide stores and will update this story if we receive a response.
In March, the Army announced that experts were conducting a safety review for the "safe removal of a chemical compound currently at the plant."
On Nov. 17, local ABC affiliate KCRG reported that local activists were planning a "peaceful demonstration" against the planned detonations.
Group organizers were reportedly demanding:
- An immediate halt to the Nov. 20 lead azide detonation, at minimum until affected communities have had an adequate opportunity to review the risks and alternatives.
- Full transparency regarding the potential environmental and public health consequences.
- Independent environmental experts to review the proposed disposal method and evaluate safer alternatives.
- A comprehensive plan for independent air, soil, and surface testing in potentially affected communities.
- A commitment to clean up and remediate any lead contamination resulting from this operation, at no cost to affected residents and property owners.

At Anthropic, AI is changing how software engineers move up in their careers.
Katelyn Lesse, the head of platform engineering at the newly public company, said on a podcast released Wednesday that AI has made the amount of time it takes to complete a project a less useful measure of readiness for promotion for engineers on her team. Because work that once took years can now take months, Lesse said her team is placing greater weight on outcomes such as lower latency and avoided incidents than on how long a project takes.
"Ultimately, the fallback is always just impact," Lesse told Gergely Orosz, host of The Pragmatic Engineer.
With AI agents speeding up projects for engineers, Lesse said making an impact is becoming more about "coordination" — getting people and agents aligned and understanding how to turn an idea into a high-quality release — and less about writing code.
"You really, really, really shrink the implementation part," Lesse said.
The changes taking place inside Anthropic may be an early indicator of a broader workplace conundrum: If an AI tool can sharply reduce the time it takes to complete difficult work, managers may have to rethink how they measure employees' expertise, progress, and readiness for more senior roles.
Anthropic has a front-row view because its Claude Code programming tool is used by hundreds of thousands of workers worldwide — including its own engineers. The company disclosed in its IPO filing that as of September 30, it had more than 11,900 customers who spent at least $100,000 annually on Claude.
For experienced engineers in particular, AI's speed boost is adding a new wrinkle as to what constitutes top performance, Lesse said.
"As you get more senior, you find people owning totally different problem spaces and totally different systems," she said. "We're kind of constantly iterating on how do we get a sense for the complexity of the work that somebody does."
AI is reshaping hiring, too, said Lesse. Her team is experimenting with interviews that test whether software-engineering candidates can use coding agents to get work done, such as reviewing agent-written code or building a system with an agent. The team made the shift after finding that some candidates who excelled in other parts of interviews had flubbed the hand-coding round.
"It's a big change," said Lesse. "We're basically trying to find what is the best way to really truly get signal on whether someone can use these tools really well to get work done."

- For years, people have claimed without proof that U.S. President Donald Trump is a Russian asset. This theory is often connected to allegations that Trump was once recruited by the KGB, the Soviet Union's intelligence agency.
- The 2021 book "American Kompromat" features an interview with a former spy who claimed the KGB recruited Trump in the late 1980s. Several years later, in February 2025, Alnur Mussayev, a former Soviet and Kazakh security official, claimed in a Facebook post that the KGB recruited Trump in 1987 and assigned him the code name "Krasnov."
- Since then, an image supposedly showing Trump's KGB file has circulated on social media. Reputable reporting indicated that document was actually a file on Trump from the Czechoslovak intelligence agency StB, which had been watching him ever since he married Ivana Trump, a Czechoslovak citizen, in 1977.
- Mussayev's post does not say whether he personally recruited Trump or simply knew about the recruitment, nor does it state whether Trump has ever actively participated in espionage or is just a potential asset.
- Trump did visit Moscow in 1987. Given his high status in society, the KGB almost certainly knew about his trip. But there is no clear evidence suggesting the KGB successfully recruited Trump during that trip or at any other time.
- Mussayev's documented career path raises questions about his credibility as a source. Several biographies of him on Russian-language websites suggest that at the time the KGB supposedly recruited Trump, Mussayev was working in the Soviet Union's Ministry of Internal Affairs, not the KGB.
- No credible evidence proving the rumor that Trump is a Russian intelligence asset has ever surfaced. The president has long denied any claims that he has worked for Russia.
For years, people have claimed that Russian intelligence services recruited U.S. President Donald Trump as an asset in the late 1980s.
In February 2025, the rumor took a new turn. Alnur Mussayev, a former Soviet and Kazakh security official, claimed on Facebook that the KGB, the Soviet Union's intelligence agency, recruited Trump as an asset and gave him the code name "Krasnov," derived from a Russian word for "red."
The claim gained traction when news website The Daily Beast published a now-deleted story (archived) titled, "Former Intelligence Officer Claims KGB Recruited Trump," using only Mussayev's Facebook post as a source. The article described Mussayev's allegations as "unfounded."
The rumor has been widespread ever since then.
Snopes has fact-checked Mussayev's allegation twice and found it to be unsubstantiated — that is, he has not provided tangible evidence supporting his claim and it is not supported by other credible sources. (We contacted Mussayev again for this story, but never heard back).
But the rumor has continued to spread since Snopes published our articles. We regularly receive reader emails asking whether the story is true, including people asking whether an image shows an old KGB intelligence file featuring Trump's photo.
(Facebook user Karen Rourke)
This article revisits and updates our previous work, including a new section on the intelligence file. Reputable reporting indicates it was from the StB, Czechoslovakia's intelligence agency, not the KGB.
In early 2019, Trump denied claims that he has worked for Russia. He has also repeatedly said that investigations into Russian interference in the 2016 election unfairly or illegally targeted him — often branding them part of the "Russia hoax," as Snopes has previously reported.
We also contacted the White House for comment on the matter. They called the rumor "absolutely insane" and said it had "no basis in reality."
Our findings — that the claim is unfounded due to a lack of evidence — remain the same. While the KGB certainly knew about Trump's trip to Moscow in 1987, there is no evidence the agency actively recruited him on the visit.
The mislabeled intelligence file
We identified the intelligence file's true origin while researching the claim: a 2018 article in The Guardian detailing Czechoslovakia's intelligence operations against Trump. According to the story, the state intelligence agency StB watched Trump for years following his 1977 marriage to Ivana, a Czechoslovak citizen. (It's worth noting that the StB was known to collaborate with the Soviets.)
That article, alongside one published in the Czech magazine Respekt at the same time, also happened to contain a much clearer view of the exact same intelligence file used in the social media posts. Both credited the image to the StB, with a watermark reading "Archiv Bezpecnostnich Slozek" That's the Czech name of the Security Services Archive, a state-funded agency that maintains old StB records.
Snopes contacted the archive with the goal of obtaining any files it has on Trump, but was informed that the files may only be viewed and copied in person at one of three locations in the Czech Republic. 
However, even if we hadn't been able to identify the file's original source, there was still a large hint that it wasn't KGB. The document is written in the Czech or Slovak Latin alphabet, not Russian Cyrillic.
Mussayev's allegations don't line up with official records
In Mussayev's Feb. 20, 2025, Facebook post, he claims that in 1987, while he was was serving in the KGB's Moscow-based Sixth Directorate, the agency recruited a "40-year-old businessman from the USA, Donald Trump, nicknamed 'Krasnov.'" The Sixth Directorate's purpose was to recruit businessmen from "capitalist countries," according to Mussayev.
Mussayev's post does not specify whether Trump participated in any spying, only that he was recruited. In a post (archived) from July 18, 2018, he describes Trump's relationship with Russian President Vladimir Putin as follows (translated from Russian to English with DeepL):
Based on my experience working in the field for the KGB and the KNB, I can say with certainty that Trump falls into the category of people who are ideal candidates for recruitment. I have no doubt that Russia has compromising information on the U.S. president and that, for many years, the Kremlin has been promoting Trump for the presidency of the world's leading superpower.
Trump did visit Moscow in 1987 to look at possible locations for luxury hotels, as he noted in his book, "Trump: The Art of the Deal." According to The Guardian and Politico, the KGB may have played a role in luring him there, though Snopes could not confirm that reporting. (Some of it may be sourced either directly or indirectly from the 2017 Steele Dossier — a private intelligence report containing allegations against Donald Trump that was published before he first entered the White House, which several reputable outlets have branded as "discredited").
But despite some circumstantial evidence behind Mussayev's claim, biographies of him on several Russian-language websites (of unknown trustworthiness, we note) reveal a possible discrepancy in his credibility as a source.
While Mussayev's post says he worked in the Sixth Directorate of the KGB in 1987, those online biographies, including one from the Moscow State Institute of International Relations, placed him in Kazakh KGB counterintelligence from 1979 until 1986, when he moved to the Soviet Union's Ministry of Internal Affairs.
Given the covert nature of the KGB, it is possible the public timeline of Mussayev's work history was fabricated by the agency as a cover. At face value, however, the short biographies suggest Mussayev's claim may not be quite as reliable as he claims.
Furthermore, other sources say the First Chief Directorate, not the Sixth Directorate, was the KGB's principal espionage arm. According to the journalist and author W. Thomas Smith Jr.'s book "Encyclopedia of the Central Intelligence Agency," the Sixth Directorate was responsible for "enforcing financial and trade laws, as well as guarding against economic espionage," in line with the counterintelligence descriptions present in the online biographies. Recruiting a foreign businessman as a KGB asset would therefore be, at best, only tangentially related to the Sixth Directorate's mission, assuming Smith Jr.'s descriptions are accurate.
Other accusations against Trump
Trump's relatively pro-Russian positions compared with those of other U.S. presidents have led to past allegations that he is or was a Russian asset in some way.
For instance, the Steele Dossier famously claimed Russia has incriminating tapes of Trump engaging in sexual activity with prostitutes in Moscow, among other scandalous accusations. In 2026, Mussayev echoed the claim that Trump was captured on tape and said Kazakhstan also has the footage, according to the Kyiv Post. The Ukrainian English-language newspaper cited an interview the former KGB official conducted with Ukrainian news station Espreso TV.
However, as mentioned above, that dossier is widely regarded as discredited. CNN previously reported that the dossier's main source, Igor Danchenko, was mainly relaying "rumor and speculation." In 2022, Danchenko was acquitted of charges of lying to the FBI about the dossier's sources.
In the 2021 book "American Kompromat," journalist Craig Unger interviewed a former KGB spy, Yuri Shvets, who also alleged that Trump was compromised by Russia, as Snopes previously reported. The Guardian reported that Shvets had said Trump was "cultivated as a Russian asset over 40 years."
Shvets claimed Trump first appeared on the Russians' radar in 1977, when he was the target of a spying operation — 10 years before the recruitment alleged by Mussayev took place. (That is also the year Trump married Ivana. The Czechoslovakians likely started their file on Trump around this time, according to The Guardian article featuring the image of Trump's old StB file).
Shvets said the KGB later went on a "charm offensive" when Trump visited Moscow and St. Petersburg for the first time in 1987 — the same year Mussayev specified. Shvets told The Guardian that Trump proved so willing to spread anti-Western propaganda that there were celebrations in Moscow. It was not possible to uncover evidence corroborating these claims.
Finally, the Mueller report documented the official findings of former Special Counsel Robert Mueller's investigation into Russian efforts to interfere in the 2016 U.S. presidential election, as well as allegations of conspiracy or coordination between Trump's presidential campaign and the Kremlin. That investigation — which found that the Russian government did interfere in the 2016 presidential election "in sweeping and systemic fashion" (Paragraph 2, PDF Page 9) and that there were "links" between Trump campaign officials and individuals with ties to the Russian government (Paragraph 6, PDF Page 9) — did not establish that members of the Trump campaign conspired or coordinated with the Russian government (Paragraph 1, PDF Page 10).

When medical student Emmanuel Oyebadejo went to watch his friend's American football game, he had no idea he would end up being scouted himself for a sport he had never even played.
He wasn't even interested in it. In fact, while still at school in Manchester he'd delivered a speech titled 'I have a dream' in which he outlined plans to do "very well in basketball, return from the NBA and be the prime minister of the United Kingdom".
But now, four years later, he is being tipped to become the first Briton to be a first-round pick in the NFL Draft.
It is a rapid rise for the 22-year-old, who had to learn the game from scratch and win over his parents who "begged" him not to play and instead focus on his medical studies.
His biggest challenge at the start, though, was finding a pair of boots big enough for his size 16 feet.
It was 6ft 6in Oyebadejo's physique that had caught the eye of the coaching staff at Exeter Demons when he was a spectator for his friend's university game that was taking place at the club's home ground, The Crumb.
"I was talking to one of the other coaches, Jack Mullins, and we sort of turned around [and thought] 'that guy's freaking huge! We should go talk to him'," Lydon Ward-Best, one of the Demons' coaches, tells BBC Sport.
Oyebadejo had been a talented basketball player, playing for Manchester Magic - one of England's top junior clubs - from the age of 11 to 18. But by the time he was at the University of Exeter he was no longer playing competitively.
Lydon Ward-Best persuaded him to give a new sport a go.
"He started coming to training and just had the most ridiculous intro to American football I think I've ever seen," the coach adds.
A straight-A pupil, who had also learned the piano, guitar and drums while studying medicine, Oyebadejo had always been a quick learner.
"I always say that American football is kind of like violent chess," says Mullins, the Demons' current head coach.
"[Emmanuel] got the violent bit pretty quickly. He was fine at that - 'I am much bigger than you, watch me go'.
"The chess bit took a little longer because there's all these things that you have to think about."
But as Ward-Best puts it, "he's not just a big sort of jock athlete, he's a smart guy. He is so dedicated and disciplined with everything."
Oyebadejo played for the Demons at the end of the 2022-23 season, before the team went unbeaten in his first full season, 2023-24. When back home he also played for the Manchester Titans and helped them win the Britbowl in September 2023.
By December 2023, he decided he wanted to take things further. Could he make it in the United States? Would college teams be interested if he sent them videos of his highlights?
Coach Ward-Best told Oyebadejo it would be "tough", adding: "You know the percentages are not on your side here, but you are 6ft 6in and 280 pounds (20 stone), so you've got a better chance than most.
"I wanted to be realistic with him," he adds. "But I said I'd do whatever I could to help get him out there."
Emmanuel's father Oladini says he thought it was a "joke" and that he did not support him playing this "dangerous" game, explaining: "He had never played this game before. He'd only done it for a few months, so why would anybody from America want him?"
But they did.
There was interest from several colleges and Oyebadejo ended up at Jacksonville State, where he would study biology and play under legendary college coach Rich Rodriguez, having managed to win his parents round thanks to the influence of an uncle who lived in Dallas and understood the sport.
His first season was hit by injury but, despite coming up against players who have played American football since they were young children, his second was a big success.
As a defensive end, Oyebadejo's job is to get past the offensive linemen trying to block him and tackle the ball carrier or claim a sack - when a defensive player tackles the quarterback behind the line of scrimmage.
He recorded 4.5 sacks, forced two fumbles and had 41 total tackles during the 2025 season.
Now the big college teams were paying attention.
College football is America's most passionate sporting pastime. While the NFL plays on Sundays, the college game dominates Saturdays during the autumn months.
And Oyebadejo transferred to the University of Florida to play for one of college football's biggest teams in the most prestigious conference, the Southeastern (SEC).
The Florida Gators are three-time national champions, have about 50 former players currently in the NFL and get home crowds of 90,000 at 'The Swamp'.
Oyebadejo was undaunted as he burst on to the scene. He had 2.5 sacks in a win at rivals Auburn in September and followed that up by impressing in big wins over Mississippi and Texas, the latter in front of 103,989 people.
After barely being on the radar of NFL scouts at the start of the season, Oyebadejo's form has propelled him into contention to be an early-round draft pick in 2027.
NFL teams do not have youth systems or academies. Almost all players have come through the US college system and they are recruited via the NFL Draft when they graduate.
One of the biggest events in the American sporting calendar, the NFL Draft takes place over three days in April, with the 32 teams taking turns to select players across seven rounds.
First-round picks in April will be guaranteed a rookie contract of at least $19.1m (£14.4m) and they are often fast-tracked into starting roles. The contract values decrease in a sliding scale so, for example, a third-round pick (top 96) will be guaranteed $7.3m (£5.5m).
Among the latest prospects, ESPN's veteran draft analyst Mel Kiper has ranked Oyebadejo as the fifth-best edge rusher (defensive end). That is regarded as the sport's second-most important position behind quarterback - and therefore the second-best paid in the NFL.
The reason is that Oyebadejo has everything needed to be a starting defensive end in the NFL. Firstly, his height and weight are ideally suited for the grappling battle required in what is known as 'the trenches'.
He has very long arms (7ft wingspan), perfect for winning a wrestling match against the kind of enormous opponent he faces, and unusually for a man as big as him, he's extremely quick. That's the money-making trait.
Although he now weighs about 300lbs (more than 21 stone), it is believed he has a remarkable body-fat percentage of about 12%. All his measurables are seen as ideal for a defensive end, if not better.
There are simply very few people with Oyebadejo's physical talent, and given the fast-tracked nature of his rise in American football, he does not look as raw as you might expect.
"He's British and has only played the sport for three [full] seasons," says his mentor and former coach Ward-Best. "You'd therefore think he must be very green, but he doesn't look that way.
"The physical qualities are clearly there but he's worked a lot on mastering aspects of the position as well."
Menelik Watson, also from Manchester, holds the record for being the highest-drafted British player. He was the 42nd pick in 2013 and spent six years in the NFL, earning a total of $16.4m (£13.7m).
London-born Osi Umenyiora, the 56th pick in 2003, enjoyed an illustrious 12-year career - winning two Super Bowls with the New York Giants.
"I have spoken to Osi, he's a really cool guy," says Oyebadejo, who is also of Nigerian heritage.
"To be a first-round pick out of the UK, it would be amazing. It would do so much for the American football community back home."
Oyebadejo impressed again in an upset win at Kentucky on Saturday and has 4.5 sacks with two regular-season games left. Florida could then play in a 'bowl' game, an end-of-season exhibition.
After that, Oyebadejo is expected to participate in a physical-testing event called the 'scouting combine', where he will be assessed by representatives of all 32 teams in March.
The draft then begins in Washington DC on 27 April, and if Oyebadejo hears his name called, he will complete an unlikely journey and make his now fully supportive parents very proud.
"It's mad," says Ward-Best. "I've been doing this for 20 years and I've never seen anything like this. We almost have to pinch ourselves."
Oyebadejo has stayed in touch with his former coaches in Exeter. The Demons hold watch parties for Florida games and there is a real sense of pride over where his journey began.
"It was just complete chance that he wanted to wander up to The Crumb and watch a game, just being there for his mate," says coach Mullins.
"If those things didn't happen, we wouldn't be having this conversation. He would be four years into his medical degree."

The All Indian Cine Workers Association (AICWA) has written to prime minister Narendra Modi seeking a ban on releasing the Pakistani series “Bachay Hain Sang Samait Lo” on Netflix India on December 4, 2026. The body has also demanded a "strong, permanent law" to keep Pakistani content off Indian television, OTT platforms and cinema. The letter, dated November 24 and signed by AICWA president Suresh Shyamlal Gupta, was shared by news agency ANI on X. It is copied to information and broadcasting minister Ashwini Vaishnaw and to Netflix India. AICWA’s four demands are listed below: that the series is not released or streamed in India on December 4 or any other date that all OTT and streaming platforms strictly comply with the May 8, 2025 advisory that the permanent law be enacted that platforms be made to understand that commercial interest can never come before national security and the sentiments of the martyrs' families The letter also appeals to Netflix India and other OTT platforms to state clearly in their social media posts that such content will not be shown in India. It ends with the line: "No Pakistani face, voice or story has a place on Indian screens." Netflix is yet to issue a statement on this. Inc42 has reached out to the company and the story will be updated based on their response. AICWA claimed that the series stars Pakistani actors — Fawad Khan, Mahira Khan and Hania Aamir — have spoken against India at times of high tension between the two countries. The association said its letter speaks for the "140 Cr people" of the country. The letter's central argument is that Netflix's release would run directly against the government's stance. AICWA pointed to the information and broadcasting ministry's May 2025 advisory, which asked OTT platforms and streaming services to stop streaming Pakistan-origin web series, films, songs and podcasts. Back then, the ministry said that several terrorist attacks in India have been established to have cross-border linkages with Pakistan-based state and non-state actors. ICWA highlighted that the government itself had banned Pakistani artists from working in the Indian film industry after the recent Pulwama attack. Notably, this pattern of cancelling things associated with Pakistan is not only limited to content. Last year, trade body CAIT asked the government to ban Pakistani flags and merchandise on ecommerce platforms. The Central Consumer Protection Authority then issued notices to Amazon, Flipkart, Etsy and three other platforms over the sale of such products.

Amazon workers around the world plan strikes and protests on Black Friday and Cyber Monday
Protests are planned in Los Angeles and Chicago, while a union called for strikes at 11 Amazon sites in Germany.
Amazon workers and their supporters are once again set to go on strike and hold protests in more than 20 countries across the Black Friday and Cyber Monday period. Trade union federation UNI Global said the workers are pushing Amazon to negotiate with unions and respect employees' right to organize.
Teamsters are planning protests on Cyber Monday (November 30) in Los Angeles and Chicago. "As part of a global day of action, Amazon workers are demanding fair wages, safer working conditions, union recognition and respect on the job," a local Teamsters union representing workers in Southern California said.
German trade union Verdi called strikes at 11 Amazon sites on Black Friday (November 27). It claimed the wages the company pays often aren't enough for workers to live on and that warehouse work puts a "considerable physical strain on employees." According to Deutsche Presse-Agentur, Verdi also said Amazon uses digital trackers to keep close tabs on around 40,000 employees. An Amazon spokesman denied Verdi's claims and said average starting pay was above the German minimum wage.
Amazon workers and their allies are also set to mobilize in Canada, Australia, India, Bangladesh, Poland, Luxembourg, Brazil, Colombia, Uruguay, Indonesia, Japan, the Philippines, Thailand, Fiji, Singapore, South Africa and elsewhere. UNI Global said this is the seventh year of the Make Amazon Pay campaign, which it convenes alongside Progressive International.
"The fact is at Amazon we provide great pay, great benefits and great opportunities — all from day one," an Amazon spokesperson told Engadget in a statement. "We directly employ more than 1.5 million people around the world, and provide a modern, safe and engaging workplace whether you work in an office or at one of our operations buildings."
Earlier this month, workers at a warehouse in Delta, British Columbia, became the first in North America to win a union contract with Amazon. The terms of the three-year pact were imposed through binding arbitration. Among other things, the contract ensures pay increases (up to $29 CAD per hour by the time it ends), an extra week of vacation for workers with 10 years of service and severance of up to 18 weeks.
British Columbia's labor relations board ordered arbitration in August despite Amazon's objections. After an arbitrator imposed the agreement, Amazon vice-president J. Ofori Agboka said the process was "improper [and] unfair" and that it "defies common sense," adding that the company would take the issue to court if need be.
In April, the NLRB ordered Amazon to recognize and bargain with a union at the JFK8 warehouse on Staten Island, New York. The company is contesting the order. JFK8 workers voted to unionize in 2022, becoming the first Amazon warehouse in the US to do so.

The bigger Netflix gets, the easier it is to miss stuff. This is true of all digital platforms, of course, but it’s especially true of Netflix of late, as the streaming service’s lineup now also includes a growing library of reality shows, live-programming, and even games. It makes it easy for some of the best shows to zoom right past you, unnoticed — which almost happened to me with Midnight Diner.
Netflix’s coziest show has made a very quiet return
A new season of Midnight Diner: Tokyo Stories is streaming now, though it’s easy to miss.
If you haven’t seen it, Midnight Diner is probably the most comforting thing available on Netflix. The show follows the patrons of a cozy little restaurant tucked away in the backstreets of Shinjuku, which is only open during the unusual hours of midnight to 7:00AM. This, in turn, attracts a unique blend of customers, who help each other out under the watchful eye of the shop’s owner (Kaoru Kobayashi), known only as “master.” The show aired for three seasons on Japanese TV, before being picked up by Netflix for a handful more under the subtitle Tokyo Stories.
What’s especially notable about the show’s return is the huge gap: season 2 of the Netflix iteration streamed in 2019, and it took seven years for it to come back. The break was so long that season 3’s first episode, which premiered in October, is about the restaurant’s struggles during the pandemic. There are a bunch of cute scenes of the diner’s regulars sneaking outside to check if the restaurant is open yet, and wondering if it will ever be able to. If nothing else, the break was a chance for the reliable master to finally take a vacation.
But once Midnight Diner’s new season gets going, it’s right back to everything that made it beloved. Each episode uses a different dish as a way of exploring a particular story. An overworked manga artist imagines the life he missed out on over plates of spicy konjac, while a pair of old friends reconnect while munching on pork cutlet sandwiches. What’s remarkable about the show is the way it balances being a charming, comforting watch with exploring truly difficult and heartbreaking topics. It’s the combination of sweetness and sadness that makes it work so well. It’s as likely to make you laugh as it is to make you cry.
And unlike most Netflix series, the whole season isn’t streaming all at once. Instead, new episodes come out every Tuesday; so far six of a planned 10 episodes are available. It’s a welcome way to spend an evening, as the show’s slow pace and warm sense of humanity can feel like all-too rare traits in the current streaming landscape.
But the main reason I’m even writing about Midnight Diner’s return is that it has been so easy to miss. There’s been next to no promotion for it — all I could find was a trailer on Netflix’s Japanese YouTube channel — and I only happened upon it accidentally after the initial premiere while browsing aimlessly through Netflix’s new releases. This, despite being someone who has watched and rewatched the previous seasons multiple times. You’d think I’d get a notification or something. Netflix has always been full of hidden gems, but now that it’s busier than ever, those gems are all the more hidden.

'Priceless' Duran proves 'the man' but is he papering over cracks at Celtic?
- Published
"Duran is priceless for us at the moment".
It would be difficult for a football manager to muster up a higher compliment for one of his players - given he should know exactly how much he did cost - but Celtic boss Martin O'Neill was rightly effusive in his praise for Camilo Duran.
With 15 goals in 23 appearances, six assists, and another late European winner on Thursday, the Colombian was once again the main man for a struggling Celtic side.
His double against Besiktas breathed life into their Europa League campaign last time out, and his late leap to nod in the winner against Torreense kept it alive.
Duran, 24, started on the bench but was brought on with just over half an hour to go as O'Neill watched his side labour against a team currently 13th in the Portuguese second tier.
Celtic would still be searching for their first European win were it not for their summer arrival from Qarabag, whose goals have played a key part in keeping his team within touching distance of a play-off spot with three fixtures to play.
"He's taken on this mantle of being the man and he's been fantastic," said O'Neill, who started Duran on the bench. "We tried a similar approach against Besiktas.
"Sometimes by the time Duran gets subbed on, you could be behind. But I think that's the sign of a brilliant player, he'll do something.
"He's not a big guy but he's just a super footballer, a super, super footballer."
Papering over cracks or quality in depth?
Duran's summer arrival was overshadowed when, just over a fortnight later, a club-record fee was paid to Bodo Glimt for another striker, Kasper Hogh.
While recent weeks have been dominated by debates over Duran or Hogh, the debate now seems settled, with the Colombian operating on a different level from his striking counterpart.
Anyone watching Celtic in Portugal would have watched Hogh find space a handful of times in the area, but repeatedly fail to find a team-mate or trouble the goalkeeper. Duran didn't need to be asked twice.
"I don't know how many touches he got, but he had the telling touch," James McFadden said on Sportsound post-match.
Duran's goals have also proved decisive in securing domestic points against Falkirk and Hibernian, and with Celtic just a point clear of Rangers, he is indeed invaluable.
Despite his late header giving the thousands of travelling Celtic fans a thrilling end to a relatively turgid game, the intervention is another significant moment in a season that is threatening to unravel if individual performances fail to continue papering over glaring deficiencies across the park.
If the lively Jota - who lasted 74 minutes - was not creating chances, tormenting full-backs or digging out enticing crosses in the first half, Celtic seemed without any real plan of attack.
Yang and Luke McCowan's involvements were limited at best, Hogh's chance to stake a claim was sub-par to be kind, and there was no driving force from the middle of the park to show some impetus.
Arithmetically, Celtic can still finish in any position in the Europa League table. But if they are to claim a playoff or automatic qualification spot, they will need Duran to remain in such a rich vein of form.

John: Celtic are just an average side these days - there should be no expectation.

In a relief for electricity consumers amid rising household expenses, electricity supply companies (Escoms) across Karnataka are likely to pass on their profits to consumers in the form of a refund of around 16 paise per unit from April 2027.
Sources in the Energy Department said on Thursday that most Escoms, including Bangalore Electricity Supply Company (Bescom), Gulbarga Electricity Supply Company (Gescom), Chamundeshwari Electricity Supply Corporation (CESC), and Mangalore Electricity Supply Company (Mescom), have recorded profits for the financial year 2025-26. However, Hubli Electricity Supply Company (Hescom) is an exception.
A senior Energy Department official said the improved financial performance would enable Escoms to return the gains to consumers. Bescom alone reported a profit of ₹293.62 crore during 2025-26, while the profit figures of other Escoms are yet to be officially announced.
Every year, Escoms are required to submit their tariff status and profit-and-loss statements, known as truing-up petitions, to the Karnataka Electricity Regulatory Commission (KERC) as part of their annual performance review. The companies are scheduled to submit their petitions on November 30.
Once the proposals receive KERC’s approval, the refund will be adjusted against electricity bills for consumption from April 2027.
While the average refund is expected to be around 16 paise per unit, consumers in some Escom jurisdictions could receive a higher benefit. Bescom sources said the company was seeking a refund of 35 paise per unit, although the proposal is yet to be finalised. The approved amount is expected to be announced on the Bescom website in December 2026.
Officials attributed the improved financial performance to a reduction in power distribution losses from 11% to around 9.13%. Escoms also reduced power procurement costs by utilising more electricity generated through hydropower instead of relying on relatively expensive thermal power.

An Amazon delivery drone that clipped a fiber-optic line before crashing onto a garage roof is now the subject of an investigation by the US Federal Aviation Administration. It’s the latest delivery drone mishap caught on video as Amazon and other companies are ramping up such aerial delivery operations across the United States.
The November 20 incident began with Jim Brennan and his wife, residents of Huntington Woods, Michigan, placing an order for shampoo and being surprised by a notification about the package arriving by drone within seven minutes, according to WXYZ 7 News Detroit. After the drone dropped the package into Brennan’s backyard, it lost a propeller when it caught on fiber-optic cable and floundered sideways before getting pinned between the neighbor’s garage roof and some power lines.
“Like a sick bird, it tried to go up, it tried to get out of here,” Brennan told WXYZ 7.
Amazon Prime Air currently operates a fleet of battery-powered MK30 drones that can deliver packages weighing up to five pounds and have onboard sense-and-avoid technology to avoid obstacles. However, the drone clearly failed to avoid the thin fiber-optic cable in this case—so hopefully the FAA investigation would take that into account along with Amazon delivery drone procedures.
The FAA preliminary accident and incident notification briefly describes the incident as “UAS struck a fiber cable, a residential garage, and became entangled in power lines during takeoff.” That notice was posted on November 23.
The National Transportation Safety Board is also gathering information about the incident but has not yet decided whether to open its own probe, according to CNBC. That US government agency holds primary responsibility for investigating aviation accidents and other transportation incidents.
