Due to the global RAM shortage, buying any kind of gaming gear that needs memory has gotten prohibitively expensive, which is precisely what makes this early Black Friday deal for an Alienware Aurora desktop for just $1,900 on Amazon so appealing.
The desktop is housed in a compact 35 liter mid-tower and the system comes with an Intel Core Ultra 7 265F processor, 32GB of DDR5 RAM, a 1TB SSD and an NVIDIA RTX 5070 GPU with 12GB of vRAM. That right there is a pretty solid foundation for a mid-range gaming rig that can handle both 1080p and QHD gaming with ease (depending on the title of course). This offer is especially enticing when considering the cost of those individual components if you bought them separately.
Let's start with the CPU, and compare it against other listings on Amazon. If you search for an Intel Core Ultra 7 265F, that particular CPU is actually sold out at the time of writing, and the next closest processor is a Core Ultra 7 265 processor that's going for $365. Next, we can move on to 32GB of DDR5 RAM, which is similar to this 2 x 16GB Corsair Vengeance kit that's listed for $470. Finally, there's the RTX 5070 GPU which is currently going for between $910 and $980 on Amazon from a couple different OEMs.
So even if we take the cheapest price for each component, you're looking at a total cost of $1,745 for just the system's three most expensive pieces of hardware, which means you're basically getting a case, a PSU, fans, heatsinks and a 1TB SSD for $150 — and without the need to do any assembly. That's one of the best deals I've seen for a gaming PC in a while. To give you even more context, if you go to the official Dell/Alienware website, you can find an Aurora desktop with the exact same specs listed at around $2,600. This means we're looking at a potential savings of around $700 compared to its standard pricing.
Meanwhile, the rest of the system is pretty well equipped. It comes with a good selection of front IO including three USB-A, one USB-C and a 3.5mm audio jack. Around back, there's even more connectivity with a total of six additional USB connectors (two Type-C and four Type-A), 2.5 gigabit Ethernet, more audio jacks and even a SPDIF optical port. And on the inside, you get a motherboard with an Intel Z890 chipset with three PCIe slots and support for Wi-Fi 7. There's even a little window on its side panel so you can see the system's built-in RGB lighting and all those pricey components.
However, anyone thinking about buying this system should be careful about reading too much into Amazon's listed specs. Details for this offer say the Aurora comes with a built-in optical drive, but I'm pretty sure that's a mistake. Furthermore, Amazon's page says the desktop comes with a 450-watt PSU, while other materials state the PC has a 500-watt power supply. Also, while you can configure an Aurora with water-cooling on Alienware's website, this particular model is merely air-cooled.
Regardless, if you've been caught off-guard by the rapid rise in PC components over the past year and a half and have been waiting for a system with a more reasonable price, this $1,900 Alienware Aurora desktop might be the deal you're looking for. Just don't wait too long because this offer seems poised to sell out fast.

This article is part of a new First Opinion series on the future of medical school.
By this time of year, the sky is black when I step outside. The day has carried me from lectures on gastrointestinal cancer disparities to TAing microbiology, from student government debates to helping free-clinic patients complete paperwork for expensive medications. With the cold nipping at my skin, I look back at the Stanford medical school building, its windows glowing. There is still so much to do, and even more to feel. I call my mother, my home base in human form. Three thousand miles away, she is preparing for bed. Circumstances beyond her control have kept her from taking a domestic flight for decades, let alone visit me in California. Her first question is always, “Did you remember to eat dinner?” Her second: “How were your classes today?”
I am a class-goer. Most of my classmates are, too, though preclinical lecture attendance among medical schools has been declining nationally since the pandemic and the Step 1 exam’s transition to pass/fail. Given the flexibility of recordings and the time students devote to service, research, and other commitments, I understand why some choose to study independently and firmly believe in preserving students’ freedom to make that choice.
For me, though, attending lectures in person has become an important part of feeling at home. It is the most powerful way I take care of my mental health and the classmates I have come to see as my newfound family. I would like to make the case why it could for other medical students, too.
Part of that happiness comes from my daily calls with my immigrant mother. What I learn gives me something to share with the woman who gave up her dream of becoming a clinician so I could pursue mine: dissecting a cadaver for the first time, suturing, administering flu vaccines for undocumented folks, wrapping wound dressing around an unhoused man’s arm. Putting these experiences into words is an exercise of understanding the unmistakably human profession I am entering.
I once worried that telling her the good parts of my day would make the distance between us more painful. Her unconditional love for me throughout the years has taught me otherwise. There are many students like me who left the comfort of our communities to pursue higher education. We should not have to compromise on maintaining relationships with loved ones, which influences medical student well-being and belonging.
In graduate school, where life is more independent, class also gives us a place to come together. During lecture breaks, I learn about friends advocating against the medical bloodletting of horseshoe crabs, making spaces more accessible to people with disabilities, and bringing care to under-resourced youth through mobile vans. We ask to become involved in one another’s work. Other days, happiness is resting my head on a friend’s shoulder, sharing my next bucket-list read — Bryant Lin’s “Sunshine: An Exploration of Living When You Are Dying” — or suggesting that we try the new cafe with robot baristas. It is remembering I am not walking this road alone.
Just as importantly, being physically present gives me opportunities to check in with others. As smartphones and artificial intelligence mediate more of our lives, I worry how easily we can grow used to being alone. Hard workers are remarkable at hiding stress. Intelligent people are good at forgetting to be kind to themselves. Class gives us a place, an excuse, not only to struggle through challenging coursework in real time together, but be part of one another’s lives. In between lectures, I am giving a friend a relationship pep talk as we complain about dating in the Bay Area. The next moment, I am making plans to cheer on another friend at a marathon. After lab, I am curled up on the reading room couch beside a peer whose mother has just been diagnosed with cancer. Our parents are getting older and sicker. It is infuriating. You would think learning medicine would brace us for inevitable losses. False. But knowing there is an abundance of people here to catch you is a peace in its own form.
In the classroom, I have also come to see my education as one I help shape. Conversations with professors following lectures have allowed me to successfully advocate to integrate various topics in our curriculum: sex differences in aortic stenosis pathophysiology, the relationship between ALDH2*2 deficiency and esophageal cancer, overdose response training. Medicine is evolving by the day, and these exchanges make education a collaboration between learners and teachers, showing students that our voices matter.
I think often of watching Celine Song’s “Past Lives” with my mother in December 2024, when I was still in New York. The film introduces in-yun, the idea that an encounter between two people is the result of countless threads from their past lives intertwining. Today, I still wonder if this, too, is a past life, and we are already something else to each other in the next. Perhaps in the next, I am the uninsured one who needs translation, and she is the medical student sitting across from me at the free clinic. In this life, it is 2 a.m. Eastern, and she is calling to ask about my day. It is 11 p.m. in California, and I am at the beach with friends, squinting into the Pacific because someone yelled that they spotted a whale. I imagine the animal’s song, sung at a frequency so low it travels for thousands of miles underwater, enough to carry me home.
I crave a big future, expansive in experience and generosity. For others, that may mean studying independently to make room for research, paid work, service, or rest. Those choices deserve grace.
For me, it begins with being physically present during these four brief years. Honoring my mother means doing good when her familiar applause is far away and nurturing the classmates who will become tomorrow’s doctors. Here is my chance to find where I fit, then widen that space for the next person. I don’t plan to squander a second of it.
Brian Zhang is a second-year M.D. student at Stanford University School of Medicine, where he currently serves as student body president.
The First Opinion series on the future of medical school will run through the end of 2026. Have an idea for a big or small way to change medical school? Email us.

Serbia sets presidential election for Dec. 27 after students won parliamentary vote
Serbia's Parliament speaker has set an early presidential election for December 27
BELGRADE, Serbia -- BELGRADE, Serbia (AP) — Serbia 's Parliament speaker on Thursday set an early presidential election for Dec. 27, after former President Aleksandar Vucic resigned in September to pursue what turned out to be a failed bid to become prime minister.
The presidential vote will be held after a student movement defeated Vucic's right-wing Serbian Progressive Party in an early parliamentary ballot on Oct. 25.
Vucic and his party had ruled virtually unchallenged for 14 years. He had run for prime minister after serving two near-complete five-year terms as president, and was banned by law from seeking a third term.
“I hope we will have a tough choice between top candidates and their programs," Speaker Aleksandar Cupic said. “Building democratic institutions is the task for all of us.”
It was not immediately clear who the presidential candidates will be. Vucic has suggested that his SNS party could sit out the election.
The presidency in Serbia is largely ceremonial. The president commands the army and has a say in foreign policy but has no executive powers. While he was in office, however, Vucic concentrated power in the presidency, facing accusations of authoritarian rule. Vucic regularly announced important state decisions and policies and even presided over government sessions.
Since losing power, Vucic has accused the election winners of imposing a “revolutionary terror,” although his government is still technically in control until a new one is formed. The change in power has led to a surge in detentions of officials and police officers suspected of abusing their positions during Vucic's rule.
The youth-led movement had led two years of street protests that started in response to a train station canopy collapse in northern Serbia that killed 16 people. Many blamed the tragedy on alleged rampant corruption and negligence during the building renovation in Novi Sad.

Amid protests, Meta has reportedly told Congress leaders that it was bound by local laws to take down flagged content and accounts from its platforms. Denying accusations of political favouritism, the tech giant reiterated that it was neutral towards all parties in India. In a closed-door meeting with Congress leadership today, Meta India executives Aman Jain and Natasha Jog reportedly cited that the removals were in fact linked to its policies on AI-generated content. To this, Congress, whose youth wing (Indian Youth Congress) has been protesting against steep numbers of takedowns on Meta platforms, cited use of AI-generated BJP posts that remained accessible. IYC has called for Meta restore accounts restricted following government directions and explain how its algorithms identify and take down posts. The tech giant, on the other hand, has raised concerns about protests targeting its offices and posters depicting CEO Mark Zuckerberg in RSS traditional attire. Meanwhile, IYC workers continued their protest, protesting outside the Bengaluru office today. "Stop dodging accountability, disclose government takedown requests, explain your algorithms and restore unfairly restricted accounts," IYC said in a post on X. With no commitment made by either side, the meeting seems to have ended at a stale mate. The proceedings of the meeting were reported by Reuters. Inc42 has not been able to verify the information independently. We'll update the story on the basis of comments from the tech giant. Meta’s Content Restrictions Surge In India IYC has been protesting the recent increase in Meta’s content deletion over the past few months. Meta restricted access to more than 5.44 Mn items across Facebook and Instagram between January and June 2026, compared with around 41,400 in the preceding six months, marking an approximately 131X increase, according to its latest transparency disclosures. The restrictions covered several categories, including online gaming, AI-generated content depicting prominent figures, threats to India's sovereignty and integrity, gender-based harassment and the promotion of enmity between groups. Meta has attributed the increase to changes in India's IT rules, which require platforms to act on government takedown directions within shorter timelines. India's social media content moderation framework is primarily governed by the Information Technology Act, 2000, and the Information Technology (Intermediary Guidelines and Digital Media Ethics Code) Rules, 2021. Under Rule 3(1)(d), intermediaries must remove or disable access to unlawful information after receiving a valid court order or a reasoned intimation from an authorised government officer. The provisions cover content relating to national security, public order and India's sovereignty, among other grounds. The government has tightened these requirements through successive amendments. In October 2025, the Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology (MeitY) notified amendments, effective November 15, requiring takedown notices to specify the legal provision invoked, the nature of the alleged unlawful act and the exact URL or electronic identifier of the content. The changes also introduced periodic reviews of government directions by senior officials. In February 2026, the government further reduced the compliance window for intermediaries. An amendment effective February 20 cut the deadline to remove or disable access to specified unlawful content from 36 hours to three hours after receiving a valid court order or reasoned government intimation. The shorter deadline has increased pressure on social media platforms to strengthen their content detection and enforcement systems, while raising questions about transparency and the potential for legitimate content to be restricted.

We see an increasing acknowledgement and fact of dual use in particularly the public cloud, but also just across the board in private cloud data centers as well. The dual use that I refer to is the utilization of compute functions within these data centers—within cloud services—by militaries, for example, to run battlefield management systems, to do their HR, to do their resource management. Once a military uses a piece of civilian infrastructure, at least under international law or in terms of the principles of targeting that are taken forward by militaries, it can sometimes become a military object and is therefore of interest to an adversary, and there’s an incentive to target it.

US too focused on Middle East and not pushing Russia hard enough, Zelensky tells BBC
- Published
Volodymyr Zelensky has voiced deep frustration with the US, saying that delays in delivering vital anti-ballistic missiles are costing Ukrainian lives and complaining that the US is not pushing Russia hard enough during peace talks.
In an interview with the BBC at his office in central Kyiv, Ukraine's president also said it was "very strange" that Donald Trump had posted a picture of himself embracing Vladimir Putin as "my friend".
"Of course it's up to the President of the United States, but... it's strange," Zelensky said, speaking in English.
"He's an aggressor, and a killer…He can't be a friend. Just cannot be," he said, suggesting it was like hugging Adolf Hitler during WWII.
Since a bruising encounter with Trump in the Oval Office in 2025, Zelensky has been careful how he handles relations with the United States.
Trump's two envoys have been trying to negotiate a peace deal between Russia and Ukraine - to end the huge loss of life. But they often seem more in tune with Moscow's position, than that of Kyiv.
The latest round of peace talks, mediated in Abu Dhabi earlier this month, made no obvious progress: "The more we know, the more problems", is how Zelensky described it.
He said talks were expected to resume in December.
On Thursday, Donald Trump posted on his Truth Social platform that at his own summit with Putin in China last week he had urged Russia to "pull back all military aggression against territories throughout Europe" and said he believed a peace deal with Ukraine was "a strong possibility".
But from its public statements, Russia appears to have regressed to its initial, hardline negotiating positions – on everything.
And Zelensky revealed that it wasn't clear whether European negotiators would be at the table, as the US envoys had announced.
The Kremlin appears to be resisting.
- Europe ready for talks with Russia on ending war in Ukraine, leaders say 
  - Published6 days ago
- Zelensky says Putin is a 'killer' after Trump calls Russian leader a friend 
  - Published5 days ago
Ukraine urgently needs the talks to move forward and bring five exhausting years of Russia's full-scale invasion to an end.
Russian strikes across the country have been growing more frequent and more deadly: the number of civilians being killed is at an all-time high.
So Zelensky called for "real helpful allies, who can push Russia" to achieve results and urged the US to live up to its reputation as a strong country with "power and respect".
"When you try to be very neutral with the aggressor... it means you support victims and you support also aggressor. It's not right," he said.
The US argues that it is neutral: in the complex search for a peace deal between the two sides that can hold.
In the meantime, Kyiv is struggling to defend its skies.
The air alerts, day and night, are now a draining feature of everyday life. As Russian ballistic missiles target power stations and bridges, jet-powered drones are launched daily at central Kyiv and other big cities.
Ukraine launches hundreds of drones at targets in Russia in response.
Zelensky said the military here are now able to destroy about 70% of Russia's fastest drones, a statistic he said was improving.
But there is a "very, very big" deficit of interceptors to stop ballistic missiles and he said the Amercians were delaying deliveries of its Patriot systems.
"It's a pity they made a focus on Middle East and they help them more… It's a pity. We have huge questions with this," Zelensky said.
"The deficit of these missiles - that is people's lives."
He also confirmed that the US satellite communications system, Starlink – and its military version, Starshield – were still being restricted in occupied areas of Ukraine.
Ukrainian drone units have described their problems to the BBC, as their interceptor drones can no longer catch up with Russian Shaheds. It means those weapons then fly deeper into Ukraine, unhindered.
So whose decision was that?
"Technically SpaceX, politically - I don't know, I really don't know," Zelensky replied. "It's like... ping pong. We are asking one side, they say it's the other."
Tough winter
Ukraine's own long-range strikes against Russian targets have increased in recent weeks, including oil refineries and ships carrying weapons or fuel.
On Thursday, Italy's Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni said an attack that sank a Russian warship docked in eastern Libya this week risked spreading war to the Mediterranean, which was unacceptable.
Zelensky defended the strikes, calling the warship Merkury an "absolutely fair goal".
He accepted that such strikes were "very dangerous" but said Ukraine's forces "never attack" without coordinating with its partners.
He declined to be more specific.
But he acknowledged that Ukraine was bracing for a difficult and dangerous winter.
Recent strikes on Kyiv have targeted bridges over the vast river Dnipro, apparently trying to cut the city in two.
Some residents have already left town for the winter and businesses closed, as power cuts and strikes on logistics networks have pushed operating costs unmanageably high.
They've also plunged much of the city into darkness.
"[Russia] wants us to run away, of course," Zelensky said.
"People can go, but we will try to defend our capital in any way. We need our capital. Without a capital, you don't have a country."

WASHINGTON — A new website launched by the Trump administration provides centralized access to more than 92,000 public records from the Department of Health and Human Services and the agencies it oversees — including partially redacted entries from health secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr.’s calendar.
While many of the records were previously available, the health department heralded the launch of the site as a sign of its “radical transparency.”
In June, after a New York Times report referred to him as disengaged with the job, Kennedy said on social media that his calendar was publicly available, though no such calendar had been made available for the media or the public before Tuesday. A number of Freedom of Information Act requests filed by STAT reporters had previously gone unanswered and even unacknowledged and do not appear to be included in the Tuesday release.
Much of the secretary’s partial calendar, which reflects his activities from Feb. 13, 2025, to June 19, 2026, is redacted, including some private calls taken by the secretary. One of his closest aides at the agency, Stefanie Spear, appears to be listed only once in the calendar. References to other notable meetings are not redacted, including one that would ultimately lead to the ouster of a short-lived director of the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, Susan Monarez.

North Korea expels Swiss diplomat in sanctions row
- Published
North Korea has ordered Switzerland's diplomatic representative to leave the country within 48 hours and called for the office to close, in a row over sanctions.
It followed Switzerland's decision to place sanctions on the Songdowon international children's camp in the eastern city of Wonsan, which is attended by Russian and Chinese children among other nationalities.
The camp has been accused of involvement in transferring children from Russian-occupied areas of Ukraine.
North Korea's state-run news agency KCNA called the sanctions "a blatant hostile act".
Switzerland is one of the few Western nations to maintain dialogue with Pyongyang.
Confirming the expulsion, KCNA said: "The Foreign Ministry of the Democratic People's Republic of Korea (North Korea) declared the head of the Swiss Diplomatic Office in the DPRK persona non grata and urged him to leave the country within 48 hours."
The diplomatic rebuke comes weeks after Swiss foreign minister Ignazio Cassis made a rare visit to North Korea, where he officially reopened the office and discussed normalising relations.
Swiss authorities said relations between the two countries would be maintained through the North Korean embassy in Bern, and the Swiss embassy in Beijing.
Diplomatic links with North Korea were first established in 1974 and Switzerland opened a co-operation office in Pyongyang in 1997. It was closed during the pandemic and remained shut for six years.
Switzerland's department of foreign affairs said the country "distinguishes between its sanctions policy and its commitment to maintaining dialogue with all countries".
It added: "The reopening of the office in Pyongyang did not in any way affect Switzerland's implementation of UN sanctions related to North Korea's nuclear programme, nor its implementation of EU sanctions targeting North Korea in the context of Russia's war against Ukraine."
Thousands of North Korean soldiers have been deployed to help support Russia's war with Ukraine.
In August, Ukraine's President Volodymyr Zelensky accused Moscow of using North Korean missiles.

Faldo urges LIV stars to 'chip in' for unpaid firms
- Published
Sir Nick Faldo has suggested those who financially benefited from LIV Golf should "chip in and take care of" businesses owed money by the Saudi-backed tour.
His comments have been welcomed by UK companies still waiting to be paid.
A BBC Sport investigation found that LIV paid millions to players and executives in the weeks before filing for bankruptcy, while bills from suppliers were already overdue.
Faldo - arguably Britain's greatest golfer - said the controversial breakaway tour risked "ruining the small businesses that help make their events possible".
"British suppliers who cleaned venues and kept events running are still owed hundreds of thousands of pounds," added the six-time major winner.
"Maybe if those on and off the golf course feel they were overcompensated for their worth, they should chip in and take care of this matter."
Since the investigation was published, more firms have contacted us about money they are owed by LIV.
They include sports communications company Soapbox, which works with the likes of Anthony Joshua and Luke Littler and is owed tens of thousands of pounds.
"I'm incredibly grateful to Sir Nick Faldo for speaking out," said Krissi Foskett, whose cleaning company BD365 Clean is £75,225 out of pocket.
"For the last couple of months I've felt powerless. Having someone of his standing recognise the injustice of what's happening to businesses like ours genuinely means a lot.
"Sir Nick's suggestion that those who have benefited financially could contribute towards paying the outstanding suppliers is something I wholeheartedly welcome."
LIV Golf has not responded to requests for comment on the original investigation or Faldo's remarks.
In August, chief executive Scott O'Neil said he hoped the tour would be able to pay its suppliers.
"What I would say to them is we're doing everything we can to make sure we can do right by them and the work they committed.
"I come from a family of entrepreneurs, a family of small business entrepreneurs and know the challenge."
Faldo's one-time on-course rival, Greg Norman, was chief executive of LIV Golf until last year.
Court filings show the Australian received $9.4m (£7.2m) in settlement and bonus payments in September 2025.
His successor, O'Neil, received a retention bonus of $6.4m (£4.9m) in June this year.
In September, Norman told The Real Deal with Bob Philion podcast that he was proud of bringing private equity into the sport.
"In a period of basically 2021 to now, close to $8bn (£6.1bn) has been brought into the game of golf," he said.
Responding to those comments, Faldo told BBC Sport: "Eight billion dollars is 8,000 million dollars. If that is a full six years, that is approximately $3.6m (£2.8m) a day.
"Before LIV filed for bankruptcy, seven executives received $15.6m (£11.9m) in retention payments, with further bonuses also paid.
"Now they risk ruining the small businesses that help make their events possible."
BBC Sport has contacted Norman for a response.
'I'm not the one who should feel ashamed'
Companies still owed money include Global Infusion Group, which provided catering at July's LIV Golf UK event and is awaiting £321,671 - which was due on 7 August.
Public records also list more than £3,000 owed to Goodysphere, a family-run Yorkshire firm that provides a sensory bus designed to help autistic children who may find busy events overwhelming.
Just $2m (£1.5m) has been proposed so far by LIV's Saudi owners to pay unsecured creditors, leaving many smaller companies unsure whether they will receive anything at all.
"I've spent months questioning myself, feeling ashamed that our financial difficulties might be perceived as poor management," said Foskett.
"When I look at the billions poured into LIV Golf and the millions reportedly paid to executives, whilst I was personally climbing in and out of skips to meet their zero-waste policy, I've come to realise that I'm not the one who should feel ashamed.
"We didn't invest in LIV Golf. We didn't gamble on its success. We simply went to work.
"Scott O'Neil talks about understanding small businesses. Sir Nick Faldo is standing up for them. Right now, I know whose words mean more to me."

SpaceX gets FCC approval to deploy 1 million satellites for its AI orbital data center
The FCC expects the initiative, called Starmind, to deploy it first satellite by November 2033.
The Federal Communications Commission (FCC) has approved SpaceX's request to deploy 1 million satellites to build its AI orbital data center. SpaceX filed its application at the beginning of the year, presenting the initiative called Starmind as the better alternative for ground-based data centers. In its filing, the company argued that "orbital data centers are the most efficient way to meet the accelerating demand for AI computing power," since they use "solar power with little operating and maintenance costs."
But can space-based data centers for AI really work? Critics doubt they can. Adam Becker, an astrophysicist and a critic of Elon Musk's space and AI ambitions, told AP that "it's not going to happen. The idea behind sending AI data centers outside our planet is so that they don't consume resources their ground-based counterparts do, like energy and water for cooling.
However, critics of the plan argue that space is a vacuum that traps heat inside objects and doesn't make cooling down hardware easier. In space, heat has to leave the satellites via radiation, and Becker explained that there are "basic physical limits" to radiating the heat out for all of them. In addition, that many satellites could cause in-orbit collisions and generate a huge amount of space junk.
FCC Chairman Brendan Carr believes that with this approval, though, America is "leading the world into the era of super intelligence." It opens a "bold new frontier," he added. Under the terms the FCC has approved, SpaceX has permission to deploy satellites into orbital layers spanning 50 kilometers, at altitudes between 500 meters and 1,002 kilometers.
The company is required to deploy at lease one authorized satellite and place it into its assigned orbit by November 25, 2033. By the same date in 2035, it must have already deployed 100,000 satellites to their respective orbits. Three years later, on November 25, 2028, it must have already deployed 500,000 of the authorized satellites. All 1 million satellites must have already been placed in their assigned orbits no later than November 25, 2040. Musk previously said that SpaceX will start launching the satellites in 2027, but we'll have to wait and see if the company can stick to that timeline.

WASHINGTON — The Trump administration on Monday said that the federal government will save $9.2 billion on drugs purchased through Medicare next year as a result of price negotiations, a net savings of 45% compared to what it would’ve paid last year had the negotiated prices been in effect.
This is the third time the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services has negotiated drug prices following the passage of the Inflation Reduction Act, but it’s the first time those drugs have included treatments administered in doctors’ offices, which are covered by Part B. Only retail drugs covered by Part D were eligible during the first two years.
The estimated $9.2 billion in savings does not account for discounts the drugmakers pay to the Part D Manufacturer Discount Program. That program was created by the same law that created the price negotiation program. If those discounts were included, the estimated savings would be about $5.5 billion, or 33% in lower net aggregate spending.

(Bloomberg) -- A drone attack on Kuwait killed two Italian civilians and injured two others Thursday, with the Gulf nation blaming Iran for the strike on what its military described as a “vital” facility.
The Italians, technicians working for German defense company Rheinmetall AG, were killed in an explosion involving several drones of Iranian origin, Italy’s Foreign Ministry said in a statement.
They were carrying out maintenance on detection antennas for the Skyguard air-defense system used by Kuwait’s armed forces, the ministry said. Falling debris also injured a Kuwaiti and a Pakistani, according to Kuwait’s military.
The attack was the second on the country this month.
Iran “firmly and completely” denied carrying out the attack.
“No military or offensive operation of any kind has been carried out by the Islamic Republic’s armed forces in that region,” senior armed forces spokesman Abolfazl Shekarchi said, according to state-run IRIB.
Renewed tit-for-tat strikes between the US and Iran have ratcheted up tensions in recent weeks, leaving the region in limbo as President Donald Trump threatens further strikes while mediators seek a deal.
The attacks on Kuwait this month followed a two-month lull in Iranian assaults on the country. Kuwait and neighboring Bahrain have been among Tehran’s targets since its April ceasefire with Washington collapsed. Iran struck an industrial facility in Bahrain on Saturday, injuring two people, one critically.
Unlike previous Iranian attacks on Kuwait, Thursday’s assault appeared to be unsolicited and didn’t follow any reported US attacks on Iranian territory.
“Iran is going on the offensive, gradually abandoning the gray area that has defined the latest phase of the war,” said Bader Al-Saif, assistant professor at Kuwait University and associate fellow at Chatham House. “Analysts fixated on the timing of renewed US-Israeli strikes are remiss in downplaying Tehran’s own agency.”
The risks of shipping energy through the Strait of Hormuz have also risen in recent weeks as Iran launched a wave of attacks on tankers.
A US blockade, meanwhile, is worsening Iran’s economic crisis by preventing it from exporting oil and restricting imports of some essential goods, while inflation has accelerated to around 90%.
Arab states in the Persian Gulf are urging Trump to end the conflict without another round of all-out hostilities after Tehran targeted them with thousands of missiles and drones during the opening weeks of the war.
“With no durable solutions in sight, the region is spiraling deeper into mayhem,” Al-Saif said.

NASA's DART mission left a stadium-sized crater in an asteroid, the ESA finds
The ESA’s Hera mission has begun capturing images of the aftermath of DART’s impact.
In March, NASA revealed it successfully altered the orbit of Dimorphos and its parent asteroid Didymos around the Sun with its Double Asteroid Redirection Test (DART), and now thanks to new images captured by the ESA's Hera spacecraft, we have a better idea of what that mission actually did to the smaller of the two asteroids. The 2022 controlled crash created an "impact crater the size of a sports stadium," according to Patrick Michel, the Director of Research at France's National Centre for Scientific Research (CNRS) and Hera's principal investigator.
The crater extends across the entire width of Dimorphos, according to Michel, yet it didn't alter the fields of boulders that cover the rest of the asteroid. Besides physically altering the surface of Dimorphos, the ESA found that the DART impact sent the asteroid tumbling in its new orbit. Hera also revealed that both Dimorphos and Didymos are surrounded by hundreds of orbiting boulders.
All of these new details were captured by Hera's monochrome Asteroid Framing Camera, multi-spectral Hyperscout H and JAXA-developed Thermal Infrared Imager from about 25 to 30km away from the asteroids, the ESA says.
"NASA's DART mission demonstrated that we can change an asteroid's orbit," Hera mission manager Ian Carnelli said. "Hera is now revealing what happened to the asteroid itself. By combining these two missions, humanity is taking a decisive step towards making asteroid deflection a reliable tool for protecting our planet."
NASA and other space agencies are exploring altering asteroids' orbits as one way of protecting the Earth from potentially dangerous future impacts. In December, the ESA plans to move Hera closer to Dimorphos and Didymos to capture even higher-resolution images of the impact site. In January, Hera will also deploy shoebox-sized CubeSats to collect other types of data. The Juventas CubeSat, created by a Luxembourg-led research team, will use radar to probe the asteroid's interior and eventually land on its surface. An Italian-led team will use the other CubeSat, Milani, to prospect asteroid dust and other surrounding materials.

Thirty-four-year-old Sundar lives in Tappal village in Khair tehsil of Aligarh district, Uttar Pradesh. His name was absent from the state’s draft voter list published on January 6, 2026. However, in the final list published on April 10, his name appears four times, at serial numbers 730, 738, 739 and 757 in booth 19. Each entry carries a different Elector Photo Identity Card (EPIC) number.
The official list of Form 6 applications, used for voter registration, records only two applications from Sundar, dated January 9 and 14. The office of the Uttar Pradesh chief electoral officer (CEO), however, said that he had filed four. The discrepancy aside, the CEO’s office’s response confirms a crucial point: Multiple applications by the same person resulted in the issuance of multiple voter IDs.
The Election Commission launched the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of electoral rolls in Uttar Pradesh in November 2025, with the removal of duplicate and incorrect entries among its stated objectives. Alt News compared the draft and final electoral rolls across 69 booths in 20 districts, covering 60,558 voters, and cross-checked newly added names against the corresponding Form 6 application lists. The analysis found 230 people whose names appeared at least twice in the final rolls, with some listed three or four times, each against a separate voter ID. Such duplicate entries were found in booths across the political spectrum.
On October 27, 2025, the Election Commission announced the second phase of the SIR across 12 states and Union Territories, including Uttar Pradesh. The exercise, covering approximately 51 crore voters, began on November 4.
The schedule for Uttar Pradesh was subsequently extended four times. The draft electoral roll was published on January 6, 2026. Those whose names were missing from the draft had to submit Form 6 to seek inclusion. Following the fourth extension, the deadline for filing claims and objections was March 6, while the final electoral roll was published on April 10.
At present a special summary revision (SSR) of electoral rolls is going on in the state. The draft roll was published on November 17.
The Methodology
For each of 69 booths in UP, Alt News read the draft list (January 6, 2026) and the final list (April 10, 2026) entry by entry, and matched the count with the totals on each list’s cover page. We treated two entries as the same person only if the name, father’s or husband’s name, age and house number all matched.
We checked every case against the scanned entry. We then looked up Form 6 applications in the Form 9 lists. The latter is a public list of every Form 6 application an election office received, with the applicant’s name, relative and address. The lists we examined cover 13 assembly constituencies. The 69 booths that we chose fall into the three following groups:
One Form, Several Voter IDs
Listed below are 11 voters (chosen randomly from the 230 to explain the nature of the anomalies) whose names did not appear on the January 6 draft list but were all added to the final list. In each of these cases, the entries share the same name, relative, age and house number, but carry different EPIC numbers. We use first names because they are private citizens.
Our findings revealed two patterns: For Ishlok, Najmeen, Himanshu, Pinki, Saurabh and Aakash, every form became a voter ID, and the entries sit next to each other on the list. Saurabh’s are serial numbers 1004 and 1005.
From Sundar to Sunita, the list has more entries than the published Form 6 list has forms. Married couple Vijay Lakshmi and Dharmendra have a cumulative total of five voter IDs. Vijay Lakshmi has three, while her husband has two.
Anushree Verma, whose husband is Akshay Verma, had filled Form 6 twice and received three voter IDs.
Sundar, mentioned at the beginning, had filled the form twice (According to Form 9) and in return got four voter IDs.
The biggest single cluster of duplicate voters is booth 449 in Chachoi, Sikandrabad (Bulandshahr), where the BJP won 94% of the votes in 2022. The final list adds 69 names to this booth.
Of these, 34 entries are for 17 people, each listed twice with a new EPIC. None of the 17 names are on the January 6 draft list. Fifteen of the 17 filed one Form 6 each on the published lists. For two, Hasmuddin and Heema Devi, we found none. Six of the 17 live at house 91. One of them, Vikas, is listed once as female and once as male.
Some duplicates were already there before the revision and were not removed. In booth 330 of Husainganj (Fatehpur), two brothers appear twice each, at serials 108 and 109 and at 110 and 111 respectively, on both the draft and final lists.
In booth 1044 of Sahibabad, a father and son already on the list at house number 306 were added again with new IDs at house number 840. We found no Form 6 for either.
The published Form 9 lists for Khair village show one applicant, Bhuvnesh, son of Sanjeev Kumar of Simrauthi village, ten times between January 31 and March 6, 2026.
Across the Form 9 lists of the 13 constituencies, 3,369 people were found to have filed Form 6 between two to 10 times.
Missing Addresses, Renamed IDs, Suspicious Deletions
In booth 330 of Husainganj (Fatehpur), 20 of the 64 new voters have no house number. The field holds a place name, Oramha, for unrelated families.
Across the 37 city booths, 62 new voters were added with house “0” or a blank. In booth 354 of Kairana (Shamli), 48 voters were already listed at “house 3” on the draft list, and eight more were added from at least seven different families.
In Khair constituency, house number 658, under which all four of Sundar’s entries are listed, is associated with 36 voters from approximately 19 families.
A shared or missing house number is not, in itself, evidence of electoral irregularity, as most villages do not have a system of house numbering. The concern, however, is how entries without a verifiable address could be physically checked during field visits.
Moreover, in booth 351 of Sidhauli (Sitapur), three women’s names appeared changed between the draft and final lists, while the EPIC number, husband’s name, house number and age stayed the same. Rekharani became Lakshmi Devi, Gayashri became Meena Devi and Shivrani became Neelam.
We found 15 such cases across 20 rural booths. These changes could be legitimate corrections. However, only the corresponding Form 8 applications, used to request corrections to electoral roll entries, can establish the basis for the changes.
The most striking example of renamed entries is in booth 327 of Gorakhpur Rural. Serial 799 was Bhathwa, male, 53, house 156, on the draft list. On the final list, the same EPIC belongs to Rusha Devi, female, 50, house 56. Rusha Devi, husband Parmeshwar, also appears at serial numbers 924 and 930 of the addition list under two new EPICs. We found no Form 6 for her among the 23,136 applications in the Gorakhpur Rural lists.
In booth 943 of Sahibabad, 298 entries from one part of the 2025 electoral roll were deleted, 280 of them marked as “absent”. The deletions occurred in consecutive chunks of 23, 17, 14 and 10 names (shown in the plot below). Since electoral rolls are arranged by house and lane, such clusters could simply indicate that an entire building or group of homes had been vacated. A door-to-door verification would establish this. Whether such visits were conducted is something the Election Commission can clarify.
It is worth noting how many voters in every 1,000 appear twice or more on the final roll. See the chart below:
Questions for the Poll Panel
The analysis above poses several significant questions for the election commission vis-a-vis the SIR exercise in Uttar Pradesh. Some of them are the following:
- How did one Form 6 become two or three voter IDs – and how many times did this happen across UP?
- Why are repeat applications from the same person, at the same address, not merged before an ID is issued?
- How did officials verify new voters at house ‘0’, blank addresses and catch-all house numbers?
- How to explain the long runs of consecutive ‘Absent’ deletions – were these homes actually visited?
UP CEO’s Response
The Uttar Pradesh CEO initially denied findings by Alt News co-founder Mohammed Zubair, who flagged Sundar’s case of four different EPIC IDs on X. The office responded with the following post:
Mr Fact-checker please fact-check your own facts.
There is no such scheme as “Buy one Get one free” scheme by Election Commission.
As per your post, the voter had submitted only two applications and he got 4 EPIC cards.
This statement is false.
The voter had submitted 4 applications.
If you want to dispute our facts then you post the reference numbers of two applications that you claim he had submitted and we will post the reference number of the remaining two.
The problem of generation of multiple EPICs on submission of multiple forms of an individual is a long standing one. We do deduplication through ECINET periodically. We are on path to achieving the objective of catching multiple forms submitted by an individual at the submission stage only. We will achieve our objective very soon.
Please do not incite people by making patently false statements about ECI and thereby trying to create disaffection among the citizens towards a Constitutional Body.
You are advised to rectify your mistake by amending or deleting your post after completing your own due diligence now that you have been informed by us about your wrong information.
— CEO Uttar Pradesh (@ceoup) October 17, 2026
The CEO claimed that Sundar had submitted four Form 6 applications, resulting in four separate entries on the final electoral roll. This contradicted the official Form 6 application list, which recorded only two applications from Sundar. However, the CEO’s response also acknowledged that “the problem of generation of multiple EPICs on submission of multiple forms of an individual is a long-standing one”.
The discrepancy over whether Sundar submitted two or four applications does not alter the central issue: the Commission itself acknowledges that multiple applications by the same voter can result in the generation of multiple EPIC numbers. Its response also indicates that the system does not consistently prevent such duplication at the application stage, necessitating periodic deduplication through ECINET.
On October 19, the CEO directed election officials to expedite the removal of duplicate entries ahead of the 2027 Assembly elections and identify cases in which individual voters had submitted multiple applications during the SIR.
Readers should note that some of the errors documented in this article were rectified by the Election Commission in the intervening period between our initial identification of these anomalies and the publication of this report.

The warden kept telling Pheap Rom not to think of himself as a prisoner. Instead, the jailer insisted, Rom and his fellow deportees from the United States were “the king’s guests.”
Here was the warden’s idea of royal hospitality: Each morning at 7:30, Rom—a chiseled, compact, 43-year-old Cambodian man with a pronounced Philly accent—was roused from a bare cell he shared with three other men in Eswatini, a tiny kingdom in Southern Africa. Then he was made to stand at attention as the country’s national anthem, “Nkulunkulu Mnikati Wetibusiso temaSwati,” reverberated through the halls of the Matsapha Correctional Centre. Most meals consisted of a portion of rice splashed with thin broth. It was late 2025, and the weather was warm and wet. For 15 minutes a day, Rom and the other men were allowed to go outside. Before they were locked up for lights out, the anthem played again; thick clouds of mosquitoes kept Rom thrashing all night.
Sometimes Rom would banter with the towering, bespectacled warden, who went by the name Kuenene. If I’m a guest, then why am I being held in a prison with criminals? Rom would ask. Why aren’t I allowed to leave? But Rom knew these exchanges with the warden were absurd, like everything else about his situation.
Before the second Trump administration, the practice of deporting immigrants to countries where they have no ties was a rare and tightly restricted move in US immigration enforcement—reserved mainly for cases where a person simply could not be returned to their nation of origin due to risk of persecution or torture. It has since expanded into a signature White House policy of mass removal. Over the past two years, the administration has inked deals with some 35 nations to accept third-country deportees from the US. The kingdom of Eswatini, which agreed to take up to 160 migrants for a fee of $5.1 million, is one of them. Some of the other destination countries—the Central African Republic, the Democratic Republic of the Congo, South Sudan—are so violent and unstable that they rank on the State Department’s “Do Not Travel” list.
Often making a spectacle of its own transgressiveness, the administration has steamrolled past public outcry, an investigation by Democratic lawmakers, and a warning from the United Nations about a “cascade of human rights violations” resulting from these removals. At least twice in the past two years, US federal courts have ordered the Department of Homeland Security to stop shipping migrants to third countries with insufficient due process. Both times, the Supreme Court has quickly stepped in to let the administration resume.
In September, during one of those brief, court-ordered pauses in removal flights, DHS general counsel James Percival went on X to publish the most comprehensive figures yet on how many migrants have been affected by the practice. He posted a GIF of Taylor Swift mouthing the words “That’s my husband” and pointing excitedly at her wedding ring. Percival’s caption: “How my wife looks at me when I tell her we have deported 25,000 illegal aliens to third nations.”
Rather than slowing down in the face of resistance, in fact, President Trump’s third-country push appears to have inspired imitators. Five European Union countries announced in November that they are working toward a plan to send rejected asylum seekers to a deportation hub in Rwanda. In the past two years, Italy has begun sending asylum seekers to Albania. The United Kingdom quietly sent an asylum seeker to Eswatini earlier this year; the man, originally from Sri Lanka, died last month, the government of Eswatini reported. According to local media, the apparent cause was suicide.
Rom’s lawyer, Tin Thanh Nguyen—who is himself the child of refugees from Vietnam—predicts that, if the administration keeps getting away with these expulsions, additional wealthy countries will be emboldened to offload their undesirables to poorer nations for a price. “This is going to be the new model for the West, not only for the United States,” says Nguyen, who also represents three other men currently held in Eswatini and Rwanda. “It’s just kind of out of sight, out of mind for these Western countries.”
But as Rom’s experience reveals, some of these removals may rest on little more than bureaucratic fiction. The US claims it has followed due process with every one of the 25,000 migrants deported to unfamiliar lands. “Their own countries say, ‘We do not want them back,’” US attorney general Todd Blanche told Fox News in early October. Yet in Rom’s case—among countless other Kafkaesque details—his own country never even appears to have been asked.
An American in virtually everything but citizenship status, Rom came to the United States as a 3-year-old refugee from Cambodia. Around 1979, his parents fled their home to escape the horrors of the Khmer Rouge, a genocidal regime that seized power in the wake of Richard Nixon’s carpet-bombing of the country. From there, the family went to a Thai refugee camp—where Rom was born in 1982—and then to a resettlement center in the Philippines. As Rom’s father was selling off possessions to raise money for their ultimate move to America, he was killed by roadside thieves. Rom sat by his side after the attack, his mother later told him, trying to wake his father up.
Rom’s first memories of America are of a cramped, dimly lit bedroom in a small apartment in the Bronx, where he arrived with his mother and six siblings in 1985. “There was just one mattress, and we all slept on that,” he says. “It was a new world to us; everything was new.”
Rom and his family had arrived in the middle of the largest resettlement effort in US history. As America’s chimerical war efforts in Southeast Asia faltered in the 1970s, hundreds of thousands of people began arriving in the US from Vietnam, Laos, and Cambodia. Of the nearly 158,000 Cambodians who gained entry between 1975 and 1994, the majority, like Rom and his family, were refugees deeply marked by the atrocities of the Khmer Rouge.
Around 10,000 of them came to be resettled in areas of the Bronx that were blighted by high crime and poverty. Many were placed in dilapidated housing, with limited job opportunities. Rom’s mother, who didn’t speak English, relied on government support checks and whatever extra income she could make sewing and scavenging. As a child, Rom would help her collect cans and carry the overstuffed bags to the grocery store to return for cash.
With the help of an uncle, the family eventually relocated to Philadelphia, where an adolescent Rom was enticed by a newly formed gang—a Cambodian clique within the Crips called the Blue Dragons. “If you don’t want to get bullied,” older members of the gang told him, “you need to link up with us.” Rom was barely a teenager. An older gang member dubbed him Menace, after Dennis the Menace, because he was “funny and bad at the same time.”
By the time he was 18, Rom had done three stints in juvenile detention and was caught in ever-escalating street beefs. At a New Year’s Eve party in 2008, rival gang members jumped him. Rom waited for a day off from his job—caring for abandoned dogs at a local rescue—to seek revenge. He parked outside the gang’s hangout, and when his targets exited, he opened fire from his car. Rom contemplated running when he heard that the police were looking for him but decided against it largely because he had a young daughter. In jail he would be able to see her, even if it was from behind glass. On the lam, he’d have to disappear. He pleaded guilty in April 2010 to multiple charges, including attempted murder.
Rom was a legal permanent resident of the US, a status he had been granted as a refugee. Though refugees are entitled to obtain full American citizenship, Rom had been told he didn’t stand a chance due to his juvenile record, an obstacle that would greatly alter the trajectory of his life.
Under US immigration law since the 1990s, legal permanent residents who commit crimes that qualify as “aggravated felonies”—an expansive and, critics say, somewhat arbitrary legal category—can lose their immigration status and become subject to deportation after they’ve served out their sentences. In a case of what immigrant advocates call “double punishment,” Rom’s conviction for attempted murder meant he would lose his green card. And he knew that in the post-9/11 era, his home country had bowed to US pressure to accept the repatriation of deported Cambodian refugees.
Rom likes to say that prison saved his life. He spent much of his time in lockup reading, exercising, and making cents an hour working in the kitchen to save up for small gifts for his daughter. As he served out his sentence, a generation of shifts in America’s immigration policy flew by—from President Obama’s support of the Dreamers and record-high deportation numbers to Trump’s policy of family separation to Biden’s border crisis to Trump’s return to the White House. But in Rom’s mind, none of that made a difference for him: His fate was already sealed. He was fully prepared to be deported to Cambodia, a country he had never visited, once his sentence was finished.
Rom’s reserved mood as his prison term neared its end confused fellow inmates. “Yo, why are you not happy?” they asked. “You’re about to be released, you made parole.” On November 13, 2024, Rom walked out after serving 15 years. He was immediately transferred to Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) holding, where what he believed would be a straightforward process turned into a bewildering journey through the American deportation machine.
From detention, Rom did what he could to hasten the process of his own removal. He frequently called the Cambodian embassy in Washington, DC, seeking information on his departure process. He was told that his questions should be directed to the Department of Homeland Security. Officers in Pennsylvania, he says, had no updates. They told Rom they were swamped by the number of cases they were trying to handle. At one point, they told him he would be deported to Thailand, his country of birth, which he told them was incorrect. After six months of detention, Rom filed a writ of habeas corpus arguing that he was being unlawfully detained.
He continued to wait for another three months. On September 24, 2025, his daughter’s birthday, Rom saw on a tablet device that his commissary account had been zeroed out. Among ICE detainees, this is a telltale sign that deportation is imminent. The following day, Rom was transferred to Pine Prairie ICE Processing Center in Louisiana. He was moved again a few days later to Alexandria, Louisiana, where the airport hums with obscure charter airlines that ferry deportees abroad. He waited there for another 72 hours before he started, again, asking officers what was happening.
At first, they said they didn’t know, a claim Rom found hard to believe. When an officer checked his case on the computer system and then quickly clammed up, Rom’s suspicions grew. Finally they told him to pack up, and Rom caught a look at the immigration paperwork. It listed Eswatini as the country of deportation. Confused, Rom turned to another detainee: “Hey, bro, is Eswatini another ICE facility in Louisiana?” he asked. The man responded that it was in southern Africa.
Rom ran to the phone and made a panicked call to his sister in Las Vegas. She searched online and confirmed that Eswatini was indeed in Africa. Rom asked her to call the Cambodian Embassy. Another detainee’s lawyer suggested the group request “reasonable fear” interviews: US Citizenship and Immigration Services conducts these interviews through their asylum officers to ascertain if a person has a reasonable fear of persecution or torture. Immigration agents seemed amused by the suggestion, Rom says. What could the men be afraid of? they asked. “Y’all a bunch of murderers,” Rom recalls them taunting.
Rom pleaded with the guards. Eventually, one officer told him and the others that if they agreed to be shackled, he would take down their request in writing. They stepped into the restraints, and the officer set about filling out some paperwork. As they sat waiting, their feet and hands in chains, Rom gave the request for a “reasonable fear” interview one last try. “Hey,” he asked, “you think you are going to give us that interview?” He realized it was “all fake” and that the officers never intended to file anything.
One by one, under heavy guard, the men were loaded onto a small airplane. When the door closed it was “like my coffin is closing,” says KV, another deportee on the flight who asked to be identified by his initials because he remains detained. The plane flew from Alexandria to Puerto Rico. The officials accompanying the men gave them no information. They tried, and failed, to disable the small TVs that showed the plane’s flight path.
The plane carried on to Senegal, where they were delayed as officials sought permission to travel onward. “They were basically smuggling us through Africa,” Rom says. When the flight touched down at King Mswati III International Airport early on the morning of October 6, the runway was lined with dozens of armed military personnel. Rom was loaded into a paddy wagon. As the van turned onto a dirt road, Rom was overcome with fear. Oh yeah, they are going to kill us, Rom thought. They’re definitely going to kill us.
Eswatini, a country about the size of New Jersey surrounded almost entirely by South Africa, is the continent’s last remaining absolute monarchy. In April 1973, King Sobhuza II suspended the constitution and banned all political parties. The ban remains in place. His son, King Mswati III, took power in 1986, at just 18 years old. Challenges to the monarchy have been met with violence. In June 2021, security forces cracked down on pro-democracy protests, killing 46 people, including two children, according to a government inquiry. Civil society organizations say this is an undercount. A leading human rights lawyer and pro-democracy activist was assassinated at his home two years later. No one has been held accountable for his death.
Eswatini has the highest HIV prevalence rates in the world. Poverty in the country is pervasive. A 2024 report from the US State Department describes Eswatini as having “significant human rights issues,” including torture, media restrictions, and the worst forms of child labor. The king is reportedly married to a cohort of wives and lives a life divorced from his country’s brutal reality. At an April event to mark his 40 years on the throne, he held an extravagant party at a luxury convention center that included a performance by Grammy-nominated singer Davido.
The men, none of whom had committed any crime in Eswatini, were deposited in a high-security area of the Matsapha Correctional Centre. Rom’s cell sat behind a large metal door with a barred window painted forest green. When the detainees arrived, the cells were dirty. They asked for cleaning products but were told that none were available. Basic hygiene supplies took four months to arrive. In a dirt courtyard outside, the men had access to a row of concrete sinks to hand-wash their clothes during their 15 daily minutes of outdoor time. One detainee was allowed to retrieve the clothes in the evening.
Rom’s 15-year sentence in the US proved to be a useful experience. He fell back into his workout routine from prison, knocking out 500 pushups a day along with burpees and sit-ups. He read books donated to the prison, churning through the Hunger Games and Twilight series. His lawyer sent him a copy of First They Killed My Father, a memoir about surviving the Khmer Rouge. Rom had expected the weather to cool down at night, but there was little reprieve from the heat. He was given heavy blankets, which meant choosing between sweltering or being swarmed by mosquitoes. He asked jailers the same question he had been asking the guards in the US. “How long am I going to be here?” No one had an answer.
Gradually, the men were granted a few freedoms. They were brought to a mobile store so those without phones could buy them using money from their families. On the way back, they were allowed to eat at KFC and buy two beers apiece. These were the first excursions Rom had taken outside of detention facilities in more than 15 years.
In a post on X, a DHS official had said that the men being deported to Eswatini were “depraved monsters,” and those statements had spread in local media. So Rom smiled and waved, saying hello to the people who stopped to gawk.
The men were permitted to make one phone call a week using WhatsApp. The calls were broadcast in a common room; a prison official would sit nearby, scribbling notes. When Rom wanted to discuss something sensitive with his sister, the two would switch to speaking in Khmer. Local lawyers were barred from visiting. Shortly after Rom was deported, his sister saw a post on Facebook that mentioned Tin Thanh Nguyen, the lawyer in North Carolina. She got in touch, and Nguyen agreed to take Rom’s case.
Thanks to a TV in the common room that was set to the news, Rom was well aware of the controversy surrounding his fellow deportees. He watched a report about one fellow Matsapha inmate from Cuba, Roberto Mosquera del Peral, who had arrived earlier and was on a hunger strike. Each morning, when officers checked Mosquera del Peral’s cell, Rom says, they would shout, mockingly asking if he was still alive.
How Rom and the others came to be trapped in Eswatini is still unclear. According to a report from Reuters, the deal was brokered in February 2025 between Caitlin Piper, a diplomat who was leading the US embassy in the capital of Mbabane, and Russell Dlamini, the country’s prime minister, who sought and received approval from the king. Neither Dlamini nor the acting government spokesperson, Thabile Mdluli, responded to requests for comment. In May, a spokesperson for King Mswati told Reuters that “the king embraced the deal as Eswatini’s contribution to world order.”
Piper has since departed Eswatini. She was most recently based at the US Consulate in Erbil, Iraq, according to social media posts from the consulate. The consulate did not respond to requests for comment on her current position.
In November 2025, more than a month after Rom arrived and four months after the first deportees were deposited at the prison, Eswatini’s finance minister confirmed that he had received a $5.1 million payment from the US. He said the money would be funneled toward Eswatini’s National Disaster Management Agency. The country said it would accept 160 deportees as part of the agreement. The State Department eventually posted a copy of the memorandum of understanding signed between the two countries on May 14, 2025, which confirmed these details. The signature of the US official includes a looping C, but no name is printed underneath. Asked for comment, the Eswatini Press Inquiries Team at the embassy directed questions to the Department of State in Washington. The Department of State did not respond to questions regarding who signed the agreement.
This payment disclosure led the men in detention to charge that they had been trafficked. “You are moving people around, and money is exchanged,” says KV. “So what is that?” If Eswatini got all that money, Rom wondered, why was he having to spend his own on basics like a fan for his cell?
The Southern Africa Litigation Centre (SALC), a human rights NGO, joined several other groups in filing a legal challenge against Eswatini in 2025, aiming to declare the deportation agreement unconstitutional, obtain the terms of the agreement, and secure an order stopping further arrivals until the matter was legally resolved. The initial challenge was dismissed. SALC and the other groups filed an appeal to the Supreme Court of Eswatini in March. (Just weeks before her reported meeting with Eswatini’s prime minister to facilitate the deportations, Piper had addressed an SALC workshop, urging participants “to bring injustice to light, to demand the respect of those in power, to advocate for a world in which our most cherished freedoms are secured.” )
Rom’s personal path to Eswatini appears to have come about through a combination of cruelty and bureaucratic ineptitude. Nguyen points out that Cambodia has been accepting deportees for more than two decades and that the country is generally responsive and professional in issuing the requisite travel documents. He says that the Cambodian government moved to begin rectifying the situation within a week of his contacting them in October 2025.
Nguyen believes that the US erroneously thought Rom should be sent to Thailand, the country of his birth, not citizenship, but never bothered to contact government officials from that country or from Cambodia. Chann Rotana, a spokesman for Cambodia’s foreign ministry, says they also do not understand why Rom was sent to Africa. He adds that the US did not contact the country’s embassy in Washington, DC, regarding Rom’s case before he left the country. Rotana described the deportation to Africa as “strange” and said the embassy only became aware of the situation when Rom’s sister got in touch. Asked about Rotana’s comments, the Department of Homeland Security directed questions to the Department of State, which declined to respond.
“There’s no rhyme or reason as to why any of my clients were picked to go to Eswatini versus the clients that I have who are actually in Vietnam, Laos, and Cambodia,” Nguyen says. “There’s nothing that makes them distinguishable.”
After an interview with Cambodian officials, Rom’s case for removal progressed while the other men sat hoping for similar developments. When he was cleared to be sent to Cambodia in early February, he requested that he be escorted by a representative from the UN’s International Organization for Migration as a form of insurance. Rom finally arrived in Cambodia on March 26, becoming the second US deportee freed from Eswatini. (The first, a Jamaican man named Orville Isaac Etoria, was deported to Eswatini in July 2025 and repatriated to Jamaica in September of that year.)
When I met Rom in June, at a restaurant in the Cambodian capital of Phnom Penh, he was dressed in all black. The sleeves of his polo shirt were taut around his thick, tattooed arms. We met within walking distance of S-21, a Khmer Rouge torture and interrogation center that is now a museum dedicated to the genocide that set his family on its path to America. He is contemplative about his journey and speaks softly.
After arriving in Cambodia, Rom enrolled in a creative writing class, hoping to detail his experience. He was taking teacher training courses, hoping to land a job at an international school, and picked up work fixing air conditioners when he could.
The jarring transition to life in Cambodia was made harder when his older sister—who had been his lifeline in detention—died in July. “Im trying to hold it together,” he texted me. In August, Rom sent a string of messages saying he’d gotten a job teaching English to a rambunctious group of third graders.
Once a week, Rom calls the deportees who remain in Africa. There are more now. A few weeks after Rom and I met, Eswatini announced that it had received a fourth batch of 11 deportees. Another group followed. Thirty-two have been forced to the country in total. KV remains imprisoned. “With the holidays around the corner,” he texted in late September, “it feels I’m wasting my life sitting here for no reason.” It is unclear when he will be released.
The fate of all third-country deportees stands to be clarified in the coming months. After at least twice granting the Trump administration temporary stays to keep deporting migrants to third countries, the US Supreme Court will start hearing oral arguments on the ultimate legality of the practice in December.
Shortly after he arrived in Cambodia, Rom noticed that Kuenene, his warden at Matsapha, had added him as a contact on Telegram and WhatsApp. Another Eswatini official requested to connect on Facebook and follow Rom on Instagram. Rom accepted some of the invitations and declined others; he couldn’t tell why they were trying to befriend him. Maybe Kuenene wanted to keep tabs on what Rom might say publicly. “He was one of those guys that tell you what you want to hear, smile at your face, make you believe that he is the most supportive guy in the world, and then he will stab you in the back,” Rom said. “I didn’t trust him.” Before he was released, Rom told the guards and other deportees that he might return to Eswatini to visit as a tourist. In reality, he has no intention of ever returning. One visit as a royal guest was enough.

On my second trip to Alaska, I wanted to get a little off the beaten path and see some of the state's stunning national parks.
My flight landed in Anchorage five days before my cruise departed, which gave me plenty of time to rent a car and explore on my own. From Anchorage, the Kenai Peninsula is a short drive away and offers access to three national parks: Katmai, Lake Clark, and Kenai Fjords.
I knew that tours would cost a pretty penny, but I didn't realize I would be paying for the most expensive single-day excursion I've ever purchased.
I thought seeing bears would be a bucket-list experience
I knew the three national parks I was headed to were known for being relatively expensive to visit. After all, visitors need to take a boat or a seaplane to get to them.
I knew I wanted to take the full-day boat ride into Kenai Fjords National Park, so my tour choices included bear viewing in Katmai or Lake Clark. I was more familiar with Katmai National Park and knew that people came from all over the world to see its brown bear population, so I decided to book my tour.
I went into the Alaskan bush
Many people who visit Katmai National Park go to Brooks Falls during the salmon run to see large numbers of bears gathering to feed. I was making last-minute plans, so almost all Brooks Falls tours were already sold out.
While researching companies, I found that some will take you into the Alaskan bush, where you can see bears in the backcountry. These tours ranged in price from $1,295 to $1,595, before tip. The company I chose was the most expensive option, but they ran small-group tours with a naturalist guide, gave visitors 5 hours on the ground, and had many five-star reviews. In my mind, I was all but guaranteed to have a great adventure.
The weather can make or break your trip
It's Alaska. I totally understand that dreary weather is a part of life. But that doesn't change the fact that walking miles in pouring rain isn't as fun as doing it in the sun.
On the tour I chose, you land either in the ocean or in a river, so they outfit you with hip waders and a waterproof rain jacket if needed. The day of our tour, it was an absolute downpour. After about two hours of persistent heavy rain, I was ready to be somewhere warm and dry.
Instead, I was walking through inches of standing water in cloudy, 50°F weather.
This was an epic experience, but I wouldn't pay this much again
Over the course of the five-hour tour, my group saw just three bears up close. Two females and one male.
More on bucket-list travel
The male tried to approach one of the females when she quickly darted away. After a bit of a staring contest, the male decided it wasn't worth it and moved on from the area. This happened toward the very beginning of our tour and was the only time we saw the bears interact with each other. The female stayed to eat, and another female nearby was sleeping in the field.
It was incredible to see these massive animals at such close proximity and in their natural habitat. But paying $1,595, standing out in the pouring rain for hours, and having to bring my own lunch for that single interaction? I doubt I'll do something like this again.

India's 'cockroach' party leader says he was stopped from flying to UK
