A leader of India's "cockroach" party has said that immigration officials at Delhi airport stopped him from flying to the UK, where he was set to attend a series of events.
Saurav Das said he was supposed to board a flight on Tuesday at 01:00 local time (19:30 GMT on Monday) but was told by immigration officers that his passport had been "flagged".
It is not clear yet why Das's passport was flagged. The BBC has reached out to the federal home ministry, Delhi police and airport officials for comment.
Das, who rose to prominence in India earlier this year after Gen Z-led protests, said that he had been invited by the Oxford Union to speak about the movement.
He said that he was also scheduled to speak at other universities in Cambridge and Edinburgh.
"Indian students put their heart and soul to organise the events but this anti-intellectual [government] was scared of me going to these prestigious institutions," Das wrote on X.
A federal home ministry spokesperson directed the BBC to airport authorities and the Delhi police for comment on Das's allegations.
On Tuesday, the London School of Economics Student Union's Amnesty International Unit, a student-led charity group, shared a post on Instagram saying that an event featuring Das had been "indefinitely postponed".
Ratna Singh, another leader of the Cockroach Janta Party (CJP), said in a post on X that she and Das had been invited by the Oxford Union but that her visa had been rejected a few days ago.
"The manner in which Saurav was not allowed to board today raises deeply troubling questions about the state of freedom of expression and the space being allowed for young voices in this country," she wrote.
Das, a former journalist, became one of the faces of the CJP - a Gen Z-led movement that began as satire but has since emerged as a youth-led pressure group.
In July, protests spearheaded by the CJP over exam paper leaks led to the resignation of India's Education Minister Dharmendra Pradhan .
In October, CJP leaders including Das were among thousands of people detained by the police for trying to hold protests demanding the resignation of India's Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar over alleged irregularities in electoral rolls. Kumar and the Election Commission have denied wrongdoing.
The same month, Das and Ashutosh Ranka, another CJP leader, were jailed for seven days after being arrested for trespassing at a banned protest site in Delhi.
Abhijeet Dipke, the founder of CJP, wrote on X that if Das "had looted a bank or committed financial fraud", he may have been allowed to fly to London, referring to billionaire bank-loan defaulters who have left India.
There have been other instances in recent years of people being prevented from boarding flights.
In September 2025, Bhanu Tatak, an environmental and anti-dam activist from India's north-eastern Arunachal Pradesh state, was stopped from boarding a flight to Dublin.
In March 2022, Rana Ayyub, an investigative journalist and outspoken critic of Prime Minister Narendra Modi's government, was also stopped from boarding a flight to London at the Mumbai airport. She was due to speak at different events on media freedom and the targeting of journalists.

Frustration reigns for Pochettino in chaotic start to Man Utd job
- Published
Two games, no wins. Two red cards, two goals scored. One goal disallowed, six conceded. Is it possible for Mauricio Pochettino to have learned anything from a crazy first week as Manchester United boss?
United and Pochettino went on the warpath before the Champions League encounter with Sporting, furious at Leny Yoro's dismissal at Liverpool which they believe was unjust and shaped the eventual 4-0 defeat.
Club officials were seething after the 2-2 draw in Lisbon as well.
This time it was 2022 World Cup final referee Szymon Marciniak in the firing line. Blowing before Amad's first-half header went into the net meant VAR had no chance to assess whether the Polish official was right to rule Youri Tielemans had fouled Goncalo Inacio before prodding the ball through to the Ivorian.
Former United winger Ashley Young didn't think so. He called Marciniak's performance "a disgrace".
That Tielemans picked up a booking that eventually led to his late red card – the Old Trafford outfit have now had four players sent off in their past five games, meaning the Belgian will miss the Old Trafford clash with RB Leipzig on 8 December - just compounded the situation.
Then, in a matter of minutes, Marciniak decided neither Manchester United keeper Senne Lammens nor Sporting counterpart Kaique had been fouled as they conceded. Their respective defences complained bitterly. Marciniak was only asked to go to the pitchside monitor by VAR for the latter incident, which he overturned.
United insiders felt the Tielemans incident was clearly not a foul and Amad's goal should have stood. They also felt any foul on Kaique by Patrick Dorgu was marginal and did not warrant their goal being disallowed.
Pochettino trod a fine path, knowing if he said something too controversial, it could land him with a fine.
A nod of a head in agreement was his initial reaction in his post-match news conference, when asked if he felt Marciniak had got it wrong.
A few minutes before, he was more expansive when he spoke to TNT.
"It's difficult to find a game where you get punished [so much] in one game," he said. "We were punished a lot in key actions."
Pochettino searching for first Man Utd win
Not for the first time this season, United controlled extended periods of a game they ended up not winning.
The goals they conceded at the Jose Alvalade were bizarre.
Seventy-five seconds after superbly saving one penalty, goalkeeper Lammens suffered a rush of blood and conceded another, which was scored.
Lammens was at fault for the second, when he dropped the ball into the path of Sporting striker Luis Suarez, who scored with an overhead kick.
"I think we dominated and we deserved to win the game, but we didn't for different circumstances," he said.
"All the teams make mistakes, but for these mistakes the punishment (for us) is too big in every single mistake. Many other clubs make mistakes or tilt in a different circumstance, in a more positive way. But that is in the way we are. We need to take responsibility."
United are still to win away from home in any competition this season. They have now won once in their last 13 matches. In the Champions League, they are 19th, two points in front of Roma, who are just below the top 24, which guarantees passage to the next phase.
Pochettino defends Lammens over error
Young said Lammens may be one mistake from being dropped.
The Belgian's performance was not good and errors are beginning to mount.
It is not what Pochettino needs right now. United showed faith in the Belgium international this summer by bringing in 36-year-old Karl Darlow as his understudy.
Darlow did end last season as first choice at Leeds but started just 30 league games in his three seasons with the Elland Road club. Tom Heaton, 40, who was also on the bench against Sporting, has not played in a senior game since February 2023.
Could Pochettino contemplate leaving Lammens out.
"This type of thing happens," he said. "That is football. Football is about making mistakes.
"I always want to support my player. I think we need to talk about responsibility. In this type of action our defensive line needs to cover the keeper better because it was very difficult.
"It's not to blame the defensive line, but it's two things that we need to improve, details that we need to work on. We need to manage his type of situation better."
It has been a whirlwind week for Pochettino, who last Wednesday morning UK time was still United States boss.
There have been a few blows to absorb, and lessons are having to be learned quickly.
But despite the clear frustrations, the 54-year-old is glad he accepted the challenge.
"I am happy to be here," he said. "I'm so excited to be the face representing this club.
"We are here because the situation wasn't the situation all the fans and people expect. We are here to take the responsibility from one week, and we are going to improve for sure.
"It's going to be tough, of course. Nothing is easy. But we have the energy and I think we have the capacity, and, most important, we have the players and the power and the energy from our fans, which is massive."

Bleeding, birth defects: Congo residents sue over alleged mining pollution
KOLWEZI, Democratic Republic of Congo — In a small cinderblock home in the scrub beside a Chinese-owned copper and cobalt mine in Kolwezi, a mother shares a story of devastating loss.
She believes pollution from the neighboring mine is responsible for her family's suffering.
She has lost three children. Two died at birth. A third suffered repeated nosebleeds before dying. One of her two surviving children has stunted growth.
Now she and 26 other residents are taking the company to court in a rare attempt to hold alleged polluters accountable in the Democratic Republic of Congo. They are also suing the government, accusing it of failing to enforce environmental regulations.
Like other plaintiffs, she asked NPR not to identify her, fearing retribution from the company or government. Although the claimants' names are public in court documents, they want to avoid further exposure. Their lawyers also fear the plaintiffs could face intimidation from other locals.
"Our children are the first victims," she said, as the sun set over a nearby mound of mine tailings. "What we're hoping for is to see justice done."
The plaintiffs, whose case began Nov. 3, describe similar problems: contaminated water, nosebleeds, skin rashes, miscarriages and birth defects, which they blame on mining pollution.
The mine, known as COMMUS, is owned by Chinese multinational Zijin and lies in Kolwezi, a city of more than 500,000 people in the heart of Congo's copper belt, a southern region with vast mineral reserves.
Congo is the world's second-largest producer of copper, and also the source of over 70% of the world's cobalt, a metal that is critical to the electric-vehicle revolution because of its use in rechargeable batteries.
Last year, the U.S. signed a sweeping economic partnership with Congo aimed at attracting American investment and challenging the dominance of Chinese companies in the country's mining industry
Despite the global importance of Congo's copper and cobalt mines, however, environmental pollution from the industry has received comparatively little scrutiny.
In Kolwezi, pollution is severe. Neighborhoods near mines are often filled with an acrid smell that residents attribute to the sulfuric acid used to process minerals. A study published in June by environmental research organization Source International — carried out with the advocacy groups RAID and Afrewatch, and scientists from Congo's University of Lubumbashi — also highlighted the scale of the contamination.
Researchers found that levels of fine particulate matter, known as PM2.5, in Kolwezi were three to six times the World Health Organization's air quality guideline. The highest concentrations were recorded near the COMMUS mine.
These tiny particles can penetrate deep into the lungs and enter the bloodstream. Exposure poses health risks generally, but is particularly dangerous for pregnant women and young children.
The researchers also tested dust samples and found residue of copper, cobalt and manganese, which they said pointed to mining waste as the main source. When the study was released, Source International's executive director, Flaviano Bianchini, said that "these are among the most concerning air quality results we have documented in years of monitoring pollution at industrial mining sites around the world."
The study did not examine health impacts directly, and the authors recommended formal epidemiological research. Residents and health workers in Kolwezi nonetheless point to a string of ailments that they blame on a polluted environment.
In a dilapidated health clinic in the shadow of a mountain of waste from the COMMUS mine, nurse Héritier Bukassa said that people routinely break out in itchy hives. "Some sick people scratch themselves with knives to relieve itching," he explained.
Bukassa added that women in the area also suffer from high rates of miscarriage, and that he had referred four babies born with congenital malformations — mostly cleft palates — to hospitals this year alone.
Respiratory illnesses are common too, Bukassa said, especially in otherwise healthy babies who develop breathing problems a few weeks after birth. "No one from the [mining] company has ever come to talk to us about this," the nurse said.
Zijin, the owner of COMMUS, did not respond to emailed requests for comment. Neither did Congo's mining and environment ministries.
The Cobalt Institute, an industry lobby, said that understanding environmental pollution requires "an evidence-based approach that considers all potential sources and contributors." It added that companies perform environmental monitoring and carry out mitigation measures.
RAID, which is supporting the plaintiffs alongside Afrewatch, described the case this month as one of "the most ambitious legal challenges yet brought by Congolese residents over industrial mining pollution."
The suit is an important test case that could lead to communities challenging other mines in the future, it added.
The plaintiffs are seeking $1.3 million in compensation for health problems and medical expenses, as well as $5 million to restore the environment. Their lawyers say they worry their clients might come under pressure or intimidation to withdraw their testimony.
The mother, however, said she had no such fears. "We have a right to a clean environment," she said, "and to health."

A video showing a woman holding a weapon and trying to protect her house and child as a mob attacks and vandalises the house is being shared on social media (here, here, and here) with claims that it depicts an attack on Hindu homes in Bangladesh. Let’s verify the claim made in the post in this article.
Claim: The video shows a mob attacking Hindu homes in Bangladesh, while a woman tries to protect her house and child.
Fact: The video shows a mob attacking the houses of two men accused of cattle theft in Dakshin Kurshi village, Sunamganj District, Bangladesh, on 25 March 2026. The woman seen holding a child and a sharp weapon while trying to protect her house is the wife of one of the accused. Police confirmed that theft cases had been registered against the accused but condemned the mob attack. Bangladeshi fact-checkers also clarified that the woman is Muslim and that the incident stemmed from allegations of cattle theft, not communal violence. Hence, the claim made in the post is FALSE.
A reverse image search of keyframes from the viral video led us to multiple Bangladeshi media reports (here, here, and here) from March 2026, which identified the incident as one involving allegations of cattle theft in Dakshin Kurshi village, Dolar Bazar Union, Chhatak Upazila, Sunamganj District, Bangladesh.
According to these reports, villagers were angered by repeated cattle theft. A man named Saifur Rahman was reportedly caught stealing cattle in neighbouring North Kurshi village. During questioning, he allegedly named Ali Hussain, his son-in-law Tarek Mia, and several others as being involved in the thefts. Following this, an agitated mob attacked the houses of Ali Hussain and Tarek Mia in South Kurshi village on 25 March 2026.
The reports stated that more than a hundred people gathered following the allegations and vandalised and looted the houses of the accused. The mob threw bricks and stones, damaged tin walls and household belongings, and attacked women and children. The viral video shows Tarek Mia’s wife, who is also Ali Hussain’s daughter, holding a child and a sharp weapon as she attempts to protect her house from the mob. She tries to fend off the attackers, but they continue to vandalise the house.
Reports further stated that Ali Hussain and Tarek Mia had previously faced theft allegations. Sub-Inspector Abdur Rahman of the Zahidpur Police Investigation Centre reportedly said that police had registered multiple theft cases against the accused and filed a case in connection with the latest incident. However, the officer condemned the mob attack, stating that vandalising someone’s house was unjustified, despite the villagers’ frustration over repeated thefts. The viral video, therefore, depicts an incident arising from allegations of cattle theft in Bangladesh and has no communal angle.
We also found an X post by Bangladeshi fact-checker Shohanur Rahman dated 1 November 2026, stating that the woman is Muslim and the wife of Mohammad Tarek. He clarified that she was trying to protect her father’s house during an attack triggered by allegations of theft.
To sum up, the video of a mob attacking houses in Bangladesh over cattle theft allegations is falsely shared with a communal spin.

Sixty years ago, after two failed attempts, Ford won the 24 Hours of Le Mans with its GT40 race car. Musk's plan to send a million SpaceX data satellites into space approved
- Published
US regulators have given SpaceX the go-ahead to launch a million satellites into Earth's orbit to help build data centres in space - the first approval of its kind.
The company, which is owned by Elon Musk, wants to use sunlight to power satellites that will process data for AI and send the results back to Earth.
The Federal Communications Commission (FCC) said on Wednesday that the project, known as Starmind, would "support America's booming super intelligence economy".
However, rival firm Amazon has criticised it as a "lofty ambition rather than a real plan", while astronomers in the US said the move would "significantly undermine" the public's ability to study and observe the night sky.
There is increasing opposition to data centres on earth, including in the US where experts say they were a factor in the Republicans big losses in the midterm elections.
SpaceX believes the "orbital data centres" are the most cost and energy-efficient way to meet the growing demand for artificial intelligence (AI) computing power that is beyond "terrestrial capabilities".
FCC Chairman Brendan Carr said in a statement that the project "opens a bold new frontier for the computing infrastructure needed to power America's leadership and growth".
"This is the kind of American ingenuity that can unite our strengths in space and advanced technology, reinforce our economic leadership, and expand prosperity here at home," Carr said.
Responding to the announcement, Musk wrote on X: "Much appreciated. This will be a great asset to America and the world."

Under the FCC licence, deployment of the satellites must begin no later than November 2033. SpaceX will be required to have deployed 10% by November 2035, rising to 50% by November 2038.
The company has already said it wants to launch its first Starmind satellite next year.
It is unclear whether a million satellites will indeed be launched or whether SpaceX has sought approval for a higher number than it will use.
Like SpaceX's current Starlink network, which provides high-speed internet via more than 10,000 satellites, Starmind's satellites will operate in low-Earth orbit at altitudes ranging between 500-2,000km (310-1,242 miles).
Starmind's satellites will communicate with Starlink's and then relay the data to Earth.
- The plans to put data centres in orbit and on the Moon 
  - Published10 April 2025
Speaking to the Today programme, on BBC Radio 4, Prof Sir Martin Sweeting, founder and executive chairman of Surrey Satellite Technology Ltd, said while the idea of data centres in space seemed "technically feasible", whether it "makes sense at scale yet" still needed to be analysed.
Being able to get the data from the network of satellites, he added, would depend on being able to use laser links from the ground to them.
"That has not yet been perfected to the level at which it would be able to support the huge amounts of data that are likely to be transferred backwards and forwards," he said.
Meanwhile, the American Astronomical Society (AAS) said it was "disheartened and dismayed" by the decision.
It said the proposed constellation would "significantly undermine decades of federal investment in astronomical facilities" as well as "the ability of astronomers and the public to enjoy and study the night sky".
It noted that the constellation "involves larger (and therefore brighter) and more numerous objects", meaning the satellites would "be visible as extremely bright objects for longer periods in the night sky".
Jan Hasselman, a senior attorney at the non-profit group Earthjustice, said in a statement: "Drastically expanding satellites in space has a direct impact on people's everyday lives as well as the future of our planet."
The orbiting data centre concept is also being explored by other firms - including Google and Blue Origin - and is being pitched as a greener alternative to traditional centres, which require enormous amounts of power to run and water for cooling.
The ever-expanding use of AI computing has seen a massive increase in the amount of data that needs to be stored and processed around the world.
New facilities continue to be built but it is becoming difficult to find places to put them. Data centres are large and sprawling, use enormous amounts of power and water for cooling, and increasingly local people don't want them built nearby.
An expert previously told the BBC that launching hardware into orbit remains expensive and that the infrastructure to protect, cool and power them can be complex - while a growing quantity of space debris puts the physical hardware at risk.
Separately, another cautioned that the growing number of low-orbit craft increases the possibility of crashes between objects - which could damage machines or send materials falling back to earth.
Starlink has been accused of creating congestion in space, something Musk denies. He has also rejected claims his satellites have been taking up too much room and crowding out competitors.

Neuralink receives FDA approval for 'pivotal' brain implant trial in ALS patients
The study will evaluate the efficacity and safety of the company’s LINK device.
Elon Musk's Neuralink has received FDA permission to launch the first "pivotal" trial for its implantable LINK brain-computer interface, the company announced. The study represents a more advanced step in the company's efforts to develop a brain implant that allows people with paralysis to control devices using their brain alone. It will be open to a limited number of patients with ALS (amyotrophic lateral sclerosis), a progressive neurodegenerative disorder that damages nerve cells controlling voluntary muscle movement.
"We've received FDA approval to launch LINK, the first pivotal trial for an implantable brain-computer interface in the US," Neuralink announced on X. "This builds off of our work with 30+ participants with Neuralink to date."
Neuralink hit a milestone last year when the company revealed that its first participant with ALS named Bradford Smith was able to communicate using brain signals alone. "Neuralink has given me freedom, hope, and faster communication. ... It has improved my life so much. I'm so happy to be involved in something big that will help many people," Smith said at the time.
We've received FDA approval to launch LINK, the first pivotal trial for an implantable brain-computer interface in the US. This builds off of our work with 30+ participants with Neuralink to date.
Those with ALS may be eligible. To learn more:https://t.co/dWhb5N4GdR pic.twitter.com/Vor7iXXCBA
— Neuralink (@neuralink) November 25, 2026
The FDA authorization was granted on an experimental basis, but it's a key step forward for Neuralink's LINK brain-implant system. The study will evaluate the ability of patients to control digital devices through thought, "with a focus on functional outcomes that improve independence in daily life," Neuralink wrote. It will also assess the system's long-term safety and reliability.
WIth Neuralink's latest system, the company's N1 implant is surgically placed in the skull, then the company uses its R1 robot to insert flexible electrodes into the brain. Neural activity from the brain associated with movement is then interpreted by software, which translates signals into commands for controlling computers or digital devices. The technology is designed to help patients communicate with the outside world, with the eventual goal to let them operate devices without keyboards or other physical controls.
Neuralink said patients with ALS may be eligible for the LINK trial, but it didn't specify other requirements or the number of participants. It now has approval recruit participants, then conduct the study under an approved clinical protocol. If the technology proves to be safe, the trial may allow Neuralink to apply for more advanced trials and eventually release LINK onto the market.

Comedian Samay Raina has become the first YouTuber in the world to cross one million channel members, marking a new milestone in his digital career. Samay Raina becomes world’s first YouTuber to cross 1 million channel members
Google India officially acknowledged the milestone in a blog post, highlighting Samay’s contribution to creator-led entertainment. The comedian currently has 12.4 million YouTube subscribers.
“From host-level banter with Grandmasters to creating the phenomenon that is India’s Got Latent, Samay turned his YouTube channel into the ultimate virtual hangout for millions," the YouTube team stated.

During the finale of India’s Got Latent Season 2, Samay also opened up about the difficult period following the controversy. He revealed that he struggled with depression while staying in Canada and often turned to ChatGPT to ask whether his show would ever return.

Kimi Antonelli was 10 when his father Marco first realised the boy sitting on his lap, operating the steering and gears, might have an exceptional talent as a racing driver.
The pair were at the Adria circuit in north-east Italy, Marco with his Lamborghini sports car team, Kimi competing in a karting race.
It was the end of the day and Marco, a former driver himself, asked his son: "Do you want to try the Lamborghini?"
Of course he did.
Marco strapped himself and Kimi into the car, belts extended around both. Dad was in charge of the throttle and brake, his son would control the rest.
"I couldn't see the track because he was in front of me with a helmet on," Marco tells BBC Sport. "I could only see beside me the marker panels before each corner - 100m, 50m.
"We started to drive, step by step, faster, faster, faster. In the end, I pushed like I was alone and I arrived at the braking point at the end of the straight, 320km/h, braked very hard and at the limit.
"The car had a lot of oversteer. Kimi controlled the oversteer perfectly, then I went on the throttle, Kimi finished the oversteer, changed gear, and went.
"I said: 'OK, stop, because it has now become dangerous.' But when I saw the video, 10 years old, on my leg, oversteer, everything perfect, I said: 'Maybe he has something special.'"
And now Kimi, who turned 20 only in August, has dominated F1 in only his second season, and become the youngest world champion in the sport's history.
This is the story of a boy his dad says was "born in a garage".
"Kimi from 15 days old was in the garage and heard the sound of the engine and the smell of the exhaust," says Marco, who worked with his wife Veronica on their racing team business.
It was the Christmas holidays when Kimi was about three, and Marco had brought home a simulator he had bought for his guests to try out at the Bologna Motor Show.
"Each evening, Kimi wanted to drive," Marco remembers.
Just like seven years later in the Lamborghini, Kimi would sit on Marco's leg, the controls divided in the same way.
"I remember one night I started to fall asleep because I had been at work very early and we had a crash because I didn't brake when we arrived at the end of the straight," Marco says.
"And Kimi said: 'Dad, dad, no sleep, no sleep. I have to drive.'"
Marco Antonelli did not originally want his son to become a racing driver, because of his own struggles during his career.
"Sometimes you are fast but not in the right position to become a professional driver," he says.
In the 1990s, Marco Antonelli was on the cusp of becoming a works driver in the DTM touring car series, then a huge hit with audiences across Europe.
He tested for Alfa Romeo, but then the team boss left and the opportunity evaporated. Another chance came up with BMW, alongside Roberto Ravaglia and Steve Soper - stars at the time. Again, the same thing happened.
"I suffered a lot for it," Marco says. "And, of course, I was scared that my son [would] relive the same situation. At the beginning, I was very stressed about the passion my son had for motorsport."
Kimi tried a go-kart for the first time when he was five, and immediately showed an awareness of racing lines, braking points and car control.
The Antonellis were what Marco describes as "a normal family". They could not possibly afford to pay for Kimi to take part in all the categories on the way to Formula 1.
Marco decided he could fund Kimi through karting and a year of the basic single-seater category, Formula 4. After that, he figured he might be able to put him in one of his GT cars and become professional that way.
But Kimi immediately started to impress. Whatever category he entered, he was quick, and won.
By the time Kimi was 11, his name was buzzing around motor racing circles. Mercedes heard about him, and their driver academy scout Gwen Lagrue flew to Italy to check him out.
It was a season in which Antonelli had ended up driving a kart with less power than those of his rivals. Marco had told Kimi this would be good for him - he should think not about the result, but about how to improve, always push hard.
"Gwen was impressed about this condition of power and driving in this category that Kimi did," Marco says. "And maybe they understood that Kimi was a different child."
Now Kimi was a member of the Mercedes driver academy, Marco could stop worrying about money, and start focusing on helping his son achieve his full potential.
Mercedes were not the only big names in F1 who had noticed Antonelli's promise.
"When he was in karting, you could already see he was one of the stand-out talents," says four-time world champion Max Verstappen, the only other teenager to win an F1 race.
At 15, Antonelli was ready to move up to cars, and, as a final preparation, did a couple of races in a karting category with gears. On his debut, with minimal pre-event testing, he took pole position. After that, he went to the world final, and stuck it on pole again.
This was the end of 2021, after which Antonelli moved full-time into cars. Through 2022, he swept the board in various championships in Formula 4, and the same happened in Formula Regional in 2023.
1 of 4
By now, Mercedes team boss Toto Wolff was already thinking that Antonelli would be his next F1 driver, potentially a replacement for Lewis Hamilton. With the seven-time champion approaching 40, Wolff was planning on taking control of that generational transition.
So when it came time to negotiate a new contract with Hamilton in 2023, Wolff played hardball. Hamilton wanted to sign for at least two firm years, Wolff only one. In the end, they compromised on a contract for 2024 with an option for 2025.
Hamilton, unimpressed, decided to look at his options, and signed to join Ferrari in 2025, telling Wolff in late January 2024, before the start of that season.
Wolff immediately phoned Marco Antonelli, to tell him the "very big news".
"'We put Kimi in Formula 1,'" Marco remembers Wolff saying. "'What do you think?'
"I said: 'Oh, [it] is a difficult question you ask me. Of course I'm happy that you think about Kimi but are you sure he's ready?'"
Mercedes were at a management away day. Wolff called his senior engineers together to tell them about Hamilton's decision.
"We were reviewing options and trying to come to a fairly rapid conclusion," says trackside engineering director Andrew Shovlin.
"We were all keen to just go with Kimi, which we knew was a bit of a risk. But it was quite exciting and we thought, based on his career to date, he had a good chance of being very good. It seemed like a good challenge."
Antonelli had not even driven an F1 car when Wolff made the call. Mercedes put together a testing programme for him, 20-odd days in cars a couple of years old at tracks all over the world to prepare him for his F1 debut in 2025.
Shovlin and the engineers were immediately impressed.
"It was how rapidly he would get up to speed," Shovlin says. "What you normally see with drivers is they're just incrementally going a little bit quicker, braking a bit later.
"If you compare with other drivers we've seen in an F1 car for the first time, the best I'd ever seen until then was George [Russell]. You suddenly saw someone who was quite similar.
"With Kimi, he took a couple of runs to work out how the car behaved and then he'd be more or less on the limit.
"The other thing you can see is the fidelity of the car control, how they can sit with it right on the edge of breaking away from them on entry to a corner, but they can just control it in that condition.
"Equally, when you looked at the mistakes he was making, they were often errors of judgement or lack of experience. They weren't run-out-of-talent mistakes."
Antonelli made one of these at the 2024 Italian Grand Prix. Wolff decided to give him his first experience of an F1 weekend in first practice at his home race at Monza.
It was a spectacular debut - for both good and bad reasons.
Antonelli set the fastest time on his first lap. Then he went for another. He was flying, miles quicker than anyone up to that point, but then he crashed heavily at the final corner, Parabolica.
"No-one on earth could have got the car around the corner at the speed he was attempting," Shovlin says. "He clearly got into his head that he would try and do something special and it was an error of judgment."
Wolff took Antonelli aside, told him it was OK, and not to worry about it. But the crash had a significant impact on Antonelli.
Wolff was very clear in public about managing expectations of Antonelli going into his debut season.
"I conditioned myself so strong that I said: 'There's going to be moments of brilliance and moments where you want to tear your hair out'," Wolff says.
There were stand-out moments, including pole for the sprint in Miami.
But the middle part of the season, through Europe, was a disappointment. A change to the rear suspension design made the car nervous and rocked his confidence. His pace was not impressive, and he made too many mistakes.
"We expected more highlights from him," Shovlin says.
Marco Antonelli explains: "Mercedes needed to have a good result after a period that was not like the Hamilton era. And, of course, needed two cars that always take points.
"Kimi felt this necessity. The crash in Monza was very tough for him to forget. It created on him a big pressure."
Wolff said the "moments of brilliance were there" but then there was "a spell of nine races that was really not good".
"Me, personally, I never doubted," says Wolff. "Other people doubted. In the team and externally."
A year on from his practice debut, Antonelli crashed again in Monza practice.
"This was the point where I said: 'Kimi, you've got to turn this around. This is just not good enough'," says Wolff. "He said: 'I know.'"
Marco Antonelli says he and his son talked a lot during this period and that Kimi "understood that everything can change".
"The period was bad but you can see light at the end of the tunnel," he says. "And step by step he started to take confidence."
Once F1 had left Europe in the autumn of last year, there was a shift.
"Suddenly, we felt like we were making really good progress," says Shovlin.
"There were signs towards the end of the year. I'm not saying any of us thought we'd see what we've seen so far this year, but that we had a decent F1 driver."
Antonelli has been rather more than that this year. He took the season by storm, and established a consistent supremacy over Russell.
In the best car in the field, Antonelli took six poles and six wins in the first 11 races, establishing a 50-point lead in the championship.
Mercedes lost their dominant form in the second half of the season in the face of challenges from first McLaren and then Red Bull.
But Antonelli remained a consistent threat at the front, and he killed off his Monza ghosts in the Italian Grand Prix with a stunning victory after an engine penalty led to him starting 19th on the grid.
He put in a drive of clinical excellence and, with help from a safety car, chased down and caught Russell in the final laps to take a win that will go down in folklore.
The extent of his turnaround in form has shocked almost everyone.
"We were all surprised," Wolff says. "My thoughts were always that he needed to make the experience of knowing all the tracks, the pressure of performing on such a high level under the spotlight of the media, the constant public feedback, whether you're doing well or not, the situations everyone wanted to be close to him.
"There wasn't one single defining factor where I would have said that made it difficult for him, but this year, he knew exactly what to expect. What was really nice to see is that the self-confidence, without feeling any entitlement, has shone."
Marco points to his son's "very strong" mentality.
"In F4 and Freca, he started with not good results, and he was able to remake everything and, at the end, work hard and win the championship," he says.
"We talk about F1. I don't know what the spark is in his brain, but Kimi in the past did the same."
Verstappen says: "For me, there was never any doubt that he would make the jump the year after and already be a lot more consistently competitive.
"It's normal in the progression of a driver. In your rookie season, it can be quite tough, but at the moment, of course, he's doing an amazing job."
Kimi pays tribute to his father, describing him as his "rock", while Wolff also praises the driver's "typical Italian family".
"They are caring, they are loving," Wolff says. "Kimi's character, he's gentle, he has empathy, he has charisma, he has the right amount of intelligence for being a racing driver."
Mercedes have been talking to Antonelli about managing his emotions, which have flared at times this season, such as in the sprint in Canada, when the racing between the two Mercedes drivers came close to boiling over.
Shovlin says: "He just says: 'I'm young, I'm Italian, what do you expect?'"
The remark reveals Antonelli's sense of humour, but also a maturity and self-awareness that might not always be expected in someone so young.
Wolff says: "He has all that. He's actually not [fitting the stereotype of] a typical emotional Italian. He's so clear [in] what he needs to do in a car. I don't see lots of emotion. I see full focus, full concentration. I see, 'OK, this is a problem, let's analyse it, and move on.'
"You see him in a debrief afterwards. You couldn't really say whether there was a bad or a good session. It's all very balanced and stable."
Antonelli took advice on this when he met tennis legend Roger Federer at Wimbledon this summer.
"We chatted about my races," Antonelli says. "About when he used to play, and about life in general.
"About pressure, he just told me to focus on one race at a time, just focus on what you can control, and also to control the emotions, especially the ones that can make you do mistakes."
Federer's words echoed something Marco has always impressed on his son.
"In our family, we use this concept in normal life as well," he says.
"We have to live every day our best day. You work hard every day to arrive at the end of the project you have."
Back in February 2024, Wolff followed up his phone call to Marco with a meeting in Milan.
"Toto said 'Of course it will be difficult, but I think after one year of experience, we can do very well with Kimi in F1'," Marco says.
"The project was 2025 experience, 2026 start to achieve results. I think we overachieved."

'Memories of a Good Meal': How food made a difference during WWII
NEW ORLEANS — Chef Alon Shaya believes there's power in a meal.
"It's always been the way that I can start a conversation, build a relationship, disagree about things, but still be able to come together and break bread," Shaya, of the acclaimed Crescent City restaurant Saba, said one recent afternoon. "When you share a meal with someone, a lot of those barriers get broken down."
The Israeli American chef also believes food can be a source of inspiration even in the darkest of times. A few years ago, he spearheaded the Rescued Recipes initiative at the United States Holocaust Memorial Museum, and that got him digging deeper into the role that food played during World War II.
Now, he's collected those stories and the dishes they inspired in a new historical cookbook, Memories of a Good Meal: Recipes of Resilience Inspired by Stories of World War II Survival.
Shaya hopes home cooks use the recipes to inspire dinner table conversations about the deeper stories behind them.
"I want people to gather and cook and eat and put their phones down, and share a meal and recount these miraculous stories of survival, resilience and heroism," he told NPR.
Stories like that of Roddie Edmonds, a U.S. Army master sergeant, whose unit was captured in the Battle of the Bulge and imprisoned in a German POW camp. (Edmonds posthumously won the Congressional Medal of Honor earlier this year for his refusal to turn in his Jewish troops to be sent to concentration camps.)
One of the ways Edmonds and his fellow prisoners distracted themselves from the horror of the camp was to talk about the foods that reminded them of home, be it Sunday spaghetti sauce, hot cakes or cherry pie.
"They're eating up this idea that they were going to go home," Shaya said. "They were going to be free, and they were going to be able to sit around and dig into that filet mignon with creamy mushroom sauce."
The servicemen sketched out detailed plans for a dreamed-of restaurant called the Jolly Chef. There, they would serve all those yearned-for dishes, including candied yams with pecans and whipped marshmallow — one of the recipes in the new cookbook.
Another chapter highlights Polish partisan fighters who lived in underground bunkers and sabotaged the Nazis by derailing trains and blowing up ammunition plants. In a nod to the fire that ensued, a recipe from their chapter also includes smashed potatoes flambéed in vodka.
"Vodka was a form of currency for them," Shaya said. "They would use it to barter. They would use it to celebrate. And so each moment of that recipe helps to really tell the story of what they were going through."
The book has stories from around the world – Hungarian Jews whose non-Jewish cook salvaged the treasured family cookbook as they were being sent to Auschwitz; a French village that took in Jewish children and hid them from the Nazis; Navajo code breakers who changed the course of the war; and Japanese Americans, convicted of no crimes, who were incarcerated in military-style camps in the U.S.
June Hersh, a food historian and writer who worked with Shaya on the cookbook, said remembering and talking about favorite recipes was a form of resistance – turning a tragic situation into something triumphant.
"You can put me in a uniform, you can make me do hard labor, you can shave my head, you can starve me if you want, but I'm not going to let go of my food memory," she said. "It's something you can't take away from me."

Last week, news broke that a mathematician had used AI to help crack one of the biggest outstanding problems in math: a proof of the Riemann hypothesis. The news follows several other major breakthroughs in math that have either been enabled by or managed entirely by large language model-based systems, a development that has left the entire field of mathematics in a state of upset.
It’s too early to say much about the proof itself—mathematicians are still in the process of digesting it. But we can say a little about how the proof came about, and what it tells us about the state of math.
Tackling Riemann
The Riemann hypothesis dates from the mid-1800s and was formulated by (you will be surprised to learn) Bernhard Riemann. There’s not an obvious way to describe the details of the actual hypothesis simply, but it has implications for the distribution of prime numbers. This gives it significance for areas ranging from number theory to cryptography. As Wikipedia accurately states, “It is considered by pure mathematicians to be one of the most important problems in the field.”
The proof of the hypothesis was announced by a mathematician named Levent Alpöge, who has been working at Anthropic, and, not surprisingly, used Claude to generate it. His announcement is written in a somewhat florid style (example: “one of which was already new and shocking, making very simple one of the shadows of Riemann over which we mathematicians felt most triumph”), and he has apparently dropped some hints that some of it was meant in jest.
But it does make clear that this proof was a longstanding interest of Alpöge’s, and he had some insights into how to connect different areas of math to reach the final proof. The process seems to have involved getting the AI started with handling a simplified “toy” form of some of Alpöge’s insights and then directing it to expand what it found there to the full scope of the Riemann hypothesis.
The proof itself comes in two different forms, and the difference between them gets at the heart of why AI usage in math has been controversial. One is a rigorous description of the proof using a programming language named Lean that has allowed the rapid verification that the proof is valid. The second is a description of the logic behind it, which may ultimately be the key for mathematics as a field to benefit from this proof.
Proof factories
It’s important to emphasize that, so far at least, AI has been solving problems that humans previously recognized as significant. That significance is typically ascribed to mathematical ideas because of their implications or utility—they either tell us something about areas of math that people care about, or they keep popping up in problems that mathematicians are working on. So far, there are no indications that AI can recognize or formulate interesting and important unresolved problems on its own.
But AI has tackled many problems humans have considered significant with impressive ease. Trained on a body of material that included a lot of advanced math, the software has provided both formal proofs as well as counterexamples that have clearly demonstrated that some proposals are incorrect.
When it comes to proofs, AI might have some advantages over people. For starters, it’s not specialized in specific fields of math and can potentially pull together tools from a variety of disciplines. AI also pays no cost (either in terms of career or emotional soundness) from going down the wrong track, giving up, and starting over.
AI models have also had one of their biggest limitations removed via humanity’s development of Lean, a computer language that allows mathematical proofs to be expressed in a way that can be readily verified. Due to their tendency to hallucinate, a description of a proof generated by an AI would still require extensive human validation before it could be accepted, a task that might radically shift the effort/reward ratio of using AI models. But by instructing an AI to include the necessary Lean code as part of its output, verification has become straightforward.
The unfortunate aspect of this for mathematics as a field is that it’s often the process of working through the reasoning behind a proof, rather than the step-by-step logic, that advances the field as a whole.
Deriving worries
Mathematicians have expressed their fears about this aspect of AI usage in a formal open letter. We’ll try to connect those fears to the recent announcement.
Before AI, proofs were typically worked through by people who recognized potential pathways connecting disparate fields of math and spent years finding ways to formalize those intuitions and validate that the math worked. It wasn’t necessarily an efficient use of time if the only output was the proof itself.
But that was rarely the case. By finding the connections between problems, this work helped many other people see new ways of tackling whatever issues they were wrestling with. Mathematicians often developed new tools, found shortcuts, or stumbled across related problems while working through their proofs, enriching math as a whole. In other words, the proof itself was often less important for math than the process of generating it.
By contrast, the internal workings of large neural networks are notoriously opaque. Asking an AI to explain its reasoning runs into the same problems that asking it anything else does: Since the software has only been selected for producing decent-sounding text, it’s likely to make something up that sounds good when asked about its own internal processes. So, an AI-generated proof has little to offer the field in terms of new ideas or unexpected advances, at least on its own.
Indeed, nobody can say much about the Riemann proof at the moment, simply because mathematicians have barely started the process of shifting through the logic as expressed in Lean. It’s possible it can eventually produce new insights and tools, but it may take years before humans can figure out what they are and how to express them in a way that other mathematicians can appreciate.
How mathematicians are expected to identify new challenges that can push their fields beyond the current body while seeing AI relieve them of the need to actually do math is anybody’s guess.
This is all new and progressing incredibly quickly; there has been no time for the field to find a new normal. It’s possible that, once Alpöge gets around to describing the approach he pushed Claude to use, mathematicians will start getting the same sorts of insights that they normally expect to receive from proofs. It could be that Alpöge’s approach, mixing human intuition with machine-generated detail and rigor, provides a model for what math will look like in a few years.
But it’s impossible to tell at this early stage in development.

How American Thanksgiving took root — and evolved — in Liberia
Yvonne Capehart Weah is from Liberia, a country in West Africa, and she's one of twelve siblings.
"I'm the second to the last one — I'm the eleventh," she says. "We have large families in Liberia."
Every year on the first Thursday in November, Weah's family gathers in Caldwell, the township where she grew up, to celebrate Liberian Thanksgiving.
"When we come together, the group become [so] large that you are not able to sit around a dining table," she explains. "So we do it outside under the tree. And when we meet, it's almost like we're having a party."
The Liberian holiday dates back to the first half of the 19th century when the American Colonization Society established the community that would grow into the country. It was founded by Black Americans — both those born free and enslaved people who had been emancipated — whose departure was sometimes voluntary, sometimes forced. "The settlers from America brought that Thanksgiving Day tradition to Liberia," says Weah. Once transplanted, the holiday evolved over time in response to national events.
Liberia gained its independence in 1847 but the British continued trying to take swaths of territory. In 1883, President Alfred Francis Russell, an Episcopalian priest, called upon God to help halt the incursions.
That invocation was a "prayer of protection against the intruders, preventing intrusion into our territory," says Weah.
The Liberians managed to maintain their sovereignty. And that year, the legislature officially established Thanksgiving as a national holiday steeped in the religious gratitude of the moment.
A sacred day for all
Weah summarizes Liberian Thanksgiving this way: "It's giving thanks to God for our freedom, for divine protection. It's giving thanks to God for unity and for the harvest."
Weah says that her family's celebration, like that of many others in Liberia, starts in the morning at church. But the holiday's for people of all faiths, and other religious communities mark the occasion as well
"The Muslims, they go to the mosques and pray," says Sekou Muhammad Sheriff, a YouTuber who travels his home country of Liberia to showcase its offerings and cultural heritage, including Thanksgiving. "And Muslims, Christians, and others — everybody observe this day as a holiday."
When Sheriff was a boy, this was the day that he counted on to get a new outfit.
"What my dad used to do for me," says Sheriff, was to purchase a "shirt-trouser suit, and then he'd buy me slipper." His favorite suit was a white one.
Over the years on Thanksgiving, he's grown accustomed to eating different stews, including one made with sweet potato leaves and another with snails collected from the garden.
"We call it king's meat," Sheriff says with a chuckle. "It is very, very nice."
The mid-afternoon meal varies from household to household in Liberia.
"We don't do turkey," says Weah, "but we do chicken. We do fried chicken, smoked chicken, roasted chicken."
Weah's family also serves jollof rice, watermelon, pineapple and a variety of stews, including one called fufu and soup. It's a mix of cassava, fish, chicken, okra, chili pepper and more. "That makes the soup very tasty," says Weah. "It has to be [at] every Thanksgiving."
(Weah doesn't especially like to cook, however. "If you tell me, 'Go in the kitchen to cook or sit in the living room and read,'" she says, "I will sit in the living room and read.")
"I'm thanking God"
This year, Sheriff didn't have the resources to host Thanksgiving. But he says that he remains thankful to God for keeping him healthy and for keeping Liberia peaceful after civil conflict tore his country apart from 1989 to 1997 and 1999 to 2003.
Weah is also grateful. "When I go for Thanksgiving," she says, "I'm thanking God for where I have come from, where I am now, and I'm also thanking Him for where He will take me because I know He holds the future."
Weah is the program manager at the We-Care Foundation, an education nonprofit that, among other things, teaches children literacy. "A reading child will become a reading elder," she says.
"And we expect informed adults to make informed decisions that affect both their social and economic life" — in ways, perhaps, that they will one day be thankful for.

It was an extra special Thanksgiving holiday for Melissa Gilbert. The Little House on the Prairie actress gave a shoutout Thursday to all those “who checked in … spoke up, testified and wrote letters” after her husband Timothy Busfield was charged with two counts of criminal sexual contact with a minor and child abuse. A New Mexico judge dismissed them in October.
The charges stemmed from alleged incidents involving two minor boys on the New Mexico set of the Fox/Warner Bros TV series The Cleaning Lady. Busfield, who directed several episodes of Cleaning Lady during its four-season run from 2022-25, said the claims were “absolutely one gazillion percent untrue. Never ever.”
“This Thanksgiving I”m incredibly grateful for all those who came running toward us this year,” Gilbert wrote on Instagram. “Our undying gratitude also, to our extraordinary team who bravely fought and continue to fight so hard for what is right and true. On this day, as we all acknowledge the blessings in our lives, we send our love and eternal gratitude to each and every one of you.”
Watch on Deadline
The charges were tossed last month after the “prosecuting attorney failed to act in a fair and impartial manner, including the failure to properly instruct the grand jury on the law for calling witnesses and in instructing the grand jurors on a procedure that effectively withheld requested witnesses,” Judge Joseph Montano wrote in an order quashing the indictment. “In doing so, the grand jury proceedings were conducted in a manner that violated grand jury statutes designed to protect the structural integrity of our grand jury system and the presumption of prejudice applies.”
Montano gave prosecutors the option to “institute new criminal proceedings” against Busfield; each count in the tossed indictment carried a maximum sentence of six years behind bars.

From Mahanadi Coalfields’ IPO drawing strong institutional demand despite a muted retail response and Jensen Huang’s return as Nvidia CEO to faster US economic growth amid persistent inflation, a slowdown in vehicle sales in the festival season and Vaibhav Sooryavanshi’s record-breaking double century in men’s List A cricket, here is this week’s news in numbers.
Selective appetite
Mahanadi Coalfields’ ₹8,981-crore IPO closed with an overall subscription of 1.52 times, driven overwhelmingly by qualified institutional buyers (QIBs), whose reserved portion was subscribed nearly five times. Retail investors subscribed to just 0.46 times their allotted portion, while non-institutional and existing shareholder categories remained undersubscribed.
The company’s shares are scheduled to list on 27 November. The IPO comprises a 10% stake sale by parent Coal India through an offer for sale (OFS), meaning the proceeds will go to Coal India rather than Mahanadi Coalfields. India’s largest coal producer, Mahanadi accounted for around 21% of domestic output in FY26, producing 218.31 million tonnes. However, its production fell 3.1% from the previous year, while revenue and net profit also declined marginally. It remained Coal India’s largest subsidiary by production.
Plot twist
Nvidia's board unanimously reinstated Jensen Huang as CEO on Monday, 11 days after his resignation amid reports of his alleged relationship with a Chinese spy. The announcement sent the chipmaker's shares soaring 31.5%, marking its third-largest single-day gain since its 1999 listing. Most of Nvidia's biggest daily gains came during the dot-com era of the early 2000s, with only three of its 10 biggest rallies recorded in the 2010s and 2020s.
The stock had fallen 24.5% between Huang's resignation on 12 November and 20 November. The decline coincided with a broader sell-off in AI-linked stocks, even as Indian equities rallied amid renewed foreign investor inflows. The controversy first emerged on 29 October, when reports linked Huang to a Singapore-based businesswoman suspected by US intelligence officials of having ties to Chinese intelligence.
Economic pulse
The US economy grew at an annualised rate of 4.3% in the third quarter of 2026, its fastest pace in three years, according to the Bureau of Economic Analysis. This was higher than the advance estimate of 3.4% and the growth of 2.2% in the previous quarter. The stronger-than-expected growth comes as the US continues to grapple with persistent inflation, complicating the Federal Reserve's efforts to bring price increases under control.
The Fed's preferred gauge, the personal consumption expenditures (PCE) price index, rose 3.8% year-on-year in October, up from 3.7% in September. Core PCE inflation, which excludes food and energy, increased to 3.3%, its highest in three years. Both measures rose 0.3% from the previous month. The combination of strong growth and persistent inflation leaves the Federal Reserve with less room to cut interest rates. Markets are pricing in another 25-basis-point rate increase at its 8-9 December meeting. The final decision will depend on incoming economic data and policymakers' assessment of inflation.
Numbers Talk
56.3: HSBC Flash India Composite PMI in October, marginally up from 56.2. Manufacturing activity rose to a nine-month high of 56.0 from 54.7, while services activity eased to 55.3.
15%: Decline expected in India’s sugar production to 26.5 million tonnes in the 2026-27 season due to smaller cane area and uneven rainfall, the Indian Sugar and Bio-Energy Manufacturers Association (ISMA) said on Wednesday.
₹15,000 crore: The value of India's development assistance project for Nepal announced by Prime Minister Narendra Modi on Monday during talks with Nepalese Prime Minister Balendra Shah.
96%: The share of employees in India who use artificial intelligence (AI) daily or two to three times a week, the highest among nine Asia-Pacific markets surveyed by Boston Consulting Group (BCG).
18.8%:The year-on-year growth in unincorporated non-agricultural establishments to 9.47 crore in July–September 2026, according to the quarterly bulletin of the ASUSE.
Lower gear
Vehicle retail sales growth slowed sharply during the 2026 festive season, with registrations rising just 2.2% year-on-year, compared with 21.3% in 2025 and 11.8% in 2024, according to the Federation of Automobile Dealers Associations (FADA). Growth moderated across all major vehicle categories. Two-wheeler sales rose 3.7%, down from 21.6% a year earlier, while commercial vehicle growth more than halved to 7.1% from 15.1%.
Passenger vehicle registrations fell 7.2%, reversing a 25.4% increase in the previous festive season. The slowdown follows an exceptional 2025, when GST rate cuts lowered vehicle prices and helped release pent-up demand, creating a high base for comparison. Higher inflation may also have weighed on spending, with retail inflation rising to 6.1% in October and food inflation reaching 8.9%. Geopolitical tensions have added to uncertainty over energy prices and the economic outlook.
Cricket sensation
Fifteen-year-old Vaibhav Sooryavanshi rewrote the men’s List A cricket record books on 24 November, scoring 204 off just 53 balls for India A against the UAE in the Rising Stars Asia Cup in Doha. He reached his double century in 52 balls, becoming the fastest batter to the milestone in List A cricket.
The previous record, held by New Zealand's Chad Bowes, stood at 103 balls—almost twice as long. Sooryavanshi also struck the fastest List A century, off 28 balls, and the fastest 150, off 40 balls. His innings included 28 sixes, the most in a men's List A innings. Shubman Gill also features among the fastest List A double-centurions, having reached 200 in 117 balls against the West Indies in September. List A cricket covers recognised senior one-day matches, including ODIs and domestic 50-over games.

Genomic testing can answer a variety of pressing health questions a person (and their clinician) might face throughout their lifespan.
Unfortunately, these valuable tests have become fragmented and iterative for most patients. A patient may receive a carrier screening test before or during pregnancy; a cancer predisposition test to screen for inherited cancer-predisposition variants like BRCA, the breast cancer gene; and a pharmacogenomic test before starting a medication. Each test is a new blood draw or buccal swab, a new wet lab workflow, a new spot on a genome sequencer, a new analysis, and new costs borne by patients and insurance companies.
With the precipitous decline in the cost of whole genome sequencing, it’s time to consolidate testing by sequencing genomes once and reevaluating them when needed.
As research has shown, patients face many challenges to accessing genomic testing including financial barriers, limited access to providers, geographic limitations, and clinician biases. Since the genome can enable diagnoses and care for so many health conditions, a more streamlined and uniform approach to genomic testing would likely benefit many patients. I call it “test once, evaluate often.”
Is one test really enough?
A “test once, evaluate often” approach could start at any age. For some families, that might be at birth, as an optional add-on to the newborn screening their baby already gets. A single whole genome sequence could be stored, along with other medical records information, for future analysis. Any time a clinician orders a new genomic test, the lab would simply reevaluate the relevant genes and issue a report.
This approach would dramatically lower the cost and turnaround time needed to answer genomic questions by eliminating the sample handling and wet lab processing of patient samples, potentially improving access to genomic information for patients who would otherwise choose to forgo testing due to costs.
Such a paradigm would only apply to tests looking at germline DNA (the DNA we are born with). Clinical genomic tests seeking to understand the genetics of other biological characteristics, such as somatic DNA in a cancer tissue, circulating fetal DNA in a noninvasive prenatal test, or circulating tumor DNA in liquid biopsy panels would still be needed to look for genomic variants beyond germline DNA when patient circumstances dictate.
What about newborns?
Newborn screening is one of public health’s great successes. For more than 60 years, nearly every U.S. baby has had a heel-prick blood test for dozens of serious, treatable conditions, catching thousands of babies each year who look perfectly healthy.
For many, early diagnosis is the difference between life and death. Infants with severe combined immunodeficiency who receive a transplant by 3.5 months survive 94% of the time. Babies destined for the most severe form of spinal muscular atrophy who receive gene therapy before symptoms emerge go on to sit independently and breathe without permanent ventilation. Any interruption to newborn screening would cost children their lives.
Genome sequencing builds on that foundation. In the BabySeq Project, 9.4% of newborns had an unexpected genetic risk for childhood-onset disease. In New York’s GUARDIAN study, 72% of families opted in and 3.7% of babies screened positive, including for treatable conditions that standard screening misses. Because sequencing alone misses some cases that biochemical tests catch, it should add to the heel prick, not replace it.
In childhood, reporting can stay focused on conditions where knowing early changes care; the rest of the genome can wait until there’s a question to answer. And as with any public health program, clear consent and transparent data use must be built in from the start.
Regular evaluation of the genome is critical
The need for genomic information changes with patient circumstances and throughout their lifespan. This is why regular evaluation of the genome is needed in place of the piecemeal approach to ordering individual tests today.
Unfortunately, genomic science is not yet in a place where a single point of evaluation is practical. Evidence about emerging gene-disease relationships and new understandings of variants associated with hereditary cancer and other diseases continue to be adopted into clinical practice, meaning that an analysis conducted 20 years into the future would likely deliver more information than is currently possible.
The genomics community has honed a version of this practice, termed reanalysis, in the rare disease space. There, it is commonplace to reexamine a patient’s exome or genome based on emerging clinical evidence about gene-disease relationships.
Reevaluation is a bit different. Reanalysis is done for the same testing indication (i.e., finding the genetic cause of a rare disease) and reevaluation is studying the same genome for a new testing indication.
The National Human Genome Research Institute envisions a future where genomic data is systematically collected and used more regularly and efficiently for patient benefit. Getting there means moving clinical and laboratory medicine toward a system in which a genome sequenced once, whether at birth or later in life, helps a person’s clinicians manage their health throughout their life.
Making this vision a reality will require several changes to the way medicine is practiced and paid for today.
First, health systems, laboratories, and policymakers need to agree on how genomic data will be stored securely for decades and who can see it. Patients already trust online patient portals with their lab results and medical records, and genomic data can be held to the same standards of security and transparency.
These questions are already being actively worked on. Leading newborn sequencing programs, such as New York’s GUARDIAN study and England’s Generation Study, ask parents for opt-in consent, keep data under strict access controls, and are studying how long it should be kept. Leftover newborn screening blood spots have also been stored for years in many states, often without parents knowing, which is why consent and transparency have become central to this work. Any program that stores genomes, at birth or later, must start with fully informed consent: patients and parents should know what is kept, where, for how long and who may use it, and be free to say no.
Second, additional genetic counseling resources would need to support patients along their genomic health journeys, helping balance clinical needs, desires for information, and the familial implications of genomic insights. That support matters even more as care becomes increasingly patient-driven, with more people ordering tests themselves, reading their own results, and coming back with new questions.
Finally, and perhaps most important, insurers need a way to pay for evaluating a genome that has already been sequenced. Today, insurance can cover reanalysis, but there is no clear path to pay for reevaluation, the step that makes “test once, evaluate often” work. Paying for it would save insurers money, too, since it could replace repeat sequencing over a patient’s lifetime. Without reimbursement for prevention-oriented sequencing, genetic counseling, and genomic evaluation, we can’t improve equity in genomic testing.
Sharing data, finding answers
Something I’ve seen again and again in the rare disease setting is that parents of a child without a diagnosis are almost always eager to share their child’s genetic data. They know that a match with another family somewhere in the world may be what finally explains what’s happening, and many new gene discoveries start exactly that way.
If we protect genomic data well and show people what sharing makes possible, more of us may come to see it the way these parents do: not as a risk to minimize, but as a path to answers, prevention, and cures.
Kelly Hagman, M.S., is a genetic counselor and vice president of medical affairs and strategic integration at Ambry Genetics, a Tempus company. She led the launch of the industry’s first clinical exome and has authored more than 55 peer-reviewed publications.
