Mushroom supplements promise health benefits. What does the science say?
Growing up in the French Alps, Julie Daoust fell for mushrooms early in life.
"So as a kid, we'd go out and forage," she recalls. "We'd come across species like lion's mane or reishi. And I became more and more interested in those species."
Daoust went on to get a Ph.D. in chemistry, searching nature for novel pharmaceuticals. Her work ultimately led her back to mushrooms, a group of organisms to which humans are more closely related than plants. And yet, many of our modern medicines and therapeutics come from plants.
"Mushrooms share a lot more in terms of their biochemistry with us than plants do," says Daoust, which means "you have more chances of finding something that's going to have bioactivity in a human than you would with other source organisms."
Daoust is now vice president of science and innovation at Monterey Nutra, a company that specializes in the genetics and cultivation of mushrooms and sells fungal extracts and powders. Her team focuses not on the poisonous varieties, nor the psychedelic ones that contain psilocybin. Rather, they are interested in the functional or medicinal mushrooms that Daoust likens to tiny cauldrons of potentially useful molecules.
"We love to look for soft things that can't run away very fast," says Daoust, "because they typically produce really interesting chemistry to defend themselves or to communicate with others in their environment to survive."
The claim
Daoust says that certain types of fungi may have specific uses.
For instance, lion's mane — a soft chandelier of a fungus — may aid cognition. Reishi and turkey tail, which are mushrooms that grow as hard brown scales on decomposing trees, could bolster immune health.
And on social media, influencers and advertisers promise that medicinal mushrooms, taken as supplements, can slow aging and improve energy levels, focus and immune health.
The evidence
Robust clinical trials proving such connections — and their safety — are largely lacking, according to Abby Langer, a registered dietitian based in Toronto. "In my opinion, I don't think that there's much evidence for functional mushrooms as of now," she says.
Langer says mushrooms accumulate and concentrate the materials in the ground they're grown in, both good and bad — so one has to be cautious.
Want the latest stories on the science of healthy living? Subscribe to NPR's Health newsletter.
She grants that in certain communities (in parts of Asia, for instance), mushrooms have been incorporated into their healing practices for generations. However, "just because something has been used for a long time doesn't mean that it's safe, that it's effective, that the dosing has been established," Langer says. "There are a lot of unknowns."
Still, she acknowledges that empirical support for the potential positive impacts of mushrooms is growing. "The clinical research on specific functional mushroom products is young," she says, "but it's accumulating fast and already includes some impressive results."
Mushrooms are a good source of vitamin D2 and antioxidants. Their cell walls contain beta-glucan, which has been linked to gut health, including a lower risk of Crohn's Disease, and immune response. Research into the effects of mushrooms on cognition have been mixed.
In addition, there's work out of Japan looking at how PSK, a purified extract from turkey tail, improved immune response in cancer patients. A meta-analysis considered 8,009 patients in eight randomized controlled trials who had undergone surgical removal of a gastric tumor and in almost all cases chemotherapy. Those who were also given PSK showed a 12% reduction in risk of death.
"This is not something that we brush off," says Santhosshi Narayanan, an integrative oncologist based at the University of Texas MD Anderson Cancer Center who recognizes the potential of PSK.
Even so, she admits that this "does not mean that PSK or any mushrooms alone cures cancer. It just shows to us that we need to pay attention to these natural products." Narayanan says there's still a lot to figure out with this particular extract, especially for populations outside Japan with different genetics or treatment regimes who might experience unwanted side effects.
"We need to do more research and understand how we can use it," she says. "Like which people, which type of patients benefit from which type of mushroom — because that itself is a whole science."
Narayanan and her colleagues also surveyed 2,349 studies examining the relationship between medicinal mushrooms and cancer, but only 39 were robust enough to be included in their 2023 analysis. Of that subset, "31 studies showed beneficial effects of the mushrooms, resulting in improved quality of life, reduced [side effect] profiles of different chemotherapeutic drugs, improved anti-inflammatory and anti-metastatic effects, and improved [disease-free survival] as well as [overall survival] in a few trials," according to the report.
Six studies didn't reveal any advantage and two highlighted worse outcomes. Overall, the analysis was unable to make clear conclusions about "the complex biological effects of mushrooms on the immune system in cancer."
The bottom line
In Narayanan's estimation, there's not yet enough evidence to support routine clinical use in cancer treatment.
And Langer recommends considering a few nutrition basics before introducing a supplement for gut health or cognition. "Take a closer look at what you're eating, how you're eating, when you're eating," she advises, "and see if there's any tweaks that you need to make."
Maybe it's possible to eat more fiber or protein, reduce consumption of alcohol or sugar-sweetened beverages, skip fewer meals, or eat out less often, she says.
"There's so many things that people can potentially improve on," Langer says, "before adding something else that's promised to be this panacea for everything that ails you."

Four years ago, NASA dispatched a small spacecraft on a suicide mission to show how humanity might deflect an asteroid on a collision course with Earth. The first-of-its-kind experiment worked beautifully as the solar-powered space probe slammed into asteroid Dimorphos, permanently altering its trajectory.
Using telescopes, astronomers measured changes in the orbit of Dimorphos around a larger asteroid companion named Didymos in the aftermath of NASA’s Double Asteroid Redirection Test (DART) mission. The spacecraft released some 10 billion joules of energy as it impacted Dimorphos in September 2022 at more than 13,700 mph (6.14 kilometers per second), shortening the asteroid’s 12-hour orbit around Didymos by about 33 minutes, 25 times the most conservative expectation.
But scientists could only learn so much from DART. The collision destroyed the spacecraft, as expected. DART recorded images as it took aim on Dimorphos, but only faraway telescopes and a small CubeSat that briefly detected the impact flash could see what happened next.
“We knew right away that the impact was successful, that DART made a really, really large mess,” said Sabina Raducan, a planetary scientist at the International Space Science Institute in Bern, Switzerland. “However, we didn’t really know what kind of mess. We were still missing pieces of the puzzle.”
Following up
The European Space Agency’s Hera spacecraft recently arrived in the vicinity of Didymos and Dimorphos after a two-year journey from a launch pad in Florida. On Wednesday, ESA released Hera’s first views of the scar left by DART on Dimorphos. The images show the car-sized impactor carved out a crater the size of a stadium, nearly as big as Dimorphos itself, a rugged chunk of extraterrestrial rock measuring about 500 feet (151 meters) across.
Mission planners selected Didymos and Dimorphos for the deflection experiment because they are similar to many near-Earth asteroids, but there’s no risk of them striking our home planet. Scientists weren’t sure what Hera would find when it got to the double asteroid, currently orbiting the Sun about 120 million miles (193.5 million kilometers) from Earth.
“I would say we had two kinds of predictions: either we made a crater, or we reshaped the asteroid,” said Patrick Michel, Hera’s principal investigator from Côte d’Azur Observatory in Nice, France. “In fact, we did both because the crater is so large that the shape has changed. Therefore, we are in a sort of a transition between just cratering and global transformation, and we are still not sure how this can happen.”
Hera found Didymos, the larger of the two asteroids, spinning on its axis just as DART observed on final approach in 2022. Dimorphos is no longer so stable.
“As Hera returned more images, it became clear that the DART impact has left Dimorphos tumbling wildly in its orbit,” says Michael Kueppers, ESA’s Hera mission scientist.
The Hera spacecraft will fly closer to Didymos and Dimorphos over the next six months to obtain more detailed observations. Hera will release two small sub-satellites to attempt landings on Dimorphos and collect data on the asteroid’s composition, internal structure, and mass.
Scientists will use this information to reconstruct the dynamics of DART’s impact four years ago and better understand how a future deflection mission might move an asteroid off a trajectory that actually threatens Earth. Near-Earth asteroids come in many shapes and sizes, with different densities and makeups, so knowledge of Dimorphos’s physical properties will anchor predictive computer models teaching scientists how best to deflect all types of asteroids.
“Once we understand, we have a breakthrough, which really solves planetary defense,” Michel said in an interview with Ars.
What a mess
In its initial reconnaissance this month, Hera spotted hundreds of boulders surrounding the double asteroid. This was not entirely unexpected. A picture taken by the Hubble Space Telescope shortly after DART’s impact showed a cloud of material streaming behind Didymos and Dimorphos, but scientists were astonished by the extent of the debris swarm in Hera’s first images.
“As we approached Didymos and Dimorphos, we quickly realized the asteroids were not alone,” said Naomi Murdoch, planetary scientist at the Institut Supérieur de l’Aéronautique et de l’Espace in Toulouse, France. “In fact, they had a lot of company.”
An image released by ESA on Wednesday combines 11 long exposure frames from Hera’s hyperspectral camera. Image processors on the ground digitally removed the relatively bright Didymos and Dimorphos to reveal a panoply of dimmer streaks and dots, each of which is a rock fragment ranging in size from a football to a washing machine, Murdoch said.
“Hera came to visit two asteroids, and we found hundreds of companions,” Murdoch said.
One obvious explanation for the boulders is they were thrown off Dimorphos when DART slammed into it. But scientists cautioned they need more information before they can say that with surety. Hera is the first space mission to undertake a sustained study of an asteroid with its own moon. The debris around the two asteroids might be relics from the creation of Dimorphos some time in the ancient past.

Ars Technica is a place that has always leaned into remote working. Since its beginnings in 1998, Ars has never had a single, central office—a setup that makes for a great commute to work, with little risk of getting stuck in traffic.
As Ars staffers step away from their desks for a few days to spend some time with family and friends, we wanted to give you a look inside our home offices. We’ve got all sorts of setups, tucked into basements, dens, spare bedrooms, apartment corners, and lofts. They run the gamut from minimalist “here’s my laptop and monitor” setups to “I really like collecting things.” Without any further ado, let’s dig in:
Jeremy Hsu
As an apartment dweller in New York City, I’ve usually set up my home work station in a small corner of my residence along with sometimes decamping for local cafes or coworking spaces. My current hodgepodge of equipment is probably on the minimal side compared to many members of the Ars team.
I’m usually multitasking on my basic monitor display and work laptop configuration, with the monitor sitting on a stack of several books (apologies in particular to Mary Beard’s excellent history of the Roman Republic, titled SPQR).
Accessories plugged into the work laptop include a simple Lekvey Ergonomic Mouse and a Logitech K380 keyboard that I’ve often brought along with me to public workspaces. Sometimes I’ll use the built-in Macbook Air keyboard, but I like having the laptop display elevated, whether I’m working at home or elsewhere.
My personal Apple M4 Macbook Air usually sits on the side, where I primarily use my old, battered pair of Sennheiser HD 518 headphones to listen to music during the work day.
I have a simple standing desk, but it’s not the easiest to change positions, so I wouldn’t recommend it for anyone who wants to adjust frequently. Whenever I’m sitting, I sometimes switch between a simple wooden chair from Ikea and a more ergonomic chair.
Aside from an assortment of coasters and a tea container turned pen holder, my desk also holds a painted dinosaur sculpture (courtesy of my young son) and two versions of the Spot It! Matching game (also for my son’s entertainment).
Last but not least, I have a pair of Powerblock dumbbells tucked under my work desk. I wouldn’t say they feature heavily in my work day, but they’re easily accessible if I have 15-20 minutes to spare.
Nick Indge
Greetings from my basement hobbit hole! My desk sits across from a workbench area that was already here when we got the house. I have labeled drawers full of PC parts, tools, and cables accumulated over decades. The drawer organization was quite the upgrade over my previous solution of “chuck everything in unlabeled storage tubs.”
My current PC setup is an AceMagic W1 mini PC running Fedora, and a Blackview Intel N150 I keep on Windows for audio recording (PipeWire is fussy). The two are connected to my inputs and monitors via a KVM so I can switch back and forth at the press of a button.
The monitors are mismatched thrift finds. One is an HP, the other Sansui. The TV is a similar story—an old Samsung LCD that set me back $10 at the thrift store. I use it as a third monitor for watching PC streams. An Onn Android box is also connected, though it rarely earns its keep.
Below the TV sits a Lenovo ThinkSmart View, a repurposed B2B video-conference gadget modded to run LineageOS. It handles smart-home controls and tracks my solar production during the day. There’s also a Flashforge 5M printer in the corner, and the pegboard wall holds tools, Mega Man figures, and about 10 years’ worth of convention badges.
The back closet is the scary part: old consoles, spare drives, boards, and parts for every project I’ll get to “eventually.” The chair is a Dowinx gaming chair I grabbed on a Slickdeals whim—it’s fine, but I wouldn’t recommend it to anyone.
The rug-patterned Dude mousepad really ties the desk together, man.
Ryan Whitwam
I’m something of an outlier at Ars, in that I use Windows most days. I’m no great lover of Windows 11, but I still use it thanks to years of computing inertia. My machine is custom, built in early 2024 with a Raptor Lake Core i7 (that thankfully did not fall victim to the overvolting bug) and an RTX 4070 Ti. It has long been my preference to build my own PC for gaming and work to ensure easier repairs and upgrades. Although with the prices of components being what they are, I hope all these parts last a very long time.
The primary monitor on the bottom is an Alienware ultrawide OLED. I got it for gaming, but it’s also a nice productivity display that gives me lots of room to keep windows visible. Above that, I have an Asus ProArt LCD calibrated in sRGB for photography work. I’ll get to the keyboard, but I do want to point out my preferred mouse, a Logitech MX Vertical. I have carpal tunnel issues, and this thing has been a lifesaver.
I believe organizing my desk before taking the photo would be a form of lying, so rest assured this is what it looks like on an average day. I have a few organizers to keep phones and various accessories from getting scattered around my Uplift sit-stand desk (seen here in sitting mode), which I quite like. The chair is a Herman Miller Aeron, which I don’t like as much. It’s fine and has plenty of adjustments, but the mesh is very hard. You should only buy one on sale, and if you do, get a cushion.
Above the desk are some Star Trek cross-stitches, courtesy of my talented wife. The dangling ’90s-era computer components are a mobile I put together many years ago, featuring a neat Intel i486 DEC socket board and some SDRAM.
Aurich Lawson
I’m not a particularly neat person. My natural state is to have two or three projects half-exploded all over every surface: piles of 3D-printed prototypes, spools of wire, a soldering iron, laser-cut acrylic for a pinball project, the packaging from something I recently opened and need to sort through. Those aren’t random examples; that’s the contents of my workbench behind me on the opposite wall of my office as I type this. It’s a bit of a mess.
To combat that tendency, I make a concerted effort to keep the desk where I spend so many hours of the day calm and a place where I can focus. It doesn’t always last! But I’m always at least striving for it, and what I find helps is having a very intentional design where everything has a place.
My desk surface is made from rubberwood butcher block, on Flexispot motorized legs. I recently picked up another rubberwood slab to build the cantilevered shelf. The supports neatly tuck away my M1 Max Mac Studio, which is still a great little workhorse with 64 gigs of RAM, and my Arturia audio interface, which I use to record line-in sources like synthesizers.
On the left is a task lamp and a pen holder with six discrete holes. This fits in with the intentional design part: I have to pick the six things I want handy, and I can’t just pack it with more and more stuff. Currently that’s my Apple Pencil, a Pentel mechanical pencil, an Olfa mini snap-off blade knife, and a selection of three Pigma Micron pens in different line widths.
The right side holds an Aiyima 10th anniversary hi-fi stack: A20 amp, D20 DAC, and T20 pre-amplifier. The speakers are SVS Ultra Evolution Nanos. They’re sitting on the latest version of some 3D-printed stands I’ve been designing. I print them with hollow legs and then fill them with concrete for mass and stability.
Since I know Ryan is going to flex on everyone with his keyboard collection, I have to try my best to keep up with my daily driver. It’s a Percent Canoe v2 case, running Holy Panda switches modified with 63 gram SPRiT springs for a slightly lighter touch, and GMK Bento keycaps. This was a pandemic build project, and it has served me well since.
I used to run multiple monitors, but I’ve found that I don’t focus as well with them and prefer a singular spot to pay attention to. I’m using an Apple Studio Display because I’m very picky about pixel density. I opted to order it without the stand so I can run it on an ergo arm.
When I built the shelf for my desk, I fabricated a mounting bracket for the arm out of schedule 40 steel pipe and a 3D-printed sleeve that sits in a pocket CNC’d out. Since it sits flush on the underside, I don’t have to use a clamp that would extend down into the space where I keep my Mac and audio interface.

My office setup is probably a lot simpler—basic?—than most of my Ars colleagues. I use an adjustable wood-top desk that allows me to stand or sit while I work. I do almost all of my writing and editing on a MacBook Air, and I have a spare available in case I need it. Sometimes I travel with both MacBooks so I can use one for writing and the other for monitoring a rocket launch, press conference, or other event. I also work a lot from my porch, where I can enjoy the fresh air and quiet mornings on our ranch in rural Texas.
An iMac and a second monitor stand behind the laptops. I generally use them to watch conferences, rocket launch livestreams, weather radar, or live news. It just depends on what’s happening any given day. One of the things I love about the space beat is there’s something happening nearly every day, and it’s possible to cover much of it from home. There are often multiple things happening the same day, so the dual-screen setup becomes especially handy then. For example, I can use one monitor to watch what SpaceX is doing at Starbase, Texas, and another to watch a rocket launch in Florida. I use a ring light behind my desk for TV interviews or podcast appearances.
Absent from my desk is my large collection of space swag stowed away in storage boxes. Perhaps I will bring it out to add to my workspace for a future Ars Staff Source. For now, I use a mouse pad from the European Space Agency that I’ve had for at least 15 years. The mouse pad features ESA’s astronomy missions that were in development or operations at the time. All of the missions have now launched, and some have long been decommissioned. It’s a good reminder of how long it takes to design, develop, build, and launch science missions. Anyone who says this stuff is easy is being dishonest.

Meta declined a suggestion from the UK’s financial regulator last week that they joint-test Muse using their sandbox, according to the watchdog’s head of innovation Colin Payne. It comes as regulators across the UK, including the competition and data watchdogs, warned Meta it needs to ensure its AI products comply with UK consumer protection laws.
“It’s another force of attack, agents hitting the streets, most of them coming from the US,” Payne, of the Financial Conduct Authority (FCA), said Tuesday in a panel hosted by AI firm Whitespace. “We’ve got a number of entrants into the market. We want to see what they’re going to be doing in the market. I think it’s just reasonable,” he later explained to WIRED. Payne told WIRED the FCA had been hoping the organizations could work together to investigate what interactions might look like between the tool, marketed as a personal assistant, and a normal customer.
His organization has been experimenting with other firms as many, including Amazon, roll out AI shopping assistants, and other agentic tools in the UK.
The FCA especially wants to understand how payments will be made by agents—as multiple British retailers, including grocers Sainsbury’s, Marks & Spencer, and Ocado, department store Debenhams Group, and electronics seller Currys said they’d been working with Meta to smooth Muse’s access to their sites. Payne is concerned about potential unintended consequences of prompts, especially when a user has a low level of understanding of how the AI product works. “If an agent is acting autonomously, we want to make sure it’s in the interest of the consumer,” he says.
Payne did note the testing would have taken time to set up. “Normally you have a long period of time speaking to a firm and then you plan it over a period of weeks or months,” he explained, but Meta only made the FCA aware of its plans last month.
“We’ve engaged constructively with the appropriate regulatory authorities and will continue to do so,” Meta Spokesperson Matthew Pollard tells WIRED.
More than 10 million users have set up Muse in North America since it was launched in September. British watchdogs say they will be monitoring Muse’s rollout closely as they are bracing for significant uptake on their side of the pond, too, given that many Brits already use Meta’s other products, like Instagram, Facebook, and WhatsApp. “If it’s going to be equally popular in the UK, we need to be able to see what it’s going to do,” Payne says.
The ICO stressed the importance of users understanding and being able to control how Muse uses their personal data. The Competition and Markets Authority has already made Meta adapt its terms and conditions for UK consumers to say Meta must exercise “reasonable skill and care/professional diligence” when providing Muse, the EU and UK terms say, with the document acknowledging that outputs may still be inaccurate and actions may not be completed as intended.
“If we have concerns, we will not hesitate to act to protect UK consumers,” the CMA said in a statement.

NEW DELHI: The Union health ministry has tightened controls on stem cell treatment for autism spectrum disorder (ASD), barring clinics from offering the experimental procedure as routine care and introducing safeguards for patients in clinical trials. Under two regulatory notices issued on 20 November, institutions must insure participants against research-related harm, researchers cannot charge for treatment or other study-related costs, and trials must follow defined approval timelines.
The notices establish safeguards for participants and a regulatory framework for researchers, while reiterating that stem cell procedures cannot be offered as routine commercial care, according to the notices, reviewed by Mint, and two officials.
In its public notice for caregivers, the ministry said the host institution or trial site must ensure insurance coverage before research involving human participants begins. This must cover compensation if a participant suffers an injury, disability or death because of the research. Compensation under the New Drugs and Clinical Trials Rules, 2019, will apply equally to participants receiving stem cells and those in comparator groups.
The ministry has prohibited researchers from collecting payments disguised as study fees. “Anyone taking part in a stem cell clinical trial must not be asked to pay for any procedure during the course of the study. This includes the stem cell treatment being studied, tests, procedures, hospital stay or any other research-related costs,” the notice said.
Parents must receive full details of the study design and risks, provide voluntary written consent, alongside child assent where applicable, and retain the right to withdraw without affecting routine care. Research teams must also explain monitoring arrangements for children in each study arm and what happens after the trial ends.
The ministry has also cautioned families that participation in a randomized trial does not guarantee that a child will receive stem cells or derive any clinical benefit. “Do not stop or delay your child's existing care or developmental support in favour of an unproven intervention,” it advised.
The notice stressed that autism has no cure and requires early identification, speech and occupational therapy, special education, parent-mediated interventions and behavioural support. Medicines only manage associated conditions such as epilepsy, irritability, sleep disorders or hyperactivity.
It also countered marketing claims around the use of a child's own cells. “Use of the child's own (autologous) cells does not make an unproven intervention safe or permissible.”
Queries sent to the health ministry spokesperson remained unanswered till press time.
Tighter controls on research
A second notice sets out a two-tier approval process based on the extent of laboratory processing of stem cells. For cells that undergo only basic processing, proposals must clear an institutional scientific panel and an ethics committee with external stem cell specialists before going to the National Stem Cell Research Regulation Committee under the Department of Health Research, which must decide within 90 working days.
Heavily altered or engineered cells are regulated as a new drug. Researchers must apply to the Central Drugs Standard Control Organisation (CDSCO), which will decide within 30 working days for therapies developed in India and 90 working days for foreign ones. Local site ethics committees must clear the study and notify the drug regulator within 15 working days. All trials must be registered on the Clinical Trials Registry of India before patient enrolment.
The new rules follow a 17 September health ministry advisory warning doctors and clinical establishments of disciplinary action and statutory penalties for offering unproven stem cell procedures as routine care. That advisory followed a Supreme Court judgment ruling that patients have no right to demand experimental stem cell treatments outside regulated clinical trials.
The regulatory push comes amid the commercialisation of such procedures, with private stem cell clinics charging families between ₹3 lakh and ₹15 lakh per treatment cycle. India has an estimated 18 million people living with autism, including roughly 2 million children. Globally, the World Health Organization estimates that about one in 100 children has autism.
Dr Anshul Dhillon, consultant paediatric neurologist at Kailash Hospital in Noida, said the safeguards were important for protecting participants and their families.
“Stem cell therapy for autism remains investigational and is not currently an established standard of care. Therefore, it is essential that such interventions are undertaken only within appropriately approved clinical trials, following established scientific and ethical guidelines. The framework also reinforces the importance of responsible research while ensuring that families have access to evidence-based interventions and appropriate developmental support," Dhillon said.
The ministry has invited public feedback via email on participation in a proposed randomized controlled trial for autism, without specifying a closing date in the notice.

Mumbai Police issues LOCs against CJP's Saurav Das, Abhijeet Dipke, Ashutosh Ranka over Dadar protest last month
The circulars were issued over the FIR registered against Dipke, Das, Ranka, as well as other CJP members and their supporters on October 3 after the protest.
Mumbai Police has issued look-out circulars against Cockroach Janta Party leaders Abhijeet Dipke, Saurav Das and Ashutosh Ranka, seven weeks after the organisation's protest in Shivaji Park on October 2.
According to Mumbai Police officials, the circulars were issued over an FIR registered against Dipke, Das, Ranka, as well as other CJP members and their supporters on October 3 for allegedly gathering illegally and sloganeering in Dadar.
The police had denied permission to the CJP’s representative Ajinkya Shinde for organising the protest on Gandhi Jayanti at Shivaji Park, saying they were not empowered to grant permission for any gathering at Shivaji Park.
Deep Dive
An LoC is an alert sent to Indian immigration checkpoints at international airports, seaports, and land borders to track or stop the person named from entering or leaving the country.
Also Read | CJP’s Saurav Das claims his passport leaked, blames ‘BJP-aligned’ social media handles
The LoC against CJP spokesperson Saurav Das came to light earlier on Thursday after the Centre informed the Delhi High Court about it, stating that it had been done at the request of the Maharashtra Police. Das had moved the HC on Monday (November 23), alleging that he was stopped from travelling to London to deliver a lecture at Oxford University. The CJP had condemned the LoC against Das, saying the outfit spokesperson had not been informed about this when he was stopped at the airport, PTI reported. There was no immediate reaction from the CJP on the LoCs against Dipke and Ranka.
Mumbai Police's FIR against CJP leaders, supporters
The Shivaji Park police had registered a case against Abhijeet Dipke, Pranav Ahire, Ashutosh Ranka, Ajinkya Shinde, Saurabh Das, Afreen Nawaz, Saumya Korde, Ankit Bharadwaj, Vijay Malangi and Yogesh Ingle over the protest at Shivaji Park last month. The FIR also mentioned 400 CJP supporters, HT reported earlier.
“We have registered a case against the organisers of CJP protests on October 2 at Shivaji Park. The case has been registered under sections 189 (unlawful assembly) and 223 (disobedience to a public servant’s lawful order) of the Bhartiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023, and section 37 (power to prohibit certain acts for prevention of disorder) and 135 (disobeying or breaking official orders issued by the police) of the Maharashtra Police Act,” a police personnel from the Shivaji Park Police Station had said.
The cops had denied permission for CJP's October 2 protest citing a judgment of the Bombay High Court in PIL 116/2009 dated January 4, 2013, and a subsequent order of the Maharashtra government dated January 20, 2016. The HC order had restricted the use of Shivaji Park for purposes other than sports. Police had also said that the organisers had not submitted the required BMC permission for using the ground.

Centre informs Delhi HC of LoC against Saurav Das
In a separate development this morning, Additional Solicitor General Chetan Sharma, appearing for the Centre, submitted before Justice Amit Mahajan that an LoC had been opened against him.
The development came days after Saurav Das claimed he was stopped from flying to London.
Senior advocate Akhil Sibal, who was representing Das, told the court that he had not been informed about the LoC and sought details of the circular from the Centre. Sharma argued that Das's legal team could obtain the details independently and challenge the LoC, issued on November 22 and 23. Many social media users have shared a 20-second video of a woman on a bus repeatedly moving closer to the man in front of her. According to the social media claims, the woman was trying to record a fake molestation video.
An X account, MenToo (@MenTooSave), shared the video claiming that the woman in the video was leaning on the man, trying to record a fake molestation video just for views. Noting that such false narrative can put an innocent man’s life and reputation at risk, the post asks, “When will society stop treating every man as guilty by default?”
She filmed herself deliberately pressing her breast against a man’s hand while he visibly tried to create distance and protect himself.
If true, this wasn’t an accident. It was a calculated attempt to manufacture a molestation clip — just for views.
One video. One false narrative. And an innocent man’s life, reputation, and freedom put at risk for content.
This is not empowerment. This is weaponizing accusations. When will society stop treating every man as guilty by default?
Innocent until proven guilty — even when the camera is rolling.
#FalseAccusations #DueProcess #MenToo #JusticeForAll
— MenToo (@MenTooSave) November 19, 2026
Men’s rights activist Barkha Trehan shared the same video on her Instagram account (@barkhatrehan16) on November 20. She also claimed the woman was trying to manufacture a molestation video for views, and the incident was from Patna, Bihar.
Social activist Deepika Narayan Bhardwaj (@DeepikaBhardwaj) also shared the video on X claiming the woman was deliberately sticking to the man so that she could “cry molestation”.
Fact Check
A close examination of the video shows that there is a release announcement poster of a film, ‘Janak’ at the end of the video. Below is a screenshot of the last frame of the viral video:
We then searched for the trailer of the movie, ‘Janak’, and found it on the YouTube channel of Marathi Cineyug, where it had been uploaded on October 14, 2026. The trailer contains the visual that is now viral. The same two people, the same background, clothing and movements can be seen at the 0:49-0:50-second mark in the trailer.
In the process, we also found behind-the-scene photos related to the movie shared on Instagram by Anushka Pimputkar, the woman in the viral clip. In one of the photos, she is seen with Avinash Narkar, the actor who is standing next to her in the viral video.
To sum up, the viral video does not show a real incident of a woman trying to record a fake molestation clip on a bus. It is a scene from the trailer of the Marathi film, ‘Janak’. Social media claims presenting the footage as real are false.

Vote for the first BBC Men's Footballer of the Year
- Published
Voting is now open for the BBC Men's Footballer of the Year 2026 award, which will be presented at Sports Personality of the Year.
Fans from the UK can vote from the five-player shortlist of Jude Bellingham, Harry Kane, Kylian Mbappe, Rodri and Lamine Yamal.
The vote closes on Friday, 27 November at 09:00 GMT.
The winner of the award - new for this year - will be presented during the live Sports Personality of the Year show on Sunday, 13 December.
Alex Kay-Jelski, Director of BBC Sport, said: "From the drama and excitement of the men's World Cup to the moments that have captivated fans across the domestic and international game, 2026 has given us so much to celebrate.
"Our inaugural BBC Men's Footballer of the Year award is about recognising the players who have made this year so special, inspired fans and left their mark on the game.
"It's a fantastic shortlist, and I can't wait to see who the public choose as our first-ever winner."
The shortlist was selected by an expert panel comprising former international players and some of the BBC's most respected football voices, bringing together a wealth of experience and insight from across the game.
The panel included Cesar Azpilicueta (Spain), Scott Brown (Scotland), Olivier Giroud (France), Shay Given (Republic of Ireland), Hassan Kachloul (Morocco), Lucas Leiva (Brazil), Benni McCarthy (South Africa), Alan Shearer, Ellen White (both England) and Ashley Williams (Wales).
Read more on the five contenders and cast your vote below.
Jude Bellingham
Age: 23 Country: England
Club: Real Madrid Position: Midfield
Bellingham made history this summer as he became the first Englishman to score as many as seven goals at a major tournament.
In a superb World Cup for the midfielder, he memorably netted twice in back-to-back games to help the Three Lions beat Mexico and Norway.
That meant he joined exalted company as the first player to score two or more goals in successive World Cup knockout games since Diego Maradona in 1986, and the second youngest in history behind Pele in 1958.
Bellingham also became the youngest European player to make an appearance at four different major tournaments, and also reached the milestone of 50 caps at a younger age than any other England men's player.
The goals continued to flow for Real Madrid, too, with Bellingham notching his 50th for the club to move above the legendary Zinedine Zidane in the Los Blancos' all-time scoring charts.
Harry Kane
Age: 33 Country: England
Club: Bayern Munich Position: Forward
In a stunning year of goalscoring, Kane become the first Englishman for 25 years (and only fifth in history) to win the Ballon d'Or - awarded to the world's best footballer.
His tally of 73 goals in 65 matches for club and country during a stellar 2025-26 season has only been surpassed in one of Europe's top five leagues by Lionel Messi's 82 for Barcelona and Argentina in 2011-12.
Kane scored 61 of those goals in just 51 appearances for Bayern Munich as he helped the Bavarians to a league and cup double. His total was 19 more than any other player in Europe's top five divisions.
Already England's record goalscorer, he surpassed Peter Shilton's mark of 125 appearances to become the most-capped Englishman in history.
Six goals at this summer's World Cup also helped him overtake Gary Lineker as the Three Lions' record scorer at the tournament, while he joined David Beckham as the only Englishmen to score in three separate World Cups.
Kylian Mbappe
Age: 27 Country: France
Club: Real Madrid Position: Forward
Mbappe came out on top of an enthralling tussle with Lionel Messi at the 2026 World Cup to become the leading goalscorer in the tournament's history.
The France forward, who is still only 27, took his tally to 22 from just three World Cups to finish one ahead of the great Argentine.
Mbappe's 10 goals from eight games this summer meant he won his second World Cup Golden Boot - a feat no player has managed before.
It also made him the first man to reach double figures at a World Cup since Gerd Muller in 1970, with only Just Fontaine (13) and Sandor Kocsis (11) having scored more goals in a single tournament.
Other achievements in a standout year included him finishing runner-up in the Ballon d'Or awards and overtaking Olivier Giroud as France's all-time leading goalscorer.
He scored 25 times to retain his title as La Liga's top scorer during a 2025-26 campaign in which he netted 42 goals in all competitions for Real Madrid.
Rodri
Age: 30 Country: Spain
Club: Barcelona Position: Midfield
Midfield maestro Rodri earned yet another accolade in his incredible career when he was awarded the Golden Ball trophy for the World Cup's best player.
By captaining Spain to glory in the US, Rodri became only the fourth male player to win the World Cup, European Championship, Champions League and Ballon d'Or - following in the footsteps of legendary Germans Gerd Muller and Franz Beckenbauer and France's Zinedine Zidane.
His achievements were made all the more special given doubts remained over whether he would recapture his best form after a long recovery from a serious knee injury in 2024.
Then Manchester City boss Pep Guardiola predicted he would return to his best at the World Cup and he was right. Rodri completed 756 passes there - the most in the tournament since records began in 1966.
His final season at Manchester City before departing for Barcelona ended in familiar fashion with a domestic cup double taking his trophy haul with the club to 14.
Lamine Yamal
Age: 19 Country: Spain
Club: Barcelona Position: Forward
Lamine Yamal continues to rewrite the record books with his astonishing exploits for club and country.
Just days after his 19th birthday, the Spaniard became the youngest footballer to have played in - and won - both a World Cup and a European Championship. The only players younger than him to play in a World Cup final are Brazil's Pele in 1958 and Giuseppe Bergomi for Italy in 1982.
For the second year running, his performances led to a podium place at the Ballon d'Or and at the same award ceremony he became the first footballer in history to win the Young Talent of the Year three years in succession.
At club level, he was named La Liga's Best Player courtesy of a starring role in Barcelona's title success. The teenager ended the season with an impressive 24 goals and 18 assists across all competitions.
He recently broke Kylian Mbappe's record for the most goals by a teenager in Champions League history.

November has been a frightening month for many people because it seems like the digital world is under attack.
With data breaches keeping entire airlines grounded and disrupting digital banking platforms, concern has quickly spread that AI advancements are fueling cyberattacks — though there has been no indication from government officials or the affected companies that AI was responsible.
According to Scott Wu, CEO of applied AI engineering firm Cognition, these problems likely won't stop.
"I do think it's worth it for the world to come to terms with the fact that on the current course that we are on over the next 6 to 12 months, there will be a lot of major breaches," he told host Patrick O'Shaughnessy on an episode of Invest Like the Best podcast on Tuesday.
Wu shared more details on his grim prediction, stating that Fortune 50 and Fortune 100 companies, as well as government institutions, will likely be at high risk.
He isn't the only one to express these concerns. The Center for Strategic and International Studies, a bipartisan think tank, recently wrote that the 2027 Congress will likely have a difficult job addressing the "dangerous data breaches" that have recently severely affected the executive branch.
Wu says that more breaches are coming.
"It's almost inevitable," Wu said. "I think there's still a big difference in whether we respond quickly to that and all these organizations start using a lot of AI for defense versus that just goes completely unchecked for the next couple years straight."
Before the data breaches began, viral AI doomsday scenarios had sparked waves of panic as some people worried it would wipe them out completely.
The recent breaches have fueled these fears, as the rapid advancement of AI models has raised concerns that hackers could use them to target US companies and institutions. Wu weighed in on this debate as well, explaining how AI breakthroughs may enable hackers to achieve new feats.
"No one has had the time or the level of effort or the ability to go and try every single option and understand what kind of attacks were possible until now," he said. "And now you have all these entire swarms going and doing attacks."
Wu highlighted the risks of the recent shift from single AI agents to entire groups or "swarms" that can work much faster, framing it as a breaking point for the technology.
He cited the July example in which OpenAI models breached the startup Hugging Face on their own, an incident that sparked strong concern in the tech community.
"How do you find that and catch that early and understand exactly what your agents are doing?" he said. "How do you set up the right restrictions and guardrails? This is something that every organization should want regardless of their view on safety."

Last week, international health authorities formally announced that the US had lost its measles-elimination status, meaning that the virus is once again endemic. But the official determination is a bit like getting the technical readout of a cracked dam while the country is already feet under water.
The national tally of measles cases is nearing 6,000 for the year, the highest count since 1991. Transmission is widespread, with 47 states and jurisdictions reporting cases. There have been 43 outbreaks this year, which account for 96 percent of the cases. Four states have case counts above 500, including Pennsylvania, which leads with 1,638 cases as of November 23. Nearly 650 people have been hospitalized nationwide. As of today, 14 people have died.
Deaths and transmission
On November 23, Pennsylvania’s health department announced its ninth confirmed death, an unvaccinated resident of Centre County. On November 24, Wisconsin reported its third measles death, an adult in Lafayette County. The report follows two other deaths in the state, an infant and a child. New York has also reported a death, which was of a 7-month-old baby. On November 20, Virginia reported the death of a child between the age of 0 and 4.
The virus isn’t slowing down. Measles is the most contagious virus known; it can linger in the air for up to two hours. Up to 90 percent of people who are not immune will fall ill after an exposure. People are considered immune if they’ve been vaccinated or previously infected. With slipping vaccination rates nationwide, the number of susceptible people is only growing.
To keep measles from getting a foothold in a community, vaccination rates need to be 95 percent or higher. According to the latest data, only 92.4 percent of US kindergartners were vaccinated with the measles, mumps, and rubella (MMR) vaccine in the 2025–2026 school year. Only 10 states have MMR vaccination rates at or above the 95 percent threshold. But even in those states, there are pockets and communities that are undervaccinated.

Jesse Eisenberg is reflecting on his work in Hollywood and why he has a very different experience with fans in public than some other actors.
In a new interview with The New Yorker, the actor, director, writer, and producer of The Debut said fans of his work are “mostly fine” when they see him in public, as his roles are not sexualized.
Eisenberg said in the interview that he goes to the New York Public Library, where he writes scripts. When asked if people interrupt him when they recognize who he is, he told the publication, “People are mostly fine.”
“It’s because there’s no sexuality to my work,” he added. “I think once the public is asked to want to sleep with a person onscreen, that person’s life is fundamentally different.”
Watch on Deadline
Eisenberg, who earned an Oscar for his role in Aaron Sorkin’s The Social Network as Facebook founder Mark Zuckerberg, recalled an interaction with a fan.
“I’d be out at a bar, and a drunk guy would say, ‘Hey, I love your website,’” he said. “And as I’m pretending to laugh, I’d just wish all of the oxygen would leave my lungs, and that I would collapse on the floor in front of this guy and show him what he’s doing to me.”
The actor didn’t return for the sequel, The Social Reckoning, and has been outspoken about his decision. Succession alum Jeremy Strong took on the role of Zuckerberg after Eisenberg declined.
Eisenberg’s The Debut opens in theaters on December 11, and the cast also includes Julianne Moore, Paul Giamatti, Halley Bailey, Colton Ryan, and Bernadette Peters, among others.
He did a great job in that movie and he looks like Zuckerberg. I understand.

Directors Laxman Utekar, Rajkumar Periasamy and Vishnuvardhan are set to collaborate with Indian studio T-Series chair and managing director Bhushan Kumar on three new films.
Title, story, cast and production details have not been disclosed yet.
Utekar directed the 2025 hit Hindi-language historical drama “Chhaava.” Periasamy won the best director prize at India’s National Film Awards for Tamil-language military biopic “Amaran,” while Vishnuvardhan’s Hindi-language war film “Shershaah” took the event’s Special Jury Award.
The three collaborations add to a busy T-Series pipeline that runs across Bollywood and South Indian cinema, with leading stars from both industries attached. Several of those titles are produced by T-Series, while others are presented by the company.
Under its own production banner, T-Series is backing Sandeep Reddy Vanga’s “Spirit,” which stars Prabhas, and an untitled Anurag Basu film with Kartik Aaryan. Also on the roster are Ram Gopal Varma’s “Police Company” and an untitled Milap Zaveri project pairing Aditya Roy Kapur and Tara Sutaria.
Kumar is producing “The Pride of Bharat – Chhatrapati Shivaji Maharaj,” a historical drama in two parts from director Sandeep Singh, with “Kantara” star Rishab Shetty in the lead. Aaryan has a second film on the slate, Shimit Amin’s “Captain India.” “Khosla Ka Ghosla 2,” “Karnika” and “Jaani Dushman” round out the list.
In the south, T-Series is presenting Hanu Raghavapudi’s “Fauzi,” which gives Prabhas a second title on the slate, and Prasanth Varma’s mythological feature “Jai Hanuman.” The company is also presenting Prashanth Neel’s “Dragon,” led by Jr NTR, and Sukumar’s next film with Ram Charan, which reunites director and star.
In all, the slate takes in action, romance, period drama and mythology, and spans both the Bollywood and South Indian industries.

Storms are disrupting Thanksgiving travel, with more severe weather expected to hit the East Coast on Thursday.
More than 6,500 flights within, into, or out of the US were delayed on Wednesday, and about 160 were canceled, according to FlightAware. As of about 1:30 a.m. ET Thursday, roughly 120 flights had been delayed and 300 canceled.
The National Weather Service wrote in a Wednesday report that the East Coast can expect "major coastal flooding, beach erosion, strong wind gusts, and heavy rainfall" during Thanksgiving.
Scattered power outages and tree damage are also likely, it added. A map from the weather service showed winter, gale, coastal flood, and wind warnings along the country's eastern coast.
NYC Mayor Zohran Mamdani wrote in a Wednesday X post that New Yorkers should expect severe weather on Thursday, including winds up to 60 miles per hour.
He said that, to protect New Yorkers, the city, along with Macy's and the local police department, had decided to postpone the 100th Annual Macy's Thanksgiving Day Parade to Saturday. This is the first time in history that the iconic parade has been rescheduled.
"The worst of the storm is expected to hit on Thanksgiving Day in the afternoon through the late evening," he added in his X post. He provided a list of steps New Yorkers should take to protect themselves ahead of the storm, such as staying indoors, moving cars away from coastal areas to higher ground, and budgeting extra time for travel.
The Transportation Security Administration said in a Saturday X post that it expects to screen nearly 17.6 million passengers nationwide between November 24 and November 30, including more than 3 million on Sunday, November 29. It recommended that travelers arrive early for their flights.
The Federal Aviation Administration wrote in a Wednesday X post that gusty winds may slow flights at LaGuardia Airport, Newark Liberty Airport, JFK, and San Francisco International Airport that day. It added that thunderstorms may cause delays at Miami International Airport and Fort Lauderdale-Hollywood International Airport.
Business Insider has put together a handy guide for passengers whose flights are canceled or delayed this weekend.

Young Americans are increasingly dependent on the stock market to build wealth as traditional paths to financial security become harder to access.
But one economist warns that historical market returns point to a potentially disappointing decade ahead.
Steven Blitz, the chief US economist at GlobalData.TS Lombard, wrote on Wednesday that long-term equity-return data suggest investors should expect zero returns over the next 10 years.
The warning comes as younger Americans face barriers to homeownership and savings deposits offer limited returns, leaving them increasingly reliant on equities to accumulate wealth for retirement, Blitz argued.
"Households' feeling that the economy fails to deliver is rooted in reality not imagination," Blitz wrote.
Millennials are particularly exposed because they rely more heavily on 401(k)-style retirement plans, whose value depends on investment performance, than traditional pensions.
Blitz found that millennials have $1.30 in such retirement benefits for every dollar in traditional pension benefits, compared with $1.05 for Gen X and just 59 cents for baby boomers.
Millennials also trail baby boomers in their asset-to-liability ratios at comparable life stages, though they are roughly on par with Generation X, according to the report.
Blitz argues that the growing importance of equities to household finances has implications for monetary policy.
The Federal Reserve traditionally influences economic activity through borrowing and lending costs, but household finances have become increasingly tied to equities rather than credit-driven spending, he said.
That dependence could also constrain the Fed's ability to tolerate a sustained stock-market downturn, Blitz wrote, because falling share prices could undermine household wealth and confidence.
"The economy is not broken, but it operates very differently, and policy has yet to adapt," Blitz wrote.

ఈ ఘటన నేపథ్యంలో, పోలీసులు కొంతమంది వ్యక్తులను ఊరేగిస్తున్నట్లు చూపించే వీడియో ఒకటి సోషల్ మీడియాలో (ఇక్కడ, ఇక్కడ, ఇక్కడ) వైరల్ అవుతోంది. ముంబైలో యువ జంటపై దాడి చేసిన వారిని పోలీసులు ఇలా ఊరేగిస్తున్నారని ఈ వీడియోను షేర్ చేస్తున్నారు. ఈ పోస్టులో చేసిన వాదనలో నిజమెంత ఉందో ఇప్పుడు పరిశీలిద్దాం.
క్లెయిమ్: ముంబైలోని కుర్లా వెస్ట్‌లో యువ జంటపై దాడి చేసిన నిందితులను ముంబై పోలీసులు రోడ్డు పై ఊరేగిస్తున్నట్లు ఈ వీడియో చూపిస్తోంది.
ఫాక్ట్: ఈ వైరల్ వీడియోలో గుజరాత్‌లోని సూరత్‌లో 18 ఏళ్ల సంతోష్ మోరే హత్య కేసులో అరెస్టైన నిందితులను చూపిస్తున్నారు. ఈ హత్య కేసుకు సంబంధించి సూరత్ పోలీసులు నిందితులను ఊరేగించారు. ముంబైలో యువ జంటపై దాడి చేసిన వారిని కాదు. కాబట్టి, ఈ పోస్టులో చేసిన వాదన తప్పు.
వైరల్ వీడియోలోని కీ ఫ్రేమ్‌లతో రివర్స్ ఇమేజ్ సెర్చ్ చేయగా, 2026 నవంబర్ 14న Gujarat Live అనే ఇన్‌స్టాగ్రామ్ ఖాతాలో అప్‌లోడ్ చేసిన వీడియో లభించింది. ఈ వీడియో ముంబైలోని కుర్లా ఘటనకు ముందే అప్‌లోడ్ చేయబడింది. ఆ వీడియోలో ఉన్న వివరణలో, సూరత్‌కు చెందిన యువకుడు సంతోష్ మోరే హత్య కేసులో అరెస్టైన నిందితులను చూపిస్తున్నట్లు పేర్కొన్నారు.
దీనిపై కీవర్డ్ సెర్చ్ చేయగా, వైరల్ వీడియోలోని దృశ్యాలతో కూడిన పలు మీడియా రిపోర్టులు (ఇక్కడ, ఇక్కడ) లభించాయి. ఈ రిపోర్టుల ప్రకారం, 8 నవంబర్ 2026న సూరత్‌లోని రసూలాబాద్ ప్రాంతంలో 18 ఏళ్ల సంతోష్ మోరేను కత్తితో పొడిచి హత్య చేసినట్లు ఆరోపణలు ఉన్నాయి. ప్రేమ వ్యవహారానికి సంబంధించిన వివాదం, గత కక్షల కారణంగా ఈ హత్య జరిగినట్లు సమాచారం. ఈ కేసులో జావేద్ అలియాస్ నవాబ్ షేక్, హన్సరాజ్ కుష్వాహా, షకీబ్ మానియార్, షాహిద్ షేక్, పీయూష్ సాహూలను నిందితులుగా గుర్తించారు.
2026 నవంబర్ 12న సూరత్ పోలీసులు తమ X ఖాతాలో అప్‌లోడ్ చేసిన వీడియోలో కూడా ఇలాంటి దృశ్యాలే కనిపించాయి. ఈ వీడియోలో అదే నిందితులను పోలీసులు ఊరేగించడం చూడవచ్చు. ఈ వీడియోకు జత చేసిన వివరణలో, ఖటోదరా పోలీస్ స్టేషన్ పరిధిలోని ఆజాద్ నగర్‌లో ఒక యువకుడి హత్య కేసులో నిందితులను ఖటోదరా పోలీసులు అరెస్టు చేసి, చట్టం గురించి వారికి గుణపాఠం చెప్పారని పేర్కొన్నారు.
చివరిగా, హత్య కేసులో నిందితులను సూరత్ పోలీసులు ఊరేగిస్తున్న వీడియోను, ముంబైలో యువ జంటపై దాడి చేసిన ఘటనకు సంబంధించినదిగా షేర్ చేస్తున్నారు.

Congress is looking increasingly likely to pass bipartisan legislation this year banning the import of Chinese autos, after the bill's Senate backers won over key parts of the auto industry.
The Connected Vehicle Security Act, sponsored by Sens. Bernie Moreno (R-Ohio) and Elissa Slotkin (D-Mich.), would ban US sales of cars that are made with components from adversaries like China and Russia. Moreno and Slotkin are aiming to pass the legislation by a voice vote in December, and are working with House colleagues to fast track the measure in that chamber, as well.
Senate leadership from both parties have already signaled support for the bill, according to a person familiar with the conversations, and Majority Leader John Thune (R-S.D.) helped advance the measure out of the Senate Commerce Committee earlier this year.
Getting European and US car companies, who had concerns about parts of the legislation, to line up behind it greatly improves the odds of that happening.
According to the same person and another familiar with the talks, the lawmakers agreed to tweak language in the bill to address concerns from several European automakers and their defenders, including GOP Sen. Rand Paul, whose state of Kentucky is an auto manufacturing hub and has courted more than $10 billion in investment from international automakers, according toAutos Drive America.
Discussions are at the "one yard line," said one of the people, with the substance of the changes resolved and only wording and text left to iron out. Like others in this story, they were granted anonymity to share details of the closed-door discussions.
A spokesperson for the Alliance for Automotive Innovation, which advocates for many of the largest automakers, including Mercedes, Volvo, GM, Ford and Stellantis told POLITICO the organization is "very supportive" of the bill.
Winning over the Kentucky senator, as well as others like Alabama Sen. Katie Britt, whose state is home to a Mercedes plant, is crucial to getting the unanimous consent in the Senate to pass the legislation by voice vote — a necessity given the end-of-year floor time crunch, as lawmakers race to complete votes on must-pass bills before this Congress expires.
Passing the legislation would be another sign of Capitol Hill's hardening position on China, in defiance of President Donald Trump, who has defended Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang amid a Chinese espionage scandal as he pushes to do more business with Beijing — and even mused about allowing Chinese car companies to build plants and sell their vehicles in the US. And it could further heighten US-China tensions as the administration continues to negotiate another extension to the two country's trade truce, which is due to expire on Jan. 10.
Chinese vehicles are already effectively blocked from the US market by steep 100% tariffs, first imposed by] Trump and raised by former President Joe Biden, as well as Commerce Department restrictions on vehicle components. But some in the domestic auto industry have been pushing Congress to codify the blockade to provide greater certainty and help firms make long-term sourcing decisions.
Moreno, Slotkin and the bill's other House and Senate backers have been negotiating with German manufacturer Mercedes, as well as advocacy groups that represent them, on provisions in the bill defining what qualifies as a Chinese vehicle, said the two people familiar and three others briefed on the talks. The original language banned sales of cars made by companies with more than 15% Chinese ownership. Chinese investors own nearly 80% of Volvo and 20% of Mercedes.
Paul told Reuters in September that he thought the bill unfairly singled out Mercedes, with its criteria for determining Chinese ownership.
Paul and Britt's offices did not respond to a question on whether they would support the legislation. The White House did not immediately respond to a request for comment on its position on the bill.
A GOP staff member who worked on the legislation and a second person familiar with the deal said that under the agreement reached with lawmakers, neither company would be blocked from selling cars in the US. The bill will now include more flexibility for companies with silent shareholders, like Mercedes, according to the people. Volvo has already been able to secure federal authorization to sell cars in the U.S. despite its China ties.
A Mercedes-Benz spokesperson declined to comment on whether a deal has been reached, but said the company "applauds the constructive discussions with key US lawmakers including Senator Moreno, Senator Slotkin and [Senate Commerce Committee] Chairman [Ted] Cruz (R-Texas)."
A Volvo Cars spokesperson reiterated to POLITICO that the company has "specific authorization to continue to sell connected vehicles in the US."
"We continue to monitor developments closely and we are actively engaged with policymakers on the potential business and consumer impacts of this US legislation," they added.
Lawmakers also kept batteries out of the list of components covered by the legislation and opted not to tighten restrictions on battery technologies, despite calls from parts of the domestic industry to do so. Ford Motor Co. resisted efforts for tighter curbs on batteries, which could have affected the US automaker's partnership with Chinese battery manufacturer CATL to license its technology.
Lawmakers will not include language on batteries in the final version of the bill, four of the people said. The language in the bill instead focuses only on battery management systems, which should leave Ford's partnership unaffected.
Ford declined to comment.
Negotiators also agreed to include a sunset provision for the vehicle ban, after some environmentally-minded lawmakers expressed concern that indefinitely banning Chinese cars, including the country's affordable electric vehicles, could slow decarbonization efforts, according to three of the people
This is "a freight train that's moving," said one of the people familiar with the discussions. "Slotkin and Moreno are putting people in rooms to make this stuff happen."

Suresh Mittal is 87. According to Uttar Pradesh’s latest draft electoral roll, his father, Vansh Mittal, is 23. Both are registered at house number 869 in booth 111 of the Dholana constituency in Hapur. The same roll lists Vansh as the son of Ajay, a 56-year-old in the same house.
Suresh is not an exception. Alt News found 1,10,875 voters in the Special Summary Revision (SSR) draft roll whose father or mother, registered in the same booth and the same house, is recorded as the same age as them or younger. The draft was published on November 17.
A Year of Revisions: First SIR, Now SSR
The draft comes at the end of a long year for UP’s voter list. The Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of the rolls began on October 27, 2025 and ended with the final roll on April 10, 2026. In those 166 days the state’s electorate shrank from 15.44 crore to 13.39 crore.
As per the process of SIR, every voter was supposed to be issued an enumeration form, which was supposed to be collected by booth-level officers (BLOs). The Election Commission’s software then allegedly went through the data looking for what it called logical discrepancies. One of these was a parent less than 15 years older than the voter. About 2.22 crore voters in UP were sent notices for such discrepancies, and the Commission says hearings were completed on all of them.
On October 15, six months after the SIR’s final roll, the Election Commission ordered a Special Summary Revision (SSR) in 17 states and Union territories, including UP. The SSR draft roll, which merges the SIR roll with all supplementary lists, has 13.58 crore electors. Claims and objections can be filed till December 16, and the final roll is due on January 4, 2027.
What We Found and How
The SSR draft rolls are machine readable. We took every voter whose entry names a father or a mother, and looked in the same booth for a voter with that name living in the same house. If that ‘parent’ turned out to be the same age as the voter, or younger, we flagged the entry.
We found 1,10,875 such cases spread across all 75 districts and 403 constituencies.
In 35,523 of these cases, parent and child are the same age. In the other 75,352, the parent is younger, and in 6,860 of them by 20 years or more.
Some of the cases are shown below for representation:
What did SIR Actually Achieve?
The SIR was designed to weed out exactly this kind of error. It had enumeration forms, BLO visits, software flags and hearings. A parent who is younger than their own child is perhaps the most basic inconsistency a voter list can have. This raises a larger question: if a process this elaborate left the most basic errors untouched, what did the SIR actually achieve?
Moreover, spotting these anomalous entries is no rocket science. Each one is a contradiction between two lines of the same booth’s roll, often on the same page: An 87-year-old whose father is 23, a 123-year-old woman whose mother is 45, two women who are each other’s mother. A simple check on the roll itself would have thrown them up. Either no such check was run, or nobody acted on what it found.
As of now, all 1,10,875 are in the draft, and the window for corrections closes on December 16.
