Around the world, people are increasingly choosing to have babies later in life for reasons both social and economic. As they get older though, they face a mounting biological challenge: genetic errors caused by chromosomes failing to separate correctly. This phenomenon, known as aneuploidy, is the leading cause of age-related infertility, failed in-vitro fertilization (IVF) cycles, and miscarriage, and it increases dramatically around the age of 40. Studies have shown that between 50% and 80% of embryos from women in their 40s carry chromosomal abnormalities.
One of the main drivers of aneuploidy is the loss of a protein complex called cohesin, which acts like a molecular glue holding chromosomes together. In a new study, researchers at the Max Planck Institute for Multidisciplinary Sciences in Göttingen, Germany, engineered a novel protein system capable of restoring normal chromosome connections in aging mouse eggs. The study, published Thursday in Science, raises the possibility of one day developing such a system into a treatment that could reduce aneuploidy in human eggs used for IVF.
“There is still work ahead, but their proof of concept was highly successful,” said Rajiv McCoy, a biologist at Johns Hopkins University who was not involved in the work. McCoy’s lab is focused on pregnancy loss, the leading cause of which is aneuploidy. It is estimated that about half of all human conceptions are lost before birth, including the roughly 15% of known pregnancies that end in miscarriage. Technologies that could reduce the odds of miscarriage and expand women’s biological reproductive windows by addressing aneuploidy would have far-reaching consequences for the IVF industry and for society at large. “The stakes are very high,” McCoy said.
When a cell prepares to divide, its chromosomes replicate, forming two copies, or sister chromatids, that are all lined up and organized by a cellular winch system known as the spindle. Within the spindle, the sister chromatids are tethered to each other by cohesin — its ring-like structure traps DNA from both sisters inside it. In most cells, cohesin only has to do this work for a few hours before other enzymes cleave it apart, freeing the chromatids to separate into two new cells. But in oocytes, cohesin has to keep this bond going for decades.
That’s because female babies are born with all the oocytes they will ever have. And already at birth, those 1 to 2 million immature egg cells have begun to divide, and the cohesin’s job is only finished when fertilization occurs. That triggers the end of the division process called meiosis in which the egg cells eject half their genetic material so they can fuse with sperm to make an embryo.
Over all that time, the cohesin molecule doesn’t seem to be reloaded, said Melina Schuh, a director at the Max Planck Institute who led the new work.
For the last two decades, Schuh has been finding new ways of peering into egg cells to better understand how meiosis works and what happens when it goes awry. In 2015, her lab showed for the first time how the structures holding chromosomes together deteriorate in human eggs as they age. Not long after, Schuh began to wonder if they might be able to engineer a system of proteins that could step in and stabilize the chromosomes in older eggs. Over the last eight years, her team tested many different designs before settling on one that did everything they wanted it to.
Called TALhesins, the proteins are designed to attach to specific DNA regions near the centers of each chromosome, tethering them together. The research team also baked a deactivation switch into the TALhesin system —based on cohesin’s natural cleavage sites — so that it would automatically release the chromosomes only when fertilization occurs. In experiments with eggs from older mice, the team found that the TALhesin system reduced premature chromosome separation, increasing the proportion of eggs with properly connected chromatids from 47% to 74% — a level comparable to that found in young mice.
Schuh told STAT her lab has already taken the next step of adapting the TALhesin system to bind to chromosomes in human eggs. “We have initial signs that there is a positive effect on cohesion,” she said. “But what we have not done yet is to really test in human oocytes whether we can reduce errors by stabilizing the chromosomes.”
That’s a critical next step, said Eva Hoffman, a molecular geneticist at the University of Copenhagen, who was not involved in the work. After that, researchers would need to establish that this method for reducing aneuploidy doesn’t introduce other kinds of problems. “The clinical potential depends upon regulatory aspects including safety studies for embryonic development,” Hoffman said. Even with the long road ahead, she commended the German group for generating data that challenges the conventional view of aneuploidy as a condition impossible (or impractical) to intervene in. “Since cohesion is established during fetal life and has to be maintained for decades, its depletion over time was thought to be irreversible,” Hoffman said.
Efforts to address age-related ovarian infertility are long overdue. For older women struggling to get pregnant, currently the only solution that’s available to most patients is to try IVF over and over. (For women between 35 and 40, the odds of getting pregnant are about one in three IVF cycles; for women over 40 it drops to one in ten.) This is both expensive and inefficient, and online support groups are overflowing with heart-wrenching stories of women spending a fortune and years of their lives on failed fertility sagas.
Many clinics also offer a panoply of “add-ons” — experimental treatments with shaky scientific backing — to boost the odds of having a baby. Some clinics overseas have even begun to market mitochondrial replacement techniques (MRT), a controversial method for reducing the risk of mitochondrial disease transmission, as a potential solution for age-related ovarian infertility. A recent STAT investigation found that hundreds of women in their late 30s and 40s have traveled to clinics in the Ukraine, Albania, and other parts of the world seeking MRT to boost the odds of IVF, despite scant evidence that it can overcome issues of aneuploidy.
Schuh has co-founded a startup, Ovo Labs, in Munich and London that has licensed TALhesin from the Max Planck Institute and is trying to commercialize the technology. A key hurdle is that most eggs retrieved in IVF have already undergone the first meiotic division, so cohesin loss could have already caused chromosome errors that can no longer be fixed. While retrieving and treating immature eggs appears to prevent some of these earlier errors, this then requires maturation of eggs in lab dishes, which is not widely used and has its own drawbacks, including that many eggs fail to mature successfully. Shuh is hopeful they can establish a system where oocytes are removed and treated a bit earlier — during the first phase of meiosis — which would require less time and fewer steps to mature.
Ovo Labs has competition from a U.K.-based startup called U-Ploid, co-founded by Schuh’s Max Planck colleague and study co-author, Alexandre Webster. U-ploid’s approach is slightly different, designed to preserve a cell’s natural structures for keeping chromosomes together.
Its lead candidate, Lyvanta, is injected into immature eggs prior to IVF.
Last month, at the 2026 meeting of the American Society for Reproductive Medicine, U-Ploid reported results from a study using immature eggs donated by patients at six U.K. fertility clinics. The study found that 65.5% of eggs treated with Lyvanta matured without detectable chromosome errors, compared to 35.7% of untreated eggs in a control group. The effect appeared in donors both under and over the age of 35, however eggs in that study were not fertilized. Lyvanta has not yet been tested in patients or demonstrated the ability to improve pregnancy or live birth rates.

For the first time in more than a year, the Food and Drug Administration has sent notices to companies for failing to report required clinical trial information.
The agency sends such notices when a trial sponsor fails to comply with a federal law that requires studies to be registered on ClinicalTrials.gov, a federal government database, within 21 days after the first human subject is enrolled. Summary results must also be posted to the database within 12 months after the trial’s primary completion date.
The FDA, however, has rarely sent noncompliance letters, despite years of criticism over lax enforcement. In recent years, calls for greater transparency have sparked a raft of studies showing a failure by drug companies, universities, and academic medical centers to comply with disclosure requirements. Following the Special Intensive Revision (SIR), the Special Summary Revision (SSR) is now underway in Uttar Pradesh, with the stated objective of preparing an error-free electoral roll. An analysis of Form 6 applications by Alt News, however, reveals a sharp and unprecedented surge in applications for inclusion in the electoral roll, with daily submissions rising from a few thousand in early November to over four lakh by November 22.
The SSR process began with the publication of the draft electoral rolls on November 17. About two weeks earlier, on October 30, Uttar Pradesh chief minister Yogi Adityanath had said at a BJP state working committee meeting in Lucknow that the names of around 1.27 crore Hindu voters were missing from the electoral rolls. He urged party workers to launch a systematic campaign to ensure their inclusion.
Again, on November 22, The Indian Express reported that Uttar Pradesh BJP had instructed its workers to focus on Form 6 additions in the SSR is to ensure inclusion of names of individuals eligible to be voters but left out during the SIR for some reason.
Tracking Form 6 application data from the SSR process, Alt News found that between November 1 and 16, an average of around 10,000 applications were submitted daily across the state. The numbers began rising sharply from November 17, the day the draft rolls were published, and accelerated dramatically over the following five days. On November 22 alone, around 4.16 lakh applications were submitted.
What Alt News Found
An analysis of Form 6 application data from Uttar Pradesh shows that around 2,000 applications were filed across the state on November 1. The numbers began rising the following day, with around 10,000 applications submitted on November 2. A similar number were filed on November 3 and 4, followed by 9,000 on November 5.
The state recorded around 12,000 applications each on November 6 and 7, before the figure dropped to 4,000 on November 8. Around 9,000 applications were submitted on November 9.
On November 10, 11 and 12, the daily figures stood at 15,000, 16,000 and 15,000, respectively. Applications declined to around 11,000 each on November 13 and 14, and further to 9,000 on both November 15 and 16.
The pace of submissions changed significantly on November 17, when the SSR process began and the draft electoral roll was published. Around 31,000 Form-6 applications were filed across Uttar Pradesh that day. The numbers climbed further over the next two days, with 46,000 applications on November 18 and 68,000 on November 19. On November 20, the figure stood at around 60,851.
The surge became even more pronounced from November 21, when around 2.31 lakh Form-6 applications were submitted. The following day, November 22, the figure more than doubled to approximately 4.16 lakh.
Who Are Filing these Applications?
Alt News’s analysis found that some of the new applicants had been deleted from the electoral rolls during the SIR.
To identify such applicants, the Alt News team matched new Form 6 applicants against the 2.89 crore names deleted during the SIR under the categories of absent, shifted, dead or duplicate.
Of the approximately 10.4 lakh applications examined between October 29 and November 22, Alt News found around 45,000 applicants whose names had been deleted during the SIR and who were now applying for inclusion in the electoral roll of the same assembly constituency. These applicants accounted for around 4.3% of all the applications examined.
Put another way, the 45,000 applicants represent approximately 1.6 in every 1,000 people whose names were deleted during the SIR (45,000 out of 2.89 crore). Most of these applicants had previously been marked as absent or shifted before their names were deleted.
A Closer Look at Form 6 Applications
A closer examination of the Form 6 applications reveals several serious anomalies, like instances of multiple applications carrying identical applicant details.
In Siwalkhas assembly constituency in Meerut district, for instance, 44 applications were submitted from the same address: “Gotka, Gotka, Gotka, Gotka, 250344, Sardhana.” All 44 applications were filed on November 5 and 6.
Alt News also identified 6,969 repeat Form-6 applications submitted between November 20 and 22.
These repeat applications were found within the same assembly constituency and carried identical applicant names and father’s or husband’s names.
For instance, in Bindki constituency in Fatehpur district, an applicant named Himanshu submitted five Form 6 applications. Four were filed on November 21 and another on November 22. All five applications carry the same applicant name, his father’s name, Baburam, and the same address.
The application serial numbers also show that three of these applications were submitted consecutively.
In another instance, Alt News identified an applicant named Aadhya Seth who submitted six Form 6 applications over three days, between November 20 and 22. In all six applications, the applicant’s name, father’s name and address are identical.
To identify similar instances, we matched applicants by name and their father’s or husband’s name within each constituency for the period October 29 to November 22. The exercise identified 10,773 individuals whose names appeared more than once, accounting for 11,684 additional applications.
According to Alt News’s analysis, approximately one in every 90 Form 6 applications was a repeat submission. The analysis also identified 427 individuals who had submitted applications in two different assembly constituencies.
The data shows that most repeat applications were filed on the same day, often in immediate succession.
A closer analysis also reveals that repeat applications increased alongside the overall surge in Form 6 submissions. On November 17, 18 and 19, the number of repeat applications stood at 340, 458 and 699, respectively. Before this, the daily figure had rarely crossed 400, reaching around that mark only on November 10 and 15.
On November 22 alone, however, 4,325 repeat applications were submitted. This means approximately one in every 100 Form 6 applications filed that day was a repeat submission.
Making Sense of the Surge
The overall volume of applications saw a sharp increase ever since the SSR draft role had been published. Between October 29 and November 22, a total of 10,56,778 Form 6 applications were submitted across Uttar Pradesh. Of these, 1,65,289 were filed between November 1 and 16, while 4,37,235 were submitted in just five days, between November 17 and 21.
On November 22 alone, the number stood at 4,16,380. According to data compiled by the Alt News team, more Form-6 applications were submitted on November 22 than during the first 20 days of November combined.
According to the figures available from November 20 to November 22, Kheri district (33,836) saw the most number of Form 6 applications. Other districts such as Ghaziabad (25,438), Agra (24,715), Barabanki (21,652), Prayagraj (21,433), Azamgarh (20,642), Bareily (20,625), Lucknow (20,369), Unnao (16,376) and Bulandshahr (16,217) also saw significant number of applications.
Interestingly, Ghaziabad and Bulandshahr showed zero entry on November 20. So all the applications for these two districts are from November 21 and November 22.
Ghaziabad district recorded the highest number of Form 6 applications so far on November 22, with 39,828 submissions. Other districts with substantial numbers of applications include Agra (39,091), Lucknow (32,324), Kheri (27,904), Prayagraj (19,764) , Azamgarh (19,135) , Fatehpur (18,253), Bulandshahr (18,120), Barabanki (15,782), Bareily (15,096) and Gorakhpur (12,474).
A similar trend was observed in constituencies such as Loni, Ghaziabad, Lakhimpur, Etmadpur, Zaidpur, Bangermau, Dadri, Chakia and Barabanki.
Across the state, an assembly constituency typically recorded an average of around 17 Form 6 applications between November 1 and 16. However, the average rose sharply to 496 applications on November 21 and further to 966 on November 22.
Amid this surge, however, some pockets of western Uttar Pradesh recorded no substantial number of Form 6 applications. For instance, in Bijnor district, eight constituencies recorded no Form 6 applications, according to the compiled Form 9 lists on November 20 and 21. In Muzaffarnagar, six constituencies recorded a similar trend on November 20 and 21, while 22 constituencies did so on November 22.
Similar patterns were observed in pockets of Saharanpur, Moradabad, Meerut, Rampur, Bulandshahr and Shamli, among other districts.
The Back Story
On April 10, the final SIR roll for Uttar Pradesh was published. The total voters in the state plummeted from 15.44 crores to 13.39 crores in the process.
In December 2025, Yogi Adityanath warned that nearly 4 crore eligible voters could be missing during the SIR, claiming that 85-90% of them could be BJP supporters. Following the publication of the draft electoral roll on January 6, which reportedly recorded around 2.89 crore deletions, the BJP expressed concern, particularly over urban constituencies, and mobilised workers to help voters re-enroll.
In January 2026, a Newslaundry report said that the BJP was worried that large-scale deletions in urban constituencies could affect its electoral prospects. In 50 constituencies, more than one lakh voters had reportedly been deleted, 47 of which the BJP had won in 2022. The final roll, published on April 10, 2026, contained approximately 13.39 crore electors, down from around 15.44 crore before the SIR, with several BJP minister held constituencies reportedly recording substantial deletions.
On October 30, Adityanath claimed that 1.27 crore Hindu voters were missing, citing discrepancies involving panchayat electoral rolls, welfare beneficiaries and young voters. He mentioned 66 lakh names allegedly present on panchayat rolls but absent from Assembly rolls, 55 lakh welfare beneficiaries and approximately 4.5 lakh young voters.
On November 14, the BJP reportedly set targets of restoring 10,000–25,000 voters per assembly constituency, with party leaders estimating that 40–80 lakh voters could be re-enrolled. Following the publication of the SSR draft roll on November 17, the party planned to launch a booth-level voter addition campaign from November 20.

As foreign troops withdraw from Somalia, could al-Shabab take over?
- Published
Somalia is facing a fresh test of its stability as foreign troops begin withdrawing, funding for its security forces comes under pressure and a bitter political dispute threatens to derail plans for the country's first direct democratic elections in decades.
The combination of challenges has raised questions about whether the government can defend itself against Islamist militant group al-Shabab while managing growing divisions among political factions.
Some analysts fear the situation could embolden al-Shabab, which is affiliated with al-Qaeda, and potentially allow it to seize control of the capital, Mogadishu.
The group already controls large parts of the country despite the presence of about 12,000 African Union (AU) military personnel supporting the government.
The withdrawal of foreign forces, alongside the activities of clan-based militias aligned with rival political factions, has heightened concerns about the government's ability to maintain control.
Ugandan troops, who make up the largest contingent of the AU force, began withdrawing last month, with the country expected to complete its withdrawal by next year.
Ethiopia, another major contributor to the AU mission with over 7,000 soldiers, is also reportedly planning to withdraw almost half of its contingent.
The US, which had earlier announced cuts to funding for the UN Support Office in Somalia (Uunsos) has since said it is extending it for a year. Washington contributes about a quarter of the annual budget of about $500m (£380) of Unsos, which supports Somali security forces, AU missions and individual troop-contributing nations.
With military support uncertain and the government facing mounting political challenges, analysts question whether Somalia's security forces are ready to stand on their own.
The concerns were heightened recently when al-Shabab claimed to have killed hundreds of elite Somali soldiers in an attack. The government acknowledged the attack but did not disclose the number of casualties.
Abdisalam Guleid, a former deputy director of Somalia's National Security Agency, tells the BBC the security situation is increasingly precarious.
He warns that the withdrawal of foreign troops could leave Mogadishu vulnerable to a takeover similar to that of Afghanistan by the Taliban in 2021, following the withdrawal of US and Nato forces.
"I don't think Mogadishu will be able to defend itself. The Taliban-style [takeover]… that's the most likely scenario I can envision now," he says.
Such a scenario has played out in Somalia in the past, Guleid explains.
In the early 1990s, clan-based rebel groups advanced on Mogadishu from several fronts, forcing then-President Mohamed Siad Barre from power.
His overthrow triggered a devastating civil war and a prolonged humanitarian crisis. The collapse of state institutions subsequently created conditions in which Islamist militant groups, including al-Shabab, were able to expand their influence.
Guleid says Ugandan troops have been central to preventing a similar collapse since their first deployment to Somalia in 2007.
They played a key role in driving al-Shabab out of Mogadishu and other major towns, while protecting strategic installations, including the airport, port, government institutions and diplomatic missions.
Troops from Burundi, Djibouti, Kenya, Sierra Leone and Ethiopia later joined the AU mission, while countries including Turkey and the US maintained separate military deployments and provided training and equipment to Somali forces.
But Guleid argues that years of international assistance have not translated into the Somali government becoming militarily independent.
He says the authorities have become so reliant on foreign protection that they have neglected to adequately prepare their own forces to take over.
Somalia's Information Minister Abdifatah Qasim Mohamud rejects suggestions that the country would be unable to cope with the withdrawals.
He tells the BBC that Somali troops had already taken over some positions vacated by Ugandan forces and were prepared to assume greater responsibility for the country's security.
He says Somalia cannot depend indefinitely on foreign troops for its protection.
"I believe there is no reason for concern over this issue. There will be no change in the country's security situation or in the areas they have vacated," he says.
President Hassan Sheikh Mohamud has also been seeking continued international backing.
During a visit to Uganda on 23 November, he and President Yoweri Museveni called on the international community to continue supporting Somalia.
Not everyone believes the withdrawal will necessarily result in a security collapse.
Ugandan security analyst Freddie David Egesa argues that years of international military support have helped Somalia establish the institutions needed to take greater responsibility for its security.
He says the withdrawal would provide an opportunity to assess how much progress has been made.
It would also force Somalia's political leaders to put aside their differences and take greater responsibility for the country's future, he added.
But other analysts warn that the timing could hardly be worse.
Omar Mahmood, an analyst at the International Crisis Group, says Somali forces are under considerable pressure as they fight al-Shabab while attempting to take over positions previously held by foreign troops.
This is a major undertaking for an army that was still developing, he says.
The military is also facing pressure in the Bay region of the South-West state, where forces loyal to ousted regional President Abdiaziz Hassan Mohamed have been fighting the federal government.
The withdrawal of Ugandan troops from the Lower Shabelle region could create further security challenges, Mahmood adds.
Mahmood further points to the long-delayed elections, which need to be secured, as another issue compounding the security situation.
Beyond the military situation, Mahmood says the government must also resolve a growing political dispute over the timing and format of the country's elections.
Somalia has been attempting to move away from an indirect electoral system in which clan elders select lawmakers, who then elect the president, towards a system of direct voting.
But the proposed changes have divided the government and opposition, with disagreements over how the elections should be conducted.
The dispute escalated this year after the president pushed through constitutional amendments extending the presidential term from four to five years, effectively delaying the next elections until 2027.
This month, the Supreme Court ruled against the extension, ordering political leaders to agree on an electoral roadmap within 30 days and to hold elections within three months.
The Somali government has rejected the decision.
A day before the ruling, the president dismissed Chief Justice Baashe Yusuf Ahmed. They have since challenged the dismissals at the East African regional court in Tanzania.
Mahmood says the political and security crises are closely connected, with the absence of consensus over the elections making it harder for the government to focus on the fight against al-Shabab.
Guleid also warns that the threat to Somalia's stability comes not only from the militant group but from clan-based militias increasingly challenging the federal government.
"Today, we have clan loyalists fighting alongside al-Shabab against the federal government," he says.
He adds that the country's leadership appears unable to anticipate the scale of the challenges ahead.
Who will fill the gap left by foreign partners?
Somalia's security challenges are compounded by its heavy dependence on international financial support.
Latest data from its finance ministry shows that donor grants account for two-thirds of its planned $1.36bn budget in 2026.
However, the ministry said it had only received about $314m of grants in the first nine months of the year, equivalent to just 35% of the expected annual aid.
Mahmood believes that although some international military support is declining, other partners could help bridge the gap through bilateral agreements and continued assistance.
But Guleid is sceptical that countries such as Turkey, Qatar and Egypt could quickly replace the military and financial contributions of Uganda and the US.
He argues that Somalia's dependence on external support makes it particularly vulnerable when international partners change their priorities.
That dependence has also contributed to increasingly strained relations with some foreign governments.
Somalia accuses the United Arab Emirates of funding armed groups and undermining its sovereignty, in the latest dispute involving an external power with significant security and economic interests in the country.
The UAE has rejected the criticism and hit back at the Somali leader, describing him as an "outgoing president" in reference to the dispute over his presidential mandate.
The two countries formally severed ties earlier this year, although the UAE has long been an important security and economic partner in Somalia.
For Egesa, the withdrawal of foreign troops could ultimately provide an opportunity for Somalia to demonstrate how much progress it has made in rebuilding its security institutions.
He believes the staggered departure of troops will allow Somali forces to assume responsibility gradually, while also forcing rival political factions to work together.
But Guleid remains far less optimistic.
He argues that unless Somalia addresses its military weaknesses, political divisions and growing influence of armed groups, it risks losing the security gains it has achieved in recent years.
For now, it faces the difficult task of fighting an entrenched insurgency, managing rival political interests and preparing for a contentious electoral process, all while some military partners are preparing to pull out.
Whether Somalia can withstand these pressures without renewed instability remains an open question.

On Tuesday, a US jury convicted one of China’s key telecommunications and AI giants, Huawei Technologies, of stealing trade secrets from US tech firms and evading sanctions against Iran.
Although the longrunning charges stem back to 2018, the verdict coming now threatens to inflame US-China tensions at a sensitive time, just as Donald Trump prepares to increase tariffs on China. In a press release, however, the US Department of Justice celebrated the outcome as critical to protecting the US financial system, the global telecommunications industry, and US national security.
The jury convicted Huawei of charges including bank fraud, conspiracy to defraud the US, money laundering conspiracy, and “substantive” violations of the International Emergency Economic Powers Act.
Among crimes, Huawei was found guilty of “repeatedly” lying to banks about its business in Iran. Huawei also frequently lied to the US government that “it did not assist Iran’s government, military, or intelligence community,” the DOJ said. In reality, the DOJ proved at trial that Huawei was conducting business in Iran under the name “Skycom” to evade sanctions, while providing Iran with “turnkey services with respect to an Internet backbone and broader accessibility for mobile networks.” Further, Huawei helped the Iranian regime “monitor and censor its users’ access to the Internet” and provided surveillance cameras to monitor protests, the DOJ said. In a statement, the acting principal deputy assistant attorney general for national security, M. Scott Proctor, said Huawei “empowered our enemies” and “harmed our national security.”
Huawei stole US trade secrets
As the DOJ successfully argued, Huawei lied about its Iranian business specifically so that it could continue obtaining billions in US dollars by participating in a global marketplace that gave it necessary access to steal US tech. Among companies targeted, US Attorney for the Eastern District of New York Joseph Nocella Jr. said that Huawei blatantly stole from T-Mobile and Cisco, as well as a semiconductor storage company called CNEX and an antenna manufacturer called Quintel.

In November, a claim circulated that Ukrainian officials found Nvidia hardware inside a Russian attack drone.
The claim spread after the U.S. technology company reappointed its CEO, Jensen Haung, who had resigned on Nov. 12 after reports of affairs with an employee and a suspected Chinese spy.
One X user who shared an image of an alleged Nvidia computer module found inside a Russian drone wrote (archived):
Ukraine has found Nvidia hardware inside Russian attack drones and a cruise missile. And Reuters found records showing that China's military bought restricted Nvidia chips. This is why the Nvidia scandal deserves a hell of a lot more attention.
The claim and image also circulated on Facebook and Reddit (archived, archived). Snopes readers contacted us about the rumor.
The image reportedly showed an Nvidia Jetson Orin computer module that the Defence Intelligence of Ukraine said (archived) in August came from a Russian cruise missile. Also in August, The New York Times, citing Ukrainian officials, reported that Russia used Jetson Orin modules to pilot drones using "an experimental artificial intelligence system" that chose its target without needing human approval.
The Times reported that one such autonomous drone killed three civilians in Zaporizhzhia, Ukraine, in July. This was remarkable for a number of reasons, including that Nvidia is a U.S. company that reportedly does not sell its products in Russia and that the U.S. has poured billions of dollars into aid for Ukraine since Russia's full-scale invasion in 2022.
At the time of this writing, Snopes found no credible evidence to suggest that the image that the Defence Intelligence posted in August and the Times' reporting on the strike in Zaporizhzhia were fake or false. However, due to a lack of primary evidence — in this case meaning confirmation from Russia of the authenticity of the Defense Intelligence of Ukraine's image and the Times' reporting — we leave the claim that Ukrainian officials found an Nvidia module inside an autonomous Russian drone unrated.
It was unlikely, given the ongoing war, that Russian authorities would provide the primary evidence Snopes would need to rate this claim.
We contacted the Russian Ministry of Defense to ask for confirmation of the image and Times report. We also contacted the Ukrainian Air Force to ask about any further developments involving Russian autonomous drones since the Times' August report. We await replies to our queries.

Our Jetson Orin modules are consumer-grade products sold to students, developers, and startups for a wide range of beneficial applications. Although we cannot track products after they are sold, if we determine that any customer is violating U.S. export controls, we will take appropriate action.
Times report on Russia using Nvidia products
According to the New York Times' report from August, Ukrainian officials were able to recover an "Nvidia chip" on the Russian drone that reportedly killed 19-year-old Tetiana Bubynets, 41-year-old Oleksiy Svirin and 48-year-old Roman Karpiy in the July 6 strike in Zaporizhzhia.
The Times reported that officials found "terrain images" on the chip that the drone used to track visual landmarks and stay on course to its target as well as descriptions of the targets it had been trained to identify and attack.
According to the report, both Ukrainian and Russian forces had previously used AI to pilot drones after a human had selected its target. However, fully autonomous drones like the one Russia allegedly used in the July 6 attack use machine learning, not human confirmation, to steer or approve a target, leaving the decision entirely up to AI.
Ukrainian officials were reportedly convinced that the July 6 drone was fully autonomous mainly because of the presence of the Nvidia module but also because it had no antenna, sent no radio signals and arrived in a wave of drones.
Kateryna Bondar, a senior fellow at the Wadhwani AI Center at the Center for Strategic and International Studies in Washington, reportedly told the Times that the Nvidia module was "the best proof" that Russia was testing fully autonomous drones and that the July 6 attack would be "the first documented case in which civilian deaths were caused by a Russian drone" outfitted with an autonomous AI system.
Resale market allows Russia to buy American tech
According to the Defence Intelligence of Ukraine, the Nvidia module found in the drone used in the July 6 attack in Zaporizhzhia was not the only product from the company that appeared in Russian weapons.
The Defence Intelligence's database tracking foreign components in Russian weapons listed at least nine different Nvidia components that Ukrainian officials had reportedly found in weapons used by Russia. Six of the nine were from the Jetson family of products.
The Times report included images of a Jetson Orin module that Ukrainian officials said they found in a separate Russian drone from the one that carried out the July 6 attack.
An Nvidia spokesperson said on Nov. 25 that Jetson Orin modules are "not available in Russia." The company reportedly suspended sales of all products to Russia after its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022.
However, as the company acknowledged in its statement, it could not control the secondhand market. In November, Wirescreen, a China-focused risk intelligence platform, reported on an established resale pipeline that allowed people inside Russia to buy products, including from Nvidia, that were not sold on the Russian market.
It's unclear how the Russian military managed to buy the Jetson modules Ukrainian officials later found in its downed weapons.
Rumors of autonomous drones cause international concern
Col. Serhiy Minaiev, the commander of air defenses in Zaporizhzhia, reportedly told the Times that the development of autonomous drones posed "a risk for the whole world" because machines rather than humans would decide when to strike and kill in war.
International organizations such as the United Nations and the International Committee of the Red Cross also regard autonomous drones with skepticism. In August, the organizations issued a joint call for nations to create legislation to govern autonomous warfare. At the time, U.N. Secretary-General Antonio Guterres called "the autonomous targeting of humans by machines" a "moral red line" that drones piloted by AI rather than humans risked crossing.
Members of the U.N. Security Council discussed the topic on Nov. 24 and 25. ICRC President Mirjana Spoljaric addressed this meeting on Nov. 24, pointing out the dangers of allowing AI to interpret international humanitarian law that governs warfare. Spoljaric said, "AI will not set its own limits in warfare. States must."

Mexico's president has accused the U.S. Drug Enforcement Administration of failing to tackle fentanyl and corruption within the United States, after the agency set up anonymous tip lines in her country.
President Claudia Sheinbaum made the accusations in harsh comments on Thursday, reading excerpts from a new investigation by The Associated Press.
That investigation revealed the DEA allowed at least 1.4 million counterfeit fentanyl pills to go unseized while spending eight months tracking a drug trafficking ring that was flooding the Southwest with deadly drugs.
“The DEA has plenty of work to do in its own country. A lot,” Sheinbaum said. “The first thing it should do is investigate corruption in the United States linked to organized crime, or what they call terrorist groups.”
The outburst came less than 24 hours after DEA Administrator Terry Cole announced the tip lines on his X account.
Cole encouraged Mexicans to denounce members of criminal networks in Sinaloa state, the corrupt officials who support them and people who launder money to finance narcoterrorism.
“Your information matters. Your identity and your safety matter,” Cole said, adding that tips submitted via Signal, WhatsApp and email would be handled confidentially.
Cole also said a channel for submitting tips about the state of Jalisco would be made public Thursday.
US offers to deploy troops in Mexico
Jalisco is a stronghold of the powerful Jalisco New Generation Cartel, known by its Spanish initials CJNG, which Washington also designated a terrorist organization.
The DEA did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
The United States has stepped up pressure on Mexico to fight the cartels and has even offered to deploy troops on Mexican soil.
Sheinbaum has ruled out that deployment while maintaining that there will be security cooperation with Washington, “but without subordination.”
On November 20, Mexican military forces captured drug lord Fausto Isidro Meza Flores, alias “El Chapo Isidro,” a key ally of a Sinaloa cartel faction who was on the FBI's Ten Most Wanted Fugitives list.
Mexico requested Washington's support for the operation, and the United States sent a drone to help gather information about the drug lord's whereabouts.
The U.S. has requested Meza Flores' extradition, but Mexican Attorney General Ernestina Godoy said he will be tried in Mexico.
Although cooperation between the two countries went smoothly in that operation, tensions arose between Mexico and Washington in late April.
Federal prosecutors in New York made public a drug trafficking indictment against Sinaloa Governor Rubén Rocha Moya, a member of Mexico's governing party.
He and nine other officials were accused of collaborating with a faction of the Sinaloa cartel, which the Trump administration has designated a foreign terrorist organization.
The ‘Fast and Furious of Fentanyl’
Amid the controversy, Rocha Moya took an indefinite leave of absence, and his bank accounts in Mexico were frozen.
Mexican authorities refused to carry out the U.S. request to arrest him.
Former Sinaloa Security Secretary Gerardo Mérida Sánchez surrendered to U.S. authorities in May.
DEA whistleblowers in June revealed how agents in New Mexico in recent years permitted hundreds of thousands of fentanyl pills to go unseized.
At the time, the DEA denied it ever knowingly allowed the trafficking of a synthetic opioid the White House has designated a “weapon of mass destruction.”
That denial was further contradicted by new findings that the DEA permitted at least 1.4 million additional pills to be trafficked between August 2024 and April 2025 as it closed in on the largest fentanyl bust in U.S. history.
The tally was based on thousands of pages of court documents, investigative records, detailed wiretap reports and 12 hours of DEA surveillance footage.
The footage showed dealers moving large packages of pills in plastic bins and duffel bags that passed through highly transited hotels, apartment complexes, Airbnb rentals and self-storage facilities in six states.
In her comments Thursday, the Mexican president called the DEA's decision to permit fentanyl to hit the streets the “Fast and Furious of Fentanyl,” a reference to the 2011 gun-walking scandal.
In that scandal, straw buyers smuggled some 2,000 assault weapons into Mexico with the intent of tracing the firearms to cartel leaders.
“What is the United States doing in the United States?” Sheinbaum asked. “We have a prosecutor’s office here, and the Security Ministry works here. So they should pay close attention to the other side of the border.”

Quick Answer
The Dreame X60 Ultra Complete offers powerful suction, heated-water mopping, a slimmer design, and smarter obstacle handling. At ₹1,34,999, it delivers an impressive cleaning experience with greater convenience, though the value of its premium features depends on your home’s needs.
When I reviewed the X40 Ultra, it was the first robot where I didn’t have to plan a backup round of cleaning. Months later, the L40 Ultra AE beat it on suction and mopping for Rs 20,000 less. The X60 Ultra Complete has to answer a question both reviews left open: what does a Dreame flagship do that the cheaper model does not?
On paper, quite a lot. It also costs more than twice what the L40 Ultra AE did, so the real question is whether the additions change daily cleaning in an Indian home or mostly change the spec sheet.
Table of Contents
Design and Build: Slimmer Robot, Smarter Moves
At first glance, the X60 Pro Complete looks like any other premium Dreame device. You get the familiar circular body, a large docking station, and a design that is more functional than flashy. But there’s one important difference. At just 7.95 cm tall, the X60 is noticeably slimmer than the X40 Ultra and L40 Ultra AE. And that’s thanks to the retractable navigation sensor that pops up when needed and slides back into the body when the robot needs to squeeze under low furniture.
This might sound gimmicky at first (remember OnePlus 7T Pro?), but it has a practical value. In 2026, most robot vacuums already do a decent job of cleaning open floors. The real challenge is getting under sofas, beds, and cabinets without getting stuck. The X60 needs just over 8 cm of clearance to enter these spaces with its sensor retracted.
The price of that slim body is a 235 ml onboard bin, which is significantly smaller than what we saw on the L40 Ultra (395 ml) and X40 Ultra (350 ml). That means the robot keeps returning to the dock to empty the bin more often than expected in heavy sessions, especially if you have a pet at home. Not a big deal, but the trips do add time.
The slimmer body isn’t the only trick up the X60’s sleeve. Dreame has also upgraded its obstacle-climbing system, allowing the robot to lift itself over raised thresholds and door tracks that might stop a regular robot vacuum. This is particularly useful in Indian homes, where bathrooms, balconies, and even some rooms have raised entrances.
Genuinely, this is a big step-up (pun intended) in the evolution of robot vacuums. But you should ask yourself this question: are the obstacles in your home tall enough to trouble a decent mid-range robot vacuum and require a top-of-the-line robot? So while the X60’s climbing ability is impressive on paper (single thresholds up to 4.5 cm and double-layer steps up to 8.8 cm), how much value it adds depends on the layout of your home. If your existing robot already moves between rooms without getting stuck, this upgrade alone won’t justify spending significantly more. In fact, your home’s layout, flooring, and the presence of pets matter far more than the specifications alone. We’ve covered these and other factors in our robot vacuum cleaner buying guide.
The dock is significantly shorter and wider than the L40 Ultra I tested last, and its gold-accented finish looks more at home in a living room than the matte black L40. The trade-off is the capacity: 4.2 liters of clean water and 3 liters of dirty water, down from 4.5 and 4 liters on the L40. The 3.2-liter dust bag is unchanged.
As I pointed out in my earlier Dreame reviews, the company continues to ship its robot vacuums with a bulky 16A plug, and the X60 Ultra Complete is no exception. Most Indian homes don’t have a 16A socket conveniently located where you’d want to place the docking station, making an adapter or a dedicated socket an unnecessary hassle for such an expensive product.
Cleaning Performance: Does the Extra Power Make a Difference?
Dreame has made a big deal of the X60 Ultra Complete’s suction power of 35,000 Pa, and understandably so. But having reviewed the X40 Ultra (12,000 Pa) and L40 Ultra AE (19,000 Pa), I’ve reached a point where raw suction figures don’t excite me as much as they once did. Both those robots were already capable of keeping my floors clean without much intervention. So with the X60, I was less interested in how much more powerful it was and more curious about whether that extra power translated into noticeably cleaner floors.
On tile and stone floors, the X60 Ultra Complete does an excellent job of picking up everyday dust, crumbs, and pet hair. The extending side brush also does a great job of cleaning along walls and around furniture legs, areas where robot vacuums often leave some dirt behind. Hair handling is noticeably better than on the X40 Ultra, which struggled with long human hair and clumps of dog fur.
Obstacle avoidance is something Dreame has mastered, and it’s no different on the X60. In my month-long testing, it easily avoided the usual suspects like cables, socks, and small toys. But that was the case with the cheaper L40 and X40 vacuums, too. While it handled thick carpets well, light fabric rugs were pulled towards its inlet a couple of times.
Two newer touches stand out on the X60 Ultra. The robot maps the house during its first clean, so there is no separate mapping run. Also, its proactive-light dirt detection spots hair and light liquids and adjusts cleaning. Image processing happens on the device, per Dreame, and the app shows when the camera is active.
Mopping Performance: Where the X60 Makes a Stronger Case
When I interviewed Manu Sharma, the head of Dreame India, he made an interesting observation: for Indians, a house isn’t truly clean until the mopping is done. And that’s where the X60 Ultra Complete brings some meaningful upgrades. Unlike the X40 Ultra and L40 Ultra AE, which used hot water only to wash the mop pads at the dock, the X60 actually mops the floor with water heated to 40°C. The pads spin at up to 230 RPM, apply 15 N of downward pressure, and extend towards walls and furniture legs to clean areas that regular circular mops often miss.
For everyday mopping, the results are quite impressive. Footprints, light spills, and the grime that builds up on floors throughout the day are handled well. Even some dried stains can be removed, although older, stubborn stains may need a second pass or a targeted zone clean. This is one area where the X60 makes a stronger case for its premium pricing, especially if you mop your floors daily rather than occasionally.
There is one catch, though. The X60 tends to leave floors noticeably damp after mopping. Not enough to make them dangerously slippery, but enough for water marks to show up on wooden-finish tiles. Thankfully, you can adjust the water level in the Dreame app, and I’d recommend starting with a lower setting before increasing it if needed. For homes with carpets, the mop pads can lift up to 21.5 mm to avoid wetting them. You can also have the robot leave the pads at the dock when vacuuming carpets, which is the safer option for thicker rugs.
Multifunction Dock: Almost Hands-Free, But Not Quite
A big part of what you’re paying for with the X60 Ultra Complete is its multifunction docking station. Once the robot finishes cleaning, the dock takes over. It empties the dustbin, refills the robot’s water tank, washes the mop pads, and dries them with hot air. This also makes the smaller onboard dustbin less of a concern, as the robot can return to the dock and empty itself whenever needed. It’s the sort of convenience that makes you forget how much work goes into keeping a robot vacuum clean.
But don’t mistake this for a completely hands-free system. During my testing, I had to refill the clean-water tank and empty the dirty-water tank roughly every other day. Your experience will vary depending on the size of your home, how often you mop, and the water settings you use. You’ll also need to replace the dust bag occasionally and clean the dock’s washboard and other parts. Then there are the recurring costs of dust bags, filters, brushes, and cleaning solution. Dreame includes a decent number of spare accessories in the Complete package, which is nice, but you’ll eventually need to buy replacements. For my usage of roughly 800 sqft home, that’s like replenishing every 6 months or so.
The dock itself is fairly large and needs a permanent spot in your home. Make sure there’s enough room to remove the water tanks comfortably, and preferably place it somewhere you won’t have to carry a tank full of dirty water across the house. These might sound like nitpicking, but when you’re spending this much on a robot vacuum, even small inconveniences are worth pointing out.
App and Battery Life: Plenty of Features, Room for Improvement
I’ve said this in my earlier Dreame reviews, and I’ll say it again. The Dreamehome app can do almost anything you want, but finding the right setting can sometimes be a task in itself. The X60 Ultra Complete is no different. You can clean individual rooms, set up no-mop zones, save up to four maps, and control the robot using Alexa, Siri, Google Home, or Dreame’s own “OK Dreame” voice commands. There’s plenty to play around with, but the app could really do with a simpler interface. Stain Recognition is still in beta, while Matter support is something Dreame has promised through a future software update.
There are some new pet-specific features, too. The X60 can recognize pet bowls, give extra attention to areas where pets spend time, and even locate your pet using its camera. You can also use the camera for live video and two-way communication. There’s an Apple Watch app for starting cleaning sessions and checking their status, along with phone widgets for quick access to cleaning routines.
As for battery life, the X60 packs a 6,400 mAh battery, the same capacity as the X40 Ultra and larger than the L40 Ultra AE’s 5,200 mAh unit. However, a bigger battery doesn’t necessarily translate into longer cleaning sessions, especially with all the extra features running. The good news is that charging is much faster than on the L40 Ultra AE. In my testing, charging times ranged from around 90 minutes to just over two hours, compared to roughly three and a half hours for the L40. Battery life itself isn’t particularly impressive for a flagship, especially in larger homes, but the robot can return to its dock, recharge, and resume cleaning from where it stopped. So, unless you’re in a hurry to get the entire house cleaned in one go, this shouldn’t be much of a concern.
Dreame X60 Ultra Complete Verdict: Worth the Price?
At Rs 1,34,999, the Dreame X60 Ultra Complete is not an easy robot vacuum to recommend, especially when the L40 Ultra AE costs less than half as much and already does an excellent job of keeping floors clean. But after spending time with the X60, I can see where the extra money goes. The slimmer design helps it reach places other robots struggle with, the improved obstacle-climbing system is useful for homes with raised thresholds, and the heated-water mopping is a meaningful upgrade over the X40 and L40. Add reliable vacuuming, better hair handling, excellent edge cleaning, and a multifunction dock that takes care of most of the dirty work, and you have a very capable cleaning system.
That doesn’t mean it’s without flaws. Despite the improvements, I still noticed some hair around the rollers. Mopping can leave floors wetter than I’d like, and stubborn stains may need another pass. The smaller 235 ml dustbin means more trips to the dock during heavy cleaning sessions, while battery life is good enough rather than exceptional. The Dreamehome app remains powerful but unnecessarily complicated, and the dock still needs regular attention. And yes, Dreame continues to ship a 16A plug, something I’ve complained about in my previous reviews. These aren’t deal-breakers individually, but they are harder to ignore at this price.
The X60 also faces some serious competition. In India, the Roborock Saros 20, Ecovacs DEEBOT X11 OmniCyclone, and Narwal Flow 2 offer their own take on premium robot cleaning. In the US, the Roborock Saros 20, Ecovacs DEEBOT X12S OmniCyclone, and eufy Omni S2 are worth considering against the X60 Max Ultra Complete. I haven’t personally tested these competing models, so I can’t tell you whether they clean better or worse than the Dreame. But based on their features, they’re certainly worth comparing before spending this kind of money.
And that brings me back to the question I raised at the beginning of this review. Does the X60 Ultra Complete do enough to justify its substantial premium over the L40 Ultra AE? For most homes, probably not. The L40 already handles everyday vacuuming and mopping well enough that the X60’s extra suction and smarter features won’t necessarily translate into noticeably cleaner floors. But if you have low furniture, tricky thresholds, pets that shed a lot, and want the most advanced cleaning system Dreame currently offers, the X60 makes a stronger case. You’re paying less for a dramatic improvement in cleaning and more for the ability to clean difficult areas with less intervention.
If you’re unsure which of these premium features you actually need, try our interactive robot vacuum buying checklist. It lets you choose features based on your home and cleaning needs, so you can decide where it’s worth spending more and where you can save.
The X60 Ultra Complete is an excellent robot vacuum, but it’s also a reminder that the best robot vacuum isn’t necessarily the most expensive one. It’s the one that cleans your home well enough that you stop thinking about cleaning. And Dreame had already come remarkably close to achieving that with its cheaper models.

- Multifunction dock reduces manual cleaning effort

- Mopping can leave floors noticeably damp
- Dreamehome app remains overly complicated
- Bulky 16A plug remains an inconvenience

The Best Keyboards for Work and Play
Featured in this article
Keyboards are important. Regardless of how little you might think about yours, you probably use it every day. A keyboard that’s comfortable and easy to use is indispensable and helps you not only do good work—but enjoy doing it as well.
Because we already have a separate guide focused on mechanical keyboards, this list instead places more focus on lower-profile keyboards and other non-mechanical options aimed at a more casual typist. There’s a greater focus on typing comfort and efficiency, instead of typing feel, and less emphasis on customization options like hot-swap sockets or keycap accessibility.
Be sure to check out our other peripheral guides for more, like the Best Mechanical Keyboards, Best Hall Effect Keyboards, Best Mouse, Best Ergonomic Mouse, and Best Computer Monitors.
Updated Noember 2026: I've added the Wallhack K-001 and Keychron K2 HE Concrete Edition to my top recommendations, as well as the Keychron V6 Ultra 8K Hybrid to my honorable mentions. I've also included a couple of recent keyboards I've reviewed that I would suggest avoiding entirely.
Other Keyboards We Like
Keychron V6 Ultra 8K Hybrid for $164: By introducing a true “hybrid” keyboard, Keychron has resolved its largest issue with Hall effect keyboards: lack of customization. Along with being compatible with standard MX-style mechanical switches, Keychron also claims the V6 is compatible with “95 percent of mechanical switches on the market.” Although it’s hard to prove that number exactly, this opens up a vast world of customization possibilities, along with providing significantly more options for repairs in the event of a switch failing. Beyond this, it also means you can have access to both mechanical switches with a tactile bump and highly customizable Hall-effect switches without needing two keyboards.
Happy Hacking Keyboard Classic Type-S for $222: The Happy Hacking Keyboard lineup has never been known for cost-effectiveness. This is shown especially with the Pro Classic Type-S, a nearly-$300 keyboard with wired-only connectivity and a distinct lack of bells and whistles. However, the unique layout and Topre switches can pretty much only be found here, and make for a unique tactile typing experience that can’t be matched by many other keyboards. Plus, the massive aftermarket community for Topre keyboards means both repair and customization are incredibly easy and well-documented. They’re a bit pricey, but one of these keyboards could last the rest of your life with a bit of care.
Wooting 80HE for $200: While the technology falls a bit behind the 60HE V2, the 80HE’s larger layout still makes it a fantastic option for anyone who isn’t quite ready to get rid of their F-row and arrow keys. The switches feel great, the magnesium case is incredibly robust, and the Wootility customization interface is both straightforward and incredibly powerful.
Logitech Pro X TKL for $140: Logitech makes great keyboards, and the G Pro X TKL is among the best gaming keyboards. It has vibrant RGB LED-backlit keys, a choice of clicky, tactile, or linear switches, and it uses Logitech’s Lightspeed wireless adapter for competitive gaming-level response time. The build quality of this keyboard is slick and stylish. It’s minimal and doesn't take up much space on your desk, and it has a subtle metallic rim around the edge that gives it a little flair that most plain keyboards lack. The volume wheel in the upper right is smooth and easy to reach, and along the top are handy media controls so you can pause your music when you finally get into a game after a long queue. For my tastes, the more clicky-clacky a keyboard, the better, and the Black Clicky switches have served me well. Each keypress feels like I'm sending tiny thunder down to my game. However, if you prefer something softer, you can choose another switch type. The only thing I dislike is the lack of a numpad—yes, I’m one of those weirdos who prefer having a numpad.
Logitech Pro X 60 for $130: The Pro X 60 (8/10, WIRED Recommends) has virtually all the benefits of the Pro X TKL in a smaller, more compact package. It keeps the volume wheel, Game mode switch, and Bluetooth/Lightspeed buttons by moving them to the edges of the keyboard, while slimming the whole thing down to a 60 percent layout.
Logitech Pop Keys for $67: The Pop Keys (9/10, WIRED Recommends) is a vibrant line of wireless keyboards that come in a wide variety of color palettes that are delightful. It also uses Logitech's system for pairing with up to three devices, making it simple to take it between your PC and laptop, or from home to work and back.
Logitech MX Keys S for $110: The MX Keys S can pair with three devices, making it easy to swap between computers. Its low-profile chiclet-style keys are comfortable, and it uses proximity sensors to activate the key backlight when your hands get near, so it's easier to see in the dark without wasting battery when you’re not using it. It supports both Mac and Windows layouts, and the keys are tastefully labeled in a way that it’s clear no matter which one you’re using at the time. Battery life is also fantastic, lasting well over a week with normal use, though it gets quite a bit longer life if you disable the backlight.
Logitech MX Mechanical for $142: With an understated, low-profile design, you can pair the MX Mechanical with up to three devices at once and swap with the push of a button. There are even a few convenient extra buttons just above the numpad to launch a calculator or lock your desktop.
Turtle Beach Vulcan II TKL Pro for $150: The Vulcan II TKL Pro has two LEDs per key, giving it a better resolution for lighting effects. It features Hall effect switches, which should cut down on wear and tear. They’re still satisfyingly clicky, and the volume knob has a comfortably grippy texture. I prefer any keyboard with a volume wheel to one without.
Corsair K65 Plus for $100: This 75 percent keyboard has some of the softest, most comfortable keys of any board I’ve tested. It’s lightweight enough to toss in a bag but sturdy enough to be your desktop keyboard. It can connect via USB-C, Bluetooth, or a wireless dongle that can be stored in a slot on the rear. A stylish metal volume knob adorns the top-right corner, and every keycap and switch can be swapped out using the included removal tool.
Razer Huntsman Mini for $65: A 60 percent keyboard has 60 percent of the keys normally found on a regular-size keyboard. The numpad and arrow keys are chopped off, and you’re left with the essentials. The Razer Huntsman Mini is one of my favorites of this size for gaming. It feels every bit as responsive and quick as a full-size keyboard, but it takes up a lot less desk space. There’s just something neat and orderly about it. Plus, like the larger Huntsman Elite, the Mini is compatible with Razer’s keycap kits, so you can customize your color scheme.
Keychron Q1 HE for $212: The Keychron Q1 HE (9/10, WIRED Recommends) is one of the best boards we’ve tested that uses Hall effect switches. You can customize the actuation point to either make keys more sensitive—so you don’t have to press them all the way down for keystrokes to register—or less sensitive, to avoid those fat-finger moments that can ruin competitive games. Keychron even has rapid-trigger settings that allow you to press a key multiple times without the key having to return fully to its resting position. Even outside the benefits of the Hall effect switches, this is another great keyboard in line with the kind that Keychron is known for, so it’s worth a look even if you don’t want to pay that much attention to every aspect of your keys.
NZXT Function 2 for $50: The original NZXT Function was a great way for anyone interested in mechanical keyboards to jump in without getting overwhelmed. The follow-up Function 2 (8/10, WIRED Recommends) improves on it in almost every way. It upgrades the keys to optical switches and comes with a spare set of switches that have a little more (or a little less) resistance, so you can customize specific keys based on your needs. I found this particularly useful for games like Overwatch 2, where I’d like to cut down on those fat-finger ultimates that are so embarrassing. The Function 2 retains many of my favorite features from the first model. It has the same left-side volume roller, super-soft keycaps, and convenient buttons along the side of the keyboard. If you’re interested in mechanical keyboards but are intimidated by phrases like “actuation force,” this is a great board to get started with.
Razer Huntsman V3 Pro TKL for $132: The Huntsman V3 Pro TKL is a robust keyboard for those who like to tweak their gaming setup. It uses Razer’s analog optical switches, which are satisfyingly clicky. On the top right, there’s a media knob that controls the volume, which you can also click to mute. However, it’s the buttons around it that are most interesting. To the left, there are two programmable macro keys you can use to customize different commands for your games (or your work). Below, on the navigation keys, are six profile shortcuts. Hold Fn and press one of them, and you can swap between several preset profiles, tailored to specific gaming needs like FPS mode, Racing mode, or High-Sensitivity mode when you need to pull off that hair trigger. All of this can be customized in the Razer Synapse app. We’ve tested a lot of keyboards with different customization options, but this one is particularly good for gamers who swap profiles a lot. The keyboard connects using a USB-C cable, included with the device, and it also comes with a magnetic wrist rest.
Razer BlackWidow V4 75% for $126: The Razer BlackWidow V4 (8/10, WIRED Recommends) has a sturdy metal casing, hot-swappable switches, and Razer’s robust Synapse software for customizing your keyboard. It’s also earned our top marks if you’re looking for a mechanical keyboard specifically for gaming. The 75 percent layout is small enough that you can leave plenty of room for your mouse, making those flicks to land a headshot that much easier in competitive games. The 8,000-Hz polling rate also helps cut down on the times that you miss activating an ability by that almost imperceptible fraction of a second.
SteelSeries Apex Pro for $150: Rather than choose one switch for the Apex Pro keyboard, SteelSeries decided to allow them all. Not only is it a colorful gaming keyboard with lots of bells and whistles, but it also features mechanical switches that can be customized per key to give you a typing experience unique to you. Plus, it has a little LED display for system alerts, volume, and other fun stuff you can toy with using SteelSeries’ included software.
Keyboards to Avoid
Keychron Q16 Ceramic Keyboard: Unlike the other novelty-focused keyboard on this list, the Keychron Q16 (5/10) falls a bit short in terms of user experience. The outer case and the keycaps are made of a plasticky ceramic that feels unpleasant to type on, and the sound profile is equally underwhelming. Ultimately, this keyboard feels less like an earnest effort and more like an attempt to chase the trend of ceramic keycaps from brands like Cerakey.
Logitech G512 X 98: While a hybrid mechanical/Hall effect keyboard may sound like a great all-around solution, it really only works as a regular keyboard when the feeling between the switches stays consistent. That’s exactly where this keyboard falls short: The “tactile” model I tested only had mechanical switches with a tactile bump, while the Hall effect switches were linear. When trying to type or do other productivity work, the two ended up constantly clashing. This means you either have to put up with an unpleasant typing experience or you’ll always have to swap out switches and recalibrate when moving between work and play.
Razer Pro Type Ergo: While this keyboard is solid and feels good to type on, the $200 price point seems far too high for what it is. Having a plastic case and laptop-like chiclet-style 66 keys, it won’t blow your socks off. Unless you desperately need Chroma RGB lighting, or have some other reason to stay within the Razer ecosystem, there are much more affordable options that offer nearly identical usability.
What Kinds of Keyboards Are There?
Generally, keyboards are defined by two specific design choices: the layout and the type of switches they use. A switch is the mechanism underneath a key that controls how the switch is pressed down. The layout can easily be seen by looking at a keyboard, but the switches can be a bit more difficult to guess from general observation. Here are the most common you’ll see:
Scissor switches are among the most widespread types of keyboard switches available today, found in nearly every consumer laptop and countless slim keyboards, including the Apple Magic Keyboard. These switches are incredibly compact and have a short travel distance, which makes them ideal for anything portable. Their low profile, flat shape, and short travel distance means they can be quick to type on, but they often lack the enjoyable tactile experience of a thicker keyboard. These switches are often also referred to as chiclet switches, a not-quite-accurate name that comes from the small amount of space between each key.
Membrane switches are one of the least expensive switches to manufacture, and are widespread even today in schools and offices. They typically consist of a sheet of rubber domes with electrical contacts inside of them, which then have keycaps put on top. When one of these keys is pressed down, it compresses the rubber dome and registers a key press. These keyboards are waterproof and reliable, but they have a key press that is typically described as mushy and unpleasant.
Mechanical switches are fairly widespread in enthusiast circles, but the actual definition of a “mechanical” switch is debatable. However, for this guide’s purpose, a “mechanical switch” will typically refer to a switch that uses the same design as a Cherry MX switch and has a metal “leaf” on the inside, which is two pieces of metal that are pressed together to register an input. ThereminGoat has a great in-depth guide on how a mechanical switch works and what all the components do. There are three main types of MX-style mechanical switches, tactile, linear, and clicky, that we discuss in-depth in our mechanical keyboard buying guide.
Low-profile mechanical switches rely on principles similar to a standard mechanical switch, but they compress the movement into a much shorter switch. They typically have a shorter key press, use unique keycaps, and are less standardized than full-size mechanical switches. Because they’re shorter, they are typically used for either low-profile keyboards or uniquely shaped keys on a standard keyboard (like the mouse buttons on the HHKB Studio).
Hall effect switches are typically similar to mechanical switches in shape, and will feel comparable to type on, but the key difference is how they register an input. A mechanical switch requires physical contact between two components, while a Hall effect switch uses magnets and sensors to determine whether a key has been pressed down. With most Hall effect keyboards, the sensor can detect how far the key has been pressed, and you can actually program the keys to only register an input at a certain distance, or even to register multiple inputs at different distances. By comparison, a standard mechanical switch will only register an input at a predetermined distance. While a Hall effect switch may seem like an all-around upgrade compared to a mechanical switch, there is still a trade-off: Nearly every Hall effect switch available is linear, which means there is no bump or click when the keyboard registers an input. Beyond that, because of small differences in their internal designs, many enthusiasts prefer the typing feel of a mechanical switch.
How to Choose a Keyboard
There are so many factors to consider when picking the right keyboard for your needs that it can get overwhelming. Not everyone has the same needs, and many aspects of a keyboard can seem universally desirable to some while being utterly polarizing to others. Here are a few things to keep in mind:
Mechanical, or no? If you like big, clicky keyboards with raised keys that make a statement, mechanical keyboards might be for you. This is also a rabbit hole that many nerds have lost themselves in, so it can be overwhelming to dive into the nuance of all the different styles in this subgroup. If you’re more a fan of the flat, chiclet-style keyboards found on low-profile keyboards (and laptops), you can save yourself a lot of time by skipping the mechanical keyboard rush. On the other hand, if you do want mechanical, we have a few in this guide you can check out, but we also have a dedicated Best Mechanical Keyboard guide you should peruse.
Wireless or wired? Wired keyboards have the advantage of never dying and never needing to be charged up. The disadvantages are, well, obvious. If you need a wireless keyboard to take with you to the office and back home, or just want more flexibility on your desk, then make sure to check a keyboard's battery life, what kind of batteries it uses (rechargeable is usually better), and what kind of system it uses for recharging.
Wireless connectivity options. Some wireless keyboards use a 2.4-GHz USB dongle to connect to your PC or laptop, which often means more reliable signal strength, while others use Bluetooth to connect to a wider range of devices. Bluetooth keyboards in general are pretty great these days, so it’s not a huge sacrifice, but pay attention to how you need to connect the keyboard to your devices when making a purchase.
Number of device connections. Similarly, some wireless keyboards can remember multiple devices they connect to and swap between them with the press of a button. If you have a desktop, a laptop, and a work computer you want to use one keyboard with, it’s a good idea to check how many devices your keyboard can remember when making your choice.
Polling rate. As mentioned, this refers to how often per second your computer receives a signal from your keyboard. Modern keyboards already approach 1,000 Hz (or once every millisecond), which is faster than what most people ever need. However, if you play a lot of fast-paced competitive games online, having a higher polling rate (commonly approaching 8,000 Hz, or eight checks every millisecond) can reduce the time between when you press a key and when the game registers it. Which, when you're dodging headshots, can mean the difference between life and virtual death.
Software. With most keyboards today advertising extensive customization options, it’s important to be sure these adjustments can be done easily and quickly. Some keyboards have great customization software with explanations, tool tips, and intuitive systems to make adjustments, and some don’t. Software like Razer Synapse, Keychron’s Launcher, and Wooting’s Wootility are some of my favorites, and I’d definitely recommend doing some research on your keyboard’s software before locking in your choice.
The Keyboard Terms You Should Know
Hz, or hertz, refers to the polling rate of a keyboard. In essence, this number is how many times the keyboard communicates with your computer in one second. Your average computer peripheral operates at 125 Hz, while higher-end equipment with a focus on speed can operate upwards of 1,000 Hz. Realistically, for everyday use, 125 Hz is perfectly serviceable. Having something higher can be beneficial for gaming, and can potentially feel smoother, but the difference is not as important as you would think.
2.4 GHz, short for 2.4 gigahertz, is a radio frequency that computer peripherals use to communicate wirelessly with a USB dongle. Most keyboards with 2.4-GHz connectivity will also have Bluetooth connectivity, but there are many keyboards that have Bluetooth without 2.4 GHz. There are many differences between how the two operate and how they perform, but the main ones are connection quality and convenience. A Bluetooth connection will often operate at a lower polling rate, such as 125 Hz or 250 Hz, but can connect directly to a Bluetooth-enabled device without a dongle. A 2.4-GHz connection, on the other hand, can operate at much higher polling rates (some devices exceed 1,000 Hz) but will require a USB port to plug a dongle into. For either connection method, the wireless range is dependent on the individual device.
Gasket mounting is a method of keyboard construction that has become popular in recent years. In a gasket-mounted keyboard, the internal assembly of the keyboard is not directly screwed into the case. Instead, rubber gaskets are placed along the edges of the top and bottom halves of the case. These press together around the internal assembly and hold it in place once the two halves have been screwed together. This allows the internal assembly to move up and down slightly when typing, along with absorbing the vibrations of typing. This kind of assembly typically results in a softer and more satisfying typing experience, while also improving the sound of the keyboard by removing any extra noises.
Function layers are secondary layouts on a keyboard that allow for inputs that don’t have dedicated keys on the keyboard. These are often accessed by holding down a key labeled “Fn” or “Function,” then pressing another key. Function layers allow for multimedia controls, setting adjustments, or access to keys like F1 through F12, or arrow keys, if they were removed from the keyboard to save space.
How I Test Keyboards
I test each keyboard on this list for an extended period of time: at least a week, and often longer. I test each under a diverse set of conditions including gaming, writing, internet browsing, video and photo editing, and even some programming. During this, I take extensive notes on how a keyboard behaves, what works, and where I run into trouble. Once I’ve finished testing a keyboard in real-life situations, I compare it to other keyboards to see how it stacks up, and I typically try to disassemble each keyboard and critique its internal assembly.
When determining what goes in this guide, I take multiple different aspects into account. The largest priorities to me are build quality, typing experience, and ease-of-use: A solid keyboard that feels good to type on will typically score better than a flimsy and boring keyboard, even if the flimsy keyboard has fantastic software, style, or typing sound. However, all of these metrics come into consideration, and if a keyboard totally fails in a certain category, that can still take it out of the running.
Keyboards are subjective, so I try to approach each review with an open mind. Even if I don’t like typing on a keyboard, I always try to imagine a user who might like it, and I evaluate its design choices from that perspective along with my own. Ultimately, you will know better than anyone else whether a keyboard is a good fit for you.

Salah scores twice as Egypt and Nigeria win Afcon 2027 qualifiers
