Much of the focus for human-caused climate change is on fossil fuels, which are creating most of our problems. But land use change is also a large component of the story, accounting for about one-third of total historical CO2 emissions. Deforestation plays a major role here, but practices like draining wetlands also factor in. Exactly how much of our history of eliminating wetlands has contributed to warming is challenging to figure out. But thanks to new sources of data that measure emissions from today’s surviving wetlands, it’s possible to put a better number on it.
A new study led by Jevan Yu at MIT focuses on peatlands—environments like bogs and fens where organic matter accumulates into thick layers of material. Some 600 billion tons of carbon are held in these vast stores of peat, which is more than you can find in all the world’s living vegetation, the researchers note.
Because these areas are permanently inundated, any oxygen in the water is quickly used up, leaving the job of decaying all that organic matter to anaerobic bacteria that work much more slowly and don’t digest everything. So instead of seeing organic carbon turning into the CO2 gas released by aerobic bacteria, in peatlands, a subset of it gradually turns into methane gas. Methane is an even more potent greenhouse gas than CO2 itself and ultimately gets oxidized into CO2. That means there’s a little trade-off from peatlands—most of the carbon they have is kept out of the atmosphere, but the carbon that does escape does so as methane.
Many peatlands have been drained by digging ditches that let water flow out to repurpose the land for agriculture or other uses. That lowers the water level, supplying oxygen to the exposed peat and ringing the aerobic bacteria dinner bell. Methane emissions get turned down, and CO2 emissions get turned way up.
History re: peats
The researchers used recent studies that measure gas emissions from peatlands to build a global model that estimated CO2 and methane release as the water level drops. The two gases respond differently to a given drop in water level, and CO2 in particular responds differently depending on where in the world the bog is located. Using reconstructions of water-level changes due to historical peatland drainage, the team ran their model starting in 1800.

Chiwetel Ejiofor started his film career by doing something that many would consider as the absolute peak: he made a film with Steven Spielberg.
“Amistad” was his very first film and, understandably, he was afraid of peaking too soon.
“I was definitely worried about it at the time,” he said at Torino Film Festival.
“You feel that there are stages to how you develop as an actor and the opportunities you get, and you think they might follow a very linear path. But of course, my first film role was with Steven Spielberg. I realized then, very early on, that it’s a deeply unpredictable profession. You can either feel disquiet or anxiety about that, or you have to go with it.”
He added: “The opportunities can be sporadic or come from different places and angles that you didn’t imagine. Part of the challenge, but also the exciting thing about being an actor, is having the capacity and ability to roll with it, to travel on the journey of it and see where it takes you.”
The British actor came to Italy to receive the Stella della Mole award for lifetime achievement.
He admitted that, for the longest time, he didn’t see himself as a film actor.
“Even though I had done the Steven Spielberg film, I still thought of myself primarily as a theater actor. I worked with the National Theatre in Great Britain, in the West End and with many off-West End theater companies,” he said. In 2008, he won the Laurence Olivier Award for best actor for “Othello.”
It took Stephen Frears’ thriller “Dirty Pretty Things” – which screened at Torino Film Festival on Thursday – to finally change his mind. Frears also received an award at the festival this week.
“I think it was around that time when I started to fall in love with film as well, with film acting and the rhythm and poetry of cinema. A lot of that had to do with Stephen Frears and Chris Menges, who was the cinematographer on that film. It became something that I started to pursue.”
For a while, he was able to “balance the two very well.”
“It was when I became more involved in writing and directing that it started taking up a lot of my time outside of acting in films. Historically, this would have been the time I spent on stage. I ended up writing or directing my own films.”
Ejiofor has directed two feature films: “Rob Peace” and “The Boy Who Harnessed the Wind.” But his return to theater is imminent.
“It’s still something that I’m very passionate about. Finding the time to do as much theater as I want can be challenging, but it’s something I’m in the midst of conversations about.”
He hopes to be involved in another theater production later on next year. In the meantime, he’s happy to reflect on some of the highlights of his career, which includes Oscar-winning “12 Years a Slave,” directed by Steve McQueen, also shown at the Italian fest.
In the film, he played Solomon Northup, a free black man who was kidnapped in 1841 and sold into slavery in Louisiana.
“I hadn’t heard of his story at all. When I was sent the script, I was incredibly moved and shocked by it. Then I read Northup’s own memoir. I thought it was an extraordinary story, an extraordinary tale,” he said before the screening, praising the story that captured a “very tragic period of absence of humanity.”
“It felt very profound to me. I was just deeply moved. Steve McQueen is a phenomenal filmmaker, incredibly passionate, detailed and thorough, with a wonderful vision and cinematic heart. It was incredibly gratifying to see the film being received the way that it was, globally and by the Academy.”
He noted: “At its heart, it was always a story about human respect and human dignity.”

Can you play GTA 6 from an external hard drive on PS5 or Xbox Series X/S?
Rockstar’s behemoth takes up a lot of storage space.
Grand Theft Auto 6 is the biggest game of the year by some distance, having racked up $3.79 billion in pre-orders and day-one sales. On PlayStation 5 alone, more than 39 million unique players took control of dual protagonists Jason and Lucia on opening weekend, making it the biggest game debut in the 32-year history of PlayStation.
There will be many other folks who want to play the game and haven't had a chance to jump in yet. One thing they should note is that, with a hefty install size, GTA 6 will take up a significant chunk of their PS5 or Xbox Series X/S storage space.
You might be wondering whether you can install GTA 6 on an external hard drive to avoid having to delete other games and data from your console. You can move GTA 6 to your external storage when you're not playing it. However, to run the game locally, you'll need to have it installed on your system's built-in storage, an SDD you've installed in your PS5 or a compatible NVMe expansion card that's plugged into your Xbox.
As with many other recent games, GTA 6 needs to take advantage of the fast-loading capabilities of the PS5 and Xbox Series X/S. The consoles are unable to load data for these titles quickly enough from an external hard drive over a USB connection. For the same reason, disc-based PS5 and Xbox Series X games are installed onto system storage before you can play them. The PS5 can run PS4 games from external storage, though. Likewise, an Xbox Series X/S can run older Xbox One and Xbox 360 titles directly from an external hard drive.
That said, there is a way to play GTA 6 without first having to free up a whole lot of console storage space. It's possible to stream the game from the cloud on Xbox Series X/S. There are two things to note if you'd like to go with that option, including that Xbox just brought in new cloud gaming time limits. Game Pass subscribers get up to 15 hours of cloud gaming included each month. You can pay extra for more access. Also, GTA 6 is limited to Xbox Series S graphics settings on Xbox Cloud Gaming.
On the PlayStation side, cloud streaming works on PS5 and PlayStation Portal if you're a PlayStation Plus Premium subscriber. There are no cloud gaming time limits on PS Plus. You'll also need to purchase GTA 6 for PS5 or Xbox Series X/S to stream the game from the cloud, as it's not included in the PS Plus or Game Pass libraries — and it probably won't be for quite some time.

North Korea's Kim vows to build more nuclear weapons after ignoring Trump's overture
SEOUL, South Korea — North Korean leader Kim Jong Un visited facilities that produce nuclear ingredients and called for building more nuclear weapons, days after ignoring U.S. President Donald Trump's offer to meet during his recent visit to Asia.
Experts say Kim likely wants to show off his evolving nuclear arsenal, the backbone of his authoritarian rule, and reaffirm his rejection of any future talks on dismantling his nuclear program.
The North's official Korean Central News Agency said Thursday that Kim inspected two nuclear materials production factories, one newly inaugurated and the other being expanded. KCNA photos showed Kim and senior military officials walking between dense rows of what appeared to be centrifuges used to produce weapons-grade uranium and touring halls displaying what were believed to be warheads. Some of the images were blurred.
KCNA said Kim visited a nuclear-powered equipment production base and a nuclear research institute as well on Wednesday.
North Korea has disclosed a uranium enrichment site a few times since it showed one at its main Yongbyon nuclear complex to visiting American scholars in 2010. North Korea didn't say where the nuclear materials production factories that Kim visited this week are located. In June, when North Korea disclosed parts of a uranium enrichment site while reporting on Kim's visit there, outside experts assessed it was likely an additional uranium enrichment facility at Yongbyon.
Kim justifies nuke program by citing threats from US, South KoreaKim said his latest inspection visit was part of efforts to strengthen North Korea's defense capabilities in response to "variable nuclear threats approaching the Korean Peninsula moment by moment." He accused the U.S. of inciting its regional allies to possess nuclear-powered submarines and committing to sharing its nuclear weapons with them, KCNA said.
"The validity and substantiality of our possession of nuclear weapons and the trend of bolstering up its nuclear capability in quality and quantity are an irreversible reality," Kim said, according to KCNA.
Kim also said the deployment of low-yield battlefield nuclear weapons across multiple domains for various missions is crucial and urgent given North Korea's "inevitable reality facing the border with the most dangerous enemy state," a reference to South Korea. North Korea has in recent years focused on developing such tactical nuclear weapons amid heightened animosity with South Korea.
"Trump has talked about a willingness to meet Kim Jong Un, but the basic U.S. position that North Korea must denuclearize remains unchanged. So Kim Jong Un wants to say 'Look at how powerful we are. Don't talk about denuclearization if you want to meet us,'" said Moon Seong Mook, an analyst for the Seoul-based Korea Research Institute for National Strategy.
Moon said Kim's visit to the nuclear facilities was also likely meant to check on how state objectives on the nuclear program have progressed this year and what future goals must be set ahead of a year-end Workers' Party conference.
South Korea's Defense Ministry said it takes Kim's comments on battlefield nuclear weapons seriously and added that Seoul maintains a firm military readiness against Pyongyang's nuclear threats under an alliance with the U.S. South Korea's Joint Chiefs of Staff declined to share an analysis of the North Korean nuclear facilities reported by KCNA, calling it confidential information for South Korea and the U.S.
Trump still hopes to meet KimTrump reiterated his eagerness to restore diplomacy with Kim as he visited China last week for the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit. But a Trump-Kim meeting didn't happen, with Pyongyang not publicly responding to Trump's overture.
In an interview with the New York Post this week, Trump dismissed the suggestion that Kim had rebuffed his outreach, saying, "No, he didn't ignore it. You know, we had many leaders there … There'll be a time when we meet … It was just not really the right time. It was a very busy two-day period."
Trump also claimed he could revive diplomacy with Kim at any time by restarting the exchange of letters they maintained during his first term, although he acknowledged that the two leaders had not corresponded "recently."
Kim has previously said he could return to talks if the U.S. drops its "hostile policy" against his country and respects what he calls the North's status as a nuclear state. Experts say Kim aims to win international recognition as a nuclear state so that he could demand the lifting of international sanctions.
Last week, International Atomic Energy Agency Director General Rafael Grossi assessed North Korea has been expanding its original uranium enrichment facility at Yongbyon, calling the move "a cause for serious concern."
Nuclear weapons can be built using either highly enriched uranium or weapons-grade plutonium, and North Korea has facilities to produce both at Yongbyon. Last year, South Korea's Unification Minister Chung Dong-young said that North Korea was operating four uranium enrichment facilities and that they were running every day.

The judge has preliminarily sided with ABC, rejecting the FCC’s efforts to dismiss the case.
Although Disney, ABC’s parent company, wasn’t set to renew its broadcast licenses until 2028, last April the FCC ordered the network to file for an early license renewal claiming it was part of an investigation into Disney’s policies on diversity, equity, and inclusivity. The FCC’s move came a day after President Donald Trump demanded ABC fire late-night talk show host Jimmy Kimmel following a skit about Melania Trump.
In response to the FCC’s order, Disney and ABC sued the agency in August and accused the FCC of “punishing ABC for its speech” by threatening its broadcast licenses. The preliminary injunction issued by the judge on Wednesday prohibits the FCC from taking any further action in the early review of ABC’s broadcast licenses and noted that the network had shown that the court’s intervention in the agency’s actions was in the public interest.
”No one doubts that the Commission may enforce the law in the manner it sees fit,” the judge wrote. “But in doing so, Defendants may not retaliate against or punish Plaintiffs and other broadcast license holders for disfavored speech.”

Nfld. & Labrador
N.L. apologizes, says it now accepts Innu history dates back more than 300 years
Letter from Premier Tony Wakeham follows months of controversy
The Grand Chief of the Innu Nation says Newfoundland and Labrador Premier Tony Wakeham has apologized following a months-long controversy over the Innu's history in Labrador.
"Newfoundland and Labrador accepts the position that the history of the Innu in Labrador goes back to the time of immemorial, prior to the arrival of Europeans," Jodie Ashini said on a Facebook livestream Thursday.
Ashini was reading a letter written to her by Wakeham dated Thursday.
- Innu Nation grand chief says N.L. premier has more work to do after meeting in St. John's
- Months after delay and ‘long, hard, painful’ path, Innu history exhibit opens in Labrador
The controversy has been making headlines since June, and boiled over when it was revealed that, according to the Innu, the province's archaeology office only considered the history of the Innu to go back 300 years — which Ashini has called "a theory."
The tension between Ashini and Wakeham boiled over in September, when Ashini walked out of a meeting with Wakeham and later committed that the Innu Nation would not vote to support the new Churchill River deal with Quebec unless the province changed its tune on the Innu's history.
The pair held a nearly three-hour meeting earlier this month. Wakeham had previously committed to an independent audit of Innu records held by the archaeology office.
“I regret the length of time the controversy around the 300-year issue has taken to resolve. I apologize for the problems which arose from the province's position," Wakeham's letter, shared with CBC News, said.
Speaking with reporters late Thursday afternoon, Wakeham said he had an emotional conversation with Ashini on Wednesday.
"To be brutally honest, it was emotional for both of us," Wakeham said.
"It caused me a lot of grief … trying to get to the bottom and understand all of it. And yeah, it was a lot of grief, I think, especially for the Innu Nation."
Federal clarification was what N.L. needed to hear: Wakeham
Wakeham was hesitant to take a stance on the timeline in the months during the dispute, often saying he wanted to wait to get the facts before making a judgment.
On Thursday, Wakeham told reporters he got those facts in October.
As part of land claim negotiations between the Innu, the provincial government and the federal government — which have been ongoing since 1977 — Wakeham said the federal government clarified that Innu have history in Labrador since time immemorial.
Newfoundland and Labrador Premier Tony Wakeham says the federal government clarifying to the province that the Innu have been in Labrador since time immemorial was what he needed to be able to move forward in addressing the wrongs felt by the Innu Nation. (Terry Roberts/CBC)
Following that clarification, Wakeham said he felt comfortable to move forward.
"Clearly, I don't see as a province how Newfoundland and Labrador cannot be on the same side as the federal government in acknowledging the Innu. And I spoke to the Grand Chief about that," Wakeham said.
"[I] apologized for the length of time that it had taken and regret the grief that it had caused the Innu Nation.”
Ashini wiped away tears several times throughout the livestream, expressing thanks for the support from "every single Innu."
“I don’t know if I thought this news would ever come, honestly,” Ashini said.
“I’m proud to bring you this letter that our history will forever be recognized that we were here longer than 300 years … and they’re not going to erase our grandparents and they’re forever marked."
Wakeham said he hopes the province and the Innu Nation can continue to work toward reconciliation.
"It was important for me to try to mend that relationship. None of us want to be at odds, and I think for both myself and Minister [Lela] Evans, that was important."

Quick Answer
Jensen Huang’s exit from Nvidia is about more than personal misconduct. It raises serious questions about conflicts of interest, abuse of power, and Silicon Valley’s habit of excusing tech leaders. His departure sends a vital message: no amount of genius, wealth, or market success should place anyone above accountability.
So Jensen Huang will not be returning to Nvidia, in spite of a groundswell of support. And though it might shock some tech bros, I think it is the best thing that could have happened to tech.
The tech world witnessed one of its most dramatic unravelings this month, perhaps the most significant one in years, if not decades. All was going smoothly; AI was still the sun the tech world was revolving around, and one of the biggest planets revolving around it was Nvidia. The company was not just in on living, breathing, and thriving on AI development but at the center of bettering AI for others, as it manufactured AI chips.
When current affairs become… well, current affairs
It all came crashing down when a report was published in The New York Times, revealing news of an affair. This was not the run-of-the-mill gossip that’s seen in the scandal section in tabloids, but news that changed the trajectory of Nvidia and possibly AI.
Nvidia CEO, Jensen Huang, was found to be having an extramarital affair with Alice Huang (unrelated, although having the same surname), a top executive at Megaspeed, a Singapore-based technology company. Alice was suspected of being a Chinese spy by US intelligence. Megaspeed was one of the major buyers of Nvidia’s AI chips, and, as per reports, it diverted chips worth USD 2 billion to China against regulations, although both Megaspeed and Nvidia deny any wrongdoing.
Following the news, A LOT went down. Huang seemed to swing into damage control and issued an apology for the affair, promising cooperation with an investigation into it. The tech world thought the worst was over. After all, what could make this worse? Then the New York Times, on 11 November, released a report citing another extramarital affair. This time it was reported that he was in a relationship with Nvidia’s Vice President of Health Care, Kimberly Powell, who reported directly to Huang. After trying to save face and his 41-year-long marriage (Jensen Huang is married to Lori Huang), Huang had to resign and leave his post as CEO at Nvidia on 12 November.
But this is not the story of a person’s personal slip-ups, or the extra-marital affair story that much of the media is making it to be. It is actually much bigger than that.
It’s not about infidelity, but about power and misconduct
While Huang has received a fair deal of criticism for his conduct, he has received a lot of support too, especially from Silicon Valley, where it seems that when there is a tech billionaire in question, the rules that apply to the rest of the world cease to apply to them. If you build an important enough product, accumulate billions of Dollars, and build some political connections, what would otherwise be a big no-no suddenly becomes negotiable, and the boundaries around right and wrong start to get hazy.
Affairs and flings are nothing new to the world of tech in particular, or the world of celebrities in general, but this case is more than just a personal lapse of judgment. Had Huang’s affair(s) been something that had happened outside of the workplace or if he had fallen for someone who had nothing to do with tech (an actress, an influencer, a trapeze artiste, et al.), this would have been an entirely different conversation. But his intimate relations with his employee and a customer – and the fact that we are being asked to overlook them – shine a light on what might be wrong with the inherent culture at not just Nvidia but in Silicon Valley.
While most concerns have revolved around Alice Huang being a Chinese spy and sensitive AI technology crossing borders, allegations which have not yet been proved, what is clear beyond doubt is that Huang misused his position as the CEO of one of the biggest companies in the world, on both the client and employee side.
In both of his affairs, Huang was the person of power, with Alice Huang and Kimberly Powell. The client in question bought billions of dollars’ worth of AI chips from Nvidia, and given her intimate relationship revelation with Huang, it would be difficult to rule out that the business deals made between the two were in no way influenced by the relationship. We are not even getting to the part of Alice Huang being a Chinese spy, and whether she managed to get sensitive information and AI chips from Jensen Huang for China, which would give China the AI leverage it needs to get ahead of the US in the AI race. Even if she was “just another client,” does it not still remain a bother that a person who has been hailed as a tech demi-god could not control his urges long enough to get through business? Similarly, his second affair with a senior employee working at Nvidia who directly reported to him, and, as per reports, was promptly promoted during her time at Nvidia, does bring up some very serious questions about preferential treatment, conflict of interest, and company power dynamics.
This is not about Huang’s infidelity, but his ability to make sound decisions. A lot of the evidence suggests that in a situation where he could misuse his position of power, he did. It was not just his moral compass that was compromised, but his professional one too. The fact that this happened, and that the former Nvidia CEO has still received a lot of support, not only raises concerns about the culture at Nvidia, but also about the overall priorities of Silicon Valley.
When the stock market decides where to draw the line
Since Jensen Huang’s departure from Nvidia, a number of executives, tech CEOs, and even the US President himself have come out in support of him. Media channels have had extensive discussions on the matter, and many have marked the (so far) two affairs as a “personal lapse of judgment” and think Huang’s potential as a tech genius outweighs his failings. Elon Musk has compared his exit as “it’s like kicking Michael Jordan off your team when you’re on a winning streak”, while other leaders like Sam Altman, Steven Chen, Tim Sweeney and many more have pushed for his comeback. President Donald Trump has said he would “not mind” seeing Huang reinstated as CEO, and Musk has even offered to hire him.
Now, there is no doubt that Jensen Huang is a genius who has built one of the most important businesses in the world of tech. Many fear that without him, Nvidia would tank, and this would have a devastating impact on AI. However, since the reports of his affairs have come out and his resignation, Nvidia’s stock has taken a nosedive, and so have many other AI stocks. In fact, many are predicting that Huang’s exit might burst the AI bubble, which, for obvious reasons, is way worse for the tech world in general than any lapse in professional and moral code of conduct. Accountability seems to count for little as long as the stock market is doing well.
Time to take the Tech God pedestal away?
Given this groundswell of support, the easy decision for Nvidia would perhaps have been to let Jensen Huang walk back in as if nothing happened and sit back and see the share prices spike. It actually seemed likely, and Huang himself had posted on X (where he was given a free blue tick by Elon Musk), offering to make a comeback if the board considered it would be in the best interest of the company. However, on 18 November, Nvidia ruled out the reinstatement of Jensen Huang. And while this led to groans of disappointment from many of the tech bros, we actually think it was the right call to take.
Over the past week, I’ve been overwhelmed by the love and support of friends, industry colleagues, and people I've never met. Thank you to everyone who has shown kindness to my family and me. It means the world to me.
I came to the United States 53 years ago, and becoming an…
— Jensen Huang (@JensenHuang) November 17, 2026
While a company has responsibilities towards its shareholders, it also has to keep its employees and clients in mind. Share prices cannot be used as an automatic defense against misconduct, especially at the highest level. Unfortunately, over the past few decades, tech brilliance has been placed on a pedestal, giving a handful of people immunity from general human misconduct. Bouts of bad temper, abusive behavior, and so much more are often turned a blind eye to because a person is perceived as a “Tech God,” a person who is part of the genius crowd that is building a better, brighter future for us all. But recent times have revealed that many of these tech gods whom we have trusted, and largely exempted from strict governance or interference, cannot even follow simple, basic rules that govern mere mortals. And these handful of people, who cannot even follow the basics, are sitting in boardrooms and are now deciding the future of billions of people, even those who have not opted for an AI-laden future or are not even aware of what AI is.
Jensen Huang’s conduct – and the support he has received – now raises the question of whether the people we were told are tech geniuses are as reliable and trustworthy as the narrative around them has painted them out to be. Or are they just a bunch of power-hungry, wealth-accumulating techies who have way too much autonomy for comfort?
The Huang affair (pun intended) marks an important phase in modern tech. While we still do not know how it will all end – there are endless conspiracy theories doing the rounds – we do hope it will teach many in the tech world not to turn a blind eye to “personal and professional misconduct,” just because a person is seen as a genius and is perceived to be good for the world in general and the stock market in particular.

It delivers up to 24 hours of battery life, with a built-in loop for easy carrying. You can also use it as a power bank and pair it with other Sonos speakers over Bluetooth when Wi-Fi isn’t available. Read our review.
LIFX Everyday Smart Light Bulbs (two-pack)
LIFX’s dimmable, color-changing bulbs offer Wi-Fi connectivity, simple setup, and Matter compatibility, so they fit seamlessly into any major smart home platform. Best of all, the smart features come at a price that makes buying multipacks more affordable than other brands.
Iniu P55-E2 Power Bank (10,000mAh)
Iniu’s P55-E2 Power Bank is an ultra-slim three-port USB charger that’s capable of fully recharging an iPhone 16 twice. It supports charging speeds of up to 45W via a USB-C port, which can deliver fast recharging for a range of gadgets.
Echo Dot Max
The Echo Dot Max features a flat design and a redesigned sound system, which delivers nearly three times the bass as its predecessor. It also offers improved conversation detection and better noise filtering, thanks to Amazon’s new AZ3 chip. Read our review.
Donkey Kong Bananza
Donkey Kong Bananza is one of the Switch 2’s first exclusive must-have titles. Its destructible environment allows you to smash your way through each of its 17 levels, and the paths you make will remain intact unless you specifically choose to reset the world. Your companion Paulene’s singing allows you to transform into animals that have abilities that allow you to reach previously inaccessible parts of levels. Read our review.
Fanttik X9 Pro Portable Tire Inflator
Whether you primarily drive a car, motorcycle, or a bicycle, the one thing in common with all three modes of transport is the need for a well-inflated tire. This rechargeable 150psi inflator might just save you from a flat (or from being dangerously close to one) when you least expect it.
Google Pixel 11 Pro
Google wants to sell you on the Pro’s software features, but it’s the underlying hardware that makes it a stellar Android handset. The build quality is incredible, the larger telephoto sensor is an improvement, and it now supports faster wired speeds and Qi2.2 for up to 25W wireless charging. Read our review.
Catan (6th Edition)
In Catan, up to four players strategically compete and trade for resources. The iconic board game ends when one player reaches 10 “victory points,” which is achieved by constructing a sprawling civilization of roads, settlements, and cities using sheep, ore, wheat, and wood.
Amazon Alexa Photo Frame
A 10-inch anti-glare touchscreen that comes in a few design options. It’s a frame that features Alexa, and doubles as a smart speaker. It works with Amazon Photos, which offers unlimited storage for Prime members.
Glocusent Bookmark Style Reading Light
Glocusent’s clip-in reading light features five brightness levels and multiple color temperature settings, ranging from a soft, warm glow that’s great for late-night reading to a brighter light that’s perfect for daytime use. The slim USB light easily slips into your pocket, too, so you can read anywhere, from a cozy bed to a dimly lit train.
Aqara Smart Lock U400
This innovative new smart lock uses the U1 ultra-wideband (UWB) chip in many iPhones and Apple Watches to automatically unlock your door as you approach. It will also work with the new Aliro standard and be compatible with Android phones for hands-free unlocking.
Roborock Qrevo Curv 2 Flow
Roborock’s first roller-mop robot vacuum, the Curv 2 Flow, features flagship specs at a midrange price, including excellent mopping, a retractable mop cover, 20,000Pa suction, AI-powered obstacle avoidance, and a compact design.
Twelve South AirFly SE
Twelve South’s entry-level Bluetooth transmitter delivers up to 25 hours of continuous use and lets you connect up to two pairs of headphones to an in-flight entertainment system, making it a great travel companion no matter where you’re going.
Kodak Charmera Keychain Digital Camera
The Chamera is not a good camera, but that’s not the point. Kodak’s charming, keychain-friendly tchotchke lets you snap lo-fi memories on a whim, with an ultra-small 1.6-megapixel sensor, a built-in LED flash, and the tiniest amount of storage.
Ghost of Yōtei
Sucker Punch’s follow-up to Ghost of Tsushima is everything you could want in a sequel. The open-world revenge epic brims with fluid combat and a host of welcome narrative twists, all set against the gorgeous backdrop of Japan’s Edo period. It’s precisely the type of game photo modes were made for, even if you never use them.
Wuben G5 rechargeable flashlight
The Wuben G5 flashlight is as small as a Zippo lighter, yet far more versatile, with a bright, rotatable light that can shine in numerous colors. It features USB-C charging and has an adjustable clip.
JBL Go 4
The last-gen JBL Go 4 has been around for a bit, but the pocket-sized Bluetooth speaker still delivers with up to seven hours of runtime, dual-device connectivity, and an IP67 rating for water and dust resistance. You can also pair it with other Go 4 speakers for bigger stereo sound, if desired.
Apple Watch SE 3
The Apple Watch SE 3 is a major glow-up, adding an always-on display, wrist-temperature sensor, a more powerful processor, and fast charging. Read our review.
Insta360 Link 2
The Insta360 Link 2 offers the same auto-swiveling design as its excellent predecessor, only in a smaller form factor. It also offers a slate of new features, including group tracking and no-follow zones.
Update, November 26th: Added a wide selection of new deals, including those for the Apple Watch SE 3 and Insta360’s Link 2 webcam.

A renovation was meant to improve these Hong Kong homes - it ended in a blaze that killed 168
- Published
It was a sunny Wednesday afternoon on 26 November last year, and Mrs Lau was attending a dance class at an activity centre close to her home.
At around 14:45 she heard the faint sounds of fire engine sirens - but didn't think much of it.
It was only a while later, when she started receiving calls from a friend, that she found out that Wang Fuk Court - the eight-block apartment complex she had called home for the past 40 years - was ablaze. And her husband - a wheelchair user - was trapped inside their home.
"I grabbed my things quickly and ran down without even putting my shoes on properly," Mrs Lau, who wanted to be identified only by her surname, told the BBC.
When she got there, the building had been cordoned off by police.
She called her 74-year-old husband but he told her not to worry - he hadn't heard an alarm so it was probably a small fire, he said.
Mrs Lau could only watch helplessly as the blaze tore through Wang Fuk Court at a peak speed of about 10m (33ft) per second - an "unprecedented" rate, a final report released by an independent committee in relation to the deadly blaze that killed 168 people found.
It was a tragedy that was entirely preventable but happened as a result of a series of human errors, fire safety failures, alleged fraud and suspected corruption, said the report.
"It was ferocious… I saw the fire jump [from one building to another] - then a huge fireball burst. It was truly hell on Earth. How could anyone possibly escape?" said Mrs Lau.
She tried calling her husband again. This time, there was no answer.
The body of Lau Man Kwong was eventually found by rescuers - he had locked himself inside the toilet.
"He was wearing his slippers, sitting on the toilet and clutching his identity card," said his wife, who added that she escaped death "by the narrowest margin".
"I would have held onto my husband and died with him.
"He was such a good person. I just don't understand why he had to die in such a terrible way."
Mr Lau and his wife moved into Wang Fuk Court in 1983 - the year the building was completed.
She recalls an idyllic life - a family with three children who were able to grow up close to the sea and spend weekends playing at a nearby park.
"All three of my children adored my husband… He could be very stern, and I was the only woman who could make him laugh."
No way out
In 2024, mandated renovations began in Wang Fuk Court.
In Hong Kong, all buildings over 30 years old have to undergo an inspection - and any necessary renovations as a result.
Like many building complexes in Hong Kong, Wang Fuk Court had a management committee that oversaw things like building repairs. As many as 57 construction companies submitted bids. But the company that won, Prestige Construction and Engineering (PC&E), submitted the most expensive bid at HK$336m ($42.8m; £32.4m).
Residents, many of whom were over 65, had to bear the cost. The hefty bills triggered protests but eventually, the contract was signed. But once the renovations began in July 2024, residents were unhappy.
Among the complaints was that workers constantly smoked on site, dropping cigarette butts everywhere.
The 1,154 page report suggested the fire was caused by a lit cigarette.
There were also complaints about most of Wang Fuk Court's eight buildings having their windows taped over with foam boards to stop debris falling in - blocking daylight or any sort of view at all, for months.
All eight buildings were also covered in a protective mesh netting and bamboo scaffolding.
The report also found that after typhoons damaged the original scaffolding nets in 2025, cheaper non-fire-retardant replacements were chosen - something that was done as a "cost-saving measure at the expense of the safety of the residents".
Residents had filed nearly 140 complaints to six government departments, including the fire services and the buildings departments, in and after 2024, but these were largely ignored, the report went on to say.
It also revealed that a staff member of the estate's property manager, ISS, had turned off the power supply to the fire alarms in all eight buildings - which is why no alarms rang on the day itself.
ISS later told the BBC it had "reviewed and reinforced its procedures [and] staff training" in Hong Kong, adding that it takes the findings of the report "very seriously".
But for those who did manage to flee their homes - the emergency staircase turned out to be another death trap. Windows were removed from some fire escape stairwells to create temporary openings for workers - letting in smoke and cutting off vital escape routes.
Dozens, including Christy's husband, died in such stairwells.
Christy, who wanted to be identified only by her first name, says her husband was at home alone when the fire broke out. She only found out about it when her friends sent her messages about it. By the time she made it to the apartment complex, it was already cordoned off.
She found out later that he had died of smoke inhalation in the stairwell, something she says that is at least of some consolation to her.
"My husband's body would have been burnt and he would have been in more pain if he was at home. At the very least… his suffering was minimal."
Christy says her family had just celebrated their eldest child's ninth birthday the day before - they had saved some leftover cake in the fridge to eat the next day. Their father never got to eat it.
Both children have been deeply affected by the loss of their father.
Her youngest child, a seven-year-old boy, had "covered his ears and yelled" when he was first told what had happened to his father.
He now often comforts his mother, saying he will take care of her as he is the only man in the family.
"He hides his emotions. A seven-year-old child should not behave this way, and I feel heartbroken," says Christy, who has herself been diagnosed with PTSD and depression.
Her daughter has "extreme thoughts" she says, and channels her emotions through art.
She turned 10 on Wednesday, but this year, there was no birthday celebration in sight.
Her birthday, she says, will now instead be a day to commemorate her father.
Bid-rigging and rubber stamps
Wang Fuk Court's problems date back to before the renovations began.
The management company hired to oversee and supervise the project, Will Power, conspired with PC&E to defraud residents in Wang Fuk Court, according to the city's Independent Commission Against Corruption (ICAC).
Although PC&E was found to have breached safety requirements and violated building department rules for multiple previous projects, homeowners at Wang Fuk Court were told that they had a clean record.
The ICAC alleges that this was part of a lucrative scheme, with Will Power's director Wong Hap-yin, along with other individuals, laundering over $5m in suspected proceeds from the tendering process from Wang Fuk Court, among other housing projects.
Once PC&E cinched the contract, Will Power's registered inspector - an individual meant to oversee the renovations - merely rubber-stamped the documents, without having actually conducted any inspections personally, the report added.
Will Power has been since liquidated and PC&E could not be reached for a response.
Both companies - Will Power and PC&E - and seven individuals have been charged with 25 counts of offences including manslaughter, conspiracy to defraud, attempting to pervert the course of public justice and tax evasion.
Four of them are still in custody but none of the cases have gone to trial yet.
The report said both companies involved were the "main culprits responsible".
But it also directed heavy criticism at authorities, saying that "no government department took effective ownership of various fire safety issues and complaints about fire hazards fell into a vacuum".
One expert, Prof John Burns of Hong Kong University, had called the tragedy the "largest governance crisis" that authorities have faced since 2020 - a reference to the controversial National Security Law that was passed in that year.
On the day the report was released, almost one year after the fire, Hong Kong's housing chief Winnie Ho resigned and the city's top leader John Lee apologised for the first time, promising that a "large number" of reforms would be rolled out.
A shell of a home
Five months after the fire, Mrs Lau was allowed into her flat for the first time to collect any personal belongings that might have remained.
In her first visit, she was given just three hours to retrieve 40 years' worth of belongings.
Pictures taken from the visit show a home that has been utterly burned out - with every surface blackened and soot covering the floor.
"I almost fainted when I saw what had become of my home. I don't understand how the home I had built, such a warm and beautiful home, could end up like this," said Mrs Lau.
Her children, who came with her, described the house as a "war zone". Among the rubble, they found broken pieces of a piggy bank that Mr Lau had dutifully filled with coins every day for the past 20 years.
"Everyone in our family knew it was his favourite possession. The piggy bank died with him," said Mrs Lau.
Mrs Lau and her daughter have since rented a place nearby to live - and she is worried about how she is going to afford a new house.
The government has said it will spend $867m (£663m) to acquire affected flats - but Mrs Lau says it is not nearly enough to buy a similarly sized flat in the area.
Still, her family was in a better position than many others, she said.
"Should I say that we are fortunate?
"I lost my husband but many families lost multiple family members... Babies less than a year old died. "
Stories have emerged of some of the other victims - a six-month-old who died alongside her 68-year-old grandmother when the fire broke out.
The bodies of an Indonesian domestic helper and the elderly person she worked for were found huddled together.
As for Christy, she says she is planning to file a lawsuit against those responsible for the fire - but acknowledges that even if she wins, she "can't [get] my husband's life back".
"I share things that happen in our daily life, as if he still existed," she says. "I often write to him, 'I miss you so much. Are you doing well on the other side?'"
It's a similar story for Mrs Lau, who says she can't go anywhere without seeing her husband.
"Every day, something reminds me of him," she said.
"I still find it very hard to accept that my husband is gone, my home is gone, and so many of my neighbours are gone…. This place was my roots. I never imagined it would also mark an ending for me."

No post-match drug testing in South Africa v New Zealand series
- Published
South Africa and New Zealand players were not subjected to a single post-match drugs test by anti-doping authorities when they contested this year's Rugby's Greatest Rivalry series.
The four-Test series, played in August and September, is a new biennial initiative between the two southern hemisphere powerhouses aimed at boosted revenues and profiles.
An agreement over how the series operates refers to World Rugby anti-doping rules; but, in practice, post-match tests, which are standard practice at most elite-level matches, were not carried out.
Players in the series could have been tested by either of two official bodies.
All players involved in the series are part of World Rugby's testing pool. The global governing body conducts on-the-spot tests on top players around the world throughout the year.
The South African Institute for Drug-Free Sport (Saids) runs its own domestic anti-doping programme, covering sporting events and athletes in the country.
With all matches, bar the fourth and final Test in the American city of Baltimore, taking place in South Africa, Saids could have demanded samples from players after games.
World Rugby would not confirm the lack of post-match testing in the Rugby's Greatest Rivalry series, but it stressed that all players are subject to the "always-on" testing regime.
"World Rugby operates a risk-based no-notice anti-doping programme in line with the World Anti-Doping Agency code," said a spokesperson.
"All qualified men's and women's Rugby World Cup team players are included within a dedicated out-of-competition testing pool which is not competition specific.
"This means that all these players are subject to testing on a no-notice, any location basis throughout the calendar year, including within international competition windows.
"This means that over the course of the year, both teams are tested in and out of competition in line with World Rugby's programme and are also subject to testing undertaken by the respective national anti-doping agencies at both the international and domestic/cross border club levels."
Saids referred queries about testing in Rugby's Greatest Rivalry back to World Rugby, saying the global body had "jurisdiction" over the matches.
The latest figures from the World Anti-Doping Agency show there were 9,583 accredited doping tests in rugby union globally in 2024, with 0.6% coming back positive.
That number of tests is fewer than those conducted in athletics (44,044), cycling (26,156), aquatics (17,447), but more than in wrestling (7,620), triathlon, (4,478) and gymnastics (4,190).
The number of rugby players tested by Saids has fallen significantly in recent years.
The most recent Saids annual report, covering the 12 months to 31 March, records 225 tests in the sport.
A decade before, the equivalent number was 753.
UK Anti-Doping, which covers England, Scotland and Wales, carried out 1,086 tests in rugby union in 2025. New Zealand's Sport Integrity Commission conducted 249 tests in rugby over the same period.
Currently two rugby union players in New Zealand – both well below elite level – are serving suspensions for doping.
The cost of testing has dramatically increased for Saids after the World Anti-Doping Agency revoked its accreditation for a sample-testing laboratory in Bloemfontein in May 2025., external
With no other such facilities in Africa, Saids has to send samples long distances for testing. It says its budget has been hit by foreign currency costs from overseas laboratories, courier costs and import charges.
While elsewhere violations have mainly been restricted to players outside the elite, the Springboks have been hit by several doping cases in recent years.
Aphiwe Dyantyi, who made 13 appearances for the team and was named as World Rugby's breakthrough player of 2018, was banned for four years after he tested positive for a cocktail of steroids.
Sbu Nkosi and Elton Jantjies, both members of the 2019 Rugby World Cup winning squad, have also been banned for doping offences.
Three-cap prop Asenathi Ntlabakanye is the latest international to fall foul of the authorities, with the 27-year-old getting an 18-month suspension in May.
Incidents of doping on the country's highly competitive schoolboy circuit are also common.
Eighteen-year-old Deon Botes, a former SA Schools prop, was banned for four years after returning a positive test for steroids at the showpiece Craven Week event in 2025., external
While Dyanti, Jantjies and Ntlabakanye's positive tests were picked up by Saids, many of the Springbok squad play their club rugby overseas and will be subject to anti-doping tests there.
World Rugby's anti-doping programme, which includes biological markers and DNA as well as urine and blood analysis, stores samples after immediate testing to allow for further investigation as new techniques and technology are developed.
South Africa play France in the Nations Championship final on Sunday evening in the last match of their Test season.

The National Weather Service in the US has confirmed that an EF1 tornado touched down south-east of Newark in the Salem Woods neighbourhood, Delaware, on Thursday. The tornado reached 160 metres wide, had a path length of 4.4 miles (7.1km) and reached estimated peak winds of up to 100mph (161km/h). There were no injuries or fatalities but windows and roofs were damaged on several homes, a large hotel sign fell on to a number of cars, and a semi truck overturned on I95. Although Delaware often experiences a few tornadoes every year, this is only the second time the state has had tornado activity in November since 1950, according to the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration. The only other November tornado recorded was in 1989.
Severe storms have also resulted in tornadoes in Argentina as well as large hailstones. A round of severe thunderstorms moved through the central Córdoba province on Friday, bringing hailstones up to the size of a baseball (about 7.5cm in diameter). Parts of the province recorded up to 73mm of rainfall in just six hours early on Saturday. Such storms are common at this time of year. Water vapour from the Amazon meeting the Andes quickly condenses, resulting in massive cloud formations often associated with heavy downpours, lightning, tornadoes and large hailstones.
India’s meteorological department has released an alert for a depression located in the Bay of Bengal with the potential to develop into a cyclone. A low-pressure system formed during the early hours of Friday before developing into a depression on Sunday. The department’s forecast is for the depression to intensify into a cyclonic storm by Tuesday before gradually drifting north-west towards eastern India, with the expectation it will make landfall on Thursday. If the storm were to develop it would become the third of the season and be named Akvan. There is a “watch” level warning for much of the eastern coast on Wednesday and Thursday, with parts of the Andhra Pradesh and Odisha states on an “alert” level.

A young couple was assaulted by a group of minors at Pramod Mahajan Garden in Kurla West, Mumbai, near Phoenix Marketcity Mall, on 20 November 2026. A viral video showed the group surrounding the couple, verbally abusing and assaulting them with sticks, kicks, punches, a belt, and stones before chasing them away. Police registered a case against eight minors after a video of the attack went viral. They were sent to a juvenile correctional home until 4 December 2026 (here, here). 
Against this backdrop, a video showing several men being paraded by the police is being shared on social media (here, here, here) with the claim that it shows the Mumbai Police parading those involved in the assault on the couple. Let’s verify the claim made in the post.
Claim: The video shows Mumbai Police parading the accused who assaulted a young couple in Kurla West, Mumbai.
Fact: The viral video shows the accused arrested in connection with the murder of 18-year-old Santosh More in Surat, Gujarat, and not those involved in the assault on a couple in Mumbai. The Surat Police had paraded the accused in connection with the murder case. Hence, the claim made in the post is FALSE.
A reverse image search using keyframes from the viral video led us to a video uploaded by an Instagram account called Gujarat Live on 14 November 2026, predating the Kurla, Mumbai incident. The text accompanying the video claimed that it showed the accused arrested in the murder of Santosh More, a youth from Surat.
A keyword search based on this led us to several media reports (here, here, here) featuring visuals from the viral video. According to these reports, 18-year-old Santosh More was allegedly stabbed to death in Surat’s Rasulabad area on 8 November 2026, following a dispute reportedly linked to a love affair and previous rivalry. The accused were identified as Javed alias Nawab Sheikh, Hansraj Kushwaha, Shakib Maniyar, Shahid Sheikh, and Piyush Sahu.
We also found similar visuals in a video uploaded by the Surat Police on X on 12 November 2026. The video showed the same accused being paraded. The caption stated, “Khatodara Police arrested the accused and taught them a lesson in the law in the case of the murder of a youth in Azad Nagar, Khatodara police station area.”
To sum up, the video of Surat Police parading the murder accused is falsely linked to the Mumbai couple assault case.

Lies, a disguise and surfboard bags: How a jealous Sydney policeman tried to cover up double murder
- Published
It was just after 09:00 on a warm February morning when CCTV picked up a man dressed as an UberEats rider hovering on a sidewalk in one of Sydney's wealthiest neighbourhoods.
He dawdled for around 20 minutes, "steeling himself for what he was about to do" prosecutors say, before disappearing out of sight. Minutes later another CCTV camera captured the sound of gunshots ringing out.
Former police officer Beau Lamarre, 31, was on Wednesday found guilty of murdering his former partner Jesse Baird, a TV presenter, and Luke Davies, Baird's new partner, with his work-issued gun.
In February 2024, the bloodied belongings of Baird and Davies were found in a skip in the suburb of Cronulla, sparking a frantic search for the couple. It culminated in the discovery of their bodies on a rural property, partially buried beneath sticks and debris.
During a two-month trial filled with at-times extraordinary testimony and a wealth of CCTV evidence, the court heard Lamarre had planned his crime over months.
Jurors watched CCTV of the then police officer purchasing a surfboard bag in which to put Baird's body, after casually sizing it up against a friend in the shop, and heard from a stream of former friends and colleagues who testified that Lamarre asked them for advice about everything from mobile phone signals to where he could buy a gun.
One recounted the chilling moment Lamarre told her that if he were ever to murder someone, he would leave their belongings in a dumpster and hide the body in bushland where they would never be found.
"What would you do if I told you I killed somebody? Would you help me hide the body?" he asked, according to her testimony.
Later, Lamarre asked for help in covering up the killings; his friends - none of whom have been implicated - say they began receiving panicked calls and odd requests from him.
One told the court Lamarre persuaded her to go for a drive in the country, during which he tried to dispose of the bodies at the family farm of a man he'd met on a dating app. Over the speakers, he played Taylor Swift's No Body, No Crime.
Dark infatuation
Baird, 26, and Lamarre - a one-time celebrity blogger who also had his own swimwear line on the side of his police work - met in a nightclub in October 2022. For Lamarre, it quickly became an infatuation, but for Baird, an AFL referee and former Network Ten presenter, the relationship appeared to be casual.
After discovering in April 2023 that Lamarre had gone through messages on his phone, and unfollowed other men on his Instagram account, Baird broke it off.
But Lamarre's obsession only grew. He watched Baird having sex with another man through his bedroom window, broke into his house multiple times, deleting contacts on his phone and turning on location settings so that he could engineer meetings with the TV presenter.
On one occasion Baird woke up to find Lamarre in his bedroom; not realising who it was, he chased him down the street. Lamarre was also convicted of aggravated break and enter over that incident on Wednesday.
Prosecutor Brett Hatfield said Baird was "oblivious to the accused's scheming and manipulations", and the pair briefly rekindled the relationship before Baird ended it definitively in November.
He'd discovered Lamarre had, again, been accessing his phone and had attempted to ward off a love rival by pretending to have received flowers from Baird.
'The beginning of the plan for murder'
His pride wounded, Hatfield said Lamarre's thoughts turned to a "darker place": "revenge".
He asked an old friend if her ex-partner could get him a gun: "This was the beginning of the plan for the murder," the prosecutor said.
In the months leading up to the killings, Lamarre bought a burner phone, a sourced motorcycle helmet, and practised shooting in the woods. On holiday with a friend in Bali in January 2024 he tried to buy a silencer.
While his murder plans percolated, he also began lashing out with petty acts of malice, prosecutors said, such as putting water in the fuel tank of Baird's car.
But at the same time as he plotted, Lamarre was still trying to win his ex back.
On one occasion he pressured a friend to send Baird a 1,600-word message he had himself composed, claiming that he had cancer, and may need to have his arm amputated.
Under questioning in court, he said a naturopath he couldn't remember the name of had diagnosed him with "a form of sporadic cancer".
By the end of 2023, Baird had met and hit it off with Davies, 29. "It was early days but they were both smitten with each other," his mother, Helen Baird, told the court. He sent her a picture of the pair at a Pink concert. "I just sent a big love heart and said 'I'm so happy for both of you'."
Early on the morning of 19 February, Lamarre picked up a hire car he had asked his mother to rent and drove to Baird's home. After waiting several hours for Baird's housemates to leave, while disguised as an UberEats driver, he let himself in with a key he had copied.
Lamarre told the court he had been at Baird's home to pick up some belongings, including a A$25,000 (US$16,500, £12,600) Cartier ring, and had disguised himself to avoid the embarrassment of being recognised if anyone was home.
He claimed he let himself in when no one answered the door, and the two men were killed in separate struggles. He argued that Baird had been holding a knife and the first shot was fired to disarm him, and the second by accident. Davies shot himself when he grabbed the gun, Lamarre said.
But prosecutors told the jury Baird was shot in the back and then once again through his temple as he lay gravely wounded on the kitchen floor.
The evidence, Hatfield said, pointed to one thing only: "an execution".
Davies was then shot through a bedroom door as he tried to call emergency services. The court heard the panic in his voice as the seconds-long call was replayed before it dropped out.
Covering tracks
After that, Lamarre set about trying to hide the evidence of what Hatfield called his "brazen and shocking murders".
One of his first actions was to call a friend. He testified Lamarre confessed he had "killed people" and asked him to take a day off work "to help him clean up his mess".
Later Lamarre pretended the call was a joke, saying, "Did you like my Oscar performance? Got you".
Meanwhile, Lamarre went to a DIY store to purchase mops, bleach and bin bags. After returning to Baird's house to clean up, he left the bodies wrapped in surfboard bags and tarpaulins in the courtyard.
Baird had been set to move out that week, and Lamarre used Baird's phone to reassure his housemates he had hired an Airtasker to move his belongings, adding, "I might be flying to Perth tonight".
Baird's housemates quickly spotted the surfboard bags when they returned home, snapping a photograph tendered in court which showed "red liquid" seeping out.
"I thought it was rusted water from the outdoor furniture," one of the women said.
The surfboard bags were gone the next morning.
Lamarre had hired a van, and over the next two days made more trips to the DIY store and a sports shop to buy gumboots, a wheelbarrow, bigger surfboard bags and 10kg weights. He squeezed in a hospital appointment for a minor procedure and paused for a sushi date with a friend, CCTV showing him laughing and eating as the bodies lay in the back of his van.
On 21 February, he picked up another friend in the van for what she thought was lunch.
There were blue tarps in the back and it smelled "lemony", she told the court. She "wasn't allowed to put the windows up or turn the aircon off" as they motored towards Goulburn, 200km southwest of Sydney, stopping only at another DIY store, where he asked her to buy an angle grinder.
His friend told the court she remembers Lamarre playing No Body, No Crime at some point: "It's a very niche song."
Arriving at a farm owned by a Hinge date's family, Lamarre used the angle grinder to cut through a padlock, making his way to a dam where he unsuccessfully tried to sink the bodies.
It was now late at night and he drove his friend, by this time upset and confused, home before returning to retrieve the bodies. He then left them in the van, parked in Sydney overnight, before driving once more to Goulburn, where he dumped the bodies near a monastery.
Later that day he visited another friend, telling her to look up the definition of schizophrenia and asking whether he could use her hose, because "there was a bit of blood he had to scrub off" the hired van, the court heard.
Lamarre faces life in prison
By this time police were closing in, and on 23 February Lamarre went to turn himself in at Bondi police station. On the way, he called a police helpline.
"I've been bullied by multiple New South Wales police force members," he told the woman on the other end of the line. "All this stress and trauma and psychological abuse and trauma - did I say trauma already? - has caused me to not sleep, get anxious, it's caused me to have some symptoms of schizophrenia."
"Actually sorry, you know what, can you just... delete that whole thing. We'll just keep it short and sweet."
He wasn't sure when he'd be back to work, he said. Shortly afterwards he was arrested and charged with murder, and the bodies of Baird and Davies were found four days later.
Lamarre's lawyer John Stratton insisted he'd acted in self-defence and had "panicked" realising how the scene would look to outsiders.
The former police officer did plenty of "foolish" and "unusual" things - "He was, it's fair to say, a poorly behaved boyfriend," Stratton said - but that did not make him a murderer.
Ultimately, however, the jury was not convinced and took just over an hour to convict him. He will be sentenced in March and faces life in prison.

Desperate appeals from women on death row in Iran after protests
- Published
Taraneh Rahimi is on death row in Iran.
In recent weeks, the 21-year-old has been unable to walk properly after her legs were beaten, and an ear-infection caused by an untreated head injury has affected her balance, her cousin says.
She is "keeping her spirits up" but "there are days she breaks down in tears," Masoud Nourmohammadi tells BBC News Persian.
He says Taraneh and her twin sister Romina were arrested after joining the anti-government protests that swept the country in January.
When the twins' mother first saw them in prison, their faces were so swollen and bruised, and their hair pulled out, that she could only recognise them by their voices, Nourmohammadi says, speaking from the US.
He says Taraneh signed a confession after interrogators threatened that her sister would be raped in front of her.
Taraneh is one of six women who have been sentenced to death this year in connection with the January protests, according to the UN's human rights rapporteur for Iran, Mai Sato.
The figure for men is much higher. However, women protesters and dissidents are being sentenced to death in numbers not seen for decades, as part of a "horrific rise" in politically motivated executions, Amnesty International's Iran researcher Raha Bahreini says.
The Iranian embassy in London told the BBC that claims of an increase in the use of the death penalty in protest-related cases were "misleading".
It categorically rejected allegations of the use of torture and any allegations that the death penalty has been imposed solely for peaceful protest, which it said is a "legitimate, and protected right".
It said death sentences in relation to the "riot in January 2026" were issued in cases involving "intentional murder" or "Moharebeh (the taking up of weapons with the intent to threaten or wreck the people's lives or property)".
The twins were seized in late January, Nourmohammadi says.
It was two weeks after the end of the protests, which began in late December over economic grievances and grew to become Iran's largest against the clerical establishment since the 1979 Islamic Revolution.
The US-based Human Rights Activists News Agency (Hrana) says it has identified more than 7,000 people killed in the crackdown that followed, most of them protesters, but believes the true figure is much higher.
The Iranian government accuses the US and Israel of fomenting the unrest, blaming "terrorists" and "rioters" for the deaths, which it says totalled 3,117 including some members of the security forces.
The twins' family did not find out where they were being held for more than three months, their cousin says. They were tried over protests in Isfahan, in an area of the city where a member of the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) security force was killed.
Court documents have not been published, but the BBC has seen part of a sentencing document which says Taraneh was convicted of moharebeh, which is a capital offence under Iran's Islamic Penal Code. The offence included "drawing a bladed weapon with the intent to endanger people's lives", according to the document.
Romina was sentenced to 25 years in jail for the lesser charge of aiding and abetting moharebeh, according to Sato, the UN rapporteur.
Nourmohammadi, who has been in contact with relatives and others in Iran familiar with the case, says both women deny all the charges against them and that there is no evidence Taraneh had a "bladed weapon".
Sato says the sisters were part of a case in which 10 people were sentenced to death, but that there was "no clarification of the acts attributed to each individual".
According to sources familiar with the case, the twins' lawyers have submitted a complaint alleging they were tortured and sexually abused during interrogation, but the investigation into it is being overseen by an official they accuse of torture.
Voice messages from other women on death row contain a mixture of desperation and defiance.
Mahboubeh Shabani - widely reported to be 33 and a civil engineer - was sentenced to death in September under Iran's espionage law after transporting injured protesters, according to rights groups.
She called for help for herself and other prisoners from jail in the city of Mashhad in north-eastern Iran: "Everyone is in a terrible place mentally, especially those whose sentences have been finalised," she said.
Also jailed in Mashhad is Najmeh Amini, reported to be 23, who was initially arrested in the wake of the January protests, and later sentenced to death after being convicted of committing blasphemy in a social media post, according to rights groups.
"As long as I am alive, I have one hope, and that is to see a free and prosperous Iran before my life ends by the noose," a voice message attributed to her says.
In addition, Mojdeh Hashemi Bazargani - reported to be aged 27 - is also facing execution, according to rights groups. They say she was convicted of charges including "espionage", after being arrested in April, during the current war between Iran and Israel and the US.
The US-based Iranian rights group Tavaana has shared audio it says is of a phone call she made from prison, describing being beaten in the head, neck and body and made to sign a confession.
The woman in the recording says: "They accused me of espionage. They say you've been paid for it. If I had been paid for espionage, I would have a car or a house. I have nothing."
Amnesty International describes the charges in all three of these cases and also the twins as "politically motivated".
In response to the BBC's questions, the Iranian Embassy in London said "any allegations of the use of torture in connection with the mentioned cases are categorically rejected". It did not comment further on individual cases, but said "confessions obtained under duress have no legal validity".
At least 39 people have already been executed in connection with the January protests, according to Sato.
She notes a "sharp" increase in arrests and sentences across both men and women, and sees the rise in death sentences for women as an "escalation and expansion" of an "established pattern of repression".
Iranian human rights lawyer Musa Barzin, who is based in Turkey, says "it appears that factors such as gender or age now carry less weight in determining the severity of punishment".
Official detail on cases is often scant and some may go unreported.
However, Sato says as well as the six women she identified as being arrested in connection with protests, a further three have received death sentences this year - for "blasphemy" and "corruption on Earth charges, in relation to the war in March" and "espionage and moharebeh".
In comparison, these nine sentences are more than Hrana recorded for women for similar offences over the whole decade to 2025 - with no more than three in any one year.
The death sentences in three of the cases Sato identified as being linked to the protests have since been overturned – though two of those have been sent for retrial. She says she is concerned by an "increasingly frequent pattern" where overturned death sentences are later "reimposed by a parallel branch of the judiciary once public attention has subsided".
Sato says there was a "turning point" for women in Iran during the 2022 protests over the death of Mahsa Amini, who died in custody after being detained over an alleged breach of Iran's dress code.
Women "were at the forefront of challenging state policies and structures of control," says Sato. "Their political agency, visibility and leadership have made them targets of state repression."
The Iranian embassy said judicial proceedings in Iran are conducted in accordance with the Constitution and rule of law. It adds: "Cases involving the death penalty have included charges such as serious criminal offences, violence, terrorism, espionage, cooperation with hostile intelligence services and Moharebeh."
Iran executes more people per head of population than any other country, according to UN experts. Human rights groups say last year saw the highest number in decades.
Hrana recorded 2,003 executions in the year to October 2026. The vast majority - including 47 women - were for crimes such as murder and drug trafficking.
Nourmohammadi says the family are trying as best they can to support the twins.
Romina enjoys music and often asks relatives to play songs over the phone, he says.
Taraneh loves horses and has always wanted to set up a horse breeding centre, he says, and they tell her they plan to help her do so in the future: "That's how we try to give her hope."

Los Angeles – Los Angeles Dodgers star Shohei Ohtani on Wednesday expressed regret about the 2026 season, during which he suffered a left knee issue and his team missed out on a third consecutive World Series title.
“Of course I feel regret,” the 32-year-old said during an online interview.
Ohtani last pitched on July 3, and toward the end of the season, his batting performance also faltered. Ohtani said it is difficult to attribute his injuries to a single factor.
Regarding his intention to continue pitching and batting next season, Ohtani said he and the Dodgers have various plans for his two-way role.
“Our shared view is that I need to be in good condition heading into October (for the postseason),” he said.
While the Dodgers have indicated the possibility of delaying Ohtani’s return to pitching, he said, “It’s not ideal for a pitcher to make too few appearances, but pitching too often would be risky.”
“There are many ways to go about it, whether that’s pushing myself harder or spacing out my appearances over the course of the season,” he said.
Referring to a possible lockout if Major League Baseball and the players’ union fail to reach a new collective bargaining agreement after the current one expires next month, Ohtani said: “If there is a wasted period, fatigue from unnecessary pitching practice would build up. That is a tricky point.”
Nevertheless, he expressed his commitment to continuing as a two-way player, saying that the role allows him to contribute the most to the team while making the best use of his strengths.
Looking ahead to next season, which will mark his 10th year in MLB, Ohtani said, “I want to make the most of this offseason and make up for this season’s frustrations next year.”

New UK-EU treaty has 10-year termination clause
- Published
The government and the EU are set to publish the texts of two treaties that were agreed last week as part of a post-Brexit reset.
The treaties will be published on Thursday afternoon, alongside legislation which is designed to enact the bulk of the deal.
The BBC understands the deal covering food exports has a 10-year termination clause that would mean if one party ended the agreement, they would have to pay to rebuild border checks infrastructure, which will be significantly scaled back as part of the new deal.
Opposition leader Kemi Badenoch has said she would scrap the deal and Reform UK's Nigel Farage has suggested he would refuse to pay.
The Brexit reset deal has already sparked debate about its benefits, its costs, and a wider discussion on the long-term UK-EU relationship.
The deal covers British food exports, emissions trading and a youth experience scheme.
Two of the three legal texts will be released on Thursday, covering the food trade and emissions trading scheme deals, alongside the government's cost-cutting bill to enact the deal.
New assessments of the impact of the deal on different sectors and regions of the country are also expected.

Under the deal, food exporters will be significant beneficiaries from the scrapping of considerable red tape and checks, and dismantling of border facilities. An internal analysis forecasts a 16% boost to agricultural exports.
The industry and government hope the reduction in costs for food producers and sellers will be passed on to customers, but there may be no clear visible impact at the checkout.
Privately, industry insiders told the BBC earlier this week that there are too many moving parts in the world economy, in particular the energy price shock resulting from war in the Middle East.
Regarding the fine detail in the text of one of the treaties relating to the 10-year termination clause, European affairs minister Hamish Falconer said: "The Cutting Costs Bill allows us to implement two major trade agreements."

The treaty text will also contain finer detail of how the UK will observe, shape but not vote on relevant EU rules.
Plans to use secondary legislation, including granting direct so-called "Henry VIII powers" to ministers to align UK and EU laws, will also be detailed in the legislation.
Such powers could enable ministers to make changes to bills with less Parliamentary scrutiny.
Outlining the agreement with the EU to MPs earlier this week, the prime minister said new agreements with the EU are "pragmatic" and "not a prelude to anything".
Andy Burnham also said it would be "unthinkable" for the UK to rejoin the bloc without a referendum.
Several former prime ministers have urged him not to reopen the Brexit debate. Burnham said they are "stuck in the past" and later claimed there would be "no banging on about Europe" from Labour.
Badenoch said Burnham has "oversold" the deal and was "trying to take Britain back to 2015".

One night in October, hackers staged one of the most unusual cyber attacks in history: cranking up the temperature in refrigeration systems at hundreds of supermarkets across France and destroying millions of euros of food.
Hackers have targeted commercial fridges and freezers before, but never at this scale and never in the heart of Europe. The brazen attack left cyber professionals unsure as to who might have executed such a madcap operation. But French intelligence agencies found traces of Farsi and other clues in the digital trail pointing to an elite hacking unit of the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps.
The unit allegedly behind the hack, Shahid Kaveh, was already well known to Western intelligence agencies. Named after Mahmoud Kaveh, an Iranian commander who died during the 1980s Iran-Iraq war, it is one of several hacking units overseen by the Revolutionary Guards’ Cyber Electronic Command.
The group, which often goes by the online persona CyberAv3ngers, has a history of targeting critical infrastructure. In 2023 and 2024, it hacked Israeli-made industrial control devices inside water, manufacturing, and transportation systems across several US states. Operational disruption was minimal, but the attackers left a message each time: “Every equipment ‘made in Israel’ is CyberAv3ngers legal target.”
State-backed Iranian hackers have rarely targeted Europe in this way, however. October’s hacks, experts say, mark an escalation in the Islamic republic’s cyber warfare strategy and a new willingness to hit European infrastructure.
“Iran has very clearly messaged that the global economy will be disrupted as a consequence of it being shut out from the world,” said Ellie Geranmayeh of the European Council on Foreign Relations.
