In the early 1500s, an Italian polymath named Leonardo da Vinci took a good crack at exactly the phenomenon that makes nervous fliers clutch their airplane seats in fear and flight attendants push their carts back to the galleys with haste: turbulence.
Da Vinci was fascinated by swirling, chaotic eddies of water, movements so complex that he made hundreds of drawings of his observations. Why, exactly, did water—any fluid, really, be it atmospheric air or blood in the heart—move in that way?
Now the world has ChatGPT and self-driving cars and solar farms, and it still doesn’t exactly know how turbulence works. “It’s the hardest remaining problem in classical physics, and it’s one we need to fly through,” says Michael Murillo, a professor of theoretical and computational physics at Michigan State University.
Now a bumper crop of data-driven efforts to predict and avoid turbulence could get fliers closer to a smooth flight. Twenty terabytes of data are created by an airplane’s engine in one hour of commercial flying, according to the International Air Transport Association, with more broadcast by airplanes midflight: GPS position, altitude, speed. An “electronic flight bag,” basically a specialized iPad, is equipped with navigation charts and manuals and can transmit its own information, as long as the airplane’s internet connection cooperates. Satellites watch and collect it all.
“Air traffic has gone up, and communication costs and the costs of putting computers on aircraft have come down,” says Larry Cornman, a physicist with the National Science Foundation’s National Center for Atmospheric Research who has been studying turbulence for decades. “The time is now to work on these things because we can do them.”
This is good news for aviation safety. More than 200 people were seriously injured on US airplanes in turbulence-related incidents between 2009 and 2023, according to FAA data. Turbulence is also getting worse. Climate change alters the atmospheric conditions around the world’s jet streams, creating destabilizing wind shear. From the cockpit of an airplane, this translates into sudden, clear-air turbulence, difficult to see or predict. Historically, pilots’ only method of avoiding turbulence is heeding the warning of those who accidentally went through it before them, and hoping that nothing had changed.
But just in the past two years, Cornman’s decades of work on turbulence has been put into the field in ways it couldn’t be before, part of several projects coordinated by the US federal government and the airline industry. One breakthrough came when Cornman and an FAA air traffic controller determined that aircrafts’ federally required broadcasts of their positions, altitude, and speed could be used to spot unexpected turbulence, without requiring new hardware or software onboard. Researchers can use this crowdsourced, public data to make predictions about when and where turbulence will pop up.
In September, the National Science Foundation announced a $30 million award to nine universities to stand up a new center dedicated to predicting turbulence—in the air, but also in the charged particles inside a fusion reactor, and in the gas clouds that stretch across space.
“Turbulence is the reason we don’t have fusion energy yet,” says Murillo, who heads up the new center, called Transformative Explorations in Multi-Physics and Engineering of Scientific Turbulence, or Tempest. The chaotic swirling of superhot plasma inside a reactor allows heat to leak out, preventing the material from reaching the temperatures needed to allow nuclei to fuse. The US federal government wants to get closer to figuring that out.
“Closer,” because turbulence is impossible to perfectly predict, scientists say. For one thing, turbulence occurs at many different, small scales at the same time. Air swirling around an airplane breaks into eddies, then smaller eddies, and then even smaller eddies, with each interacting with each other—too many variables, happening too quickly, to mathematically account for. For another, tiny changes—wind speed, temperature—can eventually dramatically alter air movement, suddenly altering the turbulence once predicted. To make perfect forecasts, one would need a perfect picture of exactly what’s going on in the atmosphere at all times.
But increasing sophisticated applications of machine learning could allow scientists to get closer to knowing what’s going to happen when, says Murillo. And while brute, computational force can’t solve the turbulence problem, AI agents might give the effort a boost. OpenAI’s blockbuster announcement this fall that it had resolved the Navier-Stokes problem—equations that are the beginning of all turbulence models—suggests LLMs could help.
“Turbulence has been a problem only human minds could work on; as of this year, that's no longer true,” says Murillo.
To make flying better, the aviation industry doesn’t necessarily need to solve turbulence. It needs to get better at knowing what sort of conditions create it and not send airplanes there.
One company in Tel Aviv, SkyPath, uses those in-plane iPads and their accelerometers to collect and share crowdsourced data between different airplanes, even if they don’t fly for the same airline. (This sort of dating sharing can be a sensitive topic for competing companies; SkyPath says it assuages these concerns by ensuring that data is anonymized before it’s shared.) More than 40,000 of these devices have SkyPath installed on them, says CEO Maya Shpak; the company says that several major airlines, including American, use the technology. SkyPath combines that collected data with additional information, including weather forecasts, and uses machine intelligence to make predictions about the future state of the air. The app helps pilots avoid turbulent air and warn passengers and crew members that choppiness is coming, 10 to 15 minutes before it happens.
One pilot named Eric who uses SkyPath, who asked WIRED not to use his full name because he was not authorized to speak to the media, said the app is a helpful tool that allows him to warn passengers what to expect. His issue is the same as those studying turbulence: One can’t take measurements everywhere all at once.
“It’s like any crowdsourced software,” says the pilot. “It only works if everyone uses it, and no one wants to use it until everyone else is.” Today, several large operators are using the app, which makes it especially useful in areas with lots of flights, he says.
Cornman, the physicist, wants to keep all these advances in perspective. “No matter what people say, we’re not getting close to 100 percent, 90 percent, 80 percent [predictive accuracy] anytime soon,” he says. “It’s too complicated a problem.” Smoother skies, if not perfect ones, are ahead.

- The claim that the Pentagon cannot account for $2 trillion in taxpayer money is based in truth but missing some context.
- It is more accurate to say that the Pentagon cannot comprehensively account for about $2.14 trillion worth of assets, based on a November news release from the Department of Defense about its annual department-wide audit. As of this writing, DOD remains the only federal agency that has never passed an audit.
- We have left this claim unrated for several reasons, including the fact that the department is composed of many agencies, and some of them are still undergoing audits as of this writing.
- Congress passed an act in 2023 mandating that by 2028 the Pentagon must obtain a clean audit, a term used to describe when auditors find no issues with an organization's financial records. The Pentagon celebrated the progress made toward that goal in 2026, despite significant issues remaining.
- Federal auditors also told Snopes that even the departments and services without clean audits could still accurately account for most of their assets.
Social media users claimed in mid-November that the U.S. Department of Defense is unable to account for $2 trillion in taxpayer funds.
"The military is unable to account for $2 trillion in tax payer money, but somehow forgiving student loans would be 'unfair to the American tax payer,'" one post on Facebook read. Users shared similar posts on X and other platforms.
This rumor began after the Department of Defense released its annual agencywide audit Nov. 16. The Pentagon said in a news release that more than 56% of the department's assets received a "clean audit," meaning auditors from the department's Office of the Inspector General and from independent public accounting firms found no issues with the agency's financial records for that percentage of its assets:
For the first time in Department history, clean audit opinions will cover more than 56 percent of DoW [Department of War, the Trump administration's preferred name for the Department of Defense] assets and over 90 percent of its liabilities. These figures include audit opinions expected in January and February of FY 2027.
The Pentagon has $4.87 trillion in assets, according to its fiscal year 2026 financial report (Page 19). In other words, about 44% — or about $2.14 trillion — of its assets, or resources owned and controlled by the Defense Department, are not comprehensively and cleanly accounted for.
We have left this claim unrated as the Department of Defense is composed of many agencies, and some of them are still undergoing audits as of this writing, as DOD notes. Those audits combined is what determines the Pentagon's departmentwide audit opinion.
The lack of a clean opinion also does not necessarily mean that the Pentagon has no idea where its assets are — just that it can't keep a detailed, transparent record of how it moves money around. Furthermore, reader opinions may differ on whether $2 trillion in assets are the same as $2 trillion in taxpayer money, given that the amount those assets cost at the time of purchase may be different from their current value.
In an email following the publication of this story, the Department of Defense Office of the Inspector General said DOD services and agencies without clean opinions can still "accurately account for most of their assets."
"For example, the military services can accurately account for military equipment and munitions but have challenges accounting for some general equipment and inventory for the Joint Strike Fighter and other programs," the email said. "There is no direct reference to $2 trillion being unaccounted for in the DoW OIG financial statement audit reports."
DOD did not immediately respond a request to explain the exact details behind its 56% calculation.
A related rumor circulating online claimed the Pentagon can't account for $31 billion worth of F-35 aircraft parts. That's a reference to a real Government Accountability Office report — separate from the audit — that found DOD's "records of its F-35 parts are outdated, inaccurate, and incomplete." The OIG's audit echoed that conclusion, finding that DOD "has not yet established an accurate, complete, or financially reportable population of F-35 property, nor implemented an IT environment capable of supporting reliable reporting."
DOD celebrates audit progress, despite major issues
Overall, DOD received a "disclaimer of opinion" rating, which means the condition of the agency's accounting is so poor, it is impossible to assess its financial records.
However, it is worth noting that the percentage of assets accounted for in 2026 is technically progress for the Pentagon, which remains the only federal agency that has never passed an audit. The Pentagon has received a disclaimer of opinion rating on every departmentwide federal audit since they began in 2018.
"This is a really big deal for us," said Jules W. Hurst III, the department's undersecretary and chief financial officer, in DOD's news release. "For the first time, by February 2027, we will have clean opinions on a majority of our assets and over 90% of our liabilities."
A clean opinion, or clean audit, means auditors have found no issues with an organization's financial records. At least one fund that the Pentagon oversees, the Medicare Eligible Retiree Health Care Fund, received the first clean opinion in its history this year.
The department's Office of the Inspector General said in the introductory memo to its report that while the Pentagon's disclaimer of opinion rating remained the same, the Department of Defense has taken "deliberate steps" to meet a congressional requirement to receive a departmentwide clean audit by 2028. For example, DOD has increased spending on auditing and overhauled its strategy toward a clean audit.
The Government Accountability Office, which has had the Department of Defense's financial management on its "high risk" list for fraud and management since 1995, said in May that DOD's "renewed focus" on a clean audit was "encouraging." However, the office said the new strategy's efforts to consolidate standalone audits of agencies under DOD oversight "potentially risks limiting accountability and transparency."
In fact, the Department of Defense Office of the Inspector General said that while the audit results seemed to suggest fewer material weaknesses — in other words, severe issues that result in a high risk of inaccurate financial reporting — that reduction comes from consolidation, not from actual resolution of the problems.
For more on the DOD's history of spotty financial records, see our in-depth look examining what the Pentagon's audit ratings actually mean.

Messaging platform WhatsApp plans to roll out a new feature that lets users buy and install international data eSIMs directly within the app. In a blog post, WhatsApp said that the offering will initially be available in select countries. Can a US-backed mineral highway bring peace and prosperity to DR Congo?
- Published
As trains carrying thousands of tonnes of copper from the Democratic Republic of Congo roar through her community, 20-year-old Manuela Julia is not thinking about critical minerals or billion-dollar investments.
She is thinking about getting around more easily.
The railway runs through Catumbela, near the Angolan city of Lobito, on the Atlantic coast.
For Julia, it has made travelling cheaper and more convenient.
"Before, I had to use a taxi, which is much more expensive. Now it is cheaper and easier to travel," she says.
But the railway has ambitions far bigger than improving local transport.
It is part of the Lobito Corridor, a US-backed effort to secure access to Africa's critical minerals and promote regional economic cooperation, which Washington hopes will help bring peace to conflict-torn eastern DR Congo.
Under agreements brokered by US President Donald Trump, DR Congo and neighbouring Rwanda have committed to greater economic cooperation, including more transparent mineral supply chains and regional infrastructure development.
The wider plan envisages linking these initiatives to the railway, which transports minerals from Central Africa to Western markets via Angola, rather than east to China as most do currently.
The hope is that formalising the mineral trade and encouraging investment could help curb illicit markets that have helped finance armed groups and fuel instability.
But can a railway built to move minerals to global markets also deliver peace and prosperity?
The Lobito Corridor links DR Congo's mineral-rich south to Angola's Atlantic coast through the Benguela Railway and the Port of Lobito.
Its importance has grown as demand for copper and cobalt rises, driven partly by the global transition to cleaner energy, as both are critical ingredients for all kinds of electrical components.
"The timing matters," says Johannesburg-based political risk analyst Wellington Muzengeza
"Electrification and the energy transition have increased the strategic importance of copper, cobalt and reliable mineral supply chains."
DR Congo is the world's largest producer of cobalt and one of its biggest copper producers, along with neighbouring Zambia. The US sees the corridor as a means to diversify mineral supplies and reduce reliance on China, which dominates much of the world's processing capacity.
A US-DR Congo strategic partnership identifies the route from the Congolese town of Sakania to Lobito as a priority for mineral exports, while the economic framework agreed by DR Congo and Rwanda envisages connecting regional infrastructure and trade initiatives to the corridor.
The project has attracted over $750m (£570m), including funding backed by the US International Development Finance Corporation and the Development Bank of Southern Africa to upgrade railway tracks, signalling systems and trains.
The railway, built in 1902 under Portuguese colonial rule, was originally designed to transport goods and minerals from Central Africa to the Atlantic coast. After years of disruption during Angola's civil war, it was rebuilt and fully reopened in 2015.
The US first got involved in the project under former President Joe Biden but backing has continued under Trump.
At Lobito's mineral terminal, the renewed ambitions are already visible.
When the BBC visited, a train carrying about 12,000 tonnes of copper cathodes from DR Congo had arrived. Workers moved the refined copper sheets into a warehouse before they were loaded on to ships bound for international markets, mostly the US.
The cargo is handled by Lobito Atlantic Railway (LAR), which has a 30-year concession to operate freight services along the corridor and manage the mineral terminal.
Chief operating officer Nicholas Gregoir says freight volumes have more than doubled since the company took over in January 2024.
LAR expects to transport about 200,000 tonnes of copper through the corridor in 2026.
For mining companies, the railway offers a shorter route to international markets.
"The Lobito Corridor is the shortest route for both Zambia and the DRC," to the Atlantic, says Kátila Vanessa Monteiro da Silva Neto, executive director of the Lobito Port Authority.
Zambia, Africa's second-largest copper producer, also plans to connect its Copperbelt to Lobito through a proposed 830km (515 mile)-railway.
But a more efficient route to market does not automatically translate into economic transformation.
"Joining a corridor is not the same as industrialising," Muzengeza says. "The test is not simply whether Zambia gains another route to the sea. It is whether that route helps build a stronger economy."
Some Angolans believe the railway's greatest value could lie in what it offers businesses and communities beyond mining.
"I call it a corridor of development," says businessman Adérito Areias.
The railway passes through some of Angola's most productive agricultural regions.
Better transport links could help farmers reach larger markets and reduce losses.
"If there isn't an artery carrying products from the interior to where there is demand, those products simply rot where they are produced," Areias says.
But the challenge is turning that ambition into reality.
The Port of Lobito handled about 1.8 million tonnes of cargo in 2025, of which around 158,000 tonnes was minerals. Its mineral terminal can handle up to 3.6 million tonnes annually.
"The port already has the capacity," says Neto. "What we need now is sufficient railway capacity and rolling stock."
For residents along the route, the benefits have been immediate.
State-owned railway operator Caminho de Ferro de Benguela (CFB), which runs passenger services, carried a record 1.6 million passengers in 2025.
LAR says it directly employs nearly 1,000 people, 98% of them Angolan.
"This job allows me to support my family," says Domingos Canhama, a father of four and a forklift operator at CFB.
"I can put food on the table, maintain a home and help support my father," he says.
Muzengeza argues that the bigger opportunity is developing local businesses in engineering, maintenance, warehousing and agricultural processing.
"Businesses in Angola need access to the railway, not just proximity to it. That means feeder roads, electricity, storage and predictable services," he says.
But can minerals and their movement along the railways line help deliver peace to eastern DR Congo, where the battle for control of mineral resources has fuelled decades of conflict?
Most recently, this has seen the M23 rebel group seize control of many mineral-rich areas.
The Congolese government says neighbouring Rwanda is backing the M23 in order to gain access to DR Congo's mineral wealth. Despite overwhelming evidence, Rwanda denies backing the M23.
The Trump-backed agreements between DR Congo and Rwanda seek to promote transparent mineral supply chains, cross-border investment and regional infrastructure, with the aim of ensuring mineral wealth does not finance armed groups.
"The US wants reliable access to minerals essential to defence, advanced technology and energy systems, while reducing dependence on supply chains in which China has substantial influence," says Muzengeza, the political risk analyst
"Lobito is therefore more than a railway but an infrastructure that can reshape trade routes and commercial power."
At a meeting in Paris in November, DR Congo urged the US to turn its strategic partnership into tangible investments, arguing that success should be measured by completed projects rather than signed agreements.
"We want the partnership to support local mineral processing, electricity access for households and businesses and peace in the east," said DR Congo's Economy Minister Daniel Mukoko Samba.
Even if more minerals move through formal channels, better infrastructure alone would not resolve the political and security tensions driving the conflict.
There is also the question of who captures the wealth. Much of the copper and cobalt transported from DR Congo through Lobito is destined for processing and manufacturing outside Africa.
While Angola can earn transit fees and create logistics jobs, much of the higher-value activity takes place elsewhere.
"When you export raw materials, you are also exporting jobs and knowledge," Angola's Foreign Affairs Minister Téte António tells the BBC.
Areias shares that concern.
"We should not export lithium but export batteries," he says, arguing that the corridor should help develop local processing and manufacturing rather than simply accelerate raw material exports.
Back in Catumbela, such debates can feel distant from everyday life.
For Julia, the railway already means cheaper journeys and easier movement.
But its ultimate success will depend on whether it can deliver more than faster mineral exports.
Whether it can also help secure lasting peace in eastern DR Congo, where the minerals are mined, remains the bigger test.

By any measure, it is one of the most extraordinary political stories of our age: a shy Italian girl locks eyes with the scion of an Indian political family, falls instantly and steadfastly in love, “transplanting herself” as a result, suffers soul-shattering tragedies, then takes the reins of power in the world’s largest democracy. It is a life that spans the extremes of privilege and distress, and half a century of seismic national history.
No wonder publishers have been keen to secure the memoirs of the famously guarded Sonia Gandhi, soon to turn 80. Yet when the chance came, the deal with the country’s biggest publisher, Penguin Random House India, fell through at the last minute over what it termed “an impasse over a particular issue” in the text, with HarperCollins stepping into the breach. For those unfamiliar with the sensitive political context, the Nehru-Gandhi family has been in charge of India for about half the eight decades since independence – and the principal opposition to Narendra Modi’s prickly BJP regime for the past 12 years.
As it turns out, Belonging does not read as incendiary. It errs, rather, towards discretion and legacy-building. It is also, at its best, a heartbreaking story of love and loss.
Gandhi’s voice is measured and generally frill-free. Flourishes do accompany the meet-cute at a Greek restaurant in Cambridge in the mid-1960s that sets off the story. “That January Sunday, which was to change my life,” she writes, “the sky [was] a beautiful azure dotted with puffy white clouds as in a Tiepolo fresco.” The introduction to fellow student Rajiv Gandhi was “a bolt of lightning”.
And, as in a film, there is parental resistance. Sonia’s father, a businessman who worked in construction in a small Italian town, is a second world war veteran, nicknamed Maino the Lion. A 1998 New Yorker profile by Patrick French, briefly a collaborator on Belonging, had him down as “an unrepentant fascist” until his death. Well, was he? We don’t get to find out. Wherever expedient, Gandhi maintains her strategic silence.
Stefano Maino, at any rate, is “padre padrone” – literally, “father master”. When he hears about his middle daughter’s love interest, he brings “his fist down on his writing table” with a shout of “Basta!” And yet, he buys her a ticket to India the moment she turns 21.
On the boy’s side is the person who would come to be described as the world’s most powerful woman, Indira Gandhi, the daughter of India’s first prime minister, Jawaharlal Nehru. Barely has Sonia landed in Delhi than Indira decides the pair must wed (the news reaches the Mainos via radio; Signor Maino stays away). Indira then manages Sonia’s first pregnancy, directs the name-giving ceremony – you get the picture. Gandhi refers to her, factually, as “my mother-in-law”, but, subverting the stereotype, she becomes a devoted daughter. Walking us through her induction into elite Indian family life, she draws an affectionate portrait of this formidable 20th-century figure.
But family and party allegiance are a distorting lens through which to view history. Charged events, such as Indira’s crushing of a huge railway strike, acquire a benign gloss. The 21 tumultuous months of the 1975 Emergency – which saw members of the opposition arrested, civil liberties curtailed, the press censored, while a despotic nepo-baby (Sanjay, Indira’s younger son) ran amok – are rendered with a brisk calm. Tenderness is reserved for the repercussions on the family in its subsequent period out of power.
Sanjay’s death at 33, just after Indira’s return to power in 1980, leaves the matriarch broken. “In her eyes [Rajiv] was the only one who could come to her rescue.” Gandhi does not interrogate the hereditary approach to democratic politics, but she does recount, affectingly, the fight to protect herself and Rajiv – a commercial pilot with no greater ambitions – and their two children from the inferno.
In the book’s strongest scene, she waits disoriented in a crowded hospital in 1984, “shivering under my dressing gown”, having ferried her mother-in-law’s bullet-ridden body there. Indira was slain by her Sikh bodyguards in revenge for ordering the army into the Golden Temple, Sikhism’s holiest site. As Rajiv embraces her with the words “they want me to be sworn in as prime minister”, Gandhi feels “a rage welling up deep inside me”. “They will kill you too!” she says. “They will kill me anyway,” he replies. The “they” is unspecified, and gives these pages an air of foretold tragedy.
Rajiv’s eventful term plays out under this death cloud. It starts with a pogrom against Sikhs, spearheaded by Congress leaders. Gandhi goes some length to eulogise her husband’s tenure: in reality, it was a troubled and contradictory record. Rajiv was 40, severely underqualified, and grieving. Miscalculations abounded, among them clumsy religious manoeuvring that played into the Hindu-nationalist BJP’s hands, and a military entanglement in Sri Lanka designed to end the civil war with Tamil separatists.
And that death cloud never blows way. The children are withdrawn from school; Gandhi, perpetually anxious, finds her hands trembling in public; Rajiv is once shot at. When he loses the election his successor vindictively withdraws his special security cover. Their son Rahul (the current leader of the opposition) predicts the worst. At a rally in Tamil Nadu in 1991, a Tamil Tiger operative makes to place a garland around Rajiv, then 46, with explosives strapped around her body.
The graphic photograph of the aftermath of that scene is seared into Indian memory. Thanks to the vigilance of her children, Gandhi has never seen it. “I had become the child to be protected, they the parents,” she writes, in a wrenching section. Years later, when she collapses in Japan, a nurse is startled to find her grown children lying on either side of her on the small hospital bed.
Gandhi’s first reaction on hearing the news about Rajiv? “I wanted to die.” Gradually though, she picks up the smithereens of her life. As the remaining Gandhi elder, she picks up the pieces of the splintering Congress party, too.There are few parallels to a life as singular as this. A century ago, Congress had its first foreign-born female president, the British theosophist Annie Besant; farther afield, Janet Jagan, the American-born Jewish wife of Cheddi Jagan herself became president of Guyana – but both women were political activists to begin with. Gandhi, in her words, “had no right – except for the fact that I carried the family name”.
The exhortations to Gandhi to take over the party reveal plenty about Congress culture, and they are eventually successful: the spectator becomes the player. We watch her bone up on her Hindi, lead campaigns, stitch up alliances (including with a party sympathetic to the Tamil Tigers), and combat the BJP, which brands her, among other things, a “Monica Lewinsky” who would establish a “Rome Raj”. In 2004, she leads an alliance of parties to victory.
To her children’s horror, Gandhi is badgered into nearly accepting the post of prime minister. Instead she handpicks a candidate, Manmohan Singh, while keeping charge of the party (eventually leading it for a staggering 22 years) and chairing the ruling coalition as well as an advisory council that keeps a hand on policy levers.
“It had been my choice to become Indian,” she reflects after the long night of the soul that leads her to decline the premiership – a source of fascinated speculation over the years. “I made it out of love for a man, but that love came to encompass his family and his country. And it was this love for India that had demanded the most from me.”
Belonging comes into its own when unpacking those demands, and showing the transition from grief to its successor emotion, resilience.

Argentina bans its central bank from printing money for the government
Argentina’s Congress has approved a law that bans the central bank from printing money to cover government spending
BUENOS AIRES, Argentina -- Argentina’s Congress voted Thursday to bar the central bank from printing money to pay the government’s bills, enshrining in law a key pillar of President Javier Milei’s fight against the country’s notoriously high inflation.
Under the new charter, the central bank’s “primary and fundamental mission” will be to preserve the value of the peso — a goal Milei has pursued in office even though, as a candidate in 2023, he promised to abolish the bank and replace the local currency with the U.S. dollar.
The 141-0 vote in the Chamber of Deputies, with 99 abstentions, comes days after preliminary figures showed Argentina had likely slipped into recession, less than a year before the libertarian economist seeks a second four-year term.
For generations, when Argentine governments spent more than they collected in taxes, they turned to the central bank to print pesos to fill the gap, fueling repeated currency crises and bouts of hyperinflation. The law puts an end to “91 years of plunder, expropriation, impunity and institutional decay,” Milei’s office said in a statement.
The new charter bars the bank from lending to any level of government or otherwise financing the Treasury. It also scraps the bank's employment and economic development goals added under former President Cristina Fernández de Kirchner, the Peronist opposition leader whose administrations leaned heavily on the central bank to fund unbridled spending.
But the law gives the monetary authority less protection than Milei sought. His original bill would have required a two-thirds vote in both houses of Congress to remove the bank’s governor, his appointee Santiago Bausili. The Senate watered down that clause, and the lower house lacked the votes Thursday to restore it. Now a president can replace the bank’s leadership with a simple Senate majority.
Milei has slashed public spending in the past three years, turning Argentina's chronic fiscal deficits into a surplus and helping cut annual inflation from nearly 300% in early 2024 to 33% last month.
Yet Milei has been reluctant to let the market set Argentina’s most important price: the exchange rate. The charter leaves currency controls in the bank’s hands and sets no clear rule for how it should respond to inflation.
Tight monetary policy has kept the peso strong, making Argentine goods expensive abroad just as factories face a flood of cheaper imports. Oil and gas exports have boomed while labor-intensive industries like manufacturing, retail and construction have struggled.
Argentina’s economy shrank an estimated 1.8% in the third quarter, after a 0.6% contraction in the second, according to official data released Tuesday. Two straight quarters of decline is the usual definition of a recession.
As Milei’s support slips in the polls, investors wary of a country infamous for defaulting on its debt nine times are weighing the possibility that the Peronists — the populist movement that has long dominated Argentine politics — could return to power and reverse his market-friendly reforms. The premium investors demand to hold Argentina’s bonds, a gauge of perceived default risk, has more than doubled since early August, according to JPMorgan.
Under growing pressure, Milei is now hoping to overhaul next year’s presidential race. The Senate on Thursday approved his bill to suspend the mandatory primaries, which the government argues waste public money on contests parties should run themselves. It now goes to the lower house for a vote.
Suspending the primaries, long a bellwether for the general election, would spare Milei an early verdict from voters — one that, if poor, could spook markets and sink the peso and his support with it.
Peronist leaders have balked at the move, which would force their fractured movement to negotiate a ticket behind closed doors or scramble to organize a primary of its own.
"Milei now wants to change the rules of democracy to improve his chances of reelection by cheating,” Buenos Aires province Gov. Axel Kicillof, a potential Peronist challenger to Milei, wrote on X.

On Wednesday morning, the US Army detonated nearly five tons of degraded lead azide outside of Middletown, Iowa.
Environmental Protection Administration chief Lee Zeldin told CNN shortly after the explosion that preliminary monitoring from the site detected no lead in the air around the site.
But the full extent of the fallout may not be certain for at least a few days. A barrage of government, university, and citizen monitoring and testing projects are underway. Air, soil, and water samples they’ve collected will determine the extent of lead exposure, if any, in Middletown and the surrounding area.
The lead azide has been on the base near Middletown for decades, but recently the Army deemed it unstable and too dangerous to move and remediate. Poor communication between the Army and towns in the path of the fallout led to a public uproar. While the federal government stepped up its mitigation measures—the Army dug a dam around the detonation site, while NASA stepped in with research jets and satellites for monitoring—universities had already been swinging into action due to the chaotic rollout.
Several departments at the University of Iowa kicked into gear to begin to set up air and soil monitoring stations late last week. “Initially we did not know that [the] EPA or Army or anybody else was going to be doing anything,” says Peter Thorne, a professor of environmental health at the university.
Scientists at Purdue University, nearly 300 miles away, also put out a call for soil samples from Middletown.
“We learned about the detonation late last week; once we learned of the initial delay in detonation date we decided to put forth the call,” says Ellen Wells, a professor of public health at Purdue who is helping lead the testing.
Surrounding towns were notified in late October that the Army wanted to conduct pre- and post-detonation soil sampling for “an intentional, controlled detonation” of a “quantity of lead azide”—seemingly the only notification that many towns in the initial modeled path of the fallout say they received before a press release issued by the Army days before the planned explosion.
The lack of communication has, understandably, instilled a lot of public distrust in the federal government, including agencies’ monitoring programs. Thorne says that efforts like the University of Iowa’s are not meant to displace federal monitoring, but rather to supplement and support it—and hopefully reassure the public.
“We and the EPA are doing similar exposure assessment efforts. If they agree, they can give us some confidence,” he says. “For people who might be concerned about the veracity of what the government tells them, if their findings are in alignment with ours, then I think that helps quell some of those concerns.”
Thorne says that the soil samples the University of Iowa scientists had measured before the detonation had low levels of lead. “If I saw something like a 10 fold increase in the amount of lead in the soil 20 miles downwind, I’d be concerned with that,” he says.
Some soil testing can be done instantaneously with devices that can image the soil’s surface, using a gun device that fires X-ray beams into a sample and measures the specific electromagnetic signature of lead atoms that bounce back. While Wells and her team don’t have those instruments in the field, they are planning on using them to analyze the samples they receive. More sensitive lab equipment can provide even more granular data, though Thorne estimates those results could take about a week.
In addition to monitoring being done by the Army and the EPA, which is maintaining a live website of air quality results, University of Iowa scientists are monitoring the plume to figure out where the highest concentration of lead may settle. They’re also collecting data on particulate matter in the air around the detonation site for analysis, sending air filters to the lab for more detailed results.
“As these data are compiled over the holiday week to the early next week, I think we'll start to have a bigger picture of roughly how much loading we have of the soil at various places downwind and what we can expect from that,” says Thorne.
A lot of concern online has centered around how additional lead in the soil may impact crops in Iowa, one of the central agricultural hubs for soybeans and corn. Jeffrey Catalano, a professor of earth and environmental sciences at Washington University in Saint Louis, says that there’s a large amount of research showing that plants like corn are actually pretty bad at absorbing lead.
“The hazard is more like, if soil with lead in it gets stuck to leaves, and you eat leaves that have lead-rich soil on them,” he says. “If you take some corn crops next year versus this year and measure their lead content, I don’t think you would see anything other than random variations. I’m not worried about food produced in Iowa.”
Municipal drinking water is also unlikely to be affected because most treatment plants are designed to remove lead from water supplies, says Patrick McNamara, a professor of environmental engineering at Marquette University. It’s more worrisome for private wells or streams on people’s property where livestock may drink. McNamara suggests that owners use at-home lead water tests for safety.
While the detonation and haphazard announcements leading up to it raised alarm bells, both Thorne and Catalano say that there are communities dealing with legacy pollution around the country that are exposed to dangerous levels of lead every day that deserve attention—and remediation.
“I've done work in places like East Chicago, Indiana, where they built a housing project and a school on the grounds of a former lead smelting plant—we were seeing soil lead levels that are roughly 10,000-fold higher than what we've measured in Iowa this week,” Thorne says. “There are a lot of places around the country where there's a much greater lead hazard than I'm going to anticipate what we’ll end up with here. I don't want to over-sell this one when we recognize that there are places where people are really suffering, and need to be remediated for the health of their children.”

Republican wants FBI and CIA answers before questioning Nvidia chief
Rep. Brian Fitzpatrick, R-Penn., on Nvidia CEO's upcoming House committee interview
Jensen Huang is back at the helm of Nvidia with President Trump's backing. But the questions surrounding the AI chipmaker and its ties to China are far from settled.
U.S. intelligence officials told congressional staff there is no evidence that Alice Huang, the woman who had an affair with the Nvidia chief, was a Chinese spy or intelligence asset, according to a person familiar with the matter who was granted anonymity to speak about a closed-door briefing.
There is also no evidence that she initiated the affair to collect intelligence for China's government, the person told NPR's Ryan Lucas on condition of anonymity because of the sensitive nature of the matter. She is, however, believed to have passed along information after the affair began.
Trump has said he helped arrange Huang's return as CEO, and Nvidia's board maintains that his reinstatement presents no national security risk. Some Republican lawmakers, however, want to understand how those conclusions were reached.
Speaking to Morning Edition on Wednesday, before NPR obtained the new information, Rep. Brian Fitzpatrick, R-Pa., said he wants to hear from the FBI and CIA before Huang appears before House lawmakers next week.
For Fitzpatrick, a former FBI special agent who sits on the House Intelligence Committee, the inquiry begins with what federal authorities knew and whether they warned the Nvidia chief of potential espionage threats.
"What briefings did they give? When did they give them?" he asked.
Huang's reinstatement, Fitzpatrick said, should not put those questions to rest.
"The public is rightly concerned, and they deserve answers," he said.
Fitzpatrick also wants to hear from Attorney General Todd Blanche, who on Tuesday described Nvidia as a good corporate citizen, and Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick, whose department faces questions over Nvidia's chip exports to China.
"Anytime you do an investigation, you follow the facts wherever they lead, and you report those facts with unimpeachable integrity," Fitzpatrick said. "You leave no stone unturned."
The debate over Huang's reinstatement extends beyond Washington.

KDgate for Montreal mayor continues with website mocking Kraft Dinner comments
Protesters ate mac and cheese in front of city hall Thursday to protest tax hike, mayor's comments
The controversy over her Kraft Dinner comments is sticking to Montreal Mayor Soraya Martinez Ferrada.
The City of Montreal unveiled a budget that featured a property tax average increase of 9.8 per cent — about three times the inflation rate – on Tuesday.
The budget is due to be adopted in mid-December.
But an ill-timed Kraft Dinner comparison over budget choices has been haunting the mayor, giving rise to a website created by a Montreal software developer presenting the city budget on KD boxes.
There is also a protest outside city hall later Thursday afternoon.
The landing page for the website, kdgate.ca, alludes to the mayor's comments. (Submitted by kdgate.ca)
Martinez Ferrada’s comments during an interview with French-language media outlet Quartre95, a personal finance site, following the budget rollout compared creating a municipal budget to decisions taken at home.
"We're going through every service to see what we can save. It's like when you make your personal budget: if you know you'll have less money one year, then, you have to make choices," she said.
"Sometimes, you'll have to eat a little more Kraft Dinner because you can't afford filet mignon."
The comments were walked back by Martinez Ferrada on Wednesday morning in an Instagram story where she described the comparison as “clumsy.”
"What I meant was that when we make choices, the city is the same as when we make personal choices," she said.
But not before it unleashed a torrent of backlash on social media, framing her remarks as out of touch with the reality of Montrealers dealing with higher cost-of-living.
The website, kdgate.ca, includes a rundown of the city budget listed in a way that mirrors the nutritional facts on the back of a food item. (Submitted by kdgate.ca)
On Thursday morning, a website, kdgate.ca, was published outlining a municipal budget in the form of nutritional information on the packaging of the popular comfort food.
Niko Draca, the Montrealer behind the site, told CBC News about what prompted him to create it.
"I saw a lot of outrage over the comment and I wanted to turn it into something positive and really get people looking at this data," Draca said.
"These documents are usually quite long and dry, so I figured a fun way to visualize could help, basically using the KD comment as a hook."
Protesting tax hike, mayor's comments
Meanwhile, a crowd gathered in front of Montreal’s city hall Thursday evening to cook boxed macaroni and cheese, some Kraft and some not, to protest the mayor's tax hike and comments.
There were portable stoves, roiling water, elbow pasta and waving signs chastising the mayor. Other people held up enlarged printouts of the famous blue Kraft Dinner box.
Sam Bélanger was among those in attendance. Speaking to CBC News as metal was clanged, drums were banged and voices rang in the background, he called the mayor’s comments unacceptable.
“I feel like she’s totally disconnected from the reality of most people in Montreal, in Quebec and in Canada — the situation with rent and food and everything we saw since the pandemic,” he said. “Everyone is feeling that pain.”
Protesters held up signs Thursday afternoon that chastised Montreal's mayor and highlighted the rising cost of living in the city. (CBC)
He said the municipal budget has nothing to do with personal budgeting. While Montreal leadership is spending tens of millions, he said he’s not even thinking about filet mignon because “I can’t afford that.”
Meghan Henderson attended the event as well, and was enjoying some President’s Choice macaroni and cheese freshly cooked from the box. She said it’s tasty, but she’s feeling bitter.
“We’re just not really happy with how the city is being run,” she said.
“I was pretty peeved by the election results initially and I guess I had a feeling things would go this way. It doesn't feel like she’s really working for us or trying to make our lives better in any way.”
Rex Beckett, holding a homemade sign, said she attended the event to express her frustration over the property tax increase that will trickle down to renters like her.
At the same time, she said there are empty housing and commercial spaces during a crisis, and the homeless population is growing every day.
“How could you be that tone deaf? Who is eating filet mignon? We’re eating lentils and rice."

WHO, the United Nations Foundation and Illumination have partnered to launch a Public Service Announcement (PSA) that reinforces safe and healthy practices during these challenging times, featuring Illumination’s globally beloved Gru and the Minions. The PSA focuses on lifesaving behaviors to help mitigate the impacts of COVID-19, including physical distancing, being active at home and remaining kind to each other —all aimed at making sure people of all ages stay safe and healthy during this pandemic.
“At this challenging time, we must find all ways possible to provide hope to people while sharing advice that can protect our health,” said Dr. Tedros Adhanom, Director-General of the World Health Organization. “WHO is excited to be working with Illumination and Steve Carell and the joys of the Minions and Gru to promote the importance of physical distancing, keeping active and connected, and being kind and compassionate to overcome COVID-19.”
The PSA is voiced by Academy Award® and Emmy Award® nominee Steve Carrell, who voices the character Gru in the Despicable Me franchise. The PSA will be localized into multiple languages including Spanish, French, Portuguese and Arabic, among others.
“Storytelling is a powerful tool to accelerate positive social change in the world. Illumination is the first Hollywood Studio to partner with WHO, the UN Foundation and the COVID-19 Solidarity Response Fund to create an entertaining and educational PSA for global audiences. Participant helped facilitate the collaboration between Illumination to the United Nations Foundation and the World Health Organization.
"As the world continues to grapple with the challenges of COVID-19, one of our most powerful weapons is kindness," said Elizabeth Cousens, President & CEO of the United Nations Foundation. "We are delighted that the Despicable Me characters are letting their love show and showing ways to keep themselves and their communities safe during this unprecedented time."

- The claim that Michigan Sen.-elect Abdul El-Sayed once said he wanted to replace the U.S. Constitution's Second Amendment, the right to bear arms, with a right to receive healthcare, circulated in November. The claim included other alleged statements such as El-Sayed wanting to ban fireworks on Independence Day.
- The rumor stems from a CNN report in August about El-Sayed making the alleged statements in videos posted to his official YouTube channel that were removed prior to the launch of his campaign for office.
- The statements appear to be correctly attributed to El-Sayed based on CNN's reporting and El-Sayed's response to the outlet. However, we've been unable to verify the videos firsthand, so we've left this claim unrated.
- Snopes will update this report if we are able to acquire the original videos or receive a response from El-Sayed.
Rumors that Democratic Michigan Sen.-elect Abdul El-Sayed once said that he believed in replacing the U.S. Constitution's Second Amendment — the right to bear arms — with a right to healthcare, as well suggesting that fireworks be banned from Independence Day, circulated in November following his midterm election victory.
People on Facebook shared posts making the claims against El-Sayed, who defeated his Republican opponent by about 7 percentage points.
One user wrote:
Abdul El-Sayed, a Michigan Democrat, is facing questions after old videos surfaced showing him suggesting that America replace the Second Amendment with a constitutional right to health care. In one video, he asked what would happen if the Constitution were changed so Americans had a right to health care instead of the right to bear arms. In another video, he criticized Fourth of July fireworks and encouraged Americans to find other ways to celebrate Independence Day.
The quotes appeared to be accurately attributed to El-Sayed based on the available evidence and previous reporting about the videos being removed prior to El-Sayed's campaign.
However, Snopes bases its ratings on primary evidence. We were unable to obtain the original videos in which the quotes were allegedly made, as they have been made private by El-Sayed and he has not yet responded a request for comment and verification of the old clips. Therefore, we've left this claim unrated. We will update this article if we're able to obtain the original videos or receive a reply from El-Sayed.
The rumor stemmed from an Aug. 11 report by CNN that mentioned the specific claims that recirculated after the midterm elections: that El-Sayed said "fireworks suck" regarding Independence Day celebrations and that he suggested replacing the Second Amendment with a Constitutional right to healthcare.
Each rumor stemmed from a separate video posted to El-Sayed's official YouTube channel but since made private. According to CNN's report, El-Sayed's office confirmed the authenticity of the videos but said they do not reflect his current views and had been removed.
"Abdul is the former captain of his high school football team, loves Michigan football on Saturdays, and celebrates the Fourth of July with fireworks like the next Michigander," CNN quoted a campaign spokesperson as saying. They added, "Cherry-picked comments from old podcasts don't reflect his beliefs today."
A wide range of major media outlets, including HuffPost, The Hill, Fox News and Forbes, picked up CNN's report, as did gun advocacy organizations such as the National Association for Gun Rights and The Firearm Industry Trade Association and independent journalism outlet The Reload, which described its aim to be the "best place to find fair and discerning reporting on firearms and how they intersect with politics."
The archived link for El-Sayed's now-private video dated April 6, 2023, showed it was titled "The Right to Bear Arms The Right to Have Healthcare!" 
The archived link did not play the video, and a thorough search for the original clip yielded no results. Based on the video's date, it appeared that it was made in response to an April 5, 2023, school shooting in Nashville.
According to a transcript of the video uploaded by The Reload, El-Sayed referenced the events of the shooting and said, "What if we tweaked the Constitution? Amended the amendment, and instead of the right to bear arms, we change it to the right to have healthcare."
The transcript further alleged that he said:
Imagine what that would mean. That would mean fewer people dying by guns and more people living because they have healthcare. Maybe two words of a change, but it would address two of America's most pernicious social ills. Literally deadly problems that we could fix with two words. So, you should think about it, huh?
The second part of the claim addressing El-Sayed's alleged comments on fireworks came from a July 10, 2024, video (archived) titled "Can we PLEASE find another way to celebrate July 4th? Four reasons why fireworks suck." That video also had been made private as of this writing.
The description for the video read:
After July 4th, the city of Detroit experienced the worst air quality in the entire world. Dr. Abdul El-Sayed explains what fireworks are made of, why exploding them over large bodies of water might not be the best idea, and the several safety risks they bring.
In addition, one chapter of the video's contents was titled "Fireworks just aren't worth it: hear us out."
While the archived link could not play the video in question, it is reasonably clear from the text on the video page that El-Sayed was not in favor of fireworks, though whether he called for a ban on them was unclear.
By July 4, 2025, the future senator seemed to have softened on fireworks when he posted, "Happy Fourth of July, Michigan! Enjoy the fireworks as we commit ourselves to building a country where all of us can thrive."

Get your daily dose of health and medicine every weekday with STAT’s free newsletter Morning Rounds. Sign up here.
Good morning. We’ve got a “Beaver Moon” today. And, of course, there’s Thanksgiving later this week. Here’s a poem for both and neither.
An FDA milestone for limb girdle muscular dystrophy
Yesterday the FDA approved the first drug to treat limb girdle muscular dystrophy, a broad collection of progressive muscle conditions that has long received scant attention from physicians and drug developers. The drug, developed by BridgeBio, is specifically approved for patients with a subtype of the disease that the company estimates affects 2,000 to 3,000 patients in the U.S. and 4,000 to 5,000 in Europe.
“I’m pretty excited about it,” Nicholas Johnson, an LGMD specialist at Virginia Commonwealth University, told STAT’s Jason Mast. “It does appear that they had actually surprisingly robust effects on clinical outcome measures… and it also looks like it’s incredibly safe, so that’s a win-win.” Read more on the approval.
Why Barbara Kingsolver stopped signing books
The Pulitzer Prize-winning novelist Barbara Kingsolver was learning to play hand drums when her fingers started curling in on themselves. She was diagnosed with a genetic condition called Dupuytren contracture, in which the tissue of a person’s palm thickens and tightens, pulling on the fingers.
While the condition is genetic, doctors believe that the gene needs to be turned on in some way — either through age or perhaps a trauma. The drums may have been Kingsolver’s trigger, according to her hand surgeon at the University of Virginia, Bobby Chhabra.
The condition quickly began to impact her work. As a sort of celebrity author, Kingsolver’s book signings are no small feat. “The way I have to do it is sign 60,000 books — that’s an actual figure,” Kingsolver said at a media briefing with UVA on Monday. “It involves hours every day of clenching a pen. And every time I did that, I’d have to go in for another surgery.”
Kingsolver has stopped signing books en masse, but she bristles when people recommend speech-to-text technology for her writing. “This is the way I write, and I need hands,” she said. “As long as I’ve got them, and as long as I can keep them, I’m going to keep writing books.”
4.9 million
In June 2026, that’s how many menopause hormone therapy medications were dispensed to cisgender women in the U.S. between the ages of 40 and 74. It’s a major increase — 141% — from the roughly 2.1 million meds dispensed monthly between July 2023 and February 2024. That’s according to an analysis of national data published last week in JAMA.
The study found that dispensing rose before and after the FDA’s removal of the black box warning in November 2025. Menopause and its precursor, perimenopause, received a flood of attention in those years, reflected in a still-booming business.
AI offers hope in the Last Frontier
Stroke is the fourth-leading cause of death in the U.S., the majority caused by occlusions that block blood flow to the brain. Survival rates are significantly worse for rural patients, and in Alaska, the challenges sound almost insurmountable.
There are five neurointerventionalists in the entire state who can extract clots. Sometimes Alaskans arrive at their village clinics by snow machine or dogsled. Every minute is precious in the aftermath of a stroke, but it can take several hours to arrange a plane, airlift a patient to the airport in Anchorage, and deliver them by ambulance to one of those specialists.
“The distances that we have to cross are enormous. The weather that we have to face is awful. Resource availability is so low,” said Kelly Isaacs, the stroke program manager at Providence Alaska Medical Center in Anchorage.
That’s why, in 2023, a small network of hospitals agreed to use the same AI software to triage stroke patients and get them to the right care faster. STAT’s Katie Palmer reported on how it’s going and what the future of stroke care looks like in Alaska.
The pros and cons of routine PSA screening
A systematic review published yesterday in Annals of Internal Medicine provides important insight into the cost-benefit profile of routine PSA screening. According to the findings from nearly 800,000 men in 13 randomized trials with follow-up for about two decades, routine screening every two to four years between the ages of 55 and 69 led to fewer cases of metastatic disease and prostate cancer deaths. However, increased screening was also linked with an increased risk of false positives (about 150 per 1,000) as well as overdiagnosis (about 20 cases per 1,000).
The review is especially timely. Earlier this month, the American Cancer Society updated its prostate cancer screening guidelines, recommending that men at average risk be tested every two years for prostate-specific antigen (PSA) levels in the blood. Routine PSA screening had gone out of favor since 2010 specifically because of the problems identified in the review, though new evidence linking it to reduced disease-specific mortality led to reconsidering the approach. — Annalisa Merelli
‘I worry how easily we can grow used to being alone’
Second-year medical student Brian Zhang is what he calls a “class-goer,” meaning he, and most of his classmates, show up physically to class each day. But in a new First Opinion essay, he notes that preclinical lecture attendance among medical schools has been declining nationally since the pandemic.
“Hard workers are remarkable at hiding stress. Intelligent people are good at forgetting to be kind to themselves,” Zhang writes. “Class gives us a place, an excuse, not only to struggle through challenging coursework in real time together, but be part of one another’s lives.” Read more.

Grocery stores and supermarkets recorded 4.15 billion transactions through the Unified Payments Interface (UPI) in October 2026, accounting for nearly 26% of all merchant payments, according to data from the National Payments Corporation of India (NPCI).
Overall, UPI merchant transactions rose 5.7% month-on-month to 16.09 billion in October, while their value increased 9.4% to Rs 9.71 lakh crore.
Compared with October 2025, transaction volume grew 23.5%, while transaction value increased 17.6%. These figures cover payments to merchants and exclude person-to-person transfers.
Groceries and restaurants lead in transaction volume
Grocery stores and supermarkets recorded more than twice the transaction volume of fast-food restaurants, the second-largest merchant category by volume.
The three leading categories were:
- Groceries and supermarkets: 4.15 billion transactions, up 5.3% from September and 26.8% from October 2025.
- Fast-food restaurants: 1.60 billion transactions.
- Other eating places and restaurants: 1.35 billion transactions.
Together, these categories accounted for approximately 44% of October’s merchant transactions. NPCI classifies fast-food restaurants and other eating places under separate merchant category codes.
Groceries narrowly surpass debt collection in transaction valueGrocery stores and supermarkets also led among individually identified merchant categories by transaction value, closely followed by debt collection agencies.
- Groceries and supermarkets: Rs 90,225.75 crore, up 7.1% from September, with an average payment of approximately Rs 217.
- Debt collection agencies: Rs 88,360.49 crore, up 15.9%, with an average payment of approximately Rs 3,547.
- Securities brokers and dealers: Rs 82,775.86 crore, up 11.7%.
- Service stations: Rs 46,154.29 crore, up 8.9%.
- Online marketplaces: Rs 12,387.56 crore, up 42.5%.
Among the ten highest-value named categories, debt collection agencies recorded the largest monthly increase in payment value, adding Rs 12,115.96 crore. Online marketplaces registered the highest percentage growth.
Despite groceries leading in both volume and value among named categories, the average payment to debt collection agencies was more than 16 times higher than that to grocery stores.
However, NPCI groups Rs 4.30 lakh crore, or 44.3% of total merchant payment value, under its “Others” classification. Since this combines multiple merchant categories, the rankings apply only to individually identified categories.

Asha Bhosle and S. Janaki, two of Indian cinema’s most celebrated playback singers, were remembered at the 57th International Film Festival of India (IFFI) in Goa by singer K.S. Chithra and actor-filmmaker Suhasini Maniratnam.
Bhosle, a two-time Grammy nominee whose name was referenced in Cornershop’s 1997 hit “Brimful of Asha,” died in April at 92. Janaki, known as the Nightingale of South India, died in July at 88. Chithra and Suhasini shared their memories of the two at the annual “Lata Mangeshkar Talk: The Voice That Echoes Forever,” named for Bhosle’s elder sister, the singer Lata Mangeshkar.
Chithra, who has recorded more than 25,000 songs in several Indian languages over a career spanning nearly five decades, spoke about the singers who shaped her musical sensibilities, among them Mangeshkar, P. Susheela and Janaki. She imitated Janaki as a child, while acknowledging that the veteran singer’s distinctive style was impossible to reproduce. Mangeshkar’s devotional songs, she said, had particularly impressed her with their emotional depth.
Suhasini recalled an episode from the making of “Iruvar” (1997), directed by her husband Mani Ratnam. Composer A.R. Rahman, an Oscar winner for “Slumdog Millionaire,” had invited Bhosle to record a song that needed to evoke the style of Tamil playback singer L.R. Eswari, but was unsure how to explain the reference to her. He asked Suhasini to help. She demonstrated Eswari’s style, and Bhosle went on to deliver “Venilla Venilla.”
Chithra spoke about Bhosle’s versatility and her ability to move between musical forms, including ghazals, and about her desire to establish her own musical identity rather than be compared with her sister. At their first meeting, Chithra said, Bhosle asked her why she was singing in such a high register.
Janaki, Suhasini said, could inhabit a character through her voice, singing like a child or a teenage boy. Chithra recalled that Janaki was a devoted fan of Mangeshkar. She would play Mangeshkar’s songs on the radio, turn down the volume during the vocal portions and record herself singing along – “like a karaoke on her own,” as Chithra described it. Offstage, Chithra said, Janaki would feed her by hand when she visited her home.
The session also touched on the demands of recording and on recognizing one’s vocal limitations with age.
Chithra sang snippets throughout, including songs from her own repertoire and numbers popularized by Janaki and Bhosle. In a closing quiz, film clips were played without their background scores and Chithra was asked to identify each song by singing it. She identified all five.
The session ended with Chithra singing “Paadariyen” from “Sindhu Bhairavi” (1985), which won her the first of her six National Film Awards, as Suhasini, who starred in the film, joined her, lip-syncing.

A video showing a massive fire near a temple is being shared on social media (here, here, and here) with the claim that Muslims set fire to the temple in Bangladesh. Let’s verify the truth behind the video in this article.
Claim: The video shows a temple in Bangladesh engulfed in flames after Muslims burned it down.
Fact: The viral video does not show a temple in Bangladesh being set on fire by Muslims. In fact, it shows a fire at a plastic warehouse near Kukra Chowk in the New Mandi police station area of Muzaffarnagar, Uttar Pradesh, on 21 November 2026. The fire reportedly broke out after sparks from fireworks during a wedding ceremony reached the warehouse. The location was geolocated to Kukra Chowk, Muzaffarnagar, by matching the surrounding structures and landmarks visible in the viral video with those at the site. Hence, the claim made in the post is FALSE.
A reverse image search of keyframes from the viral video led us to multiple social media posts (here, here) dated 21 November 2026 featuring the same video. According to these posts, the video shows a massive fire at a warehouse near Kukra Chowk in the New Mandi police station area of Muzaffarnagar, Uttar Pradesh. The fire reportedly triggered panic among nearby shopkeepers and residents, while several fire engines rushed to the spot to extinguish it.
Using clues from these social media posts, we searched relevant keywords and found several news reports (here, here, and here) with the same visuals. According to these reports, a massive fire broke out at a plastic warehouse near Kukra Chowk in the New Mandi police station area of Muzaffarnagar on 21 November 2026. The fire reportedly started when sparks from fireworks set off during a wedding ceremony, particularly during the bride’s farewell, reached the warehouse. Eleven fire engines and water tankers from nearby factories were deployed to extinguish the blaze, which took over five hours to bring under control. The fire caused panic among nearby shopkeepers, prompting the evacuation of surrounding shops. The warehouse reportedly stored crockery used for wedding ceremonies, and the owner said the fire caused significant losses. Officials said the cause was based on accounts from residents, while the extent of the damage was yet to be assessed.
We also geolocated the incident to Kukra Chowk, Muzaffarnagar, Uttar Pradesh. The surrounding structures and landmarks visible in the viral video match those at the location. The comparison can be seen below.
To sum up, a video of a warehouse fire accident in U.P is falsely shared as Muslims burning a temple in Bangladesh.

In November, a video (archived) circulated that social media users claimed authentically shows a group of Muslims calling themselves "Soldiers of Allah" and demanding Shariah be put in place in Manchester, England.
According to the Council on Foreign Relations, a U.S. foreign policy think tank, Shariah is "the divine counsel that Muslims follow to live moral lives and grow close to God." Interpretations of Shariah, the principles of which stem from the Quran and hadith, the latter of which are sayings attributed to the Prophet Muhammad, form the basis of Islamic law.
The video in question shows people gathered on Wilmslow Road in Rusholme, south of Manchester, a stretch of road that is also known as the "Curry Mile" for its large number of restaurants specializing in South Asian and Middle Eastern food. The footage shows large groups of people, who appeared to be majority male, chanting and beating their chests.
One Instagram user who shared the video wrote:
A large group of military-age men took to the streets in a Manchester suburb calling themselves soldiers of Allah and demanding sharia law be put in place because they now form the majority in the neighborhood. The march was open and organized, not a quiet gathering. When a neighborhood shifts demographically and then the new majority starts openly calling for a different legal system, the question is how far that demand is expected to go. Local officials and residents are left deciding whether this is just free expression or the start of parallel rules. Do you think this is being handled the right way in the UK?
The footage also circulated on Facebook (archived). Snopes readers searched our site for information about the clips.
The video appears authentic, meaning it shows an event that actually happened and wasn't created used artificial intelligence. However, people who shared in it November miscaptioned the footage.
It doesn't show Muslims calling themselves "Soldiers of Allah" or calling for Shariah in the U.K. Rather, the videos show Shiite Muslims marking Ashura, the culmination of 10 days of mourning to mark the martyrdom of Husayn ibn Ali, the grandson of the prophet Muhammad, on June 21.
According to the Encyclopedia Britannica, Shiite Muslims mark this day with assemblies such as the one seen in the video that feature, "sermons, poetry, chest-beating, and passion plays reenacting Husayn's martyrdom."
The Ashura assembly on the "Curry Mile" is an annual event in Manchester that local news media has covered for more than 10 years. The Manchester Evening news called the event a "ritual self-flagellation procession" in 2015 but did not report that the people participating called themselves "Soldiers of Allah" or demanded Shariah be imposed in the U.K.
The source of the video that circulated in November was unclear, though at least two of the clips featured (at 0:06 and 0:16) camefrom a separate video (at 1:20 and 1:59, archived) posted on Instagram by 
Murtaza Ali Shah, a journalist for a Pakistani news outlet.
Shah confirmed to Snopes via Instagram he recorded the footage and it showed the Ashura event in Manchester in June.
In addition to misrepresenting what the video showed, the social media post above also made a false claim about the alleged "Soldiers of Allah" calling for Shariah in the U.K.
The poster wrote (emphasis ours): "A large group of military-age men took to the streets in a Manchester suburb calling themselves soldiers of Allah and demanding sharia law be put in place because they now form the majority in the neighborhood."
Manchester, where the June Ashura assembly took place, is not majority Muslim. According to the latest U.K. Ccensus data from 2021, 22.3% of people — less than one in four — within the Manchester City Council governance area identified as Muslims. Rusholme, where the "Curry Mile" is located, is part of Manchester City Council. According to census data, 38.5% of people in the Rusholme East census area, which borders the "Curry Mile," identified as Muslim.
For further reading, Snopes previously investigated whether a video showed U.K. shoppers standing in gender-segregated lines and another video of Shiite Muslims marking Ashura in Dearborn, Michigan.

“We’ve received an extremely high volume of messages due to multiple providers in our area retiring or leaving their practice very recently,” the woman’s voice said with a hint of exasperation, “so please understand it may take longer than normal to receive a return call back.”

Xi's anti-corruption campaign ensnares rising star in Chinese Communist Party
- Published
Chinese authorities are investigating Shanghai's party chief, a rising star in the Communist Party, as part of Xi Jinping's sweeping anti-corruption drive.
Chen Jining, 62, is suspected of "severe violations of discipline and laws", according to a statement published on Tuesday by the party's anti-corruption body.
Chen is now the fourth member of the elite Politburo to be investigated, in the widest purge yet of the party's top executive body since the end of the Cultural Revolution.
As the party prepares to appoint fresh leaders at next year's National People's Congress, uncertainty looms over what its new command will look like - except that Xi will remain at the helm.
Before Chen, three other members of the current Politburo - appointed in 2022 - were investigated and subsequently expelled: ex-generals He Weidong and Zhang Youxia, as well as former Xinjiang party chief Ma Xingrui.
While Chen has not been removed from the Politburo, it's rare for officials to return after such investigations.
"Who on this Politburo feels safe, especially as the personnel machinations for next year's Party Congress intensify?" China analyst Bill Bishop wrote in his Sinocism newsletter.
Chen's investigation came as a surprise, according to Bishop, given rumours were swirling that another senior official, not Chen, would fall next in the anti-corruption campaign.
The role of Shanghai party chief, which Chen assumed in 2022, is known to be a prestigious springboard to the country's top office.
Chen's long list of predecessors include former president Jiang Zemin, his premier Zhu Rongji, incumbent premier Li Qiang and Xi Jinping himself.
As Shanghai party chief, Chen hosted foreign leaders visiting the city, including former UK Prime Minister Keir Starmer in January and former US Secretary of State Antony Blinken in 2024.
Chen was also a prominent champion for the development of the city's artificial intelligence industry - a sector that the party has stipulated as an area of strategic focus.
Chen graduated with a degree in environmental engineering at Tsinghua University, where he returned to teach in 1998 and became its president in 2012. He also spent a few years in the UK, and received a PhD from Imperial College London.
Since Xi's anti-corruption drive in 2012, more than two million individuals have been disciplined for cases related to "pointless formalities, bureaucratism, hedonism and extravagance", according to the party.
Specific charges are often not made public, and broad allegations about disciplinary and legal violations have become routine in the crackdown.
Analysts note that corruption also extends to ideological impurity - or simply put, disloyalty.
Party discipline took centre stage at the fifth plenum last month, which had the most empty seats ever seen after a record 33 members were expelled from the party's central committee.
Chen's ongoing probe suggests that the crackdown is not slowing down.
Shanghai's communist party standing committee said in a statement that its members "unanimously expressed their firm support" for the decision of the party.
The investigation of Chen, the committee said, shows that "the fight against corruption will not stop".

Two attacks in eastern Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) have killed 4 workers responding to the Ebola outbreak and injured 5 others.
The attacks occurred overnight on a shared living camp in Biakato Mines and an Ebola response coordination office in Mangina.
“We are heartbroken that people have died in the line of duty as they worked to save others,” said Dr Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus, World Health Organization Director-General. “The world has lost brave professionals.”
The dead include a member of a vaccination team, two drivers and a police officer. No WHO staff are among those killed, one staff member was injured.
“My heart goes out to the family and friends of the first responders killed in these attacks,” said Dr Matshidiso Moeti, WHO Regional Director for Africa. “We are doing everything possible to bring the injured and front-line workers in the impacted areas to safety. These constant attacks must stop. We will continue to work with the DRC Government, partners and MONUSCO to ensure the security of our staff and other health workers.”
In the last week, there were 7 cases of Ebola, down from a peak of over 120 per week in April 2019.
“Ebola was retreating. These attacks will give it force again, and more people will die as a consequence,” said Dr Tedros. “It will be tragic to see more unnecessary suffering in communities that have already suffered so much. We call on everyone who has a role to play to end this cycle of violence.”
The situation is still evolving. WHO will provide updates as new information comes in.

The post garnered 106,700 views and over 2,000 reshares.

The same clip was shared by X user @yadavanoop08, with the claim that certain “RSS goons caused a ruckus” at a restaurant in West Bengal after they were asked to pay their bill. (Archive)
