"The impugned order does not call for any interference by this Court in exercise of its revisional jurisdiction. The impugned order dated 13.10.2025 is upheld," Justice Sharma said in the judgement.
The bench said, "A conspiracy rarely unfolds in the open. It is woven through separate acts, divided among different hands, and is revealed only when the threads are seen together."
The High Court said that the material placed before this Court prima facie indicates the involvement of Lalu Prasad Yadav in the policy decisions concerning the budget hotels and the BNR Hotels at the time when the process leading to their award was underway.
It is alleged that Lalu Prasad Yadav, while serving as Minister of Railways, had entered into a criminal conspiracy with the Kochhar brothers of M/s Sujata Hotel Pvt. Ltd. and others.
In pursuance of the alleged conspiracy, he had abused his official position and extended undue favour to M/s Sujata Hotel, through officers of the Indian Railway Catering and Tourism Corporation Limited, New Delhi (IRCTC), in the award of contracts for sub-leasing the existing Railway Hotels, known as BNR Hotels, at Ranchi, Jharkhand, and Puri, Orissa.
The CBI alleged that, in consideration for the said favour, the Kochhar brothers had sold prime land situated in Patna, Bihar, to M/s Delight Marketing Company Pvt. Ltd. (DMCPL), a company run by a close associate of Lalu Prasad Yadav, namely, Prem Chand Gupta, and his associates. The said company was subsequently taken over by members of Lalu Prasad Yadav's family.
It is thus alleged that the prime land situated in Patna ultimately came into the hands of Lalu‘s family for a nominal consideration. After completion of the investigation, the CBI filed a detailed chargesheet.

At Albuquerque's Indian Pueblo Kitchen, Native American dishes are the main course
There are plenty of kitschy diners and barbecue joints along Route 66, but just a couple of miles off the highway in Albuquerque, N.M., Native American dishes are the star at Indian Pueblo Kitchen.
Late on a weekday morning, the restaurant was already starting to fill up. Most of the tables were taken up by locals, like Merlyn Liberty and Rolf Pendall.
"I started with breakfast dessert. The blue corn waffles. And now I'm finishing up my sweetheart's plate of enchiladas and pinto beans," Pendall said.
The restaurant is attached to the Indian Pueblo Cultural Center, a museum and cultural center founded in 1976 by the 19 Pueblo tribes of New Mexico.
The center sits on land where the Albuquerque Indian School operated. Open from 1881 to the early 1980s, it was one of the hundreds of federally funded boarding schools designed to strip Native American children of their family bonds, languages, culture and spiritual practices.
The Indian Pueblo Cultural Center's president and CEO, Monique Fragua, said visitors can start in the museum's galleries and then visit the restaurant to experience Pueblo culture and hospitality.
"Whether that's through our exhibits, or our food, or in our gift shop, we can celebrate the art of our Pueblo communities," Fragua said.
Museum cafés are not a typical destination for foodies, but this one is.
The menu is all Native American and Southwestern-inspired. Dishes include blue corn enchiladas that you can get "Christmas style," one with red chile sauce and the other with green chile sauce. There's a chile posole with beef short ribs served on the bone, as well as Indian tacos on homemade fry bread. Then there's a dish that's really popular on social media: pickles marinated in cherry Kool-Aid and then deep-fried and served with a green chile ranch sauce.
Rita Toledo, from Jemez Pueblo, is Indian Pueblo Kitchen's star baker. One of her specialties is biscochitos — fragrant shortbread cookies spiced with anise and rolled in cinnamon sugar that are New Mexico's state cookie. Toledo has made some twists on the traditional biscochito, like making a chile pepper version that has just a little kick at the end with a nice balance of sweet and heat.
Indian Pueblo Kitchen's version of biscochitos is so popular that the restaurant also sells them at its café inside Albuquerque's airport. Toledo turns out at least 48 dozen biscochitos each week just for the airport location.
While we chatted, Toledo was wrestling to open a giant tub of one of her main ingredients — lard. These cookies can be made with butter or shortening, she said, but "lard's the only way to make good biscochitos."
Toledo said that she has been baking all her life and that her favorite part of her work is rolling out dough.
"It calms me. You know, your energy comes out on your dough," Toledo said. "I always tell my bakers, 'Come in happy and in a good mood. That way, your products will come out nice and everybody's gonna love it.'"
Along with locals flocking to visit, the restaurant is also a hit with tourists like Kathy Allio and Jeff Allen from Pennsylvania. While we chatted, Allio was finishing a bowl of bean chili with elk meat.
"The red chiles are just very flavorful without being hot," Allio said, "so it's delicious."
One thing Fragua, the center's president, is particularly proud of is that the Pueblo community can see itself reflected in the museum's galleries and programming and on the restaurant's menu.
"We're lucky to have that history here on our campus, that we've taken lands that were once created to really change the identity of Native people and change that story of who Native people are," Fragua said. "We've created a campus that's built on resilience, empowering our voices and truly telling the stories of who we are as Native people."
Additional reporting by Jeanette DeDios of member station KUNM.

- The claim that the U.S. Army intended to detonate more than just lead azide during a planned explosion in in Middletown, Iowa, in November remains under investigation.
- The rumor stems from an authentic emergency permit issued by the EPA to the Army. The permit contained redacted text, which the Environmental Protection Agency noted was for "critical infrastructure security purposes at the request of Department of Army."
- It's unclear whether the redacted portions pertained to other material that was detonated, contained further details related to the lead azide or something else.
- Snopes will update this report if, or when, additional information surfaces. We have reached out to the Army and the EPA and are waiting for responses.
On Nov. 25, the U.S. Army destroyed 68 barrels of lead azide, a highly explosive compound, in Middletown, Iowa. Officials announced the blasts were successful, and according to the Environmental Protection Agency, its real-time air monitors had not detected any airborne lead more than an hour after the detonation.
In the days leading up to the explosions — which raised widespread alarm due to the public health risks — a rumor spread online that the Army actually planned to detonate more than lead azide, according to a redacted document.
A screenshot of the purported "Emergency Permit" spread across social media, apparently showing that in addition to 68 drums of lead azide, the Army was permitted to treat other, hidden materials as "hazardous waste."
"Is the 68 barrels of lead azide not even the most scary, dangerous, poisonous part?!" One X post read (archived).
The document was real. It was an emergency permit issued by the EPA to the Army, allowing it to treat the lead azide cache as a hazardous material (clearing the way for the military to move forward with the detonation plan) "upon the EPA's finding of an imminent and substantial endangerment to human health and the environment."
Because it remains unclear what text was redacted, Snopes has left this claim unrated. We reached out to the Army and the EPA. We will update this story if we receive a response.
On Page 2, the permit read:
Name: Lead Azide
Hazardous Waste Codes: D003 (reactivity), D008 (toxicity characteristic for lead)
CAS Number: 13424-46-9
DOT Shipping Classification: Hazard Class 1.1A, UN0130
Quantity: There are 68 drums of Lead Azide, [REDACTED]
- [REDACTED]
- [REDACTED]
On Page 12 (Section IV.N.1), it read:
N. Permitted and Prohibited Waste Identification
1. The Permittee shall only treat the following hazardous waste in accordance with this Emergency Permit
Quantity: 68 drums of lead Azide, [REDACTED]
[REDACTED]
Another widely circulated screenshot apparently showing the lead azide properties alongside heavily-redacted details related to what appeared to be other materials. That image also was authentic — it was sourced from another EPA document (PDF page 74).
It's unclear whether the redacted portions pertained to other material that was detonated, contained further details related to the lead azide or something else.
On Nov. 23, the EPA noted that "the permit and permit application materials contain redacted elements for critical infrastructure security purposes at the request of Department of Army."
In our questions to the EPA and Army, we asked why the redacted information was considered a security threat and whether the public should be concerned about what, if anything, else was detonated along with the lead

Electronics design and manufacturing startup Elecbits is in talks to raise fresh capital in the range of $12-15 Mn in a fresh funding round led by PE firm Xponentia Capital, sources familiar with the development told Inc42. Existing investors, including Nexus Venture Partners, are also likely to participate in the round. Inc42 reached out to Elecbits and Xponentia Capital for comments on the proposed fundraise. However, neither responded to queries at the time of publishing this story. The capital to be raised is yet to be finalised. Founded in 2019 by Saurav Kumar Singh and Nikhil Rawat, Elecbits operates a full-stack electronics design and manufacturing platform, helping businesses take hardware products from concept and prototyping to manufacturing and delivery. The startup offers services across the electronics manufacturing value chain, including printed circuit board (PCB) design, firmware development, component sourcing, PCB fabrication and assembly, quality control and final product manufacturing. It also operates Elecbits XOR, an AI-powered electronics engineering and manufacturing platform that offers instant quotations, component intelligence, supply chain visibility and risk management tools. The platform aims to simplify the traditionally fragmented electronics manufacturing ecosystem by bringing engineering, procurement and manufacturing workflows under one roof. Elecbits caters to businesses across digital payments, power electronics, IT hardware, automotive and consumer electronics. It claims to work with over 200 companies, including Panasonic, Schneider Electric, Motherson, Maruti Suzuki, Urban Company, Zetwerk and Ola Electric. The startup positions itself as a vertically integrated manufacturing partner for companies looking to diversify their supply chains beyond China under the China+1 strategy. In December 2025, Elecbits raised $5.5 Mn in a Series A funding round led by Nexus Venture Partners. The round also saw participation from SE Ventures and Riverwalk Holdings. The fresh fundraise comes amid growing investments in India's electronics manufacturing ecosystem, supported by government initiatives such as the Production-Linked Incentive (PLI) scheme and the Electronics Component Manufacturing Scheme (ECMS). As India looks to deepen its domestic electronics manufacturing capabilities and reduce reliance on imports, startups building design, engineering and component supply chain capabilities are looking to capitalise on the opportunity. For Elecbits, the proposed $15 Mn round could provide additional capital to expand its manufacturing capabilities, strengthen its technology platform and scale its enterprise business.

Independent Android app developers are worried about their privacy after Google announced that from next year many of them will be required to share a phone number and address publicly. The policy change is intended to meet European Union regulations under the Digital Services Act, but Google says contact details will be made public worldwide.
Android app developers will soon have to share their address publicly
The change is to meet EU regulations, but Apple gives its developers more privacy.
Developers have until February 1st 2027 to declare whether or not they’re a “trader” under UK and European law. Broadly speaking, Google says the definition applies if you earn revenue from your apps, especially if that revenue is regular or at high volume. Developers are exempt if their apps are only a hobby or non-commercial, or if they simply don’t publish them in the UK or Europe.
If they self-declare as a trader, developers’ contact details will be shared publicly starting March 1st, including a phone number and address. Google doesn’t accept PO boxes for developer payment profile addresses, meaning many independent developers without an office will either have to share their home address online or pay for a registered agent or other service that provides a business address. One independent developer told The Elec they were considering renting a private office solely to comply with the new rules. We’ve asked Google to confirm why developers aren’t permitted to publish a PO box address, and why details are being shared globally, and will update this article when we hear back.
Apple is subject to the same regulations, but is handling them differently to Google. It will only display developer addresses within the relevant European countries, rather than publishing them worldwide. It’s also allowing developers to supply PO box addresses, so long as they provide Apple with a receipt or bill that links the PO box to their regular address.
Update, November 26th: Added mention of developers’ option to use a registered agent service for a business address.

Zerodha’s cofounder Nikhil Kamath, via his investment platform WTFund, has backed influencer Diipa Büller-Khosla-led BPC brand indē wild. The undisclosed funding was finalised in October and announced yesterday (November 25). Apart from investing in the brand, Kamath will also be endorsing the brand's haircare line, Moonlight Growth. This would be the first time Kamath would be endorsing a brand. “We’re used to seeing celebrities endorse products. But having an investor choose to put his name behind one is a different kind of vote of confidence,” she wrote in an Instagram post today. The Business Of indē wild Mumbai-headquartered indē wild was cofounded in 2021 by influencer Khosla and her husband, Oleg Büller-Khosla. It is a digital-first beauty and personal care brand that claims to combine traditional Ayurvedic ingredients and rituals with modern skincare and haircare science. According to the startup's website, indē wild offers a range of products across haircare, skincare and lip care, among others. Its products are sold through its own online channels and retail partners, including Nykaa, Tira and Sephora. The startup bids to differentiate its BPC offering by combining traditional Ayurvedic skincare remedies with a high-power influencer marketing engine. indē wild’s best-selling product over the years has been Champi Hair Oil, which traces its roots to the early 1980s, when the cofounder's mother began making hair oil at home in Chennai. Inspired by a ritual practised in the Khosla family, she eventually developed the formulation into a family haircare recipe. indē wild was initially launched with a focus on skincare but later decided to double down on the hair oil market. Over the years, this marketing story has become central to indē wild’s distribution. This also contributed to indē wild’s financial story. As per its latest financial disclosures for the fiscal year FY25, the D2C brand reported a net profit of ₹38.5 Lakh while its revenue more than doubled YoY to ₹25 Ce. Inc42's Take: Can indē wild Sustain Itself Amid Intense Competition? indē wild’s expansion through Sephora and other retail partners gives it an opportunity to reach consumers beyond its digital-first base. However, the bigger challenge for the startup will be converting this initial appeal into sustained demand, repeat purchases and profitable growth, particularly as it expands into international markets. The landscape, meanwhile, is crowded. indē wild faces competition from established Ayurvedic and premium beauty brands such as Kama Ayurveda, Forest Essentials and Biotique, as well as digital-first players such as Mamaearth, Minimalist, Plum and Pilgrim. While their positioning and product portfolios differ, they compete for overlapping consumer spending across skincare and haircare. Rising customer acquisition costs, the expense of offline expansion and the need to prove product efficacy could put pressure on indē wild's margins as it scales. Its ability to stand out will depend on building a distinct product identity, retaining customers and translating its international visibility into consistent sales, rather than relying mainly on founder-led marketing and its Ayurveda positioning.

440 players, three days, one venue - the Nations Championship logistics logjam
- Published
Earlier this year, when planning their Nations Championship finals week, Argentina's staff had a request.
Would their hotel in Shepperton allow the team to scorch a patch of the hotel garden for an asado – a traditional Argentine barbecue, in which meat on a low grill is cooked over a bed of hot charcoal?
Japan were also making arrangements. The Brave Blossoms had a special rice cooker shipped over to supplement the kitchen facilities at their Kensington base.
Such are the countless details that go into an unprecedented logistical juggle.
The maths makes the bottleneck clear.
The Nations Championship brings together more than 550 players and support staff from the world's top 12 teams for six matches funnelled into three days and just one venue - Twickenham.
The new tournament has made new, unprecedented demands on organisers.
The first was to find enough accommodation in one corner of London, on a notoriously busy shopping weekend, kicked off by Black Friday sales.
A block booking was therefore made back at the start of the year to secure beds in hotels from Brentford, Guildford, Cobham and beyond.
Not all those establishments had experience of hosting elite rugby teams.
So, chefs and team nutritionists convened to ensure that the hotels were braced with sufficient supplies of eggs, chicken and the rest, to cater for the high-energy, high-protein diets of rugby's best players.
The demands continue.
While their fellow hotel guests might hit the sights, Nations Championship sides hit the pitch.
Individual, private training facilities have had to be sourced for each team, with pitches hired out at local clubs, schools and universities.
Teams were given the choice of hotels and training grounds based on their world ranking at the start of the tournament in July, with world number ones South Africa nabbing the Teddington base that usually hosts England's opponents on a regular autumn internationals weekend.
The choice is all the more important given the logjam of matches means teams will do their eve-of-match captain's run session at their training ground, rather than, as traditional, at the match venue.
To get their players, staff and equipment between hotel, training base and Twickenham itself, organisers have given each team use of four vehicles; a team bus, a people carrier, a van for training kit and a truck for moving scrum machines and other heavy items.
Once they finally do arrive, Allianz Stadium, which has hosted Sevens, double-headers and schools finals days in the past, has enough changing rooms to comfortably accommodate four teams at once.
The higher-ranked team is given the home dressing room in each fixture.
Had England lost to New Zealand last weekend, they would be in the unfamiliar away dressing room. Victory however bumped them up to fourth, the All Blacks down to fifth and secured their usual spot.
Even if they dodge the traffic however, there is tunnel congestion to be dealt with.
The first match on each of the three days kicks off three and half hours before the headline fixture.
Barring extraordinary levels of intervention from the Television Match Official, the final whistle should blow in the first fixture before the team buses for those involved in the second arrive.
However, with post-match media duties, feeding and debriefing to be done, a window between five minutes and half an hour after kick-off in the second fixture has been identified for the teams involved in the first to make a hassle-free getaway.

"We sell out at 99.9% of England men's games and we have a very clear picture of what we need to order for those," says Nils Braude, the managing director of the Twickenham Experience.
Nations Championship finals weekend will be different. Filling the 82,000-capacity Allianz Stadium, with only a week's notice on which teams will be playing when, has proved trickier.
It is estimated that Italy v Fiji and Ireland v Australia - Friday's double-header - may play out to a half-full stadium.
Braude is dealing with different numbers, demographics and demands.
"If you are a member of the public that doesn't get to go to rugby very often, now is your chance to come in," he adds.
"We are anticipating it is going to be much more akin to a general event-goer or a Red Roses game, so a more family orientated, mixed generational crowd.
"That causes a bit more just thinking about what we order
"New fans generally arrive a bit earlier than a rugby fan who has their habits well established.
"The new fans tend to eat more, particularly if it's a long day. If they are arriving an hour or two before the first game and leaving an hour after the last game, they are here for a significant amount of time.
"So having enough food on site to satisfy that demand is a key.
"As for drinks, we're known for serving a lot of Guinness, and so we can always do that. But we are anticipating a crowd that tends to look for more cocktails, Proseccos, non-alcoholic drinks and soft drinks, so we do ramp those up a little bit for these type of games."
While the stadium's bars, which number close to 80, are loaded with enough drink to see out the first two days of the Nations Championship, there are beer kegs stored in the car parks around the stadium in place to fill any unexpected shortfall.
Equally Twickenham's partner breweries and suppliers are on alert to truck in more if required.
That restocking is part of a 24-hour operation that will be in place across the Nations Championship finals weekend.
Chefs tend to be first on site from around 05:00, with a central kitchen preparing meals for the stadium's hospitality suites. After the match has taken place and the crowd has cleared, the cleaning crew descend.
They will work through the stadium seat by seat in the couple of hours after the final whistle and then to concourses and removing empties, rubbish and hospitality table linen.
Deliveries happen overnight to take advantage of an empty venue and the clearer roads around it.
For a stadium keen to host more events throughout the year, it is also a chance to show its consideration for residential neighbours, even on compressed timeframes.
The crash of glass recycling and reversing beep of forklift trucks will be restricted to certain hours.
Braude is also keen to ensure his own team get the rest and recovery they need over a weekend that comes on the back of a busy autumn.
But alongside the challenges, there is an opportunity.
"It's exciting," says Braude. "It is certainly an event that shows up. You can really flex your muscles as a venue when you have these type of events."
Brawn and brain is being deployed well beyond the white lines this weekend.

A dish with a story, Thanksgiving with culinary historian Michael Twitty
Culinary historian Michael Twitty on tracing familial connections through food
This Thanksgiving, Morning Edition host Leila Fadel left the studio for her kitchen, where she was met by the two-time James Beard Award winner Michael Twitty, who came with a spice blend, fresh sage, fish peppers and onions from his garden.
His book, The Cooking Gene, planted him as one of the nation's foremost chronologists tracing his ancestry through African American culinary history.
Kush, the forerunner to Southern cornbread dressing
Kush is one of Twitty's most beloved Thanksgiving offerings and one he's been making since he was a teen. The name and the ingredients show the way food became a tool for the enslaved in the Americas to preserve their cultures.
"The name comes from Hausa, the language of West Africa. They are a predominantly Muslim people, but Muslim in the way that West Africans do Islam – which is Islam with a lot of the influence from the traditional culture and spirituality," he said on the origins of the side dish. "And so the name Kush, it's like, couscous," he added.
The dish is one that connects Twitty to his ancestry.
"There was a time when I couldn't tell you what particular African ethnic groups I came from, but now that I know that I'm part Wolof, Hausa, Fula, and Serer and so many others," he said. "Now, I know this dish has a connection to who I am and my roots and where I came from."
In the making of this dish, Twitty also shared his work documenting the ways African American Jewish people create hybrid dishes in the kitchen.
"It's Matzah ball gumbo, and it's black-eyed peas and quiche," he said of his Black and Jewish identity. "It's a lot of dishes that were from North Africa or from Ethiopia, it's kosher jollof rice and Shito. Shito usually has shellfish in it – we don't put that."
What Thanksgiving and this dish mean to Twitty
The author of four books tracing the deep roots of the foods he loves says for him it's less about the lore of Thanksgiving, and more about the people the day brings together.
"I have to say that along with a lot of other African Americans, not everybody, but a plurality of us, Thanksgiving, as it's been expressed, means very little," he said of the holiday. "Which means we're not attaching ourselves to the myth of Thanksgiving, we don't really care for that. But we do love tradition, we love cooking, we love food, we love gathering."
And in that spirit, Kush in particular, remains one way for him to taste history.
"It means I haven't forgotten who I come from. And it means I haven't forgotten that I have a legacy to leave," he said.
You can find the recipe for Twitty's Kush in his book, Recipes from the American South.
